News.title: The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
News.content:
Jensen Huang, known for sporting a black leather jacket to shareholder events, appeared to have it all. He was courted by leaders in both Washington and Beijing, worshipped by investors and seen as a loyal family man. But a rockstar approach to his personal life has ultimately led to his resignation.

The 63-year-old has been married since 1985, long before the foundation of Nvidia, the company that propelled him to tech stardom.

He is known as a workaholic and a demanding manager, with high standards for those who worked for him, which included his own children, promoted within the company. But he has seen his personal reputation go into free fall this week, undone by romantic entanglements, that throw doubt on his focus and his judgement.

On Thursday he resigned following back-to-back revelations of two affairs. News of the first - a relationship with a businesswoman, alleged to be a Chinese spy - ricocheted around the world, raising eyebrows among investors. It was followed on Wednesday by reports that the tech boss had also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague.

His departure creates uncertainty in the global stock market, which was already knocked-off balance in recent weeks. Nvidia is a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China.

Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.

The company, which is still valued at nearly $4 trillion despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.

Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President XI Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession has led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" and seen him amass an estimated fortune of $145bn (Â£109bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.

They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at their father's firm.

The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.

News.title: Faisal Islam: Why the UK economy is surprisingly resilient
News.content:
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

"Top gear" and "strikingly strong" were among the descriptions of the 0.7% growth offered by the economists who track every minor murmur of Britain's economy.

It is an upgrade on "solid" and "resilient", and in turn a world away from "hardest hit by the Iran War".

Against the backdrop of the world's biggest disruption to energy flows, rising market borrowing costs - and the cruel summers since the pandemic - it is impressive growth.

It should reset some of the swirl of self-reinforcing negativity.

The UK's economic growth has averaged less than 0.1% in the four Q3s [ie July to September] since the pandemic.

The average prediction just months ago for this July to September was just 0.1%.

Even the UK's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) effectively pencilled in 0.3% at the Budget just 3 weeks ago.

This figure has not been exceeded outside the pandemic since 2017. It puts the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy after the US across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.

It is tempting to think about what the economy would have done if the Iran War hadn't happened. If interest rates had been cut instead of their recent rise.

News.title: Some childhood offenders may no longer have to reveal convictions to employers
News.content:
Some job applicants in England and Wales would no longer need to declare criminal convictions they received as children under government proposals designed to improve the employment prospects of rehabilitated young people.

The changes would mean criminal records for people detained when they were under 18 years old would no longer show up for life during checks carried out by employers.

The Ministry of Justice has also launched a consultation on relaxing disclosure requirements for some specific drug-related and violent crimes committed by children.

Young people who have not re-offended as adults struggle to find work because of their past behaviour, the government says.

Many employers require applicants to undergo a background check, which in their most basic form require people to self-declare if they have a criminal record.

For more sensitive roles, such as working with children or joining the police, an employer can carry out a standard or enhanced check, which allows them to request information from the Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS).

How long a criminal record must be volunteered for or will show up in those checks differs depending on the severity of the offence, the punishment received and how long ago the crime was committed - sometimes referred to as whether a conviction is 'spent'.

For example, a young person who was convicted and fined for an offence when they were under-18 will have that information show up in checks for five-and-a-half years. If they were given a custodial sentence, that will be disclosed for the rest of their lives.

The government wants to reduce the number of young people those disclosure rules apply to if an applicant has not continued to offend as an adult.

Five offences would be removed from a list of crimes which will show up in background for checks for life if committed by an adult. They are: affray, violent disorder, supplying a controlled drug to a child, robbery and assaults occasioning actual bodily harm.

Between March 2022 and March 2026, around 8,500 under-18s were convicted of those offences, according to Ministry of Justice data.

The government says that type of crime is often a result of peer pressure, exploitation and "adolescent impulsivity" by individuals who are still developing, as opposed to a broader propensity for crime and violence.

Under the new rules, they would cease to show up in checks after five-and-a-half years.

Lifelong disclosure would also be removed for offences which led to a detention period of less than two years, the maximum which can be handed out by a youth court, and replaced by a new 11-year disclosure period.

In cases where a child was given a sentence longer than two years - which can only happen if the severity of the crime meant they were dealt with by an adult crown court - the rules would stay the same.

The most serious offences - including severe violence, terrorism-related crimes and sexual offences - would be exempted from the reforms.

Other proposed changes include:

Cutting or removing altogether the disclosure period for offences which led to a fine, the majority of which are for driving-related crimes

Ending disclosure of offences which were dealt with via an out of court resolution, which have primarily been used to tackle knife possession and assault

Reforming how long earlier offences appear in checks for young people who committed more than one crime as a child

Announcing a consultation on proposals, justice minister Jake Richards said: "Many young people who offend do not go on to lead lives of crime.

"They take responsibility, turn their lives around and want to make something of themselves.

"When they do, we should recognise that progress and support them â not put unnecessary barriers in their way."

The proposals come as the government prepares to publish a long-awaited report authored by former Labour minister Alan Milburn on tackling the number of young people not in work or education.

In May, he warned the UK was at risk of a raising a "lost generation" as almost one in eight young people are not working or studying.

Richards pointed to that intervention as he announced the disclosure reforms, saying barriers to employment can be "particularly difficult to overcome" for people who committed crimes as children.

News.title: Washington DC shooting leaves one dead and four injured as suspect dies after standoff
News.content:
One person has been killed and four others injured after a gunman opened fire in Washington DC.

The shooting began on Thursday morning local time inside a gym in an apartment building in the Logan Circle neighbourhood, which is about a mile (1.6km) north of the White House.

Police said the male suspect was "contained" after barricading himself in one of the apartments. They later confirmed he had died.

Of those injured, one is in a critical condition and the others have non-life-threatening injuries.

While the suspect was barricaded, "he did fire through the door at officers at least on two occasions", Jefferey Carroll, the interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department, said at a news conference.

Negotiators had been on the phone with the suspect when they heard a gunshot and he stopped communicating with them, according to Carroll.

Officers forced their way into the apartment and saw the suspect had what appeared to be a "self-inflicted gunshot wound", he said.

Carroll added that police "believe there was a fire that was set", which has been contained.

Authorities are still working to understand the exact timeline, suspect's motivation, and other details of the incident.

"We believe there was some sort of a conflict with the apartment building, but we don't have much more than that," Carroll said.

Washington DC Mayor Muriel Bowser called it a "senseless act of gun violence" and said the White House had been briefed.

News.title: Two men found guilty of spying for Iran over plan to target UK-based journalists
News.content:
Two Iranian men have been convicted of spying for an Iranian intelligence service by carrying out surveillance on journalists and a lawyer in the UK.

Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, were convicted of "assisting a foreign intelligence service" at Woolwich Crown Court on Thursday.

They were tasked by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) with monitoring the targets. Sepahvand intended to carry out a "violent attack" against at least one of them, while Manesh helped with planning.

A third man, Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, was cleared of the same charge.

Sepahvand was in contact with two men with Iranian telephone numbers.

Police seized 534GB of data that showed Sapahvand and Manesh were given documents that included pictures of targets, their work addresses, the make and colour of their cars and the names of pets. They then used ChatGPT to carry out further research.

The pair, from west London, are asylum seekers who had been granted temporary leave to remain. Sepahvand arrived in the UK in a lorry in 2016, and Manesh arrived via small boat in 2019.

Sepahvand conducted surveillance and reconnaissance in preparation for inflicting violence on several "subjects" in the UK.

These included journalists Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, who worked for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran international, Jonathan Turner, a founding member of UK Lawyers for Israel, as well as a media production professional.

News.title: Teenage girl admits murder in row over boy
News.content:
A teenager has admitted murdering a 16-year-old girl who she stabbed to death in a pre-planned fight over a boy.

Leeds Crown Court heard that Chloe Watson Dransfield was attacked by 18-year-old Kayla Smith after going to Smith's home with her boyfriend Blake Dowling in the early hours of 28 March.

Smith had pleaded guilty to manslaughter but denied murder. She then changed her plea to guilty on the second day of her trial.

Dowling, 18, who took Chloe to the house in Kennerleigh Avenue in Leeds, and Archie Rycroft, 20, who followed Smith to the fight, are also charged with murder and manslaughter and their trial will continue. They both deny the charges against them.

The judge, Mr Justice Cavanagh KC, said he would sentence Smith once the trial was over.

He told her the only sentence he could give was life imprisonment, but that he would need to set the minimum term she must spend in custody.

The trial previously heard that Dowling had been in a relationship with both Chloe and Smith and "knew of the bad feeling between the two females".

Dowling's mother told the court that Smith was "jealous and obsessed" over her son's relationship with Chloe.

News.title: Watch: 'Life-changing moment' boy turns on Tourette syndrome device to help stop tics
News.content:
A wrist device developed by researchers in the University of Nottingham is changing the lives of people with Tourette sydrome in an "instant".

The small device works by delivering electrical pulses to the median nerve at the wrist, which trials have shown can change the activity in the parts of the brain involved in movement control.

Tourette's syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition with symptoms usually starting in childhood.

Among the users of this device is 15-year-old Ollie, from Cheshire, who started making involuntary neck movements nearly two years ago.

The BBC's Navtej Johal has this report.

More on this story.

News.title: How Pochettino came on Man Utd's radar - and what sacked manager Carrick was told
News.content:
Michael Carrick must have known what was coming.

Not just because reports of his imminent dismissal were widespread - followed by information about who would be replacing him as Manchester United boss.

But because, effectively, he and his representatives were given heavy enough indications of what was to follow.

On Monday, according to well-placed sources, Carrick's agent was contacted by chief executive Omar Berrada to be told he and director of football Jason Wilcox would be heading to Monaco for a planned meeting with co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe that would include a discussion about the head coach's future.

A day later, it is believed Wilcox had a similar conversation with Carrick.

It is understood that on both occasions it was communicated that a recommendation regarding Carrick's future at the club would be made.

What is not clear is whether Carrick and his representatives knew that recommendation was to relieve him of his duties.

By that point, BBC Sport has been told United were aware of a $10m (Â£7m) release clause in Mauricio Pochettino's contract with the United States national team. One source even indicated it was representatives of the Argentine who told the Premier League side.

There is some regret behind the scenes at United that machinations leading to Carrick's departure on Thursday were played out so publicly.

But with football clubs the size of United, keeping such developments completely private is extremely difficult - and there is a feeling they were as transparent with Carrick as they could be.

Following heavy defeats by Como and Bournemouth, United placed huge importance on the following three games - against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa.

It is understood United's leadership team were clear with Carrick that results and performances needed to improve. A defeat, a victory and draw weren't enough to save him.

There is a feeling that during that three-game period, there was not enough progress, particularly in terms of team structure - underlined by the fact they conceded eight goals.

News.title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
News.content:
ï»¿The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the previous three months, official figures, external show.

The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war.

Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers.

Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by cloud computing and AI-linked spending.

The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.

But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages.

However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".

"Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future," he said.

Chancellor John Healey told the BBC the figures showed a "remarkable resilience" in the face of global conflicts, and hopes they "bring back confidence in Britain".

Asked about how government decisions could be the reason for growth when AI investment has been a main driver, Healey said ministers can always "help or hinder" business confidence and investments.

News.title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
News.content:
Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.

As reported in the Times,, external Alan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits.

Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet".

He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.

His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Disabled people in Scotland can claim the devolved Adult Disability Payment.

Instead, under Milburn's plan, under-25s would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.

Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes.

People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work.

In his interim report,, external Milburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work.

Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.

Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.

Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.

News.title: Activist Daniel Thomas admits criminal damage after slashing migrant dinghy in Channel
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, has admitted criminal damage after slashing a dinghy with a knife in the English Channel.

The 37-year-old changed his plea to the single charge when he appeared via video link from prison at Portsmouth Crown Court on Thursday.

A court previously heard he had taken a boat into the English Channel on 22 September and observed the migrant occupants of a dinghy being assisted by the RNLI, Border Force and the French Coastguard.

Thomas admitted using a knife on the dinghy, which had French personnel on board.

Prosecutor Kevin Lucie told Basingstoke Magistrates' Court in September the defendant instructed his vessel to be steered towards the empty rigid inflatable boat (RIB) that was adrift.

The court heard he then armed himself with a knife as rescue crews also approached the dinghy and a Frenchman boarded from a rescue vessel.

After slashing the boat with the knife, Thomas could be heard on a livestream saying: "This is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats.

"Right, you're on English territory, This is England, this is not France anymore.

"Get off the boat, you have time to get off the boat. This is not France. Take them back."

News.title: Burnham says climate consensus 'gone' but pledges 'new era of leadership' in COP31 speech
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned that the consensus on both science and climate change has "gone".

Addressing other world leaders and delegates at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, he said that despite this, the UK was ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on the climate change issue.

But environmental campaigners at the summit said the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions.

In recent months, the UK government has announced policies which critics say have weakened its green credentials, such as reducing support for heat pumps, approving the Jackdaw gas field and doubling down on support for Heathrow Airport's expansion.

Burnham opened his speech on Thursday by talking about the heat experienced in the UK this past summer.

He said "it was not normal" - in fact it was the hottest on record, made 130 times more likely because of climate change, according to the Met Office.

Hundreds of schools were closed, cereal harvests were down 11%, and ambulance services were inundated with calls beyond levels seen during the Covid-19 pandemic.

As a result of the threat to people's health and homes, the PM said he was creating the UK, and the world's, first climate security envoy, Dame Madeleine Alessandri.

Alessandri, the former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee, said: "Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates."

As a result this was "placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world", she added.

This will be seen as a strong indication of the focus of the UK's priorities when it takes up the G20 presidency next year.

The current president is the US, which has been a notable absentee from the COP process over the last two years since President Trump withdrew the country from the most important global climate treaty - the Paris Climate Agreement.

Professor Lord Nicholas Stern, who identified 20 years ago that climate change could cost the global economy up to 20% of GDP if left unchecked, praised the PM's words.

"The Prime Minister was right to identify climate change as a threat to security around the world, and the importance of investments in clean electricity generation as the best way of protecting households and businesses from the high prices and volatile markets for fossil fuels," he said.

News.title: Poundland gets more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
News.content:
Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended to find a rescue deal.

A deadline to secure a buyer for the retail chain was set to expire at midnight, but a court has given Poundland an extra 10 days to find a buyer.

The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by owners Gordon Brothers from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 shops and stock piecemeal.

Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just Â£1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock shops, and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

The investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claims.

However, pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

About Â£50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.

The BBC understands that Gordon Brothers agreed to release a further Â£10m to Â£11m from Poundland's accounts, on top of Â£11m announced earlier, as the firm seeks to find a new buyer.

Gordon Brothers said it was in talks with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and it had received "several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business".

News.title: King Charles appears on Elton John's radio show in secretly-recorded birthday episode
News.content:
King Charles III has appeared on Sir Elton John's radio show in an episode set to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.

During the Rocket Hour show, the King said the pop star had become "a national treasure after all these years", to which the singer joked: "I'll be on the Antiques Roadshow."

"Join the club," the King replied.

The pair discussed some of their favourite musical performances, as well as the role music has played in the King's charity, the King's Trust. The show was recorded in secret last month and will air this Saturday.

Sir Elton has long been a supporter of the trust, most recently donating a pair of his rose-tinted glasses to its 50th anniversary auction this year.

In a trailer for the upcoming episode, the King and Sir Elton are seen laughing together as they chat.

In a voiceover, the singer said he was "excited to hear what he's got to say about music, about the King's Trust and memories that we both share".

The King's Trust - previously known as The Prince's Trust - was established by Charles in 1976 to help young people from disadvantaged backgrounds overcome challenging situations, become employed or launch their own businesses.

During the radio episode, the King called it "an opportunity too good to resist" when he was asked to showcase music from the "talented performers who have so generously supported us over the years, together with some of the newer artists the trust has helped to launch".

The full list of their chosen tracks is under wraps until the episode airs but Skye Newman's Hairdresser, Raye's Joy and Muse's rendition of Feeling Good are said to be among them.

The pair will reminisce about some of the most memorable performances for the trust, from the Wembley Arena rock galas of the 1980s - which Sir Elton participated in - to charity shows at the Royal Albert Hall and pop concerts in Hyde Park.

The episode was recorded at Apple Music Studios - which hosts the show - in Battersea Power Station when the King and Sir Elton visited for the launch of the Apple x King's Trust Creative Labs.

The mentorship programme aims to help young people explore careers in creative industries.

News.title: Russell Brand's social media accounts disabled by Meta
News.content:
Russell Brand's social media accounts on platforms owned by tech company Meta have been disabled.

It comes after the 51-year-old former entertainer was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years in jail for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault earlier this week.

He was found guilty of the charges involving four women and relating to offences between 2004 and 2009.

Meta owns social media platforms including Instagram and Facebook.

Brand is currently in prison and is expected to serve seven years of his sentence behind bars before being released on licence.

On Wednesday evening, a post appeared on his X account, which remains active. "There was never a Russell Brand, according to @meta," it read.

"Thank God for @elonmusk," the message added, referring to X's owner. "Stay tuned," it concluded.

The BBC has approached X for comment.

The post included what appeared to be screenshots showing Brand's Instagram account having been disabled.

Meta's community standards policy says that "in order to maintain a safe environment and empower free expression" it restricts or removes accounts that are "harmful to the community".

That includes accounts owned by convicted sex offenders.

In 2023, after a media investigation revealing allegations about Brand's behaviour - which he denies - YouTube suspended his channels from making money from adverts for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy".

At the time, the video platform said it was taking action "to protect" its users.

News.title: Schools, libraries and parents face 'difficult decision' over David Walliams books
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Mr Di'Iasio urged the government to give schools national guidance, so they are "not leaving this open to one or two head teachers making one decision and others making a different one".

Darren Morgan, head of Kings Road Primary School in Manchester, told the programme that he has taken the decision to remove Walliams' publications.

The stories have been useful to promote reading, but "when there are these allegations it's really difficult to keep these books on the shelves", he said.

Steve Chalke, head of Oasis Academies, which runs more than 50 schools, said it was impossible to stop children seeing the current stories about Walliams.

"So when a child wanders into a school and into the library and sees his name or perhaps sees his photograph on a book, it can be very traumatising for some children," he said.

Author Chloe Combi, who has written about "how it feels to be young in modern Britain" and Generation Z, said banning Walliams' books is not appropriate, and could mean that important conversations about him "get swept under the carpet".

"I think by talking about it and what has happened - and the responsibility of parents to have that conversation with their kids - that actually makes more sense," she told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I'm totally sympathetic with schools for withdrawing him and bookshops withdrawing him as an individual decision. But the point is, none of that is going to erase what's happened."

The Department for Education has been asked for comment.

News.title: New analysis reveals there will be 250,000 more NEETs in five years unless action is taken
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The crisis with under-25s out of work and education is set to escalate with more than a quarter of a million more destined for benefits, according to new analysis seen by The Independent.

The number of so-called NEETs (not in education, employment or training) aged 16 to-24 years old will rise by 280,000 to reach 1.26 million by 2031, accounting for one in six of that age group.

The analysis carried out for the Liberal Democrat is based on former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn's review, which estimates the crisis already costs the country £125 billion a year.

Based on the Milburn findings the extra young people would add around £36 billion annually to the bill unless the government acts to “shut off the NEET pipeline at source”, Andy Burnham has been warned.

open image in gallery Sir Ed Davey visit to youth employment programme ( PA )

The Lib Dems are calling on the government to introduce a 100-hour work experience guarantee and a careers coach for every young person - to ensure everyone leaving school is equipped with the best possible skills to succeed in life.

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said: “Every teacher knows a child that started secondary school bright and eager, but over the years drifted to the back of the class. Too often, nobody notices, and they slip through the cracks to become one of the almost one million young people not in education or training.

“As a young carer for my mum, and now as a dad to a son with complex needs, I know how much it matters when someone truly notices what a young person is going through.

“Unless we act now, hundreds of thousands more young people will slip through the cracks, stuck without the education, training or guidance to succeed. Milburn's report is a once-in-a-generation chance to shut off the NEET pipeline at source. Ministers must seize it.”

Currently, nearly a million young people (981,000) are already NEET, up 30,000 in a year. Milburn's interim report found the system already has the data to spot those at risk, but lacks the architecture, funding and accountability to act on it.

The Lib Dems want Andy Burnham’s government to commit to a 100-hour work experience and enrichment guarantee.

This would mean every young person would be guaranteed at least 100 hours of work placements, career-focused enrichment or volunteering.

They also want to see personalised careers coaching provided.

This would involve “a real person” rather than online platforms meeting young people multiple times a year, helping each young person build a five-year plan for life after education.

The proposal draws on best practice from the Netherlands and Germany and would be delivered in partnership with the third sector.

Milburn's interim report found careers guidance in schools to be underpowered, with NEET young people far less likely to feel ready for work when they leave education.

They are also calling for an overhaul of A-Levels into a baccalaureate-style system, alongside T-Levels and V-Levels, so no young person is forced down a narrow pathway at 14 or 16 that doesn't suit them.

open image in gallery As a report on Neets from Alan Milburn, right, is awaited, No 10 said the Prime Minister ‘has already been clear that we need fundamental change in how we support young people to grow up in this country’ (PA) ( PA Wire )

The party warned that Labour's plans to make pupils choose between academic and technical qualifications at 14 could funnel disadvantaged children into narrower routes. The Conservatives let more than £2 billion set aside for apprenticeships go unspent while in government, allowed the pupil premium to wither, and now want to cut 100,000 university places a year.

Savanta polling found 56 per cent of 16-to-24-year-olds had hit major roadblocks finding work in the past year, and one in five (19 per cent) had given up looking altogether.

Education spokesperson Munira Wilson said: “It is nothing short of a national moral failure that we now have nearly a million young people out of work or training. We all have a responsibility to provide the next generation the same opportunities we were afforded - but we have not held up our end of the deal. Enough is enough.

“Our plan is ready to go. 100 hours of real work experience and a proper careers coach for every young person - we urge the Prime Minister to use this plan so this is the last generation that ever has to experience a NEETs crisis.”

Labour housing minister Matthew Pennycook admitted the current system for NEETs means the government is “paying for failure,” and that the focus should shift to investing in their futures with intensive support rather than writing cheques and forgetting about them.

He told LBC that suggestions "need to be taken as a package and looked at in the round".

He said: "We've got to invest in their futures rather than paying for failure.

"The prime minister has been absolutely clear that the status quo isn't working."

News.title: Construction worker with pregnant wife identified as one of eight people killed in New York City building collapse
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A young dad is the first identified victim of a New York City building collapse that left two children and six adults dead.

José Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 26, was one of the victims, friends told the New York Daily News. The migrant from Ecuador is survived by a 4-year-old son and a pregnant wife.

“She’s heading to the hospital tomorrow for the baby to be born,” the president of the Club Deportivo La Bahía soccer team where Jose was a member, told the outlet.

The three-story building collapsed into an open construction site along Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn around 4 p.m. Wednesday. Six people were dead at the scene and two more died at the hospital, officials said Thursday. Another 18 people, including 14 civilians and four firefighters, were injured.

Crews continue to search the scene for survivors as officials now work to determine what caused the collapse.

open image in gallery Six adults and two kids were killed when a building next to a construction site collapsed in a New York City neighborhood ( Reuters )

“This has been a devastating evening and morning for our city,” New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday.

Mamdani said at a press conference that the investigation will not only try to determine why the building collapsed, but also examine other sites operated by the same construction companies.

The names of the other victims have not been released.

The building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. housed both retail and apartment space. It’s unclear how many people in total lived at the site. The property was next to a construction site at the intersection with Bedford Avenue.

Inspectors had discovered violations at the site months before the collapse, according to the New York Post. A stop-work order was issued in March, and the Department of Buildings concluded that the building was being demolished without overhead protection, such as netting, to protect nearby buildings. In April, demolition work had resumed despite the stop-work order.

Work was eventually allowed to continue in May.

The site is owned by a company linked to Robert Fischman, who wanted to build a 56,000-square-foot building there, according to WNBC.

open image in gallery City officials are now trying to determine the cause of the collapse ( Reuters )

open image in gallery Rescue efforts were ongoing Thursday ( AFP/Getty )

As rescue efforts continued on a rainy Thursday, some were praising the saving of one pregnant woman from the wreckage. Video captured dozens of firefighters lifting her out of the rubble and passing her along their line so she could be taken for care.

​Speaking to CBS News, a man revealed that his wife, who is six months pregnant, was among those rescued. However, for some time, he did not know if she was alive or dead.

“This is tough, man. He's looking for his pregnant wife, and she's not picking up the phone,” Jumaane Williams, a New York City public advocate, told the outlet amid the search.

By 6.30 p.m., the news that his wife was alive was relayed to the as-yet-unnamed man, ABC7 reports.

​“I have an update. She is alive, she is still alive. I am very happy,” the man said.

open image in gallery A pregnant woman was rescued from the scene of a collapsed building in Brooklyn ( AP )

City Councilwoman Farah Louis told the outlet that the woman, who had been taken to receive medical care, remained in critical condition as of Wednesday night.

Anderson Velez, who lived at the collapsed building, told The New York Post that his two children, aged 2 and 7, were rescued after being trapped under the rubble. He was at work at the time.

“She called me when the building collapsed while she was inside with rubble on top of her,” Velez said, referring to his wife. “She was screaming for someone to help get my son out and then the call cut off.”

News.title: Manhunt launched for two Rotherham rapists who fled before verdict
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A manhunt is under way for two of the three men convicted of raping a teenage girl who was groomed, trafficked and exploited in Rotherham 20 years ago.

The National Crime Agency said Mudasar Hussain, 37, and Kamir Ifzal Khan, 37, absconded ahead of their trial, and at least one of them has fled abroad.

The pair were found guilty at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday alongside Ghazanfar Hussain, 42, the NCA confirmed.

Ghazanfar Hussain is the brother of Mudasar Hussain. Of the three defendants, only he was in court to hear Thursday's verdicts, the NCA said.

The agency said its officers working to locate the two men are now appealing to the public for any information that could help.

Mudasar Hussain had been on conditional bail awaiting trial and had surrendered his passport to the NCA as one of those conditions.

An NCA spokesman said that, while he may still be in the UK, it is also possible that he has left the country illegally.

Khan, who was on unconditional court bail ahead of his trial, is known to have fled the country on a flight to Qatar on 22 September. Investigators believe he travelled on to Pakistan.

open image in gallery The three men were found guilty at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday (Dave Higgens/PA) ( PA Archive )

The agency confirmed that Mudasar Hussain was found guilty on Thursday of 12 counts of rape, Khan was found guilty of two counts of rape and one count of trafficking for sexual exploitation, and Ghazanfar Hussain was found guilty of one count of rape.

The CPS said Mudasar Hussain and Khan separately targeted the girl when she was 13 and 14 years old.

The complainant, who is now in her 30s, was groomed and sexually abused first by Mudasar Hussain, then separately by Ghazanfar Hussain and Khan between 2008 and 2010.

Mudasar Hussain, who she knew as "Muddy", was around 20 at the time.

He plied the girl with drugs and alcohol and, after a few months, took her to a house in Rotherham where he raped her for the first of many times.

The NCA said the girl was abused by Mudasar Hussain “countless times over the course of around 18 months, at the house, in local public spaces and in his car”.

She told officers that Hussain used violence to coerce her, including threatening her with a baseball bat.

The agency said Ghazanfar Hussain – nicknamed "Gucci" – raped the girl when his brother left the UK for a period. She did not know they were related.

The NCA said the girl met Khan, who was about 20 at the time, when she began frequenting a local takeaway where he worked.

Khan – nicknamed "Kammy" – gave her food, money and cigarettes, and took her out on deliveries, leading her to believe that they were in a relationship. But he raped her during the abuse which lasted around seven months.

According to the NCA, there were a number of times when Khan took her to a house where he asked her to have sex with other men who were present.

She always refused, but Khan took her to a different address where he left her alone with a man, who raped her.

The NCA said that, when Khan returned and found the girl in distress, he told her that he had owed the man a favour.

Ghazanfar Hussain has been remanded in custody ahead of his sentencing at Sheffield Crown Court on Friday. Mudasar Hussain and Khan will also be sentenced on Friday in their absence.

The trio were arrested as part of Operation Stovewood, the huge NCA investigation set up in 2014 in the wake of the Rotherham child exploitation scandal.

open image in gallery The three men were arrested as part of Operation Stovewood ( PA )

The NCA says Stovewood is the largest law enforcement operation of its kind undertaken in the UK and has identified and supported around 1,150 potential victims, securing 60 convictions against 55 people.

Head of Operation Stovewood Philip Marshall said: “The victim has shown tremendous courage in reporting the predatory grooming, exploitation and sustained sexual abuse these men subjected her to as a child.”

Mr Marshall said: “Mudasar Hussain and Kamir Khan have attempted to avoid justice but my officers are determined to find the men, to ensure that both of them serve the sentences handed down to them in due course.”

He said: "Officers have been working with partners, pursuing numerous lines of enquiry in the UK and overseas, to locate Mudasar Hussain and Kamir Khan.

“I am now appealing for anyone with information that could help our enquiries, no matter how insignificant that information may appear, to report it.”

Melissa Garner, specialist prosecutor for the CPS, said: "These defendants have now been convicted of their horrific and appalling crimes. I want to recognise the victim for her strength throughout this case.

“Her determination in seeing this case through has been crucial in bringing these offenders to justice.”

She added: "Their abuse has caused the victim serious and lifelong harm. These defendants have now been convicted of their horrific and appalling crimes.”

News.title: Richard Posner, prolific legal scholar and outspoken appeals court judge, dies at 87
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Richard Posner, a prodigious legal scholar and outspoken former federal appeals court judge who pioneered the use of economic theory to resolve legal questions, has died. He was 87.

Posner's opinions have been cited extensively in textbooks that have educated generations of lawyers.

The University of Chicago Law School, where he served as a senior lecturer and one of his sons, Eric Posner, is a professor, said Posner died Tuesday.

Over a nearly 40-year career on the Chicago-based 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, Posner developed a reputation as an acerbic and witty writer and tough questioner.

He was appointed to the court in 1981 by Republican President Ronald Reagan, but his legal opinions ran from conservative to liberal, and Posner described his approach to judging as pragmatic. Posner was a leading figure in the use of economic theory to analyze legal rules and institutions. His 1973 textbook, The Economic Analysis of Law, was foundational and remains in print today.

As a judge, he wrote thousands of legal opinions, including in a seminal 2017 ruling that found the 1964 Civil Rights Act also barred discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender workers.

“I don’t see why firing a lesbian because she is in the subset of women who are lesbian should be thought any less a form of sex discrimination than firing a woman because she’s a woman,” Posner wrote.

Outside the court, he authored hundreds of academic articles and dozens of books, and did not withhold his opinions about American institutions. In 2016, he called the Supreme Court “highly politicized,” saying that “probably only” a couple of the justices were qualified, and even they were “not great.”

As a legal scholar, Posner was uniquely “prolific, influential, and endlessly curious," University of Chicago Law School Dean Adam Chilton said.

"He was a giant whose influence on our legal system, the field of law and economics, and on our law school cannot be overstated,” Chilton said in a statement.

News.title: 2 beloved street vendors identified as victims of the Los Angeles metro station crash
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Authorities have identified two of the three women killed when the driver of a minivan crashed outside a Los Angeles metro station this week.

The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner identified the women as Teodora Villalobos, 57, and Maria Peck, 73. Both were killed on the sidewalk Tuesday by blunt force injuries, the medical examiner's office said.

Authorities did not immediately release the identity of the third victim, pending the notification of family, the medical examiner's office said in an email on Thursday.

Peck and Villalobos were food vendors in Los Angeles' North Hollywood neighborhood who were killed when the minivan plowed into a busy intersection during the height of the evening commute. Friends and family members built a memorial to the women, who were widely known for selling hot dogs and other street food, by leaving flower bouquets, notes, photos and candles on the sidewalk where they were struck.

Police arrested the driver, 61-year-old Ihor Demianenko, for investigation of driving under the influence and three counts of murder. His bail was set at $6 million. It was not immediately known when he would appear in court.

Melissa Villalobos told KABC-TV that her mother worked hard and tried to help those in her community.

“When she sold here, if people didn't have money to pay for the food, she would still give food to those who didn't have anything,” she said.

Peck worked as a vendor for more than a decade six days a week, even on holidays, according to a GoFundMe page set up to support her family. The page said Peck found joy in being part of the community and didn't want to scale back her hours even as she aged.

News.title: Maika Monroe shows how much more than 'Scream Queen' she is in 'Victorian Psycho'
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

After years spent fleeing serial killers and worse, Maika Monroe goes on the offensive in the gothic triller “Victorian Psycho.”

On the surface, the movie appears to extend Monroe’s reputation as the preeminent “Scream Queen” of her generation. Horror films like “It Follows,” “Watcher” and “Longlegs” have made the 33-year-old Monroe synonymous with the genre.

Bodies get bloody in “Victorian Psycho,” too. But in the film, written by Virginia Feito and based on her 2025 novel, Monroe’s deranged protagonist is archly hilarious. As much as Monroe may be associated with horror, she might be even better at comedy.

“I didn’t know if I could pull it off. I decided to take the leap,” Monroe says. “Man, it was just so much fun. There’s so much freedom in this role. It will definitely be the character I’ll miss the most.”

In the film directed by Zachary Wigon, which Bleecker Street releases Friday in theaters, Monroe plays Winifred Notty. In the 1850s, she arrives at the Ensor House, the grand manor of the Pounds family, to serve as the eager governess to two children (Evie Templeton, Jacobi Jupe).

It doesn’t take long for the children to realize Winifred has a screw loose. But their governess is comically chipper, even when making excuses for a stray ear found under a bed.

As distant as the part might be from Monroe — the laid back Santa Barbara, California, native is here doing a British accent for the first time — it’s the first role to really capture Monroe’s natural comic energy.

“I’ve never done anything remotely close to a role like this,” Monroe said in an interview earlier this year at the Cannes Film Festival, where “Victorian Psycho” first premiered. “I’m usually more introverted and internal with my roles, and this is very outward.”

Monroe’s range as an actor has always exceeded any neat genre identification. She brought Hitchcockian depth to “Watcher” and psychological intensity to “Longlegs.” She'll return to her breakthrough role in the much anticipated “They Follows,” David Robert Mitchell's recently shot sequel to his 2014 hit.

But in “Victorian Psycho,” Monroe is a hoot. Her Winifred is almost always grinning ear to ear. That came from one of Monroe’s heroes.

“One of my favorite actors is Jack Nicholson. I think every project he does he’s fascinating,” Monroe says. “Of course in ‘The Shining,’ he’s pretty much smiling through the whole thing, through all the pain and the anguish. That was a huge influence.”

Monroe is also a professed fan of Olivia Colman. And it’s easy to see how wildly mischievous characters, like those often played by Colman or Nicholson, might be even more in Monroe’s wheelhouse than horror. It’s enough to make you wonder: Does she ever chafe at the term “Scream Queen?”

“I can’t be mad at it," she says. "I’m so proud of ‘It Follows,’ ‘Longlegs,’ ‘Watcher.’ So, what can you do?”

But if a certain side of Monroe has been rarely seen on screen, “Victorian Psycho” lets it out.

“In the Victorian era, there was suppression. In this industry, I can find that I need to present a certain way or come across a certain way,” Monroe says. “You have to suppress certain things and not say certain things. That’s what was such a joy in this.”

___

This is an updated version of a story that first moved May 21, 2026.

News.title: RFK Jr faces Senate probe over ‘lies’ to Congress about Samoa trip
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Two senators have launched an investigation into whether Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. lied to Congress about the reason for a 2019 trip to Samoa.

The probe was launched after reports by The Associated Press and The Guardian in August, refuting his testimony. It is among a vast array of investigations planned into the Trump administration after Democrats regained control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., announced the inquiry in a letter sent Wednesday to Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine nonprofit group previously chaired by Kennedy.

The senators requested a broad range of documents from the group concerning Kennedy’s Samoa travel, his 2024 presidential campaign, and his Senate confirmation process. The letter also asked for all communications between the organization and federal officials since President Donald Trump's second term began in January 2025, setting a compliance deadline of Dec. 4.

Reporting in August revealed that while Kennedy repeatedly told key confirmation lawmakers last year that his visit to Samoa before a lethal measles outbreak had "nothing to do with vaccines," a pre-trip letter sent to the Samoan prime minister on Children's Health Defense letterhead showed otherwise. Kennedy used the words vaccine or vaccination eight times in the letter.

RFK Jr repeatedly told lawmakers last year that his visit to Samoa before a lethal measles outbreak had ‘nothing to do with vaccines’ ( AFP/Getty )

"We intend to hold Secretary Kennedy accountable for the grave harm he has caused to vulnerable children," Wyden and Alsobrooks wrote in their letter. "We also intend to hold him accountable for any false statements made to Congress, a crime that undermines the Senate’s ability to fulfill its constitutional duties."

The Department of Health and Human Services has maintained the Samoa trip "was unrelated to vaccines." In response to an AP query in August, HHS said "any claim or insinuation based on these letters that Secretary Kennedy lied under oath or to Congress is not only false but outright defamatory."

Kennedy was not under oath during his confirmation hearing. Knowingly giving material false testimony to Congress is a crime carrying a potential prison sentence regardless of whether an individual is under oath, though it is rarely prosecuted.

Spokespeople for Children’s Health Defense and HHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday.

Wyden is slated to chair the Senate Finance Committee, which has oversight of Kennedy’s health department, when Democrats take control of Congress in January. Alsobrooks serves on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, which also oversees the department.

The same senators on Wednesday announced a separate inquiry into hundreds of thousands of dollars in gifts reportedly given to Kennedy last year by a donor and former employee.

News.title: Experts hail a “milestone” as TB deaths fall by more than a third in 10 years
News.content:
The number of people dying from tuberculosis has dropped by more than a third over the last 10 years but progress against the disease is still too slow, according to the World Health Organization.

Figures from WHO’s annual TB report showed that the lung disease took the lives of an estimated 1.13 million people in 2025, down from 1.7m in 2015, a drop of 35 per cent.

While WHO hailed this as a major milestone in achieving global targets - albeit five years too late - it said that progress in wiping out TB was still too slow.

Africa and Europe have made the greatest progress in reducing deaths, with numbers halving on both continents over the 10-year period. India and China - countries that have high burdens of the disease - also cut deaths by 35 per cent.

The report also showed that an estimated 10.6million people contracted the disease in 2025, a reduction of just 75,000 since 2024.

TB - still the world’s leading infectious disease killer - is preventable and curable, and is caused by the bacillus Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which is spread when infected people cough or sneeze.

The disease has been around for centuries, and has been described as the quintessential disease of poverty as it spreads in areas of low quality housing, among people with poor nutrition and immunity. It is a particular risk to people who are HIV positive.

Treatment requires a six-month long regimen of medication, and while treatments have become less toxic in recent years, they still take a heavy toll on patients and have a range of side effects, including at the most extreme deafness. Adherence to medication is also a problem.

News.title: Low-cost parenting app halves rates of sexual violence amongst teenagers in Tanzania
News.content:
A low cost parenting intervention has more than halved rates of sexual violence among teenage girls in Tanzania, a study has shown.

The ParentApp digital parenting programme for families is aimed at reducing rates of violence experienced by teenagers of both sexes.

Researchers found the programme helped bolster family relationships and enabled mothers and fathers to better communicate with their children at what is often a tricky stage of their development.

The programme, led by Oxford University and the University of Cape Town in partnership with the Tanzanian government, the World Health Organization and Unicef, combines in-person and mobile parenting support.

Parents have an introductory session with a facilitator and then undertake 12 weekly sessions online. They also join a WhatsApp group with other parents where they can discuss problems and support one another.

The randomized controlled trial, published in The Lancet, included 2,396 children aged 10–17 and 2,396 parents and carers across 80 urban and rural areas.

Families were randomly assigned to receive either ParentApp or a comparison app focused on safe water and hygiene. Researchers analysing the results did not know which app each family received.

At the 14-month follow-up, girls in families participating in the ParentApp initiative reported a 67% reduction in sexual violence; a 54% reduction in sexual exploitation and an improvement in parent-child relationships. The successes were less marked in boys, however.

Violence against children is widespread globally: Unicef data shows that around one in five girls and women and one in seven boys and men globally have experienced sexual violence as children.

Lucie Cluver, professor of child and family social work at Oxford University and one of the authors of the study, said the intervention was aimed at helping parents and children talk to one another and discuss situations before they arise.

In Tanzania, for example, teenage girls might get a motorbike taxi late at night, potentially putting them in a dangerous situation.

“What you’re doing is making plans and problem solving ahead of these risky situations that teenagers end up in. And you’re building trust and the relationship so you can have these difficult conversations,” said Prof Cluver.

She said she was surprised at how big an impact the intervention had on sexual violence: teenage girls reported that because the app helped improve communication with their parents and carers they did not feel the need to go out as much.

The programme cost around $6 per family but researchers calculated that it goes up to around $10 per family if 20% are given smartphones. A traditional in-person parenting intervention generally costs around $120 per family.

Engagement in the sessions was high - around 70 per cent of participants completed the course - and some parents kept in touch with one another after the programme.

However, the authors of the study stressed that while the app focused on families there remains a need to prevent violence against children in other settings, such as schools and religious institutions. There also needs to be a broader societal push to address the scourge.

“The app isn’t the answer to everything - it’s just one part of the puzzle,” said Prof Cluver.

Prof Cluver said she hoped future versions of the programme would include greater focus on digital harms and test whether parents could take the lead themselves.

The programme is being rolled out in other countries, including Mexico, Panama and South Africa, and is easily adaptable for different contexts.

“Tanzania only has 20% smartphone use and we thought if it works in one of the hardest places to do a digital intervention it could work anywhere,” she said.

She said the study showed how parenting was a universal experience, with the majority focused on what is best for their children.

“Parents feel powerless. We live in a world where our kids are facing risks and parents just want to help,” added Prof Cluver.

News.title: AI fuels fastest economic growth in two years
News.content:
The Prime Minister and the Chancellor should not claim credit for the AI-fuelled expansion of Britain’s economy in the third quarter, a think tank said.

Julian Jessop, economics fellow at the Institute of Economic Affairs, said the 0.7pc expansion in the economy was “a tribute to the resilience of the private sector in the face of the energy shock and policy headwinds”.

He said: “This resilience is despite rather than because of anything the Government has done. In particular, the persistent weakens of the construction sector underlines the failure of flagship policies to boost housebuilding and infrastructure spending.

“The Government’s clumsy interventions are also continuing to add to labour and housing costs, including rents. Instead, the key driver of growth and business optimism has been the rollout of AI. This is an area that the Government has not got round to messing up, though that may yet be coming.

“In the meantime, the Government is still borrowing more than expected and the labour market remains weak.

“The full impact of higher inflation and higher interest rates has also yet to be felt. Early surveys for the fourth quarter already show that consumer confidence, retail spending, private sector hiring and housing market activity are all starting to slide again.

“2026 will still be a year when the economy performed much better than expected – at least in terms of GDP. But the new year will start with further increases in energy bills and high levels of job insecurity, which will matter far more to most people.”

News.title: Bird flu viruses gaining function through natural mixing, warn scientists
News.content:
The bird flu virus’ resurgence began with an 11-year-old. In February 2023, the schoolgirl was admitted to a hospital in Phnom Penh with severe pneumonia – within a day, she was dead.

Tests soon revealed that she had contracted avian influenza: Cambodia hadn’t reported a human case of bird flu since 2014, but the hiatus was over. Since then, 39 more people have been infected and 15 have died in the Southeast Asian country – a case fatality rate of roughly 40 per cent.

Researchers have been scratching their heads as to why, after nine years, this particular stain of H5N1 suddenly started jumping from birds to people again. The strain or clade called 2.3.2.1 had been circulating for almost a decade without spilling into humans. What changed?

Now, a paper in Emerging Infectious Diseases offers clues.

Scientists say the apparent rise in human cases has coincided with the virus gaining new genetic material and, potentially, new powers of infection, from a second flu virus via a process known as “reassortment”.

News.title: The country where diabetes is more feared than HIV
News.content:
Furthermore, even when antiretrovirals suppress the virus, the immune system can stay chronically activated, causing a low-grade inflammation that damages organs and blood vessels. The Lancet HIV Commission reported that, by one measure of biological ageing, people with HIV appeared about five years older on average than peers without the virus.

HIV also makes other infections more dangerous. For example, those living with the virus are more likely to contract human papillomavirus (HPV), the leading cause of cervical cancer, and they are less able to clear HPV from their bodies.

“With HIV, you don’t channel your mind into dying,” Ms Shongwe said. “But when I got to know that I have cervical cancer, I thought it was the end of the world.”

In 2018, Ms Ginindza moved from the Ministry of Health’s HIV programme to its NCD programme, but almost immediately, she asked to go back to her old job. “There is nothing here,” she recalled, “no tools, no data collection system, no guidelines”.

Even today, the ministry doesn’t have any dedicated NCD posts. While there are hundreds of people working on HIV, there are just 10 NCD staff, all borrowed from other programmes, Ms Ginindza said.

Although latest figures show that NCDs account for almost half of Eswatini’s deaths the government’s programme for NCDs, injuries and mental health received about one million emalangeni - roughly £45,000 - or 0.03 per cent of the health budget.

Foreign aid hasn’t filled the gap: international partners cover about five per cent of NCD spending, Ms Ginindza said, compared with 60 per cent of the HIV response. Donors “cannot give you money when they also need that money to address their own NCDs”, she added.

So, when it comes to these chronic diseases, patients struggle to get diagnosed, obtain their medicines or see a specialist for complications. In a 2024 government survey, fewer than 30 per cent of people with high blood pressure were on medication, and only 14 per cent had their hypertension under control.

The government’s own NCD report puts the stock-out rate for key medicines at 79 per cent, and the public system has no nephrologists, endocrinologists or cardiologists, Ms Ginindza said, relying instead on private specialists and Taiwanese medical missions to provide these services.

Faced with one of the worst HIV epidemics, Eswatini poured almost everything into fighting it. “The focus was HIV,” Ms Ginindza said, “so we forgot about the other conditions.”

Fighting on two fronts



Now, Eswatini is trying to turn its HIV machinery towards chronic diseases.

Since 2020, a government-led scheme has delivered NCD medication refills, blood pressure checks and glucose tests in hundreds of community settings, integrating this with existing HIV services. As it once did with antiretrovirals, the ministry is also shifting NCD care from hospitals to local clinics, Ms Ginindza said, aiming to train at least two nurses at each.

For Mr Mamba, that means he sees the same clinician for his HIV, diabetes and blood pressure. It saves time, he said, since he can get everything under one roof.

The challenge is not just extending HIV services to NCD patients but finding the money to sustain both. The Eswatini government aims to increase NCD funding to 20 million emalangeni, or £900,000, by 2028.

But last year, the Trump administration gutted the US President’s Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar), the backbone of Eswatini’s HIV response.

In December, Eswatini signed a five-year deal with the US to restore some HIV funding - on the condition that the government shoulders more of the cost itself. So, as the country scrambles to protect its HIV gains, NCDs risk remaining a secondary priority.

With his diabetes and blood pressure medicines so often out of stock, Mr Mamba has come to dread his check-ups, convinced each one will show his numbers have climbed again - and that his luck is running out.

Many of his neighbours have the same conditions and probably share these fears, he said, but much as people once kept quiet about HIV, they rarely discuss such things.

Over 30 years ago, Ms Gwebu contemplated suicide after being diagnosed with HIV. But today, she hopes Eswatini can sustain its hard-won progress against the virus without leaving those with other diseases behind. “What is going to kill our people,” she said, “is not going to be HIV.”
