News.title: Ebola could be raging in DRC for another year, expert warns
News.content:
The Ebola epidemic currently raging in the Democratic Republic of Congo could last at least another year, a leading UK epidemiologist has warned.

Experts have struggled to contain the current outbreak since the first cases of the rare Bundibugyo strain of the disease were reported in May.

There have so far been almost 11,000 cases including 5,000 deaths, making it the second largest outbreak in history, after the devastating West Africa epidemic of 2014-16. Cases have also been reported in Nigeria and Kenya, although transmission has not been widespread.

The outbreak is taking place across a vast area of DRC - North Kivu and Ituri - where conflict and widespread mistrust of authorities, including health workers, have hampered the response.

Neil Ferguson, professor of epidemiology at Imperial College, London, told a press briefing that at the current rate of disease spread that the epidemic could still be ongoing at the end of next year.

“Controlling Ebola outbreaks takes a long time so it is highly likely we’ll still be seeing transmission in a year’s time,” he said.

“We’re ticking over at about 70 confirmed cases a day at the moment and that’s almost certainly quite a significant underestimate of the true number of infections,” said Prof Ferguson, who rose to prominence at the beginning of the Covid pandemic when he advised government on the likely trajectory of the outbreak.

News.title: Many more cattle ranch workers infected with H5N1 than reported, says US farming union
News.content:
Far more US farm workers are infected with bird flu than officially reported, with some suffering “very severe” symptoms, according to the country’s largest farming union.

H5N1 is currently spreading rapidly across US cattle farms in dozens of US states.

Officially, just three people have been diagnosed with the virus in the past month, all following close contact with infected cows.

In total, 73 people in the US have been officially been recorded as infected with H5N1 since 2024, mostly dairy farm workers. Three have died.

But United Farm Workers (UFW), which represents thousands of workers across the US, said it was aware of many more farmers experiencing symptoms consistent with H5N1 who had not been tested.

“We have now connected with a number of workers and have confirmed that more workers are sick with avian flu symptoms who have not been tested,” the UFW wrote on X.

Symptoms range from “very mild to very severe”, the post added, including mild upper respiratory infections and conjunctivitis to severe flu-like symptoms, bone pain, persistent coughing and high fever.

The ongoing outbreak is worrying disease experts.

“H5N1 is not a virus to be casual about- or to let spread unchecked, given every mutation is like the virus buying a lottery ticket to acquire human-to-human transmission,” said Dr Devi Sridhar, a public health researcher at the University of Edinburgh.

Referring to the statement by the UFW, Professor Francois Balloux, director of the UCL Genetics Institute, added: “The most puzzling aspect to me is not even the incompetence and paralysis of the authorities but the resignation and fatalism. It feels like reading some chronicle by a mediaeval peasant.”

Of the roughly 1,000 people infected with H5N1 since the virus was first identified in the late 1990s, almost half have died. However, most historical cases have resulted from contact with wild birds, while the strain circulating in cattle, known as genotype B.12, is thought to cause much milder illness.

Concerns have nevertheless grown after an unidentified farm worker in Washington state died in late October from the cattle-derived H5N1 strain, raising questions about whether the virus may have mutated.

The Trump administration has been heavily criticised for allowing bird flu to run rampant through America’s wild and domestic animals, putting people at risk.

Deep cuts to the federal agencies responsible for managing human and animal health, the US Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and the Department of Agriculture (USDA), have resulted in the scaling down of surveillance and testing programmes amongst both livestock and farm workers.

Every infection, animal or human, raises the chance the virus could mutate and eventually gain the ability to spread between people – something which experts have long warned could trigger the next pandemic.

As flu season begins, experts are concerned a dairy worker infected with ordinary seasonal flu could catch H5N1 at the same time, and the two viruses could mix to create a new, more dangerous strain that could spread between people – a phenomenon known as “reassortment.”

“It is clear that workers are not being informed of the risks of handling sick cattle and infected milk. They are being given no information on flu shots or avian flu testing,” the UFW said.

Estimates suggest that over half of the 150,000-strong dairy workforce in the US are immigrant or undocumented workers, driven in part by high demand for intensive year-round labour and a lack of domestic applicants.

Many are reportedly worried about coming forward for testing over fears they will come into contact with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the federal agency emboldened under Trump, which has been tasked with deporting one million immigrants every year.

Yakima Valley, the region of Washington State where the three recent H5N1 cases have been reported and where the virus is spreading through dozens of dairy herds, is in the midst of an ICE crackdown.

News.title: Young women must ensure they are vaccinated as measles cases surge, doctors say
News.content:
But the dangers for pregnant women, say experts, are often ignored.

There has been relatively little data on maternal and infant measles deaths related to pregnancy in the West since the late 1960s, after the MMR vaccine was introduced and case numbers fell significantly.

Pregnant women are known, however, to be much more vulnerable to illness from measles than others, as the mother’s body, to stop it from rejecting the pregnancy, shifts its immune response significantly and becomes more susceptible to disease.

Between 2000 and 2025, 36 children and adults died from measles or related infections in England and Wales, according to NHS data, but whether or not any of those people were pregnant has not been made public.

“Given the recurrence of measles outbreaks and the number of cases occurring in adults, there may be value in better understanding the impact of measles infection during pregnancy in the UK,” Kirsty Le Doare, professor of vaccinology and immunology at City St George’s, told The Telegraph.

One study by the US CDC conducted in Namibia looked at 55 unvaccinated women who contracted measles during their pregnancies.

Of them, 53 required hospitalisation for complications arising from the virus, ranging from severe diarrhoea, pneumonia, and encephalitis (swelling of the brain).

Another meta-analysis, published in The Lancet in 2018, analysed data from 19 academic papers from countries including France, Germany, and the UK that had studied pregnancy-related measles between 1941 and 2012.

Of 420 pregnancy-related measles cases, 18 deaths occurred, mostly from pneumonia.

“Measles in pregnancy is serious and can cause stillbirth, premature labour and miscarriage,” the NHS website reads. “There is no medical treatment for measles; MMR vaccination is the best protection against becoming seriously unwell,” it adds.

“We know that if you catch measles during pregnancy, you are very likely to end up in hospital,” Professor Helen Bedford, a professor of children’s health at Great Ormond Street Hospital, told The Telegraph.

“You are much more likely to have pneumonia, and there are higher rates of encephalitis. These are all complications that can happen in adults with measles, but they do seem to occur at much higher rates during pregnancy,” said Prof Bedford.

Sports.title: Forgotten Chelsea star who cost £52million ‘lined up for winter transfer by Napoli’ after rival summer bid rejected
Sports.content:
Next

NAPOLI are reportedly eyeing forgotten Chelsea forward Jamie Gittens ahead of the January transfer window.

According to Italian outlet Corriere dello Sport, Gittens‘ name is on the Italian giants’ watchlist.



Napoli could offer the England Under-21 international an escape route after a frustrating spell at Stamford Bridge.

And a January switch could give the 22-year-old the chance to revive his career in Serie A.



Napoli currently sit tenth in the league, and boss Massimiliano Allegri is said to be keen to bolster his attacking options as he looks to turn their season around.

Gittens was close to joining Roma this summer, with the side offering a loan deal worth around £2.6million upfront, plus a potential permanent fee of around £34.5m.



But the Blues rejected their advances, as they wanted an obligation to buy, rather than an option.

After an impressive stint at Borussia Dortmund, the winger earned himself a £52m move to Chelsea last summer.

But Gittens has struggled to settle in and found the net just once since pulling on a Chelsea top.

He also spent the final four months of last season on the sidelines after suffering a hamstring injury.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

The winger has made just two appearances in the Carabao Cup this season, with further injury woes limiting his opportunities.

Despite returning to fitness, Gittens has faced stiff competition for places in Chelsea’s star-studded attack.

The club splashed £117m on Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa in the summer, adding to their already packed forward line.

Napoli could now test Chelsea’s resolve when the January transfer window opens.



However, the Italian side may have to pursue a loan deal as they look to strengthen their squad without spending big.

The club is also monitoring Serie A top goalscorer Gustavo Varela, 21, who is seen as a strong favourite.

Meanwhile, Noa Lang is expected to leave the club permanently in January, while Lorenzo Lucca could depart on loan.

And Gittens could be among the players brought in as Allegri looks to inject fresh life into his squad.

Sports.title: How Michael Carrick’s summer tactical tweaks alienated Bruno Fernandes and set ex-Man Utd boss on road to sack
Sports.content:

MICHAEL CARRICK was sacked as Manchester United manager after tactical changes that didn’t land well with a number of players.

SunSport understands captain Bruno Fernandes was one of the senior stars who preferred Carrick’s style of play during his caretaker stint.



MICHAEL CARRICK SACKED: LATEST ON NEXT MAN UTD MANAGER

Manchester United beat both Man City and champions Arsenal under Carrick, with masterful counter-attacking displays.



And performances like those propelled the Red Devils to third place in the Premier League and Champions League qualification for the first time in three years.

But in summer, Carrick and assistant Steve Holland decided to introduce a more expansive and ball-dominant style, similar to the way the former England star’s Middlesbrough team had played.

A United source told SunSport: “Bruno was butting heads with Carrick because last season the team was having great success, but the tactical changes this season had led to a huge downturn in results.

“Bruno basically said ‘why can’t we just carry on? We would have won the league at the rate we were going’. But Carrick and Holland wanted to change things.

“A number of the players also wanted to go back to the previous tactics, but Carrick stuck by his principles and tried to ride out the bad results.

“Now United are back to square one. New manager, new ideas, new tactics. And no idea if any of it will work.”



The rift between Fernandes and Carrick became public after the captain’s interview after a 4-1 loss at Como.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Man Utd had been criticised for their poor running stats, but Fernandes, 32, said those stats were a reflection of the way Carrick had asked the team to play.

He commented: “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball by waiting for them.

“But sometimes, when you give space to these teams, they get confidence.

“Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable.”



Following that criticism, Fernandes was left out of the starting XI for the next game against Bournemouth – though officially for tactical reasons.

After being asked about the criticism from Fernandes, an unimpressed Carrick said: “Whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win.”

In what may have been a further blow to Carrick’s authority, Fernandes was immediately restored to the starting XI after United lost 3-0 to Bournemouth in the match he sat out.

Mauricio Pochettino has reportedly agreed to take over as manager from Carrick.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick breaks down in tears bidding farewell to Man Utd players after being sacked in farcical circumstances
Sports.content:

MICHAEL CARRICK bid a tearful goodbye to his Manchester United players today after being sacked for leading the club into the relegation zone.

The former United midfielder turned boss, 45, was summoned to a meeting at the training ground and dismissed after just ten months in charge.



He and his staff will pocket £5million in compensation – bringing United’s spending on dismissing managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 to more than £100m.

A source told SunSport: “[Carrick] was in tears when said goodbye to the lads. He basically said ‘I’ve gone lads’ and shook a few hands, got in his car and left.”



Many first-team players are away on international duty, though four first-team players are understood to have trained with the Under-21s on Thursday.

Carrick has been expecting the sack since Monday when it was widely reported that United bosses had made former Spurs and Chelsea boss Mauricio Pochettino their No 1 target.

Carrick’s position became untenable after a run of just one win in 11 games saw the club drop into the relegation zone.

Despite knowing he was going to lose his job, Carrick continued to go into United’s Carrington training base during the international break to coach the remaining members of the squad.

A source said: “The players were as confused as anyone else about what was going on this week.

“Everyone was reading that Carrick was going to be sacked, but he kept turning up and getting on with his job.”



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Sources told SunSport that despite captain Bruno Fernandes and defender Lisandro Martinez giving outspoken interviews about the direction of the club and Carrick’s tactics, the dressing room remained behind Carrick.

A source said: “The players really liked him and wanted to do well with him. Unfortunately, things stopped working and it always ends with the manager losing his job.”

The dressing room believe Carrick was let down by chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox with a poor summer transfer window.

The club bought in Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba for £155m to replace Casemiro, but failed to bring in Lewis Hall as left back cover for injury prone Luke Shaw.

A source said: “There was a meeting and some of the players brought up that the club had brought in three midfielders to replace Case, but done nothing to bolster left back and the striker position.



“Even Luke Shaw thought it was madness not to bring in some competition, given his age and injury issues.”

The source said that meeting sparked Martinez’s outburst following United’s 2-1 defeat against Atletico Madrid in the Champions League last month.

Martinez called out Wilcox for failing to bolster the squad which meant Ayden Heaven was forced to play left back because Shaw was unavailable due to injury.



Argentinian defender Martinez later apologised but his comments saw the club tell the players to cancel a team-bonding meal at Cibo restaurant in Hale, Cheshire, with the Wags also told to cancel their plans.

The source said: “At the meeting Carrick told the players the issues would be addressed in the January transfer window, but the players remained angry at Berrada and Wilcox and feel like Carrick wasn’t given the tools to be successful.

“Some think he was sold a lie while others think he wasn’t tough enough.

“The players liked him because he’s been there and done it as a player.”



But just eight days after Martinez’s outburst, Carrick was left fire-fighting an interview by captain Bruno Fernandes in the wake of a humbling 4-1 defeat to Como in the Champions League.

Fernandes criticised the tactics, with Carrick firing back that players needed to run during a game no matter what the tactics are.

SunSport understands Fernandes’ frustration came from tactical tweaks which Carrick and assistant Steve Holland tried to introduce at the start of this season.

Sports.title: Inside Mauricio Pochettino’s £40m fortune and life with ‘rock’ wife singer Karina ahead of his imminent Man Utd return
Sports.content:
Next

MAURICIO POCHETTINO is poised to return to the Premier League after his stint as USA boss.

The former Southampton, Tottenham, and Chelsea manager is set to take the reigns at Manchester United after Michael Carrick was sacked by the club.



There’s still a few minor details that need to be ironed out, including a buyout clause of around £7.5million due to the US Soccer Federation, but no hiccups are expected with his appointment at Old Trafford.

The Argentinian coach has reportedly amassed a £40million fortune from his playing and management career.



Although modest in his personality, it has allowed him the freedom to keep abodes in London and Barcelona.

As manager of the USA, Pochettino opted against relocating to the States, preferring to divide his time between Europe and the federation’s training centre in Fayetteville, Georgia, outside Atlanta.

Over the years, he has been supported by his wife of three decades, Karina as he became one of football’s most sought-after coaches.

His ‘rock’ of a wife

Pochettino and Karina’s paths first crossed at a nightclub in 1991 in Rosario.

At that time, he was a teenager building on his football career at famed Argentinian side Newell’s Old Boys.

They dated for three years, until they married in a small, intimate ceremony in 1994 in their homeland.



Months later, Karina moved with her husband to Spain, when he was transferred to Espanyol.

Unlike many football spouses, she has intentionally avoided the media limelight.



Karina reportedly studied pharmacy at university and previously worked as a chemist.

She later went on to become a singer and songwriter, according to other reports.

But, as Pochettino’s career would see him move across Spain, France, and England, Karina would focus on raising their family.

Pochettino has frequently described Karina as his “rock” and credited her with encouraging him to accept the Southampton job in 2013, a move that launched his Premier League career.

He also joked that she is his fiercest critic, particularly regarding his English grammar and demeanour during press conferences.



When asked what Mrs. Poch criticises him for in particular, he said: “Many things. Many, many times.

“It’s more than 25 years now she’s been next to me, and in the last few years the one thing that she criticises most is my press conferences.

“Because she is very focused, ‘why you say that’, ‘you need to say to, not for’, ‘that is why, not because’.

“She is fixing me after every press conference and criticises me a lot. But it is part of it to improve, no?”



Pochettino is well known for being superstitious and holds a strong belief in universal energy.

In 2017, he put a ban on Karina attending games at Tottenham’s White Hart Lane because Spurs were on a winning streak.

He wanted her to stay home to avoid jinxing their good luck.

Family life

Together, Pochettino and Karina have raised two sons, Maurizio and Sebastiano. Both are currently involved in football.



The elder of the two, Sebastiano, 31, joined his dad on his American adventure as the fitness coach and sports scientist for the US national team.

Previously, he became the youngest sports scientist in the Premier League when he joined Spurs in 2017, and was a popular figure among the team’s players.

Pochettino brought Sebastiano to Chelsea, too, so it is more than likely they will link up again at Old Trafford.

Maurizio, 25, plays as a winger for Andorran club Inter Club d’Escaldes.

He had spells in the Southampton and Tottenham youth set-ups, before going alone on his own path to Watford and Spanish clubs Gimnàstic and Ibiza Islas Pitiusas.



Net worth

Pochettino grew up on a farm in the small town of Murphy in the Santa Fe province of Argentina.

It was a humble beginning to life for the aspiring footballer, who would drive tractors and help his dad Hector as farm hand, alongside his older brother Javier.



Poch has come a long way since then, building a £40million fortune thanks to a storied career in football.

It’s in management where he has made real money. His contract with the USA national team worth around £4.6million-per-year is small fry in comparison to the deals he had in Europe.

In 2019, when he was dismissed by Tottenham, he received a reported severance package of around £12.5 million.

The year before, he agreed a contract extension at Spurs worth around £8.5million annualy.

In 2022, following the termination of his contract with PSG, £8.5million was split between him and his coaching staff.



At Chelsea, he reportedly earned a further £10 million payoff when he left the club by mutual consent in 2024.

Poch’s riches have allowed him to keep homes in London and Barcelona.

RECOMMENDED STORIES



In 2022, he was believed to have bought a property in the upscale 8th arrondissement of Paris.

Next stop is Manchester, where the property prices in Alderley Edge might not Pochetinno off from making the north his permanent base.

Sports.title: The trilingual son of Mr Universe makes homecoming - NFL Gameday Guide
Sports.content:
Amon-Ra St. Brown. The globe-trotting trilingual son of Mr Universe, named after an Egyptian god, returning for the most special of homecomings to his mother's native land. This time, as one of the stars of the NFL.

Some five years ago, St. Brown spoke to Sky Sports about the importance of his German heritage ahead of entering the NFL Draft. And now he gets to honour it by doing what he does best.

The Detroit Lions will play an international game for the first time since November 2015 this Sunday when they host the New England Patriots at Munich's Allianz Arena.

His mother Miriam hails from Leverkusen and predominantly spoke to the Lions wide receiver and his two brothers in German growing up, while also taking them back to Europe each summer to spend time with their grandparents and play soccer.

St Brown even represented the German national team alongside brother Osiris during his sophomore year of high school, and since landing in the NFL, has worn decals of the German flag on his helmet and returned to host football camps in the country.

St Brown sat his SATs in English, German and French, spent time in French academy Lycee International de Los Angeles, spent a semester in Paris and joined his mother in travelling across the world with trips to Spain, Italy, London, France, the Caribbean, his German home from home and beyond. It was his mother Miriam who revealed the Lions would be playing in Munich on a FaceTime call set up by the Lions back in February.

At long last, he gets to take centre stage overseas as the NFL reaches the final stop on its European tour with the eighth of a record nine international games in 2026.

His own global connections travel as far as Egyptian nomenclature, after his father John - a three-time Mr World and two-time Mr Universe body-builder - named his son after Amun, the ancient Egyptian deity.

It is Germany the NFL can thank for one of its most gifted players, with St Brown's parents having met at a fitness trade show in Cologne in 1987.

His transatlantic ties have naturally forged a love of soccer as he pitches up in the home of Bayern Munich, where Ballon d'Or-winning England captain Harry Kane has often spoken of his own ambitions to step into the world of St. Brown - as an NFL kicker.

Has he got the leg to do it? Sure. Would it ever happen? Most would say no. Funnily enough, his age by the end of his football career - he is 33 now - is probably a primary reason above all as to why it wouldn't happen.

"If I was going to do it, I would take it seriously. I would probably dedicate six months to a year to training," said Kane earlier this year. "Maybe if I am in the MLS in the future or somewhere like that it might be a thing where you could connect the two maybe with the seasons."

As far as growing the game is concerned, it is a no-brainer of an easy win.

The Lions arrive 6-2 in a fiercely competitive NFC North, St. Brown continuing to be Jared Goff's prized weapon on the outside with a team-high 61 catches for 657 yards (10th most in the league) and five touchdowns within an offense ranked fifth in yards per game and fifth in scoring.

Detroit have won four straight games, including divisional victories over both the Minnesota Vikings and Green Bay Packers in the last three weeks. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs is also at the heart of their success with an NFL-high 1,132 yards and 11 touchdowns from scrimmage.

New England are 5-4 and coming off a 45-27 defeat to the Packers during which Drake Maye, struggling to live up to his MVP-contending heights of last season, threw three interceptions.

The Patriots are battling to swerve a Super Bowl hangover after February's one-sided defeat to the Seattle Seahawks and return to play in Germany for the second time after losing to the Indianapolis Colts in Frankfurt in 2023.

Germany remains one of the NFL's largest fanbases outside of North America, with millions of listeners having previously tuned in to the Armed Forces Network radio station based in Frankfurt during World War II.

The first broadcast out of AFN Frankfurt was on July 15, 1945 from a confiscated house, after which thousands of US troops remained stationed in Germany.

There were later five preseason NFL games in Germany from 1990 to 1994, while the country was also represented by the Hamburg Sea Devils, Rhein Fire, Berlin Thunder, Cologne Centurions and Frankfurt Galaxy in the former World League of American Football/NFL Europe/NFL Europa between 1991 and 2007.

It is Germany's time once again.

5 things to watch live on Sky:

No 1 player in football?

Is there another player in football who reigns as his position's outright No 1 more so than Fred Warner? Arguably not.

The San Francisco 49ers stalwart has occupied top spot among inside linebackers for multiple years now, and remains an unrivalled difference-maker from his role within Raheem Morris' defense.

Warner has been electric in his first campaign back since suffering a season-ending injury in Week Six of 2025, racking up 77 total tackles, five forced fumbles, a fumble recovery, half a sack, 5.5 stuffs and three pass breakups. Few, if any, diagnose the game better than Warner, whose film study is as refined and as expertly-exercised as any player in football.

An incredible sequence against the Las Vegas Raiders last week saw him punch the ball from the hands of Brock Bowers, recover Michael Mayers' fumble in the end zone and deny Kirk Cousins on a quarterback sneak with an incredible leaping stop over center Tyler Linderbaum in the space of about 10 minutes.

Wonder why teams are scared to throw over the middle of the field against the 49ers? Fred Warner.

Kirko chains is back

The Minnesota Vikings would be Super Bowl contenders if they could just figure things out at quarterback, and on Tuesday they rolled the dice once more by trading to bring back Kirk Cousins.

Any scenario in which Justin Jefferson isn't getting the ball thrown his way becomes a major concern; the Vikings had no choice. Kyler Murray could not get it done, the Vikings traded away J.J. McCarthy to the New York Giants and on Monday night Carson Wentz epitomised this hobbling offense, which has failed miserably in its bid to back up Brian Flores' defense.

Cousins may be 38 years old, but has been impressive for the Las Vegas Raiders this season and gives Minnesota a significantly better chance of reigniting Jefferson, who has been starved of production.

Cousins is 202 of 315, passing for 2,340 yards, 20 touchdowns, eight interceptions, and a passer rating of 97.1 as he re-joins the franchise he played for from 2018-2023. Would be quite the story, huh?

Surging Love

Jordan Love is flying, and it feels as though the Green Bay Packers are gathering Super Bowl momentum by the week as their offense begins to takeover.

Love now leads the NFL in passing yards with 2,618 for 19 touchdowns to six interceptions as the league's most aggressive splash-play merchant.

He ranks first in intended air yards (3,251), intended air yards per attempt (9.5) and completed air yards (1,553) at the heart of the league's second-best passing attack, within which his receivers have notably dropped a league-high 23 passes.

They have become box office viewing, with two No 1 receivers emerging in Christian Watson - third in the league with 879 yards - and Matthew Golden - fourth in the league with 783 yards.

Matt LaFleur has typically built his offense around run game foundations that he can tee off from through the air, but even through the NFL's worst rushing attack he is finding success thanks to Love's arm.

AFC North decider?

Sunday Night Football stages one of the biggest games of the weekend when the Cincinnati Bengals take on the Pittsburgh Steelers in a possible AFC North division decider.

Both sit 6-2 with the Steelers holding the head-to-head advantage after their 30-27 win in the reverse fixture back in September, Jaylen Warren starring out of the backfield on that occasion with 176 yards from scrimmage.

But the Bengals have hit their stride with a four-game winning streak over the last month, Joe Burrow rising to MVP contention while playing some of the best football of his NFL career within the league's most potent passing attack.

Across that four-game span, Burrow has completed 77 per cent of passes for 1,215 yards with 18 total touchdowns, three interceptions and a 132.0 passer rating.

Cincinnati look like legitimate Super Bowl contenders again, producing their best start through eight games since 2015.

Sean McVay's side were dealt another crushing blow this week when it was revealed Puka Nacua had suffered a right knee injury set to land him on injured reserve and miss at least a month of action, adding to an absentee list already featuring Davante Adams.

Sports.title: Overeem vs Manuwa added to Jake Paul's Christmas Eve fight card
Sports.content:
Alistair Overeem will make his professional boxing debut against Britain's Jimi Manuwa as the MMA stars collide on Jake Paul's comeback show on Christmas Eve.

Most Valuable Promotions (MVP) have confirmed that Overeem, known as 'The Demolition Man', and 'Poster Boy' Manuwa will meet in a six-round professional heavyweight boxing bout on the undercard of Paul's cruiserweight clash with Cedric Doumbe in Dubai.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Jake Paul’s new opponent, Cedric Doumbe, leave Kylian Mbappe stunned with this nine-second knockout in the PFL

Former Strikeforce heavyweight champion and K-1 World Grand Prix winner Overeem said: "I've fought the best in the world, and I've been a world champion in multiple disciplines. Now I'm starting a new chapter in boxing, and I'm not here to make up the numbers.

"Jimi Manuwa is a dangerous man with serious knockout power, but I've built my career on taking the toughest challenges in combat sports"

Image: British knockout artist and former UFC light heavyweight contender Jimi Manuwa will go up against Overeem

Manuwa, who began his professional MMA career in 2008, won his first 14 professional fights before establishing himself among the UFC's most dangerous strikers.

He retired from MMA in 2019 with a 17-6 record, with 15 of his 17 victories coming by knockout or technical knockout. The 46-year-old returned to competition in August 2026, making a successful professional boxing debut with a second-round TKO victory over former UFC heavyweight Chase Sherman.

Manuwa said: "London is in everything I do. Where I come from, pressure makes you, and it makes me.

"I've watched Alistair since I was coming up, and I know exactly what he's capable of. That's why I wanted this fight.

"After my win in Orlando, I wasn't looking for an easy opponent. On Christmas Eve, one of us is going to sleep, and it's not going to be me."

Overeem vs Manuwa adds another explosive encounter to the card headlined by global superstar Paul, on his return to the ring a year on from suffering a broken jaw in a sixth-round stoppage loss to former two-time unified heavyweight world champion Anthony Joshua.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jake Paul and his opponent Cedric Doumbe face-off for the first time ahead of their boxing match on December 24

MVP chief executive Nakisa Bidarian said: "Netherlands' Alistair Overeem and the United Kingdom's Jimi Manuwa are two of the most recognisable names in combat sports, with decades of experience competing against the best in the world and a combined 40 knockouts in MMA.

"Bringing these two legends together in a professional boxing match adds another compelling matchup to an already massive Christmas Eve event.

"With Jake Paul facing Cedric Doumbe in the main event, we're assembling a card that brings together some of the biggest personalities and most dangerous strikers in combat sports for fans in Dubai and around the world."

Sports.title: Neville 'disgusted' at Man Utd's treatment of Carrick
Sports.content:
Sky Sports' Gary Neville has described Manchester United's treatment of Michael Carrick as "disgusting" after the club legend was sacked as head coach, with Mauricio Pochettino set to succeed him at Old Trafford.

Neville believes United have handled the situation poorly, with Carrick taking training in Manchester while club executives met in Monaco on Wednesday and pursued Pochettino as his replacement.

Sky Sports News understands a full agreement in principle has been reached between United and Pochettino. Talks between the club and US Soccer Federation are at the paperwork and regulatory processes stage.

Neville also warned the incoming head coach that the club's problems run much deeper than the manager, insisting Pochettino must take control of recruitment and demand significant investment.

'It's quite simply disgusting'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol discusses whether the club has let Michael Carrick down as they agree a deal in principle with Mauricio Pochettino to take over as head coach if Carrick is sacked

Neville believes Carrick deserved greater respect from a club he represented with distinction as a player.

The former midfielder was initially appointed in January, following Ruben Amorim's departure, and earned a permanent two-year contract after winning 12 of his 17 games to secure Champions League qualification.

But three wins in 15 matches this season have ultimately cost him his job.

Neville had questioned Carrick's appointment at the end of last season and felt the writing was on the wall after United's 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth.

"I think after the Bournemouth game I said at the time that Manchester United effectively watched Michael Carrick resign on the pitch at the end of the game with that lap around, that wave goodbye. I think he was expecting it to come at that point and they were indecisive," he said on Sky Sports News.

"They obviously felt that they might be able to get to the international break and there could be some sort of pick-up in results, but it's been a difficult two weeks. Indecision, lack of authority, just basically really poor leadership.

"In the last 24-48 hours it's been spectacularly bad to be in Monaco as an executive and an owner whilst your manager, who's a club legend, is taking training on the pitch and simultaneously approaching the US Soccer Federation to approach Mauricio Pochettino.

"It's just quite simply disgusting. That falls well below the standard of what you would expect in any other business, in any other industry. It would be constructive dismissal and you'd be getting sued.

"The optics of being in Monaco whilst the team, the staff, the people who are running the club on a day-to-day basis are in Manchester, it's just not good and it reflects badly on the leadership.

"I don't think anybody comes out of this well at all."

'You don't even get angry anymore'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Breaking News: Michael Carrick has been sacked by Manchester United

Neville accepts Carrick must take responsibility for the results that have left United in the relegation zone, but believes the wider circumstances surrounding his departure are symptomatic of a club that continues to make poor decisions.

Carrick's departure will make him another name on a growing list of managers who have failed to restore United to the top of English football since Sir Alex Ferguson's retirement in 2013.

Neville believes supporters have become numb to the cycle of appointments and sackings, particularly given the money spent on players and the continued failure to build a squad capable of competing.

Asked whether the club had hit a new low, he said: "I think this is a low but it just feels like you don't even get angry anymore; you don't get animated. You just feel like nothing.

"It sort of knocks you numb because we've seen it so many times. Everybody's sick of it. The fans are sick of it.

"Michael felt that he was the right man for the job. He wanted to take it and you can't blame him for that.

"But at the end of last season, similarly to when they made the decision a few years ago with Erik ten Hag, they had to make better decisions and better choices and the people who are running the club are not making good choices in the football department.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Adam Binnie shares six stats that show Manchester United's troubles so far this season, and why Michael Carrick's job became untenable

"I mean there's some off-the-pitch stuff as well that you could argue is questionable, but the on-the-pitch stuff for the last 12-13 years has been absolutely terrible.

"I think eight managers, £1.6 billion has been spent on football players and they ended up with a back four on Sunday of [Patrick] Dorgu, [Noussair] Mazraoui, [Leny] Yoro and [Ayden] Heaven and you've spent £1.6 billion on players.

"That's very difficult to do. You could put every single one of those Manchester United fans in charge of that club or put them in the dugout and you wouldn't end up with that back four if they were running the club.

"It's unbelievable what's happened.

"And Michael's demise in the end is because obviously he's not been able to get the same tune out of the players. That's the accountability he has to carry as a manager.

"But when you sign those midfield players in the summer that are well below the standard of the other midfield players that have gone to other clubs. United were at the bottom of the queue when midfield players were being handed out.

"They needed midfield players; they needed to bolster that department and they ended up with players ultimately that weren't wanted by Tottenham, by [Manchester] City and others.

"And then the back four needed strengthening. That back four, five, six that are playing currently have been there for five, six years, seven years, and they've been failing for four, five, six, seven years.

"Some of them have injury problems as well and some of them are getting on. The likes of Luke Shaw, [Matthijs] De Ligt, [Lisandrp] Martinez are injured quite regularly.

"They're inconsistent when they play, and then the rest of the players who are fit, to be fair, don't meet the standards.

"So this is not unsurprising totally. I am shocked it's come this early in the season. I didn't think it would happen this quickly and I thought Manchester United would have a half-decent season, but it's come a lot quicker than anybody thought and it seems to be something that happens quite regularly at the club and it's really disappointing."

'Pochettino has got to protect himself'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Dave Reed compares Michael Carrick's playing style at Manchester United to Mauricio Pochettino's time at Chelsea

Pochettino has been considered for the United job on previous occasions, but Neville has warned him against believing that a change of manager alone will solve the club's problems.

Neville remembers visiting Pochettino at Tottenham during his early days in charge, when the Argentine was already identifying which players he wanted to build around and which he needed to move on.

"I think the mistake that Mauricio could make if he comes in is that he may get an initial bounce out of them. He may get six months of bounce out of them," Neville continued.

"I actually remember going to see him at Tottenham in his very early days. We used to, when I was coaching with England, train at Tottenham's training ground.

"He set out very quickly within the first six to eight months in the job. He had a whiteboard in front of him in his office with all the players' names on little markers and he actually moved a group of players over to the left-hand side of the board and said: 'These are the ones I know I need to get rid of. These are the ones I know I can work with and build around.'

"He's got to identify that very quickly at United and I'm sure he will do that. He's more experienced now than he was when he was at Tottenham.

"But he's got a big job to do in exiting players. Manchester United have been really poor at exiting players over the last 10 years. They've not done it very well at all."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gary Neville says he has always wanted Mauricio Pochettino as Manchester United manager but he has to take control of recruitment

'Pochettino needs control over recruitment,' says Neville

Neville believes Pochettino must also ensure he has sufficient financial backing and, crucially, control over recruitment.

United's summer business has done little to convince him that the existing structure can deliver the players required, and he believes the new head coach must make strong demands before taking the job.

"I'm hoping Mauricio Pochettino has done a couple of things on the way in and I'm hoping he protects himself on his contract because he'll need to.

"I'm sure he's stated that he needs a massive budget. I think he needs defenders straight away to get Manchester United anywhere near where they want to be this season.

"And the other thing is to make sure that he takes control of the recruitment because it's quite clear that what happened in the summer is well below the standard again.

"He's got to come in here and protect himself against actually the people that he's working with. They are currently trying to employ him.

"He needs to make sure he takes the club into his own hands, into his own destiny, make sure he controls his own outcomes and make sure he's absolutely unequivocal in getting money to improve the defence initially in January and improving the midfield and forward line next summer."

Neville's admiration for Pochettino - but is he the right appointment?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Transfer Talk, Henry Winter discusses what Mauricio Pochettino can bring to a struggling Manchester United side

Neville has made no secret of his admiration for Pochettino and believes the Argentine has the coaching ability and personality to manage a club of United's stature.

But he has also seen too many different types of manager fail at Old Trafford to believe the challenge will be straightforward.

David Moyes, Louis van Gaal, Jose Mourinho, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Carrick have all experienced the difficulties of the job, while Ralf Rangnick also failed to turn things around.

For Neville, that history should serve as a warning to Pochettino.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Manchester United fan Bradley Tooth says he would rather the club opted for Sean Dyche over Mauricio Pochettino as their new manager

"I can't believe Mauricio would have looked at the last 13 years, looked at managers like David Moyes, Jose Mourinho and Louis van Gaal who are very experienced, brilliant operators in what they do and seen them fall short.

"He's then seen talented managers from Europe like Amorim and Ten Hag fall short.

"He's seen club legends who have got a lot of love for the club, who understand the values, understand how to play for Manchester United, understand what the fans want and can communicate that. He's seen those guys fail.

"He's seen Ralf Rangnick come in, who's got more of a sporting director background and a business background, come in and fail and tell the club they need open-heart surgery.

"So he's seen every type of manager fail at this football club over the last 13 years.

"He's got to come in and basically wipe the slate clean and start from scratch and imagine that this football club is a blank canvas because everybody that's been there in that period has been part of the failure."

Despite those concerns, Neville has consistently backed Pochettino as a candidate for the job and believes he has the qualities to succeed.

"I've always wanted Mauricio Pochettino as the manager at United. I've said it numerous times that I wanted him.

"I think he's a brilliant person. I think he'll handle the media. I think he understands the size of the club.

"But it's a monumental task to win everybody else over and get everybody on side and make sure he has a team that can compete.

"He's a brilliant coach with great experience and he's a good man.

"He also believes in young players and bringing players through and developing them and coaching them, which is what he's going to have to do at Manchester United.

"I've always liked Mauricio Pochettino. Whether this is the right point for him to take the Manchester United job, who knows? We'll find out in the next year or two.

"But I'm hoping that he's made some pretty strong demands on the way in and that he's got control of the club."

'You're probably looking at about 10 players to be sold'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Transfer Talk, Sam Tighe shares his thoughts on why Manchester United are struggling so badly

For Neville, United need a complete defensive overhaul, further midfield reinforcements and a new centre-forward, with only Kobbie Mainoo currently convincing him in midfield, in a reflection of the rebuild that the incoming boss faces.

He estimates that Pochettino could need around 10 new players to get United back to where they want to be.

"If I said that the midfield that I've seen this season, only Kobbie Mainoo to me looks like he's good enough," said Neville.

"The back line, I think it needs a complete rebuild and I think we need a centre-forward.

"So I don't know how many that is and probably you could argue we need back-up in goal as well.

"So my view would be probably, I don't know yet, there's probably five or six in defence, there's two or three in midfield, there's a goalkeeper and there's probably a centre-forward.

"And I think you're probably looking at about 10 players that you would need to basically rotate out.

"Lisandro Martinez told us that basically the sporting director should have brought more players in the summer, so the players know it themselves.

"So Mauricio Pochettino, who's been around the block and knows how to manage football clubs, he'll have a pretty good idea, having watched Manchester United many times over many years.

"He'll know what he needs to do."

Sports.title: Greaves 'excited' to face Littler at Grand Slam of Darts
Sports.content:
Beau Greaves says she is "excited" to face Luke Littler on the opening day of the Grand Slam of Darts this weekend.

Greaves has been drawn in the same group as Littler and Dutch player Niels Zonneveld with only the top player from each group progressing to the knockout stages.

Littler and Greaves will meet for the first time since the latter beat the world champion at the World Youth Championship 12 months ago in Saturday's night's Grand Slam of Darts session, which begins at 7pm, live on Sky Sports.

"I think he's the best [player in the world] in my eyes, I think he's fantastic to watch, he's been amazing, so I always imagine he's going to play really well," said Greaves.

"I don't want to go in there thinking, 'oh he's not on form', or he's struggling, because then I would just be terrible, so I've got to go in there thinking 'he's going to absolutely smash me', and just play my game, and try and take any chance I can, and just enjoy it.

"I think it's going to be a good game just to watch, and just to be a part of it is special. I look forward to playing it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Beau Greaves lands double one to beat Daryl Gurney and make PDC European Tour history earlier this year

Greaves has played in the last three Grand Slam of Darts and won two matches but is yet to get out of the group stages.

The 22-year-old narrowly lost to Michael van Gerwen and Gary Anderson, despite averaging over 100, last year and is hoping to perform well on the big stage once again.

"I played decent at the Grand Slam last year. I have good moments, but I just don't do it consistently enough," she said.

"It's something that, if I am going to do really well in the sport, I'm going to have to get better at. It's a challenge for me, but I look forward to it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Beau Greaves was agonisingly close to a sensational win over Michael van Gerwen at the Grand Slam of Darts after missing a match dart in their final leg decider

"I always look forward to kind of getting better and improving. I'm aware that obviously I'm not up to that standard as I do play on the floor, but it's just a work in progress at the minute, I would call it.

"But I'm just trying to look forward to everything rather than dread anything and obviously look forward to playing on stage rather than think I'd rather play on the floor. So, I'm just trying to switch it around a little bit."

Greaves: I didn't have a clue about the format change!

The Grand Slam has expanded this year from 32 to 48 players and sees 16 groups of three, rather than four players in a group.

The format adds jeopardy as anybody who loses their opening match will be under serious pressure and could be eliminated, even if they win their second match.

"I didn't know. I didn't have a clue that there was only three in the group! I don't know why they've done it really. It didn't make much sense to me, but again, I don't really know," said Greaves.

"It's just odd, but I suppose you've still got to do well to win your group regardless but it's different, I was a bit shocked."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Beau Greaves reeled off five consecutive legs to beat Niko Springer in the group stage of the Grand Slam of Darts

Greaves says she has felt "relaxed" when playing Littler in the past and is "excited" to face the world No 1, who has won the last two Grand Slam of Darts titles.

"I know Luke's loads better than me, but I kind of have to at least convince myself I can win," she said.

"I can't go up there wanting to get beat but I know it's obviously, he's 10 times better than me, but strange to think about if you get beat.

"Luke Littler is the heavy favourite to come through that group obviously, so it's strange, but there is a big jump in prize money if you finish second or third, so there's still a little bit to play for on the ranking, so just trying to not think about it and just try and enjoy every game, and try and do my best."

Sports.title: McIlroy boosts Race to Dubai hopes as Luiten grabs shock lead
Sports.content:
Rory McIlroy made a strong start to his bid for a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title, as Joost Luiten grabbed a shock early lead at the DP World Tour Championship.

McIlroy, who needs to finish fourth or better to have a chance of surpassing Eugenio Chacarra in the season-long standings and win the Race to Dubai for an eighth time, carded an opening-round 69 at Jumeirah Golf Estates.

The world No 2 mixed five birdies with two bogeys in breezy conditions on the Earth Course, where he missed an eagle opportunity at the par-five last that would have moved him above Chacarra in the projected Race to Dubai standings.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rory McIlroy made a careless bogey on the par-four fifth, three-putting from 15 feet

McIlroy sits in tied-third on three under and within two shots of Luiten, the last player in the field and 56th in the season rankings, who jumped top of the leaderboard after a five-under 67.

Jacob Skov Olesen briefly shared the lead but is one behind Luiten on four under, with Victor Perez, Gregorio De Leo, Freddy Schott and Francesco Laporta all two back alongside McIlroy, while Race to Dubai leader Chacarra opened with a level-par 72.

How McIlroy boosted Race to Dubai hopes

McIlroy can guarantee Race to Dubai victory by winning this event for a fourth time, with The Masters champion making the dream start by rolling in an eight-foot birdie at the first.

He responded to a three-putt par at the second by birdieing the par-three fourth, then bounced back from a sloppy three-putt from 15 feet at the fifth by taking advantage of the par-five seventh.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from Rory McIlroy's opening round at the DP World Tour Championship

Chacarra was over-par until his three-birdie run from the seventh, seeing both reach the turn in 34, before McIlroy holed a birdie from the fringe to briefly get within two of the lead.

The leading pair in the Race to Dubai stumbled slightly over the closing stretch, with Chacarra making two bogeys in three holes from the 13th and McIlroy dropping a shot at the par-five 14th after missing the green with his third shot.

Image: Rory McIlroy was playing alongside Race to Dubai leader Chacarra on the opening round

McIlroy hit a glorious approach to within 15 feet at the par-five last to leave a late eagle look, which would have seen him leapfrog Chacarra, although he had to settle for a two-putt birdie after leaving his effort short.

Several see Race to Dubai hopes fade

Luiten was in the first pair out on the opening morning and raced to the top of the leaderboard with a front-nine 31, then cancelled out back-to-back bogeys from the 11th by birdieing the 13th and 18th to reclaim top spot.

Image: Luiten is only in the field because six players elected against featuring at the DP World Tour Championship

Olesen is also among those looking to secure PGA Tour membership - available to the top 10 eligible players in the Race to Dubai rankings, with the Dane's final-hole birdie getting him within one of Luiten, on a day where only 22 of the 50-man field finished under-par.

McIlroy was among nine players starting the week with a mathematical chance of topping the Race to Dubai rankings, but Jon Rahm and Daniel Hillier - who both carded one-under 71s - the only others to break par on the opening day.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tyrrell Hatton was left in shock at missing a short putt on the par-five 14th during his opening-round 71

Casey Jarvis, Jayden Schaper and Ryan Fox - who need a victory to have any chance of claiming No 1 - all started the week with a two-over 74, while major winner Aaron Rai struggled to an opening-round 76.

Chacarra and McIlroy take positives from start

Rory McIlroy, following a three-under 69: "Anything in the 60s today I felt was a good score. And sort of held it together nicely when I needed to. It was nice to finish with a birdie at the last, and obviously in a pretty good position going into the next few days."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player McIlroy was pleased to find encouraging signs in his performance during a three-under 69 in Dubai

Race to Dubai leader Eugenio Chacarra: "I need to do a couple of things better to be able to have a chance on Sunday, and that's what I'm going to focus on. I think if I fix those, a little strategy-wise and I can putt a little better, I think I'm going to have a chance.

Joost Luiten, following his opening-round 67: "A good opening round. Had a great front nine, five under after nine, then you hope you can push on. The wind picked up and I made two annoying bogeys on 11 and 12. I'm quite happy finishing five under."

Sports.title: Beirne captains strong Ireland selection vs Fiji as Gibson-Park returns
Sports.content:
Tadhg Beirne will captain a strong Ireland selection vs Fiji in the Nations Championship on Saturday, despite head coach Andy Farrell making seven changes.

Two of those changes are enforced as hooker Dan Sheehan (concussion) and No 8 Sean Jansen (knee) were ruled out, but several other injury concerns have been allayed.

Indeed, wing Rob Baloucoune is fit to start again, as is Mack Hansen despite an ankle knock - the latter shifting to full-back with Hugo Keenan rested and Tommy O'Brien brought into the back-three.

Josh van der Flier is also fit despite his own ankle complaint, starting at openside flanker with Nick Timoney shifting to No 8 in the absence of Jansen, Jack Conan and Caelan Doris due to injury.

Experienced scrum-half Jamison Gibson-Park returns to the starting XV, with Craig Casey dropping down to the bench.

Sports.title: Barcelona v Arsenal: Women’s Champions League – live
Sports.content:
It’s a maze around the Camp Nou building site, and finding the media entrance involved a lot of confused stewards and different directions. We’re in though, and what a stadium it’s going to be when the work is done. It’s really hard to know how Arsenal will fare here. They could snatch a cheeky 1-0 win or lose by five, and neither would be that much of a surprise. It’s great to see Frida Maanum in the 10 and Alessia Russo in the centre-forward position. Russo’s been on fire playing in either role but sometimes any change, whether it impacts or not, can act as a spark for a struggling team.

Hello world! And don’t worry Arsenal, it’s only Barcelona away! Sure, they’ve won the Champions League in three of the last four seasons, and only missed one final since 2018, and they’re averaging 6.34 goals a game in Europe this season and 4.62 in all competitions, but it’s not like they’re perfect: they lost 2-1 at Real Sociedad just a few weeks ago. And yes, it’s true that they have lost no other games in the last year – that’s a run of one defeat in 53 – and even including that hiccup the aggregate scoreline of their last seven games is 34-3 (Arsenal’s is about-as-third-as-many-scored to about-three-times-as-many-conceded at 13-10), but they are demonstrably and recently beatable. Hold on to that. And also the fact that the Gunners have beaten Barcelona on three of the five occasions they have met in the Champions League, most recently in the 2025 final. And, for as long as possible, hold on to that clean sheet.

“We play against a fantastic team with some very good players. They play very well and have a very clear game model. It’s a difficult match, and we’ll approach it knowing we’re facing a great team and that we’ll have to do things very well,” is very much what Arsenal coach Renée Slegers might have said ahead of this match, but is actually what an extremely generous Pere Romeu, her Barcelona counterpart, had to say of the side currently sitting sixth in the WSL having won three of their nine league games so far this season (Barca meanwhile have won nine out of 10).

“We know how good they are on the ball. We know that we have to be comfortable without the ball as well,” said Slegers. “We will have to suffer. We’ll have to put bodies on the lines. We’ll have to be really disciplined.” It might just be one of those games.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick was just the latest fall guy for Manchester United’s dysfunctional hierarchy | Jamie Jackson
Sports.content:
For a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking, consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one.

The former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick. Howe was also the favoured candidate of Dan Ashworth, Wilcox’s predecessor as United’s director of football, to follow Erik ten Hag after the Dutchman’s sacking in October 2024. Except Wilcox disagreed and Sir Jim Ratcliffe went with Wilcox’s man, Ruben Amorim, and that December Ashworth departed only five months after joining.

At that juncture Wilcox was the technical director. Now he is United’s highest-ranking football executive, the powerbroker. He was able, apparently with a straight face, to recommend to Ratcliffe that Howe, nearly two years after he rejected him, should become United’s eighth permanent No 1 in the 13 and a half years since Sir Alex Ferguson retired.

If following this is difficult, making sense of it is near impossible. Should London’s West End need a new farce then look no further than the wacky world of Ratcliffe and the football department he leads, which is also headed up by Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and is proving a disjointed, illogical operation.

Yet if this meant Carrick was dealt a treacherous hand, it is also true that he should have played it better. This, after all, is the job of a football coach: to somehow make wine from water – even if the water is murky, and may need purifying first.

José Mourinho, one of Carrick’s predecessors, from May 2016 to December 2018, showed how – to a degree. Mourinho stated famously that leading United to second place in 2017-18 (with 81 points, 19 behind Manchester City) was one of his finest achievements. This from a serial winner who broke the United-Arsenal duopoly of the Premier League to take Chelsea to consecutive crowns (2004-05 and 2005-06), and made history in Italy by guiding Inter to the treble in 2009-10.

View image in fullscreen The Manchester United chief executive, Omar Berrada (left), and the director of football, Jason Wilcox, have come in for plenty of criticism. Photograph: Conor Molloy/ProSports/Shutterstock

Mourinho’s billing of that second place was down to having to negotiate a similar shambles, overseen by Ed Woodward, the then executive vice-chair.

The Portuguese’s opening campaign ended with the Carabao Cup and Europa League collected despite, like Carrick, having to deal with a hierarchy convinced that it knew better than the man it hired as the football expert.

Here we arrive at a fundamental quality Carrick lacked: an ability to be streetwise when really required. For an example of Mourinho’s nous, rewind to a pre-season tour of America when this correspondent was offered an off-the-record sounding about a player he wanted out of the club but the executive did not.

The manager wanted his message out – that this was a player non grata. Machiavellian or pragmatic? A guess says Carrick would never dream of employing a similar tactic to achieve the best result for the team. But why not? Mourinho wanted a bad egg gone before the dressing room was stunk out and on-field prospects undermined.

Carrick, in his last month, encountered two of his own malevolents: Lisandro Martínez, a de facto captain who dared to criticise Wilcox’s recruitment after the 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid; and Bruno Fernandes, Carrick’s official leader, who betrayed his manager by questioning his tactics after the 4-1 humiliation at Como.

Each crossed a line and were emblematic of a chaotic changing room, a major factor in the dismal run of three wins from 15 games this season, including elimination from the Carabao Cup, and the league return of eight points from 10 matches that has United in the relegation zone.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Fernandes, Martínez and a club run like a banana republic are the next man’s problem, just as Mourinho inherited from Louis van Gaal, who was sacked the day after winning the 2016 FA Cup, the faults at boardroom level embodied by Woodward.

View image in fullscreen José Mourinho won the Europa League and Carabao Cup for United in 2017 and came second in the Premier League the following season but could not build on that success. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

Here we see the recurring problem at United: a new gun is hired and is bequeathed a sorry mess that is impossible to clean up because there is no true will to eradicate it. Why? Because the only real reset of culture would be for Ratcliffe, who owns 29.4%, Wilcox, Berrada and the Glazer family, whose ownership since 2005 has left the club about £1.2bn in debt, to accept they are the problem and depart.

Carrick is a good guy whose adoration of United was returned to him by the support, underlined by the reception he got from the Stretford End after the 3-0 humbling by Bournemouth last month. Yet being a decent man and head coach was not enough.

In elite sport the fine margins are often trumpeted as the difference between triumph and failure. Last season, from mid-January, Carrick worked these his way as Manchester City, Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea were defeated and United lost only two of his 17 games as interim head coach.

This season, though, the fall-off was startling – and Carrick was found wanting. Who knows what might have occurred if United were the “best-in-class” organisation Ratcliffe insisted they would be under him. As with the muddled thinking regarding Howe, “worst in class” may be a more apt characterisation.

The agonising, overlong process to decide Carrick should be sacked was the latest illustration. On Monday evening the Guardian broke the news that Wilcox and Berrada would recommend to Ratcliffe that Carrick should be removed. Yet days passed during which Carrick still took training and it emerged the deal for Pochettino was being finalised. A proper functioning organisation would have acted more swiftly and with more style.

This is what the next manager has to grapple with. He may succeed. But the odds are stacked against it owing to the deep structural faults that undermine the modern Manchester United.

Sports.title: Crystal Palace sack Pierre Sage and in advanced talks to appoint Thomas Frank
Sports.content:
Pierre Sage has been sacked as Crystal Palace’s manager after 16 games, with Thomas Frank in advanced talks to succeed him.

The Frenchman, appointed in mid-June on a three-year contract to replace Oliver Glasner, has gone after Sunday’s 3-1 defeat by Liverpool left his team bottom of the Premier League. Frank, out of work since his dismissal by Spurs in February, has emerged as the main candidate to succeed Sage. He spoke to Palace in the summer and is keen for a new challenge after a successful spell at Brentford. It is hoped that he will take charge before next Saturday’s trip to Coventry.

The decision to sack Sage was made on Sunday evening but negotiations over compensation delayed his exit. It is understood Palace have agreed to pay him 18 months of a deal thought to have been worth about £4m a season. That means they will have spent more than £10m on Sage after paying more than £4m to buy him out of his contract with Lens when he replaced Oliver Glasner.

There remains a strong possibility that Sage could rejoin the French club after they sacked Yannick Cahuzac on Tuesday. The Lens owner and president, Joseph Oughourlian, has remained in close contact with Sage and is understood to have held talks about a return. Sage won the Coupe de France and qualified for the Champions League in his final season there.

Palace, who confirmed that Sage’s backroom staff would also depart, said in a statement: “The club would like to place on record its thanks to Pierre and his staff for their efforts during their time in south London, and wish them well for the future. An update on the process of appointing a new manager will be provided in due course.”

Sunday’s defeat was Palace’s fifth in an eight-match run that also included a painful 5-0 hammering by their arch-rivals Brighton. Their only victory in the sequence came in the Carabao Cup at Fulham and they have lost four league fixtures in a row.

Palace have seven points from 10 games, their league victories having come against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, and have conceded the most goals in the division: 24. They have been juggling domestic matches with the Europa League, where they sit 21st in the 36-team table.

Alternatives to Frank include the former Nottingham Forest manager Sean Dyche, who also has his backers at Palace, and Vítor Pereira, another former Forest manager.

Palace have lost their two main central defenders this year, Marc Guéhi moving to Manchester City in January and Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea in the summer. Two loan players – Axel Disasi and the teenager Honest Ahanor – were signed as replacements. Palace did not land one of Sage’s top targets, the winger Malick Fofana.

Sage is understood to have fallen out with the board over their failure to sign what he regarded as adequate replacements for Guéhi and Lacroix. The Palace chair, Steve Parish, was unhappy with Sage’s treatment of Jaydee Canvot, another centre-back, after the France Under-21 international was dropped from the squad for September’s home defeat by Ipswich, and expressed displeasure after Adam Wharton was substituted in that match.

Sports.title: ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts
Sports.content:
Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.

Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright announced her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal.

“I think it’s becoming more common. You’re seeing it more often, especially in America,” says 32-year-old Emslie, who trained at high intensity throughout her pregnancy, with a three-person team looking after her. She gave birth to her son, Jamie, in December 2025 and returned to competitive action by May 2026; scoring her first goal since coming back for Scotland in October, and her first club goal this month. “It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.”

For many years, says the physiotherapist and Women’s Football Hub founder Carolyn Kent, there was huge caution around high-impact sports and pregnancy. The fear was that overexertion and physical contact – a heart rate going too high, a bad fall, a mistimed kick to the abdomen – could cause miscarriage. But slowly this is changing. In July Fifa launched its Stay in Play guidelines and research, which offer a groundbreaking framework for decision-making around football participation during pregnancy.

View image in fullscreen Claire Emslie on her return to football: ‘It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.’ Photograph: Elsa/NWSL/Getty Images

“I was always told that once you hit that first trimester, 12 weeks, all contact stops. But actually they’re now saying, no, we need to be a little bit more nuanced than that,” says Kent. The research suggests that while that timeframe should still be considered the loose recommended cut-off point for full-contact football (due to the uterus growing over the pubic bone and offering less protection for the growing foetus in the second trimester), low-contact and modified training can continue in the absence of any medical reason for it not to.

“Pregnancy does not mean game over,” adds Kent. “It does not mean that ‘OK, I’ve got to automatically stop’. That again feeds into this narrative that females are fragile. Your body’s amazing.”

Up to 2021, only 6% of sports science research was done on women, which means gaps are still being filled in. But as the women’s game continues to grow, this is happening at speed, says Sinéad Dufour, a pelvic health physiotherapist and academic who was one of the researchers who developed the Stay in Play guidelines. She gives Fifa credit for recognising the development of the women’s game – its popularity and intensity has soared in the past 10 years with more than six million women and girls playing football in England alone.

“More and more players are now staying through until they’re having families … And they put all this money into research,” she says. They have identified “clear cut” physical and mental health benefits for women to keep up with football, including a lower injury risk postpartum.

“There’s always been a notion that women just aren’t strong and robust the way we actually are, and now the science is proving otherwise,” Dufour says. “I do think some of it relates to the foetus. That’s going to supersede what’s actually good for the woman, right?”

Some of the main considerations players should have, whether professional or amateur, as to whether they should keep playing and training throughout pregnancy, relate to pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, and motor control and movement, she adds. But the decision whether or not to continue playing during pregnancy is ultimately personal.

When Emma Kelly, who plays for Newcastle United, unexpectedly became pregnant earlier this year at the age of 29, she was anxious. She had never played with a pregnant teammate before and she had been out for much of the season due to injury. How isolating would the experience be? Was it going to jeopardise her career? “I was questioning whether this is the right time,” she says. “It’s not that I’m ungrateful but it’s just finding it hard being out of the team again and not being able to play the sport that I love.”

View image in fullscreen Newcastle’s Emma Kelly became pregnant earlier this year. Photograph: Michelle Mercer/Newcastle United/Getty Images

Though she continued to train, she and her partner decided she would stop contact football immediately, prior to 12 weeks, as “football is so unpredictable”, she says. As she didn’t want to announce her pregnancy until she was into the second trimester, in the interim she told her teammates that she was unwell. Like Emslie she has been documenting her training with the encouragement of her club and feels as if she is noticing more and more athletes doing the same. “I want to continue as long as my body allows me to,” she says. Her club has been “extremely supportive” with specialised training, physio and equipment.

But for all the newfound positivity around pre-and postpartum for footballers, Emslie says candidly, there are some hard truths that players have to face: namely that pregnancy is a sacrifice. The pitch is their stage and no player wants to be relegated to the role of understudy, relearning how to bend their body to their will. “If I wasn’t worried about [fertility], I wouldn’t have gotten pregnant till I was retired,” she says. “I could have had a full football career.”

The other is that football is a business. “You’re used as a player,” she says bluntly. “As soon as you turn a certain age, or if you’ve got a kid, they look at you different … As a player, you’re wanted until you’re not.” Though she made it clear she wasn’t talking about her own club, which was very supportive of her pregnancy and return, at the time of interview she was two months away from her contract ending with Angel City but had no news of a new deal being offered.

Even so, Dufour says, the body works hard during pregnancy; aerobic capacity is pushed. “The biggest stress test you’re ever going to go through is pregnancy,” she says. Her data shows that some women will achieve personal bests on their return. In short pregnancy could be a secret superpower. In an industry as capitalistic, brutal and data-driven as football, that’s an important fact.
