Sports.title: ‘Second ball’ may be a Sunday league mantra but Yates showed its top-flight relevance
Sports.content:
Modern football is more systematised and data-driven than ever but some things never change. Winning the first ball is important but the second ball – the holy grail for Sunday league footballers – is often more so.

Nottingham Forest’s 3-1 win against Manchester City last weekend featured a classic example. Forest led 2-1 inside the last 20 minutes but City, lifted by Rayan Cherki’s sweet half-volley, were pushing for an equaliser.

Another City attack comes down their right: after Jair Cunha’s clearing header from a deep Matheus Nunes cross, the ball loops up in the air before descending inside the home penalty area.

Ryan Yates, Forest’s old-fashioned midfield general, is being pressed from behind by the Argentina international Enzo Fernández as the ball drops. Yates stands his ground, using his strength to hold off his opponent’s muscular challenge. Fernández tries to impose himself, too, but ends up on the turf.

Not only does Yates win that crucial one-on-one, by cleverly improvising an overhead kick to shift the ball away from danger he inadvertently begins a counterattack that arguably changes the course of Forest’s season.

Liam Delap shepherds the ball to Morgan Gibbs-White. Enzo Maresca’s team are hopelessly exposed and Gibbs-White devours the space in front of him with a driving run.

View image in fullscreen Ryan Yates wins the ball ahead of Enzo Fernández, leading to a goal by Liam Delap during Nottingham Forest’s win against Manchester City on Saturday. Photograph: Sky Sports

He lays a pass off to Delap, who takes one touch before swerving a sensational shot into the far corner for 3-1. It is a memorable move that will surely compete for goal of the month. But none of it would have been possible without the dirty work of Yates: a show of strength and desire from the captain at the other end of the pitch.

Oliver Glasner understands the importance of the moment and sprints to celebrate with his players. After a barren scoring run Delap suddenly has two goals in one afternoon. The home fans are delirious. Twelve seconds after Yates won the duel, Forest have a two-goal cushion rather than a desperate fight to maintain their lead.

The second ball is a pleasingly old-school term but remains of paramount importance. Visit your local amateur club and you are likely to hear it being shouted as a motivational mantra.

At grassroots level it’s a reminder to teammates that finesse and creativity are all very well, but it’s hard work, desire and a refusal to let your opponent get the better of you that win matches.

View image in fullscreen ‘I’ve never heard such an inspiring speech,’ Oliver Glasner said of Ryan Yates’s team talk before Forest’s win against Manchester City. Photograph: Nigel French/PA

And it remains part of the elite game’s lexicon. Premier League managers sometimes point to upcoming opponents’ second-ball prowess – a back-handed compliment if ever there was one. The hidden meaning: “They feed off scraps at set pieces. They don’t create from open play.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

After seeing Southampton Under-21s lose to Wealdstone in the National League Cup a couple of years ago, I mentioned to the then Saints manager, Simon Rusk, that his goalkeeper had been shouting “second ball” throughout.

“To be honest,” Rusk replied with amusing frankness, “I’m not sure some of them even know what second ball means.”

Managers like relying on data. They like predictable outcomes. They prefer to remove risk, reduce chaos and exert control over as much of the game as possible. But while the outcome of a one-on-one duel can never be certain, the consequences can often be far-reaching. That’s why second balls matter.

Against City Yates was named in Forest’s starting lineup, and given the captain’s armband, for the first time this season. Glasner, asked how he had motivated his players, revealed: “Ryan Yates spoke. I played more than 500 games as a player, I’ve managed, I don’t know, 500 games … and I’ve never heard such an inspiring speech.”

Glasner’s captain backed up stirring words with action. If there was a sense Yates’s star was fading – that his attributes of graft, tenacity and box-to-box drive were losing currency – then it was emphatically extinguished at the City Ground.

Win the first one if you can. But it’s the second ball that often makes the difference.

Sports.title: Archive, 1990: Peter Shilton wins 125th and final cap of record-breaking England career
Sports.content:
Harry Kane is expected to break the record for England men’s appearances tonight against Croatia at Wembley in the Nations League, overtaking goalkeeper Peter Shilton’s 125 appearances, a record set nearly four decades ago at the World Cup in Italy.

Shilton wore the captain’s armband in his final England appearance in the unloved third-place play-off against Italy in Bari. The Three Lions had previously lost on penalties to West Germany in the semi-finals.

The Guardian’s Ian Ridley, pitch side, reported that Shilton, who announced his retirement from international football that night, said: “I would just like to say how much I have thoroughly enjoyed the last 20 years.”

That joy must have been tempered slightly, though, when, in the 71st minute, Shilton, who had made his international debut against East Germany in 1970, untypically lost concentration, allowing Roberto Baggio to steal the ball as he casually cleared a back pass and scored Italy’s opening goal.

Despite a pinpoint headed equaliser by David Platt, England went down 2-1, with Schillaci scoring a penalty to win the tournament’s Golden Boot. It was also England manager Bobby Robson’s last game in charge. On his rare error, Shilton said of his teammates: “No one, though, seemed to mind much.”

England double act take their bows and exit with honour – Third place play-off: Italy 2, England 1

By Ian Ridley in Bari

9 July 1990

It was goodnight from him and it was goodnight from him. Bobby Robson ended his eight years as keeper of the England keys and Peter Shilton his career as keeper of the England goal, after 125 appearances, in footballing debit but moral credit.

At times, too, it must have seemed like a custodial sentence for Robson, but not on a windy, moonlit Saturday night by the Adriatic at the San Nicola stadium. The loss to Italy was honourable, like the man and certainly in this tournament the team.

View image in fullscreen Guardian match report: England v Italy, World Cup third-place play-off, 9 July 1990.

The draping banners for Italy saying “Thanks anyway” applied equally to England. “Bravissimo” was the verdict on them of Azeglio Vicini, the host nation’s manager. Robson exuded bonhomie, except that he could not resist a bit of manager-speak about the two goals “which I’m not very happy about”.

Unfortunately for Shilton, 30 minutes before announcing his retirement “I would just like to say how much I have thoroughly enjoyed the last 20 years” his error gave Italy their first goal. No one, though, seemed to mind much.

Robson “made” Shilton play because he wanted him to finish at the top, even though the venerable one was ready to stand aside for Woods. For Robson “I shall miss it greatly. It has been my life for eight years” it was “nice” that the two should end at the same time. ‘No doubt we’ll both be missed,” he added with a smile.

Shilton saved excellently from Ferrara in the first half, tipping his shot on to a post, but after 70 minutes found himself Gary Crosbyed by Baggio as he tried to dribble the ball. Baggio was offside when Schillaci fed him the ball to cut inside Parker and score, but then again Shilton had brought him down as punishment for robbing him. It all evened out.

So did the game 10 minutes later, England’s favourite time. The next manager might even consider beginning his team talk: ‘Right lads. Just imagine we’re one down and there’s 10 minutes to go ...’

Dorigo, who had an excellent first start proving again that as a left-back he is an outstanding left-winger crossed and Platt beat Baresi and his ball-watching defence to thump home a header.

No one could contemplate extra-time, least of all the referee Joel Quiniou, it seemed. Having apparently decided earlier that these teams had had enough of penalties hence his decision to ignore Ancelotti’s handling of Beardsley’s free-kick he changed his mind with five minutes left.

Schillaci fell over Walker’s legs and the ‘little hero’, as Robson called him, stepped up to move out on his own as the top scorer of the tournament with his sixth goal. Italy were denied a third in injury-time when a badly erring linesman flagged Berti offside after he had beautifully headed home Baggio’s cross.

England played their part in an entertaining game. It was less tame than might have been expected and was certainly taken seriously by both sides.

The record will show that Robson’s teams played 95, won 47, drew 29 and lost 19 and that Shilton was one of three Bryan Robson and Butcher the others who spanned his tenure. Indeed, it was the passing of an era, but one that should not be allowed to end.

ITALY: Zenga; Baresi, Bergomi, De Agostini (Berti, 65min), Ferrara, Maldini, Vierchowod, Ancelotti, Giannini (Ferri, 89), Baggio, Schillaci.

ENGLAND: Shilton; Stevens, Walker, Wright (Waddle, 73), Parker, Dorigo, Steven, McMahon (Webb, 73), Platt, Lineker, Beardsley.

Referee: J Quiniou (France).

Sports.title: Less drama, more listening, but is Kozo Tashima the candidate to topple Infantino?
Sports.content:
Not many remember Japan’s bid for the 2022 World Cup, when the country finished the race with only two of the final 22 votes. Kozo Tashima was involved then, and now the honorary president of the Japan Football Association is going it alone in the hope of ousting Gianni Infantino.

The 68-year-old Tashima is an unlikely insurgent and an unlikely challenger to Infantino. He is, however, a familiar and respected figure in Asian and global football politics, and ready to take the Fifa presidency out of the headlines into a quieter era.

In 2010, during the JFA’s failed World Cup bid, Tashima proved himself to be an affable campaigner, impressing with his efficiency and, in the words of an official from one European association, displaying a rare ability for a football leader to listen more than talk. He may not have the ability for an easy quip, or as much charm and charisma as Infantino or his predecessor, Sepp Blatter, but that could count in his favour.

Since entering the Fifa Council in 2015, Tashima has rarely made an international headline and it is this, he hopes, that will make a difference. Tashima is ready to put principles to the fore before March’s election. “It’s not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built,” Tashima said as he announced his candidacy for the Fifa presidency on 5 November. “What Fifa needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world.”

Tashima became the JFA’s technical director in 2002, moving up to the role of federation president as Japan became Asia’s leading football nation. Off the pitch, however, the power has moved westwards, from Tokyo to Riyadh, Doha and Manama. There has been disquiet about how the Asian Football Confederation has, from Japan’s perspective, become too close to Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

The feeling about Fifa is worse. JFA officials were dismayed at Infantino’s closeness to Donald Trump. Given how crucial a partner the United States has been to Japan in terms of security and as an export market for more than eight decades, the president’s actions in regards to tariffs and cosying up to China and North Korea went down badly in Tokyo, as did Trump’s favourability, going below 30% in May.

View image in fullscreen The close relationship between Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump has not gone down well in Japan. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

The summer was the last straw, with the Folarin Balogun affair during the World Cup and then the leaking of Infantino’s plan to sell off the tournament’s commercial rights to private investors. Yet in October the JFA president, Tsuneyasu Miyamoto, the former defender who succeeded Tashima in 2024, followed the AFC leadership and backed Infantino. Miyamoto’s decision resulted in the resignation of the JFA vice-president, Takeshi Okada.

“I have always believed that sports should be noble and have cherished their social value,” said Okada, a former Japan defender and national team head coach. “However, the recent actions surrounding the Fifa World Cup have created a significant gap between my beliefs and the actions taken, and as a sportsman I could not accept them, which led me to this decision.”

Okada led Japan at the 2010 World Cup in South Africa but only after surviving calls from fans and the media for him to be sacked due to poor results in preparation for the tournament. Tashima’s support as JFA president was key to this and his loyalty was rewarded with seeing the Samurai Blue reach the knockout stages on foreign soil for a first time. Now it was Okada’s turn to back Tashima and he did just that as the latter announced his candidacy for the Fifa presidency, one that came as a surprise to most in Asia.

There is an expectation that Uefa’s candidate will be announced soon, but if no one is put up by Europe’s governing body then Tashima becomes the main challenger to Infantino’s supremacy, ahead of the former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega, who has also announced his candidacy. He would automatically get some support from Europe and Concacaf members but may not have the international connections to pick up enough votes elsewhere.

View image in fullscreen Takeshi Okada at the 2010 World Cup, where he led Japan to the knockout phase for the first time abroad. Photograph: Luca Bruno/AP

Tashima, who earned seven caps for Japan in the late 1970s and early 1980s, is not going to unite Asia, but there will also be backing for him from the east and south-east, where the JFA has worked hard over the years building relationships with national associations such as those of Singapore and Thailand. Tashima has put his chances of winning at between 20% and 30% but, as he said, this isn’t really about winning but about standing up for what is right.

If Tashima does win, there will be a Fifa president who looks to build consensus behind the scenes and make as few headlines as possible. There will also be no cosying up to world leaders, or certainly not any more than is absolutely necessary. Football fans may well appreciate a quieter, less visible, less controversial man at the top of the sport’s world governing body. Kozo Tashima could be that man.

Sports.title: US withdraw from U-17 World Cup in Qatar due to safety concerns
Sports.content:
The US men’s national team have pulled out of the Fifa U-17 World Cup, which is due to kick off in Qatar in just over a week. In a letter sent to players explaining the decision, the US Soccer Federation cited safety concerns for players and staff, referring them to the US state department’s travel advisory for Qatar, which encourages citizens to reconsider travel to the country “due to risk of armed conflict” and asks government employees to obtain special authorization to do so.

“Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances … we are no longer able to participate in the tournament,” US Soccer’s letter to players reads. “The wellbeing of our players and staff will always be our top priority.

“Please accept our deepest appreciation for your commitment to US Soccer and our shared disappointment about these circumstances.”

A US Soccer spokesperson said the federation would not go into details about how it reached its decision. The Guardian understands Fifa was informed of the federation’s decision on Wednesday.

Fifa’s regulations for the U-17 World Cups stipulate that qualified nations must participate in the tournament or be fined, with withdrawal within 30 days of the tournament’s start resulting in a fine of CHF20,000 (about $24,000).

“Fifa has been informed of US Soccer’s decision to withdraw from the Fifa U-17 World Cup Qatar 2026,” Fifa told the Guardian in a statement. “The applicable tournament regulations will be followed. Fifa’s security assessments remain unchanged, and no new developments affecting the security situation around the tournament have occurred. Fifa understands that US Soccer’s decision was made in light of the existing US Level 3 travel advisory.”

The ongoing situation in the Middle East – involving interconnected conflicts among multiple states – has already led to postponements or cancellations of international sporting events. The 2027 Asian Cup, the continental soccer championship, was due to be held in Saudi Arabia in January 2027 but has been postponed nearly a year due to the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthi rebels, and the Iran war. More recently, Qatar pulled out of hosting rugby’s 2028 Nations Championship finals due to uncertainty around the conflicts. The final races of the Formula One season are still going ahead in the Middle East, on 29 November in Qatar and then 6 December in Abu Dhabi.

Fifa told the Guardian it had taken the situation in the Middle East into account.

“The safety and security of all participants and fans remains paramount,” Fifa said in its statement. “As with all Fifa tournaments and events, we are in close contact with the relevant authorities and are looking forward to the tournament kick-off in Qatar. In recent months, Qatar has successfully hosted several international events, including the FIP Padel World Cup, the FIVB Volleyball Boys’ U17 World Championship, the Doha Diamond League, the Fiba Basketball World Cup 2027 Asian Qualifiers, the MotoGP and the UN ITU PP.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Multiple missile strikes by the Houthis on Riyadh’s international airport killed 13 people and wounded hundreds in October. Later that month, US diplomats were told to leave Saudi Arabia amid ongoing Houthi attacks.

Qatar has been acting as a mediator in talks between the US and Iran aimed at ending the countries’ conflict, which started with attacks by the US and Israel on Iran earlier this year. A tanker off the coast of Qatar was attacked in October amid thetensions.

The U-17 World Cup is still due to begin on 19 November in Doha. The US were placed in Group J along with Montenegro, Algeria and Chile. The US roster that was due to compete in the tournament does not contain any household names, but features a number of promising young players in MLS and abroad.

Sports.title: Man United set to appoint Mauricio Pochettino as head coach: Club make formal approach to US Soccer after agreeing personal terms - with Michael Carrick's exit confirmed on Thursday
Sports.content:
Manchester United are set to name Mauricio Pochettino as head coach to replace Michael Carrick following a day of talks over both men. United moved closer to putting Pochettino in charge at Old Trafford after reaching a verbal agreement with the US national team boss on Wednesday. The club then made a formal approach to US Soccer. Meanwhile, the club’s chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox flew back from Monaco, where minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe was expected to ratify their decision to sack Carrick with the blessing of co-chairmen Joel and Avram Glazer. Carrick’s departure could be confirmed on Thursday, but official confirmation of Pochettino’s appointment may take a little longer with more talks planned overnight on Wednesday. Pochettino is currently at the US Soccer base outside Atlanta preparing for a CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final double header against Haiti, and is due to speak to the media on Friday. It’s unclear if he will remain in charge for those games, with United said to be relaxed over the Argentine taking the team. It is possible he could stay for the first leg in Kingston, Jamaica at the weekend and then travel to Manchester. Manchester United are set to name Mauricio Pochettino as their new manager - but he took training as usual on Wednesday Pochettino, who has managed Southampton,Tottenham, and Chelsea, will succeed Michael Carrick Carrick checked in at Carrington at 7.45am on Wednesday with his fate in the balance He was pictured leaving Manchester United's training base at around 1.15pm Pochettino is pictured working on United States national team duty on Tuesday (Source: X/USMNT) The second leg is Cincinnati is not until the early hours of Thursday, and Pochettino may even would only take over at United on Friday with a huge game against Liverpool at Anfield 48 hours later. It’s understood that the US Soccer Federation are ready for this contingency and have a succession plan in place should he leave. It will cost Pochettino around £7million to buy himself out of his contract with the US Soccer Federation, with United ready to foot the bill. The cost of bringing in his back-room team, including trusted assistants Jesus Perez and Miguel D’Agostino, will take the cost above £10m. The 54-year-old only signed a new deal after the World Cup meaning that United could have got him for nothing in the summer. Amid the secret talks between United and Pochettino’s camp on Wednesday, there was more intrigue when the federation cancelled media access to the players at late notice but allowed cameras to film an open training session. Sources said the decision was made out of respect for Veterans Day in America, but it also meant the players didn’t have to field any awkward questions over their coach’s future. Bournemouth midfielder Tyler Adams was quoted by the US media as saying: ‘Why would his name not be on it (United’s list)? Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox are meeting in Monaco for talks today The United execs meet in Monaco today (Pictured is the Casino Monte-Carlo in Monaco)

Your browser does not support iframes.

‘I mean, the credibility, the resume speaks for itself. It goes to show for us how lucky we are to be able to work under a manager of his quality and the person he is.’ Meanwhile, Berrada and Wilcox flew back to Manchester from Nice on Wednesday with United expected to announce Carrick’s departure imminently after 10 months in charge. The 45-year-old took training at Carrington for the second day running, arriving at 7.45am and leaving shortly after 1.30pm. However, it has been clear for some days that Carrick would lose his job after United dropped into the relegation zone following the club’s worst start in 40 years.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino faces nightmare Man United start as it emerges he WILL take charge of USA game in early hours of Wednesday - cutting preparation time for debut trip to Liverpool
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino will face a brutal start to life at Manchester United with the prospective Red Devils boss set to manage the United States days before his debut at Liverpool. United have moved closer to putting Pochettino in charge at Old Trafford after reaching a verbal agreement with the US national team boss on Wednesday. The club then made a formal approach to US Soccer. Daily Mail Sport understands Pochettino will take charge of both of the United States matches during the international window. The US take on Haiti in the CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final first leg on Saturday, with the second fixture then taking place in Cincinnati on Tuesday evening, but would likely finish at around 2am GMT. Pochettino would then have to travel to Manchester following the match to link up with the Red Devils' squad for the first time, likely on Thursday. The Argentine would then have limited time with his players before a daunting trip to Anfield to face rivals Liverpool on Sunday in a blockbuster first match in charge. Mauricio Pochettino will take charge of the United States upcoming matches against Haiti Pochettino will coach in the early hours on Wednesday morning in Cincinnati before travelling to Manchester The Argentine would have limited time to prepare his side for Sunday's match at Anfield Man United are said to be relaxed over Pochettino taking charge of his final two matches as US boss before starting as their new head coach. It will cost Pochettino around £7million to buy himself out of his contract with the US Soccer Federation, with United ready to foot the bill. The cost of bringing in his back-room team, including trusted assistants Jesus Perez and Miguel D’Agostino, will take the cost above £10million. The 54-year-old only signed a new deal after the World Cup meaning that United could have got him for nothing in the summer. Pochettino is set to take over a Man United side languishing in the Premier League relegation zone following just one win in their opening ten matches. The trip to Anfield would be the first of a run of eight matches in 29 days, as Man United juggle Premier League and Champions League football. Pochettino is set to succeed Michael Carrick, whose departure as the Red Devils' boss was officially announced on Wednesday morning. Pochettino will face a tight turnaround to prepare his new side for the daunting clash on Merseyside

Carrick arrived at United's training ground at 7.50am this morning and was dismissed. He left at 10.18am, less than two and a half hours later. He is the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season, followed hours later by bottom-of-the-table Crystal Palace boss Pierre Sage. In a statement released at 10.37am, Carrick's sacking was confirmed. United's statement read: 'After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions. 'Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club. His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.'

Sports.title: Jimmy Anderson completes stunning move to Surrey: England legend U-turns on retirement after brutal Lancashire axe and will play on next summer aged 45
Sports.content:
Jimmy Anderson completes stunning move to Surrey: England legend U-turns on retirement after brutal Lancashire axe and will play on next summer aged 45

Sir Jimmy Anderson will have a chance of winning the County Championship next year after completing a stunning move to Surrey.

Anderson, who will turn 45 during the 2027 season, thought he was heading into retirement when his boyhood club Lancashire sensationally snubbed him last month, disregarding the opportunity to offer their captain a new contract.

However, after being inundated with offers over the following fortnight, England’s most prolific bowler re-considered playing on elsewhere beyond 26 seasons as a first-team player at Emirates Old Trafford.

Daily Mail Sport understands that he chose Surrey despite receiving a couple of more lucrative offers from other counties, lured by the chance to challenge for the title.

Speaking after the move was confirmed, Anderson said: 'It’s an honour to join a club like Surrey and I can’t wait to start a new chapter in my career. Surrey have a great squad and are a team that expects to be fighting for Championship titles and I’m excited to be a part of that.

'I still feel like I have a lot to offer, taking wickets, trying to help the team win games of cricket. I also think that I can bring a lot to the team off the field and help those young players who are looking to develop their skillset and go on and represent their country.

Sir Jimmy Anderson, 44, has completed a stunning move to Surrey to prolong his career

Anderson, who will turn 45 next summer, was brutally axed by Lancashire despite claiming 50 County Championship wickets at an average of just 17.68 in the 2026 season

'I’ve always loved playing at the Kia Oval. For me it’s one of the best grounds in the world. It’s a place that I have some incredibly special memories at and I hope to create some more next season.'

Surrey's Director of Cricket Alec Stewart added: 'We’re delighted to bring someone of the calibre of Sir James Anderson to Surrey. Jimmy brings quality with the ball. His 50 championship wickets last season prove that he is still one of the best bowlers in the country.

'Jimmy also brings a wealth of experience to the group that all our bowlers will learn from. Much of our squad have international aspirations, and they will learn a great deal from training, playing and being in the same dressing room with Jimmy.'

Anderson had gone into the bombshell meeting with Lancashire chief executive Richard Kenyon and director of cricket Paul Farbrace on 19 October - in which he was informed that the rebuilding of a team that finished next to bottom in the County Championship last summer would not involve him - intent on standing down from the captaincy but retained a determination to return the side to the top flight.

But this segue means he will make a personal return to Division One even sooner and get the opportunity to set the tone with the new ball at the country’s most powerful club. When Lancashire won the Championship pennant in 2011, Anderson appeared just twice due to England commitments.

The decision to head to London on a season-long contract follows a 2026 campaign in which he claimed 50 Division Two victims at a cost of just 17.68 runs apiece. Of the division’s 20 most prolific bowlers, only Matthew Potts, of champions Durham, bettered Anderson’s strike rate of 38.66.

It means Surrey supporters will get the mouth-watering prospect of watching Anderson opening the bowling with Australian Dan Worrall, who has 199 first-class victims in 50 appearances at just 22 runs apiece since moving here on his British passport.

Surrey director of cricket Alec Stewart is also thought to be excited by the influence Anderson will have on emerging England Lions seamer Tom Lawes. And the competition for places could also inspire Yorkshireman Matthew Fisher.

Being moved on from Old Trafford, which has an end named after him, follows his abrupt departure from an international career in 2024 when, with the 2025-26 Ashes in mind, England’s think-tank of Rob Key, Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes made the impulsive call to inject their attack with new blood.

Of this latest farewell, he said on the Tailenders podcast recently that although he’d wanted to finish his career where it began, and that ‘it would be nice at some point if someone would let me retire.’

The legendary bowler will wear the No 99 shirt and will just play in the County Championship

Anderson is arguably England's greatest ever bowler, having taken 1193 first-class wickets

Adding: ‘I am sad the way it ended with the club I supported as a kid but now I have thought about it I am quite excited for the future. I am always going to support Lancashire.

‘I was born there, grew up watching them, had some of my most memorable days out with dad watching them, got to play for them and captain the club, which is something most people dream about.’

This move to Division One means a bowler with 1193 first-class career wickets is unlikely to play against the Red Rose, although his deal does not preclude him featuring in white-ball matches for Surrey.

Sports.title: Tone-deaf Australians are taking us for fools with Sandpapergate cover-up that shames their nation - if they won't punish cowardly cheats before the Ashes, the ICC must do it for them
Sports.content:
Tone-deaf Australians are taking us for fools with Sandpapergate cover-up that shames their nation - if they won't punish cowardly cheats before the Ashes, the ICC must do it for them

Oliver Holt Chief Sports Writer

It started with a young player, Cameron Bancroft, scuffing up a ball with sandpaper and being caught live on the big screen at Newlands during a Test match in South Africa eight years ago.

Now, in the second flowering of a scandal that Australian cricket thought it had buried, ‘Sandpapergate’ is engulfing it in an existential crisis that is only just beginning.

Back in 2018, Cricket Australia made scapegoats of three men – Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner – for the ball-tampering that was exposed during the third Test of the tour in Cape Town. It allowed the rest of the side to bathe in barely believable protestations of ignorance.

Those protestations were exposed as falsehoods by Usman Khawaja, Australia’s opening batsman during the tour, when he wrote in his new autobiography Sabr that the whole team knew what had been happening. His accusations sent sections of the Australian game scrambling into attempts at denial and damage limitation.

‘We have said we're comfortable with the outcome of the investigation based on the information we've received,’ Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg said this week. ‘That includes what we've seen from Usman, and our position hasn't changed on that. We don't see any compelling reason to open the investigation or revisit this again.’

That cannot be allowed to stand. Greenberg’s statement is already looking outmoded, ill-judged, arrogant and tone-deaf. Australian cricket is tearing itself apart in front of him, its bedrock of ‘mateship’ replaced by accusations of selfishness, disloyalty and betrayal. Its integrity is shot to pieces along with its reputation.

Usman Khawaja (second right) has lit a fuse under the Australian bowlers' claim that they knew nothing of the 2018 plan to rough the ball up with sandpaper

Cricket Australia made scapegoats of three men – (L-R) David Warner, Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith. It allowed the rest to bathe in barely believable protestations of ignorance

And as the sport heads rapidly towards the beginning of an Ashes year, it is fair to suggest that if Cricket Australia will not discipline the rest of the players that Khawaja insists were in on the cheating, then the game’s governing body, the International Cricket Council (ICC) must step in to do it for them.

Because bear in mind, too, that Khawaja has also claimed Australia cheated in the Ashes Tests against England in Adelaide and Perth a few months earlier, by picking at the quarter seam to raise flaps on it and help the ball reverse swing. That Ashes series of 2017-18 feels tainted now. Whatever punishments are visited on these Australia players, next summer’s Ashes will be stained by the deceptions they have perpetrated.

The ICC’s rules may say a country cannot be punished for the same offence twice but it appears the nature of the offence to be prosecuted has changed. The ICC toughened their code of conduct after the Cape Town scandal and players found guilty of ball-tampering can now be banned for up to six Test matches.

The circumstances are very different but Sandpapergate 2 is fast becoming cricket’s version of the Manchester City cheating scandal that has left an indelible stain on that club’s recent history. Sandpapergate 2 is threatening to define a generation of Australian cricketers and hang a label around their neck they will find it hard to remove.

Smith and Warner, of course, were banned from international cricket for 12 months soon after the original offence came to light and Bancroft for nine months. If Khawaja’s allegations are true, then any players from that side who are still active ought to be facing similar sanctions.

Given that current Australia captain Pat Cummins, as well as Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon, were also part of the Cape Town side, that could mean Australia going into next summer’s series in England without the majority of their bowling attack, something that would deal a hammer blow to Australian hopes of retaining the Ashes.

Impatience with Australia’s increasingly awkward attempts to insist that the bowling attack knew nothing about the ball-tampering in South Africa is growing all the time and curdling into anger and ridicule. ‘Why tamper if you ain’t going to tell the bowlers?’ former England bowler Derek Pringle asked yesterday.

I spoke to one England insider yesterday who said Australia were turning themselves into a cricketing laughing stock. ‘There is no way in the world that the rest of the lads in that team did not know what was going on,’ he said. ‘For reverse swing, the ball has to be in a certain condition. As the ball gets passed around, everybody knows why it is reversing and everybody knows how to treat the ball.

A statement from Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg (left) dismissing the new revelations is already looking outmoded, ill-judged, arrogant and tone-deaf

Whatever punishments are visited on these Australia players, next summer’s Ashes will be stained by the deceptions they have perpetrated

‘They were all in on it and everything else is b******s. They took the whole cricket world for fools in 2018 when they blamed it all on three players and now they’re trying to take us for fools all over again.’

Former England wicketkeeper Matt Prior also told Daily Mail Sport earlier this week that the claims of Australian bowlers to have known nothing about the cheating defied belief and that ball-tampering had to be a team effort.

‘There is just no way in any of the dressing rooms I played in that a conversation would have been had where the bowlers are not aware of what the plan is with the ball, and what you're all trying to do with it,’ Prior said. ‘Once that decision is made, it has to be a collective effort. A team effort.’

There are increasing signs that the crisis in Australian cricket is starting to spin out of control. Khawaja has abandoned his book tour after the scale of what he unleashed became apparent, Starc has disputed his claims, and Warner, who corroborated Khawaja’s claims, has ridiculed the views of Australia batting coach Graeme Hick that they were 'absolutely false'.

Cummins, who has stayed silent, is promising to speak to the media in the coming hours. Former Australia skipper Michael Clarke has admitted that the Australian cricket fans ‘can't trust what's real. They don't know the truth until this gets reopened… allow(ing) people to finally tell the truth, and move on.’

It is hard to see how Greenberg’s ‘nothing-to-see-here’ stance can survive much longer. As so often with controversies like this, it is the cover-up – or the attempted cover-up – that causes more damage than the original offence and Australian cricket is now deep in the process of eating itself.

What will cause it the most long-term damage is the abandonment of its principles of mateship that the scandal is exposing. To allow three players to take the fall for the actions of a team is the antithesis of the spirit of the Baggy Green that is supposed to be at the heart of Australian cricket. This is now a side and a sport at war with itself in Australia.

The team is now in a desperately difficult situation. If Cummins, Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon escape without censure and play in the Ashes next summer, they will be the subject of brutal and relentless mockery by the Barmy Army and sell-out crowds. The team will be led by four players accused of letting their mates swing when the going got tough.

If Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon and Mitchell Starc escape censure to play in next year's Ashes, Australia will be led by four players accused of letting their mates swing

Former Australia captain Michael Clarke (right) said that without a new investigation, fans 'can't trust what's real', while Matt Prior (left) rubbished the idea that the bowlers didn't know

‘The worst thing about all this for Australian cricket,’ the England insider said, ‘is how un-Australian it all is. What happened to mateship and standing by your pals? The Baggy Green cap is supposed to be a sacred symbol of togetherness and they might as well be trampling all over it.’

Former England batsman Mark Butcher also identified the loosening of the team bond as the most grievous blow for the Australians. ‘It is utterly inconceivable that the bowlers had no idea this was going on,’ Butcher said. 'Anybody who knows anything about reverse swing, everyone has to know or you screw it up and the ball stops reversing.

‘And so three of them had to take the fall. If there was some way of getting some recompense for loss of earnings or loss of career, I wouldn’t blame them. I don’t know how those three have slept. They have been utterly thrown under the bus and that was apparent from the very start.’

‘The three players did wrong,’ former England skipper Nasser Hussain said yesterday. ‘They did the crime and served the time but how a side can move on and say we are just going to let those three…

‘I remember the team, the Baggy Green, the mateship, they used to be together. That was what playing Australia was like. For an Australian team to say it was just those three, it was never going to be just those three.’

Sports.title: Man United's appointment of Mauricio Pochettino proves the Glazers are back calling the shots at Old Trafford - with Jim Ratcliffe's henchmen Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox looking like irrelevant also-rans, writes IAN HERBERT
Sports.content:
Man United's appointment of Mauricio Pochettino proves the Glazers are back calling the shots at Old Trafford - with Jim Ratcliffe's henchmen Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox looking like irrelevant also-rans, writes IAN HERBERT

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada once cited a line from the John Lennon song Beautiful Boy, when relating how an intended 12-month attachment at Barcelona had ended up with him staying there for 13 years. ‘Life is what happens to you while you’re busy making other plans.’

Lennon’s lyric seems far more appropriate to what Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment tells us about Berrada and his dubious grip on United, today.

While Berrada and his director of football Jason Wilcox have been busy making plans for United’s world domination – ‘to create the new history,’ as he described it to the journalist and broadcaster Andy Mitten just five months ago – a Glazer family petrified by the shocking descent of their Premier League asset have simply stepped in to get Pochettino installed.

If Berrada and Wilcox had got their way, we would seemingly have been treated to the sight of Eddie Howe wandering into the Old Trafford madhouse in the next few days. The Glazers said ‘no’, insisted that Pochettino would have the keys and Sir Jim Ratcliffe and his men fell in line with that.

Should Berrada and Wilcox both survive the latest embarrassment – and it would be a travesty if they do, as United pay US Soccer £7.5million in compensation for Pochettino, who would have been out of contract if they’d moved for him in August – then both will be a virtual irrelevance now. Also-rans, bypassed by the latest executive dice roll for United.

Perhaps the TV cameras will pan to them celebrating in the executive seats during some United upturn under Pochettino, weeks or months from now. If so, let it be remembered that it took the intervention of others to bend things United’s way.

If Jason Wilcox (left) and Omar Berrada (right) had got their way, we would seemingly have been treated to the sight of Eddie Howe wandering into the Old Trafford madhouse

Instead the Glazers insisted that Mauricio Pochettino (pictured) would have the keys and Sir Jim Ratcliffe and his men fell in line with that

Let us not pretend there’s been any visionary executive oversight from the Glazers. They’ve already rejected Pochettino twice, in favour of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in 2018 and Erik ten Hag four years later.

But sources close to Joel and Avram Glazer, the members of the dynasty who take some interest in their British sports asset, have indicated the brothers have been pushing to get him installed for some weeks.

The Glazers’ connection with US billionaire hedge fund owner Ken Griffin seems significant. Griffin was the main financial contributor to the salary which saw Pochettino hired by US Soccer in 2024 and again to that contract extension he signed in August.

It was also Griffin, the then youthful founder of Citadel, who provided substantial funds for the Glazers’ takeover of United in 2005.

It means that the Old Trafford hierarchy, like so much about the club, will be skewed from now on. Pochettino does not answer to Berrada and Wilcox in the same way that Ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick have.

He transcends the structure imposed by Ratcliffe, the so-called controller of football operations, and becomes the most powerful man at Old Trafford. The individual on whose vision the futures of Berrada and Wilcox now rest. Should they stay, this is the last chance saloon for them.

United's slump in form this season has been so severe, the club have been forced to dispense with Michael Carrick just six months after giving him a two-year deal

Sources close to Avram (left) and Joel Glazer, the members of the dynasty who take some interest in United, indicate they have been pushing for Pochettino for some weeks

There should be optimism. Pochettino, more than Howe, Julian Nagelsmann, Unai Emery, Antonio Conte and all other available candidates, has the faculty, charisma and fundamental toughness to instil some mettle into United and drag the club from what Ratcliffe and Co have reduced it to. To instil the identity and culture missing for so long.

Time will only tell if he can actually make a go of the most complicated and challenging job in world football, which Ratcliffe has rendered so much harder, by stripping away so many good, essential people from the Old Trafford payroll. That really is a monumental ‘If’.

One United insider spoke for many today when observing: ‘I haven’t got a clue who can make a go of it with the people above them.’

Pochettino will find United no longer command the same spending power, for transfers and wages, as other top clubs, though their name still carries a cachet, if only they can be nimbler and smarter.

He will discover that one of the most godforsaken parts of the operation is the interminable decision-making process: multiple individuals sitting around the table whose opinions must be sought in rule by committee. Some of those who have been shown the door by Ratcliffe consider themselves well out of all that.

The individual United most need now is actually David Gill, the stellar chief executive who left in the same summer as Sir Alex Ferguson, 13 years ago.

Gill would bring a command and intellect way beyond the remotest comprehension of Berrada. He probably wouldn’t want the association with Ineos but nevertheless, United do need to find a proven, world-class chief executive officer. And a sporting director befitting the biggest club in the world.

In that interview with Mitten back in June, Berrada seemed very pleased with himself – sitting on a large sofa in a United meeting room with immaculately bright white adidas trainers and declaring that United had travelled a long way in 12 months.

‘I’m naturally optimistic by nature, although my wife says I should smile more,’ he said. ‘We’ve made some very difficult decisions, but they have put us where we are today.’

It was his 'aspiration’ to ‘make United great again’, he declared. He is a footnote to another unhappy chapter in the modern history of Manchester United, now. The monumental task lies at Pochettino’s door.

Sports.title: EFL asks clubs to stop targeted 'banter' on social media amid fears over reputational damage in the wake of 'Spygate' fallout
Sports.content:
The EFL has written to clubs calling for a halt in reputationally damaging social media posts disguised as ‘banter’ - believing the line has been blurred when it comes to regulatory matters.

The letter expressed concern over a ‘growing pattern of posts that use disputes, disciplinary matters, alleged wrongdoing or rival Clubs as material for public “banter”.’

A letter, seen by Daily Mail Sport, has been sent by EFL chief executive Trevor Birch to club chairs and executives following a board meeting.

‘While any one post may be viewed as an isolated lapse, taken together they risk creating a culture in which short-term engagement is prioritised over judgement, responsibility and long-term reputation,’ the letter read.

‘This is not about removing humour, personality or rivalry from Club channels. It is about recognising when content becomes disparaging, prolongs a dispute, targets an individual, or calls the integrity of a Club or the competition into question.

‘The impact extends beyond the Clubs directly involved. Repeated public exchanges can inflame relationships, undermine confidence in the fairness and professionalism of our competitions, and weaken the collective EFL brand.

The EFL have called for clubs to halt 'banter' social media posts. Pictured: Wrexham owners Rob Mac (left) and Ryan Reynolds (right) spoofed Southampton's Spygate case in September. Source: X/Wrexham_AFC

Wrexham were among the clubs to mock the case by putting a not to 'check training ground for unauthorised visitors' prior to their match with Southampton on fixture release day. Source: X/Wrexham_AFC

Birmingham City also referenced the case by revealing the date for their fixture by showing the club badges cut into hedges and visible through binoculars. Source: X/BCFC

‘Recent media interest in perceived public disputes between Clubs illustrates how quickly individual posts can become a wider reputational issue.’

Daily Mail Sport understands the EFL are keen to avoid being seen as killjoys. Rather, they are taking a preventative approach to posts that could end up breaching FA or EFL rules.

The Southampton ‘Spygate’ scandal is among the most prominent disputes that have been referenced by clubs in social media content in recent months.

Both Birmingham City and Wrexham shared posts on the Championship fixture release date in June, using the case to highlight the dates of a fixture with Southampton.

Birmingham’s official X account posted a graphic of both clubs' badges cut into hedges which were viewed through binoculars. The account added: ‘One of the other key fixtures to keep an eye on...’

Wrexham’s calendar for their matches in September included a reminder to 'check training ground for unauthorised visitors’ two days before they played Southampton. An image of a man behind a tree was included in the Southampton badge.

The club also included their Hollywood owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac in a spoof video in the build-up to the match. The actors were seen behind a tree similar to one which Southampton intern William Salt was caught spying near ahead of their play-off semi-final with Middlesbrough.

Following the revelations by Daily Mail Sport, Southampton were eventually thrown out of the play-offs.

Last week, Blackburn hit back at a video of West Ham manager Scott Parker declaring he ‘didn’t see a Blackburn fan’ by showing images of their supporters celebrating goals in their 2-1 win over the Hammers.

Blackburn hit back at West Ham boss Scott Parker last week after he declared he ‘didn’t see a Blackburn fan', with the club then showing supporters celebrating goals. Source: X/Rovers

The EFL reminded clubs in their letter that regulations called for clubs to ‘to act towards one another with utmost good faith’. The organisation called for clubs to consider whether their content is ‘punching down’ or ‘targeting a specific Club or individual’, adding they would likely cross the threshold if it does.

The organisation stressed that its preference is for ‘engagement and prevention’ and was not requesting clubs to make ‘bland or risk-free’ content.

However, the EFL warned it is prepared to take ‘proportionate and consistent action’ where ‘conduct which doesn’t meet the standards we expect is repeated or serious.’

Clubs have been asked to ensure a senior leader owns the standard applied to the club’s content, as well as formalising approval arrangements, briefing relevant people and exercising restraint.

Sports.title: 'You can't keep out of it... you were part of the plot': Lipreader gives verdict on what Pat Cummins' wife Becky said in heated public row with Aussie captain amid fresh Sandpapergate claims
Sports.content:
'You can't keep out of it... you were part of the plot': Lipreader gives verdict on what Pat Cummins' wife Becky said in heated public row with Aussie captain amid fresh Sandpapergate claims

Pat Cummins wife Becky told him 'you can't keep out of it' amid Australia's explosive civil war following Usman Khawaja's fresh Sandpapergate claims - with the pair caught in a heated public row.

The pair were spotted in an animated conversation on a street in Sydney on Wednesday, with the Australia captain due to speak to the media for the first time in the coming hours to address former team-mate Khawaja's allegations made in his new book, Sabr.

News Corp published images of the married couple in a heated discussion beside their car and reported that the exchange lasted about five minutes before they went inside a property.

Cummins was barefoot and alternated between pacing and leaning against the car, while Becky did much of the talking.

Cummins's management declined to comment on the exchange.

Nicola Hickling, professional lipreader and founder of LipReader via Covers.com, has analysed the conversation between Cummins and his wife - detailing what she believes was said.

View this post on Instagram

Pat Cummins and his wife Becky (pictured at a different time) were filmed in a heated exchange on Wednesday, as his old team-mate Usman Khawaja's claims reignited Sandpapergate saga

Cummins celebrates with his wife after winning the Ashes outright last December in Adelaide

While it is unclear the exact context of the conversation, according to the lipreader's analysis, it begins with Becky stating: 'It's too general, you could say you didn't know,' to which Cummins nods in agreement with, before she adds: 'I just watched.'

Cummins then replies: 'I can't stop it. I don't have any say in this matter, frankly that's full my take on it.'

The 33-year-old's reply causes Becky to reply with four-straight sentences. 'You can't keep out of it, right? But you have to stay here. It doesn't mean you're right. And you were part of the plot.'

Following their discussion, Becky later shared a loving picture on her Instagram story with Cummins and their daughter Edith, whose face was hidden, with the caption: 'My loves'.

On Friday, Cummins will address the media at a press conference to have his say on Khawaja's ball-tampering allegations that have reopened the 2018 sandpaper scandal.

Cummins has been rested from the white-ball series against England which begins on Friday in Perth, but has publicly invited a media grilling in Sydney on Friday morning to respond to the accusations which have followed the publication of Khawaja's new autobiography.

Khawaja's memoir Sabr has reopened old scars in Australian cricket, specifically with his claims that knowledge of the sandpaper plot was widespread within the team and coaching staff even though Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft alone were punished.

In an interview with the Sydney Morning Herald, Khawaja said blame was shared by 'all of us', said his calls for collective responsibility were shot down by specific unnamed team-mates and suggested tampering had been going on prior to the Cape Town Test where Bancroft's cheating was exposed.

Becky later shared this family selfie with Pat and their daughter Edith on her Instagram story following their exchange on Wednesday

The Australian captain is under scrutiny following his ex-team-mate Usman Khawaja's claims

Khawaja's autobiography Sabr has reignited questions about Australia's 2018 ball-tampering scandal

His revelations have invited renewed speculation over the role of the bowling group which benefitted from the ball manipulation – with Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon having previously distanced themselves from the episode.

In 2021, the quartet issued a carefully worded statement responding to 'rumour mongering and innuendo' in which they denied knowing that a foreign substance had been taken on to the field to alter the ball.

That line may no longer hold water, given Khawaja's suggestions that the matter was openly discussed and had taken place in the previous match.

Now Cummins, who could find his position as captain of the national team called into question, is set to confront the issue head on.

'I'm training at Cricket Central (in Sydney) tomorrow morning before the Blues play in the Shield match,' he wrote on X.

'Happy to speak with any and all media about the events of this week at 9.30am. I've taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly. Afterwards please stay and support the Blues! I'll ask CA (Cricket Australia) to send out details.'

Starc appeared at a sponsor's event earlier this week, offering a stiff response that reiterated his previous position.

'As far as our statement said, we weren't aware of things being taken on the field, that's where I'll leave it,' he said.

'I'll stick to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people, and I'll leave it where I left it back then.'

Sports.title: Revealed: Shocking attack on UFC star in luxury Abu Dhabi hotel was revenge mission four months in the making - here's why brotherhood of ruthless Dagestani fighters were out for blood
Sports.content:
Revealed: Shocking attack on UFC star in luxury Abu Dhabi hotel was revenge mission four months in the making - here's why brotherhood of ruthless Dagestani fighters were out for blood

Offend one Dagestani and you offend them all. No region on earth has a higher concentration of lethal fighters than the North Caucasus of Russia on the edge of the Caspian sea.

They regard themselves as a brotherhood and UFC star Merab Dvalishvili's brutalised face from Wednesday's extraordinary hotel brawl was the result of a revenge mission four months in the making.

Of those highly-trained Russian killers, the Nurmagomedov name inspires the most reverence and pride, with retired Khabib – who famously destroyed Conor McGregor in the UFC's biggest ever fight – receiving almost a mythical status.

It was his 28-year-old cousin Usman, trained by Khabib's venerated late father, who initiated the violent 10-man melee in the lobby of Yas Hilton in Abu Dhabi, a plush five-star beachfront hotel. Everyone involved has been arrested.

Usman, 28, is a free agent and had been hoping to sign with the UFC – so why did he jeopardise his own future by slapping one of their biggest stars?

The Georgian-American Dvalishvili has a pre-existing rivalry with Usman's older brother, Umar, having beaten him for the bantamweight title last January, calling him a 'brat' and 'spoiled', suggesting the only reason for his title challenge was the connection to Khabib, who retired a national hero with a 29-0 record.

WARNING – Graphic content

UFC star Merab Dvalishvili was left battered and bloody after being attack in the lobby of Yas Hilton in Abu Dhabi

Umar (top and bottom left) and his brother Usman (top and bottom right) are part of a large cohort of Dagestani fighters who regard loyalty above all else

But that defeat and those tame jibes weren't the primary cause of the hotel retaliation.

Back in July, Dvalishvili was competing in a RAF event in Georgia, which is a freestyle wrestling show the UFC allow their fighters to compete in outside of the day job.

While milling around at the event, a Dagestani wrestler and friend of Umar, Ahmed Gadzhimagomedov, confronted Dvalishvili about refusing to entertain a rematch of any kind with Umar.

'I was super relaxed, super chilled and then somebody (Gadzhimagomedov) came and grabbed my neck and pulled me over and started yelling at me in Russian language, which I hardly understand,' Dvalishvili told Ariel Helwani.

'And he mentioned Umar. It took me a couple of seconds to realize, "Who is this guy to tell me what to talk about him?"

'It’s between me and Umar… I have so much respect for all Dagestani people, especially fighters. The only guy who I don't like from Dagestan is Umar and his sneaky manager, Rizvan. The guy who was helping Umar disrespect me on X and Threads.'

After Gadzhimagomedov squared up to him, Dvalishvili shoved him in the neck, shouting: 'What's your problem, b***h!'

The situation, unlike the hotel brawl that escalated into a complete bloodbath, was quickly diffused and there was a child in close proximity.

Umar was cornered by his cousin, UFC legend Khabib (right) in his 2025 defeat by Dvalishvili

Islam Makhachev, another high-profile Dagestani fighter and current UFC welterweight champion, all-but confirmed that the row in Georgia was behind the gang of his countrymen attacking Dvalishvili.

He wrote on his Instagram story: 'To those who are now condemning Usman and the guys, writing insults to them, why were you silent when Mirab hit the Dagestan wrestler for nothing and insulted him?

'A man approached to talk to him without any evil intention. What happened today, Merab started in his homeland, allowing himself to hit a guest and hitting his mother.'

Interestingly, Dvalishvili is due to fight on Saturday and if his injuries now rule him out of that, it could have more severe legal implications for Usman.

According to Abu Dhabi law, an assault that leads to 'incapacity from personal work for a period exceeding twenty days' fits into the upper tier of potential punishments – which can be more than a year in prison. Even the lower end of severity is up to a year in prison and a fine.

At this point, there are no official charges for Usman and his group of attackers but the infamously strict Abu Dhabi authorities may want to make an example of them after such shocking footage of the attack went viral.

In the footage, the group appeared to approach Dvalishvili, 35, from behind, before one man said a couple of words to him and punched him in the face.

Dvalishvili was rocked, then kicked, and was held back by a man he appeared to be with.

He tried to fight back but a number of men overwhelmed him as his companion was attacked too. Eventually, the groups were separated, and Dvalishvili took to social media to respond to the incident.

Usman (left) is a free agent who had hopes of signing with the UFC but that is now in doubt

He said in a video, bloody and bruised as he received treatment: 'What a sneaky way guys. Just two of us, me and my friend, came here in Abu Dhabi and Usman and his friends came like snakes from behind. What kind of fighters are you guys? What kind of man does this? If you want to fight, let's do it the real way.

'You guys came when there was two of us, you were prepared. What the f***.'

His companion then added: 'From behind? You call yourselves men? You're a little b***h.'

Dvalishvili continued: 'You are sneaky guys. You are not real men. It shows your guys' character, what the f*** guys? If you want to fight, let's fight. We are fighters. I talk straight, but you guys came from behind. I don't know how many guys, all your friends waiting for us in a sneaky way, wow.

'I knew guys, I knew what kind of guys you were. Usman, Umar and his friends came sneaky from behind, so many guys. Wow. I am fine guys. All my friends and family, I am f***ing fine. I am a fighter. This is nothing for me, but it shows what kind of people you guys are. P***ys do this bro. We are warriors.'

Dvalishvili said in a separate post on social media: 'So funny, my young friend, he is only 21 years old, a wrestler from Georgia. He was with me and he fought both brothers, Usman and Umar, and he only has this face, nothing else. He said I'm moving to MMA, if they can do only this to me, two guys...

The Georgian-American Dvalishvili (right) won a unanimous decision over Umar in 2025

'Oh my God bro, security was holding me, and they were kicking and punching us, and what the heck. Life is good, guys, everything is good.'

There's a couple of weight divisions difference between Usman (lightweight) and Dvalishvili (bantamweight).

If the UFC were to conveniently overlook the kind of behaviour they'd condemn from their own fighters and sign the free agent, a fight to settle the score would be a guaranteed money-maker.

For now the more serious contest for Usman will be with the Abu Dhabi authorities.

Sports.title: Harry Kane is waiting for ‘perfect situation’ before return - could Man Utd now provide it?
Sports.content:
“I’ll be honest, I am really not sure,” was the diplomatic response from Harry Kane during his latest interrogation this week.

On the eve of the match which will see England's captain become the most capped player in Three Lions history, Kane, the newly minted Ballon d'Or holder, still cannot escape talk of a romantic return to the Premier League.

Perhaps understandably so. That Kane has gone on to become the very best player on the planet since swapping Tottenham for Bayern Munich only serves as a reminder of the unfinished business he has on these shores.

A return to the Premier League, where Kane is just 47 goals short of eclipsing Alan Shearer as the outright leading scorer, is still viable even with the striker committing himself to Bayern until 2029 earlier this month. As does another crack at the domestic title that eluded him during some of Tottenham's finest days.

‌



Kane has been respectful if not totally dismissive when pressed on the prospect of him gracing the Premier League again. “When I think about coming back, it isn’t just about the record (top goalscorer in the Premier League), there are things I haven’t achieved yet," he told talkSPORT.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

“But since I’ve been away, it has really opened my eyes that there is a big old world out there, and I think people are appreciating my game more.

‌



“So, I think it would have to be a perfect situation for me to ever come back, and I can’t see where that would be… One day, anything is possible.”

Spurs are believed to hold an option which would enable them to position themselves ahead of any suitors should Kane deserve to bring the curtain down on his storied career in familiar surroundings. That, coupled with Kane's affection for the club, naturally make them seem the most likely option should he decide to depart the Bundesliga in a blaze of glory at some point between now and 2029.

But is the idea more romantic than realistic? And, if it is, then perhaps one of the most influential figures from Kane's past at Tottenham has the scope to throw a spanner in the works.

Mauricio Pochettino will soon become the latest name tasked with rejuvenating Manchester United, with the club currently languishing in the relegation zone after an abysmal start to the campaign. Kane flourished with Pochettino at Spurs, scoring 169 goals in 242 appearances under him. Together, they took Spurs to a Champions League final and to the cusp of Premier League glory before things slowly unravelled.

‌



View 4 Images Kane excelled under Pochettino at Tottenham (Image: PA)

The prospect of reuniting with Pochettino in Manchester, rather than north London, would be an intriguing one. And while Spurs may have Kane's heart, prospective interest from United and Pochettino could make things more difficult if it's a case of head over heart.

After all, Tottenham may be better off in terms of league position but few would deem them to be in significantly better health than United, even in their current state. After all, six months ago Spurs only narrowly escaped relegation on the 38th and final league outing of their 2025-26 campaign. And with results under Roberto De Zerbi largely proving to be as volatile as their incumbent head coach, it's anybody's guess as to where Tottenham will find themselves in six months time.

Of course, none of that should take away from United's own malaise. Pochettino is no fool and will know he is far from entering anything close to the ideal work environment. The manner in which Carrick's position went from indisputable to untenable in six short months tells the story there. As does the fact that nobody is solely directing the finger of blame at him for United's current woes.

‌



Of course, none of that particularly adds up to a persuasive sales pitch for the newly minted best footballer in the world.

But Kane also knows better than anybody what Pochettino is capable of building. Only time will tell whether or not the Argentine is able to rehabilitate Manchester United with the current hierarchy in situ, but the same coach who elevated Tottenham to challenging for major honours should certainly be capable of it.

View 4 Images Pochettino will succeed Michael Carrick at Manchester United (Image: Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire)

First, Pochettino will have to reinforce that he still possesses the magic that has seen him become a permanent resident on United's radar over the last decade. His stint at Paris Saint-Germain finally brought an end to Pochettino's silverware drought in an arc that bears stark similarities to Kane's own odyssey to reach champion status. But his frolic in Paris, plus his subsequent spell at Chelsea, have failed to yield the same acclaim as his Tottenham tenure.

‌



If Pochettino can prove his powers have not waned, then Manchester United - and their pulling power - inevitably will rise again.

A player of Kane's calibre will always be attractive to a club like United. And even with his advancing years, United would not be turning down the chance to acquire a world-class player, particularly given their current striker options are hardly ultra enticing.

From Kane's perspective, he will want to play in a team capable of ensuring he continues to dine on silverware. If there is a desire to return to England, that non-negotiable significantly narrows the field in terms of elite teams available to him.

Liverpool spent in excess of £120m on an elite striker last year. A move to Arsenal would torch his affiliation with Spurs and we can probably take Manchester City out of the equation for now given the current goings on. Who does that leave? United, Spurs and perhaps Chelsea, although again you wonder if Kane would be reluctant to join one of Tottenham's local rivals.

‌



View 4 Images Kane has won some of the biggest accolades in football since joining Bayern Munich (Image: Jeff Spicer - UEFA, UEFA via Getty Images)

Of course, neither United or Spurs fit the bill in terms of title contenders, but Kane isn't going anywhere right now. In terms of which is the more likely to reach that level over the next couple of years, if this is still the Pochettino of old, then you would feel safer backing him over De Zerbi and Spurs.

Pochettino's influence on Kane cannot be discounted. There is a reason he has been admired by Manchester United for years.

Pochettino previously claimed that the 'ideal scenario' for him to manage United never materialised despite previous flirtations - language which is not too dissimilar to that used by Kane when asked about a return to England.

‌



For Pochettino and United, the stars finally aligned. They could yet in terms of a Pochettino-Kane reunion down the line.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino must learn from Michael Carrick's biggest flaw to turn around Man Utd
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino must learn from Michael Carrick's biggest flaw to turn around Man Utd

Michael Carrick leaves Manchester United with his popularity in tact, but his relaxed demeanour was part of his downfall and Mauricio Pochettino can't afford to follow suit

View 3 Images Michael Carrick's time as Manchester United boss is up (Image: Getty Images)

One of the good things Michael Carrick did during his time as Manchester United manager - and he did a few - was to disband the leadership group that had been formed by Ruben Amorim.

‌



‌



Quite how he had found six leaders in the squad in the first place was anybody’s guess, but Bruno Fernandes, Harry Maguire, Diogo Dalot, Noussair Mazraoui, Lisandro Martinez and Tom Heaton formed a leadership group under Amorim. Carrick put an end to it. And the subsequent antics of some of those members showed it was a sound move.

‌



But what Carrick should have put in its place was another leadership group. A leadership group of ONE. The manager.

‌



Carrick had his moments. He was decisive. He sanctioned Martinez and Fernandes for what he clearly saw as ill-advised comments. He was not afraid to make contentious selection decisions. But it is hard not to wonder if Carrick was too protective of his players when things began to go badly awry.

And it is hard not to wonder if Carrick was too indulgent with his players after they had served him well in his 17 matches last season.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

They performed excellently for Carrick but returned for the start of this campaign - what should have been the manager’s first full one at the helm - looking complacent and not fully fit. There was little snap in the tackle, little aggression in duels, little urgency in ball retrieval.

‌



Carrick should have been furious with complacency that was a product of doing decently for half a season and a product of the mentality that appears to have undermined so many United playing careers in recent times. You have signed for United, you have made it - the hardest of yards are no longer needed.

It is a mentality that every manager since Sir Alex Ferguson has had to fight against. To a man, to varying degrees, every manager has lost that fight.

‌



Make sure you don't miss the best Man Utd coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

View 3 Images Michael Carrick was perhaps guilty of being too friendly with his players (Image: Catherine Ivill - AMA, Getty Images)

‌



Perhaps Mauricio Pochettino has the spirit and the single-mindedness to win it. Perhaps he has the ruthlessness to win it. Perhaps he has the nasty streak to win it. He comes across as a charming character, a nice guy, personable and compassionate.

But let’s face it, he’s an old school Argentinian centre-half. And that’s what he needs to be at heart when he takes over at Old Trafford. No prisoners, no mercy. No treading lightly.

‌



This is a United squad that needs home truths. The captain needs home truths - stop the histrionics and knuckle down. The coasting midfield needs home truths - get fitter and run yourselves into the ground. A whole raft of under-performing players need home truths - signing for United is when the hard work should start.

The people who are employing Pochettino need home truths - the defence is not fit for purpose and needs rebuilding with big money as soon as possible.

‌



View 3 Images Mauricio Pochettino has a huge task ahead of him (Image: Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire)

You could go on and on. Pochettino will, no doubt, be enthusiastic and diplomatic on his arrival. He will pay tribute to the job Carrick has done, as he should. After all, Carrick has left him a squad in the Champions League.

‌



And he will tell the media that he is looking forward to working with the owners and others upstairs. But after that there can be no more Mr Nice Guy.

He has spent the last couple of years in the United States. He knows what hardball is. He needs to play it.
