Ghana News.title: Facing our past and shaping our future together
Ghana News.content:
Dr Christian Rogg, the British High Commissioner to Ghana with President John Mahama

Britain and Ghana cannot change the past, but we can face it honestly, listen carefully and strengthen a modern partnership founded on dignity and mutual respect.

A few weeks ago, I sat in Ghana’s National Theatre and watched The Darkest Chapter, a moving play by Latif Abubakar. It traces a path from the horrors of the transatlantic slave trade through decolonisation and independence to modern Ghana. One line has stayed with me: “before diplomacy, before policy, before resolutions, there were human beings”.

That is where any conversation about the slave trade must begin. With the millions of people torn from their homes, families and communities. With those whose labour and suffering enriched others. And with the descendants and societies that continue to live with that history today.

The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation. People were denied their humanity, separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths. The UK Prime Minister has expressed his “sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people” and recognised the way this history “still shapes our world today.”

Ghana has helped ensure that the world does not look away. Its leadership in shining a spotlight on the slave trade has brought renewed attention to questions that are difficult, deeply felt and important. Ghana’s perspectives have helped shape the wider Commonwealth conversation.

At the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) last week, Commonwealth leaders agreed it was time for a meaningful, truthful, and respectful conversation to forge a common future based on equity. They welcomed the UK Government’s agreement to engage in a structured, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties, addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms. The Prime Minister also met with President Mahama during CHOGM to set out these plans and welcomed the President’s support.

This is an important step, and the United Kingdom enters the dialogue seriously and respectfully. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of the process, and the Prime Minister has said that he is open to them. A dialogue of this importance must allow those most affected to help shape it. Its outcome should not be predetermined, but neither should we underestimate the depth or difficulty of the conversation. The first responsibility is to listen.

One privilege of serving as British High Commissioner is gaining a view of the many layers of the UK’s and Ghana’s shared history. At the British Museum this summer, I saw how one object, the Asante Ewer, can tell a story spanning medieval England, trans-Saharan trade, Asante ceremonial life and the violence and pillage of the Anglo-Asante wars. Such objects do not offer simple stories. They ask us to confront complexity and understand what they mean to different communities.

Other moments remind us how relationships can change. Last year at the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park, I stood with the Duke of Edinburgh before the image of Queen Elizabeth II dancing with President Kwame Nkrumah in Accra in 1961. Ghana had won its independence only four years earlier and was inspiring movements across Africa. That photograph captured our countries’ relationship at a decisive moment as it was reshaped.

Today, the United Kingdom and Ghana meet as sovereign partners. Our relationship is rooted not only in history, but in people, education, culture, business, security and a shared interest in prosperity. That modern partnership gives us a strong foundation for difficult conversations. We should be confident enough to discuss both progress and pain, allow space for honest disagreement, and recognise that listening is part of an equal partnership.

As Ghana approaches its 70th anniversary of independence, there will be many opportunities to reflect on the journey from colonial rule to the Black Star of Africa, and on Ghana’s continuing influence in the world. The United Kingdom should take part in those conversations with humility, openness and respect.

We gather to remember. We also need to listen. The dialogue agreed at CHOGM will not be simple, and some views will be strongly held. But our bilateral relationship is mature enough to face difficult history honestly, to hear each other with respect and to work together towards a common future based on dignity and equity.

*****

The writer, Dr Christian Rogg, is the British High Commissioner to Ghana.

Ghana News.title: Fix produce markets, reduce input costs – 2019 Best Farmer runner-up urges gov’t ahead of 2027 budget
Ghana News.content:
Hours before the government presents the 2027 Budget this evening, one of Ghana’s most decorated farmers has sent a blunt message: fix the market, or farming will collapse.

The Chief Executive Officer of Antika Company Limited and second runner-up at the 2019 National Best Farmer Awards, Alhaji Antiku Abdulai, says farmers are trapped between low produce prices, expensive inputs and the absence of a guaranteed market.

“The marketing policy is important. There is a lot of mess in the system,” he said.

“We expect that the government should come out with a policy that will always mop up the excess produce we produce within the country.”

His argument is that farmers cannot return to the fields for another farming season if they are unable to sell their produce.

“If we are not able to sell as farmers, how do we go back into the farming season? The prices are low; our produce are not being bought,” he lamented.

On the cost of inputs, Alhaji Antiku said existing subsidies were not sufficient to make farming affordable.

“Fertilisers are subsidised, but the farmers are saying it is not at the lowest they can afford,” he said.

“As it is now, all the inputs — the seed, fertilisers and what not — they are very expensive. And the prices of the grains are low. How do we afford those things so that we can go back to the field?”

He is therefore appealing to the government to introduce deliberate measures to reduce the cost of fertilisers, chemicals and certified seeds.

He also raised concerns about the increasing cost of ploughing and harvesting, calling for greater government support for mechanisation to reduce the financial burden on farmers.

“Ploughing cost is going high. Harvesting cost is going high. That is why I talked of mechanisation. If the government brings in the equipment to help the farmers, the prices will come down,” he said.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Prominent Israeli settler denied entry into France
World.content:
The head of an organisation representing illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has been denied entry into France.

Israel denounced the move as “completely unacceptable” on Wednesday after prominent Israeli settler Yossi Dagan said French authorities turned him back last week when he flew into a Paris airport.

Dagan, who is a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, was “subject to an administrative ban from the territory due to his active role in implementing the settlement policy in the West Bank” according to his office.

“Settlement building is contrary to international law and undermines the two-state solution,” the French ministry said.

According to the ministry, Dagan was “pulled aside and questioned” at the airport’s passport control before being informed that he was banned from entering French territory “due to his active role in implementing the settlement policy in the West Bank.”

Dagan said Wednesday that he was undeterred by the ban and was proud to “build the historic homeland of the Jewish people”, while Israeli’s foreign ministry said the measures against Dagan were based on “political and ideological grounds”.

“Israel will demand an explanation from the French government and consider its next steps accordingly,” it added.

Increasing friction

The incident comes amid growing tension between Israel and European countries around illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, which have proliferated under Netanyahu’s government.

France, along with 11 other countries, announced its intention to restrict trade with ⁠⁠⁠⁠illegal settlements in the Palestinian territory in September, which spurred outrage from Israeli officials.



On Monday, a French parliamentary committee approved a bill banning the imports of settlement goods and services contributing to settlement construction, with further discussion scheduled for November 19.

There are at least 148 illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and 15 in occupied East Jerusalem, now home to about 750,000 Israelis, according to Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.

Earlier this year, France banned far-right Israeli ministers, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who are both members of Netanyahu’s cabinet.

World.title: UAE says 14 killed, 30 injured in Fujairah traffic accident
World.content:
At least 14 ⁠⁠people have been killed and 30 others injured in a major traffic accident involving 18 vehicles and 5 trucks in the emirate ⁠⁠of Fujairah, according ⁠⁠to preliminary reports from the ⁠⁠United ⁠⁠Arab Emirates’ Interior Ministry.

The accident happened shortly before midnight (20:00 GMT) at the entrance to the emirate, the ministry said on ⁠⁠Thursday. A truck driver lost control of his vehicle and collided with another, causing both to veer off the road and smash into several vehicles that were stationary due to slow-moving traffic. The truck caught fire before the flames engulfed several other vehicles, the ministry said.

Emergency and specialised teams were continuing to ‌‌deal with the aftermath of the ‌‌accident, the ministry said in a ⁠⁠post on ⁠⁠X. It said 15 people were discharged from hospital after receiving medical care, while 15 others remained in hospital.

Police said the 14 people confirmed killed included Emirati nationals and several foreigners, and that DNA tests are being carried out.

The injured included nationals from the UAE, Oman, India, Brazil, Pakistan, Jordan and Egypt, the ministry added.

World.title: BDS claims win as energy giants quit Israeli gas project off Gaza
World.content:
NewsFeed BDS claims win as energy giants quit Israeli gas project off Gaza

The Boycott, Divest and Sanctions movement is claiming victory after a second international company exited an Israeli-led gas project off Gaza. But who controls the gas reserves in waters claimed by Palestinians? Al Jazeera’s Mikail Malik spoke to campaigners.

World.title: Four people shot in Washington DC
World.content:
NewsFeed Four people shot in Washington DC

A major police operation is underway in Washington DC where four people have reportedly been shot in what has been described as a possible active shooting. An Al Jazeera correspondent at the scene reported seeing dozens of police vehicles at the scene and the suspect may still be at large.

World.title: Manchester United sacked manager Michael Carrick
World.content:
NewsFeed Manchester United sacked manager Michael Carrick

Michael Carrick has become the third recent Manchester United manager to be sacked midway through the season, which leaves the club looking for its eighth boss in 13 years.

World.title: UK court finds two Iranian men guilty of spying for Iran
World.content:
The pair were promised rewards to send intelligence back to Iran, while one was prepared to commit a ‘violent attack’.

Share UK court finds two Iranian men guilty of spying for Iran on social media

Two Iranian men have been found guilty of spying for Tehran by a court in the United Kingdom after being accused of conducting surveillance on several people, including journalists for a Persian-language broadcaster in London.

Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, were convicted on Thursday following a six-week trial at Woolwich Crown Court in south London for engaging in conduct likely to assist Iran’s intelligence service in a bid to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.

These included journalists for Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founding member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner. Iran International is banned by the government in Tehran.

A third defendant, Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, was acquitted on all charges.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was outlawed by the UK in July under new powers to counteract state threats, with penalties of up to 14 years in prison for anyone convicted of supporting or assisting the organisation.

“This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime,” Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service’s special crime and counterterrorism division, told reporters.

He said the pair were promised rewards to send intelligence back to Iran, while Sepahvand was willing to go beyond surveillance to commit a “violent attack” against at least one of the targets.

London’s Metropolitan Police said this was the fourth case in recent years involving direct threats to Iranian journalists in the UK and that it is “working hard to keep them safe”.



“The threat from hostile states to the UK is increasing and Iran continues to adapt its approach to using ‘proxies’,” said Vicki Evans, deputy assistant commissioner at the Met.

“We have seen examples where people who fly into the country to carry out criminal activity and then leave shortly afterwards, others where they use British nationals or, in this case, Iranian nationals with settled immigration status,” she added.

Most recently, Iran has been linked with a plot against a United States-run military airbase in England.

Sepahvand and Manesh were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online.

The pair will be sentenced at London’s Central Criminal Court, better known as the Old Bailey, on December 17.

World.title: Spain approves housing reforms after nationwide strike over costs
World.content:
The Spanish parliament has passed measures to limit evictions and real estate speculation in an attempt to make housing more affordable, a day after a nationwide general strike over the country’s housing crisis.

Spain’s interim lower house of parliament ratified the housing measures on Thursday; however, their duration will depend on the outcome of a snap election scheduled later in November.

The leading opposition party, the conservative Popular Party, has said that it will repeal the measures of the left-wing government if it takes power, which polls indicate could happen.

Large demonstrations over unaffordable housing swept the country in September when televised images of the eviction of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, from her home, shocked many Spaniards.

Protest camps sprang up in several cities, the largest in Madrid’s emblematic Puerta del Sol square. Maricarmen’s subsequent death in October caused national uproar, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority government to rush to present two decrees.

Sanchez called the general election, which had been scheduled for 2027, in response to the parliament’s failure to pass the decrees that included greater protection for tenants against evictions and the automatic renewal of tenant contracts.

The Popular Party and other conservative parties aligned to reject the measures, saying the laws would negatively affect the housing market, and proposed a building spree as the solution to the crisis.

On Wednesday, hundreds of thousands of Spaniards took to the streets in a 24-hour walkout over soaring rents and the high cost of living that the main unions called after the decrees were blocked.



Sanchez introduced another two decrees that were almost identical to the rejected ones. They were presented to a smaller parliamentary council on Thursday, giving the government a better chance of passing the laws.

Housing decrees

The first decree passed in a 35–34 vote and includes a measure extending protections against evictions for tenants deemed by social services to be in a precarious financial or social position, as long as regional authorities cannot offer them an alternative residence.

Another measure attempted to reduce real estate speculation by stopping any company involved in the real estate market from buying properties for less than 70 percent of their value.

However, it was rejected 34-35 after the centre-right Basque party voted with the right-wing bloc after having supported the other decree, on grounds that the measure could lead homeowners to withdraw their properties from the rental market, triggering a drop in supply and even higher prices.

World.title: Ukraine says military Starlink disrupted again as US envoys meet Putin in Moscow
World.content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Ukraine's military is again facing "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv is struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

It came as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, a day after the latest talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.

Zelensky told European leaders in Dublin that Ukraine was trying to clear up the Starlink situation with the American side.

But he added "some things" were already clear: "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going."

He did not elaborate further.

Starshield was developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX company for government and military use. Along with Starlink, it has come to play a vital role in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

A similar issue with connectivity affected the front line in late October and lasted about a week before it was fixed. It remained unclear who had ordered the temporary restrictions on Starlink services at the time, with US officials and SpaceX offering differing explanations.

Zelensky said the current disruption had been ongoing for several days and was "helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine".

World.title: 'We've got to run': Inside ruined Ukraine power plant under constant drone threat
World.content:
As peace talks between Ukraine and Russia continue, Ukrainians are facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts because of intensified Russian attacks on their energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.

Officials are concerned that life will quickly become unsustainable for millions of Ukrainians if power supplies cannot be maintained for at least four hours per day. Some privately warn that's close already, as some families are living with outages of up to 20 hours in Kyiv.

Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson visits one of the country's power stations on the front lines of the war. Devastated by a direct ballistic missile strike, repair work is hampered by frequent air raids.

Read the BBC's dispatch from Ukraine.

World.title: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
World.content:
Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.

Some 1,800 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported receiving a similar threat to one that created chaos in Italy on Wednesday - even though no devices have been found anywhere.

The Italian government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated".

Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.

On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.

The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.

Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.

Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".

Some officials say it originated in Taiwan.

A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has spoken of "a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern".

World.title: Democrat Scott Colom makes history as Mississippi's first black senator since 19th Century
World.content:
Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.

Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be seated in the US Senate since Blanche Bruce served from 1875 to 1881.

Fewer than five thousand votes out of nearly a million counted separated him from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The result means the Democrats will hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.

World.title: Pentagon backs war memorial guard who reprimanded Hegseth's group
World.content:
The Pentagon has given its backing to a US Army guard who reprimanded a group that included US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Arlington National Cemetery.

A video of the Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife, and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

The footage showed the army sentinel on duty stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored - and will always honor - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."

On Thursday, he presented an award to the soldier who reprimanded his group.

Hegseth "welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026," the Pentagon said in a statement.

In a post on X showing the soldier, Hesgeth said: "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist."

The Arlington National Cemetery etiquette requests that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.

The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.

A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.

It is not unusual for them to admonish visitors to the site, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. They reportedly do so a few times a day.

World.title: Millions of Ebola dollars missing with staff unpaid while virus spreads, charity says
World.content:
Hundreds of millions of dollars meant to help tackle Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo are not reaching the intended recipients, a medical charity has warned.

A report from MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF) said that while the outbreak remained "out of control", front-line workers were going unpaid, lacked proper training and were struggling with shortages of essential supplies.

It added that in some cases ambulances had run out of fuel.

More than 5,400 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.

This makes it the second-most deadly outbreak of the disease ever recorded.

MSF has urged the Congolese government and UN agencies to "strengthen oversight and accountability" to ensure money already disbursed is effectively utilised.

This means "ensuring response personnel are properly trained, paid, equipped, and supported, and directing resources towards areas where needs are greatest", it said.

The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.

MSF's warning adds to concerns raised by Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) last month, when it said that $700m (Â£527m) out of $962m disbursed to organisations implementing Ebola response was unaccounted for.

At the time, Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya said it was too early to describe it as embezzlement, characterising the issue as a major transparency and financial reporting failure.

The Congolese health minister echoed these concerns, saying that aid agencies were required to provide details of their work so the ministry could provide oversight but that only 22% had done so.

"Our requirement is clear: transparency must be total. The response relies on a single plan, a single budget, and a single coordination," Health Minister Samuel-Roger Kamba said on X., external

World.title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says
World.content:
The Israeli military said in a statement that its "precise strike" had targeted the commander of Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade, who it named as Mohammed Abu Ismail, alongside other fighters who were "hiding inside" Nasser hospital.

"The terrorists were struck in order to remove the threat they posed after turning the Nasser hospital compound into a headquarters and operating from there to advance dozens of terrorist plots against our forces and restore the brigade's force," it alleged.

The military added that it had issued advance warnings before the strike and released an audio recording of what it said was one given to a senior Gaza health official. But Fara insisted the hospital had received no warning of an attack.

A Hamas statement rejected the Israeli military's accusations, calling them "a blatant attempt to justify a documented crime targeting a civilian medical facility whose function and purpose are well known".

"The nature of the targeted site and the casualties inflicted on patients, doctors and medical staff expose the falsity and weakness of this narrative," it said.

However, local activists circulated claims overnight that the strike may have targeted a senior Hamas security figure who was hiding inside the building.

Fara said this was the seventh time that Nasser hospital had been struck during the war. In August 2025, a double Israeli strike killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and health workers.

The World Health Organization (WHO) said it had documented a total of 1,056 attacks on healthcare in Gaza over the past three years, resulting in 1,010 deaths.

"Gaza's health facilities are lifelines for its people. They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked," warned Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the UN agency's director general.

Later on Thursday, at least four more Palestinians were reportedly killed in separate incidents in northern and central Gaza.

Medics said three were killed in Israeli air strikes in Gaza City, Jabalia and Deir al-Balah, while the fourth was killed by Israeli gunfire in Bureij refugee camp.

The Israeli military said it struck a "terrorist" in Deir al-Balah and another in Gaza City.

Israeli strikes on Gaza take place almost daily despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas in October last year.

More than 1,620 people have been killed in Gaza since then, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza also remains dire and has recently deteriorated further as a result of heavy rains last weekend that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

World.title: Five new miniature frog species found in eastern Himalayas
World.content:
Scientists have discovered five new species of tiny horned frogs in India's eastern Himalayas, more than doubling the number of known species in the group.

A team of scientists from University of Delhi and Harvard University made the discoveries after five years of fieldwork, identifying the frogs as members of the Jingophrys group.

Among them is Jingophrys tanogogo - or the snail-eating horned frog - the first frog known in India to feed on snails and the first member of its family recorded with such a diet.

The research suggest the Himalayas have played a much larger role in frog evolution than previously thought and highlight the region as an overlooked hotspot for biodiversity.

World.title: Alleged Defamation: FIJ founder Soyombo visits detained colleague, says he’s ready to appear in court
World.content:
Investigative journalist Fisayo Soyombo says he will appear before the Federal High Court in Abuja on 1 December for his arraignment over reports published by the Foundation for Investigative Journalism (FIJ), even though he has yet to be officially served with police charges.

Mr Soyombo announced this on Facebook on Thursday after visiting his colleague, Daniel Ojukwu, at the Kuje Correctional Centre, where he has been held since his arraignment on Monday before the Federal High Court in Abuja.

In a Facebook post, Mr Soyombo said he decided to appear in court after FIJ’s lawyers briefed him on the proceedings.

He stated that he had not been served with the criminal charge and proof of evidence, either personally or through substituted service, but would attend the proceedings out of respect for the court.

Mr Soyombo also noted that the Inspector-General of Police had reportedly described him as being at large and sought a bench warrant for his arrest.

“I will be in court,” he said, adding that he had no reason to run.

He described Mr Ojukwu as being in good spirits during the visit, saying he was smiling and cracking jokes despite his detention. He, however, expressed concern about his colleague’s long-running battle with asthma.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Soyombo was accompanied by Funke Adeoye, founder of Hope Behind Bars Africa, and Busola Ajibola, deputy director of journalism at the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID).

Press freedom groups demand Ojukwu’s release

Mr Ojukwu was remanded at the Kuje Correctional Centre on Monday by Justice Joyce Abdulmalik of the Federal High Court, Abuja, after his arraignment on 12 counts of cyberstalking and criminal defamation.

The charges stemmed from FIJ reports on alleged irregularities involving Adeojoke Orelope-Adefulire, a presidential aide on sustainable development goals and former Lagos State deputy governor.

Mr Ojukwu pleaded guilty to the 12 counts. Justice Abdulmalik ordered his remand for 21 days in the first instance after ruling that his bail application was not ripe for hearing. The application was adjourned until 1 December.

The Wole Soyinka Centre for Investigative Journalism (WSCIJ), the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and the Coalition for Whistleblowers Protection and Press Freedom (CWPPF) have condemned his detention and called for the withdrawal of the charges.

In separate statements, the organisations questioned the use of criminal laws against journalists reporting on public spending and government activities.

CPJ’s Africa director, Angela Quintal, called on Nigerian authorities to drop the charges against both Mr Ojukwu and Mr Soyombo and repeal laws that criminalise journalism.

The CWPPF also questioned why Mr Ojukwu should remain in custody until December before his bail application is heard. It argued that the offences are bailable and that his continued detention raises concerns about the constitutional presumption of innocence.

The coalition cited Sections 22 and 39 of the 1999 Constitution, which recognise the press’s responsibility to hold government accountable and guarantee freedom of expression.

Mr Ojukwu was previously arrested in May 2024 over FIJ reports concerning the same government office. He spent 10 days in police custody before his release on 10 May following public pressure.

The current prosecution relates to four FIJ investigations published between November 2023 and January 2024. The reports examined alleged irregularities in government contracts and expenditure under the Office of the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Sustainable Development Goals.

Mr Soyombo thanked those who had spoken out against his colleague’s detention and urged them to continue defending press freedom.

“The quest to protect the freedom of the press requires relentless courage in the face of fire; none of us must give up!” he said.

World.title: Afreximbank facilitates $3 billion investment in 21 countries – Official
World.content:
The African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) says its African Sub-Sovereign Governments Network (AFSNET) has facilitated investment opportunities worth over $3 billion across 21 African countries, including Nigeria, in five years.

Gainmore Zanamwe, director of Trade Facilitation and Investment Promotion at Afreximbank, disclosed this on Thursday in Calabar during a news conference at the sixth edition of the AFSNET platform.

Mr Zanamwe said the initiative had also trained more than 2,000 people in investment promotion, entrepreneurship and project development to strengthen their capacity to identify opportunities and attract financing.

He explained that the platform was established in 2021 to extend Afreximbank’s development interventions beyond national governments to states and other sub-national authorities.

According to him, the initiative seeks to connect entrepreneurs, investors and financial institutions while enabling states to maximise opportunities in agriculture, manufacturing, tourism and the creative industry.

He said the platform was also designed to ensure that young African entrepreneurs benefited from opportunities created by the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).

Mr Zanamwe explained that although AfCFTA was negotiated by national governments, sub-national authorities and businesses needed to understand its provisions and position themselves to benefit from emerging continental markets.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the initiative was helping businesses identify investment opportunities, develop bankable projects and access potential investors beyond their immediate environments.

He added that Nigerian entrepreneurs could explore markets in countries such as South Africa and Ghana, as well as other destinations across the continent.

The director said Afreximbank was targeting all 55 African countries but prioritising those that need technical support to build their investment promotion capacity.

He disclosed that the bank had also committed a two-billion-dollar facility under the initiative to support agricultural production, processing and exports.

“Some people say funding is a problem. From Afreximbank, we say no. The $2 billion is there.

“We have this facility ready to finance projects. We will be showing you how you can tap into the $2 billion to do your projects,” he said.

Clear investment visions

Mr Zanamwe urged state governments to develop clear investment visions, identify priority projects and package them appropriately to attract investors and financial institutions.

He said Afreximbank was also strengthening state investment promotion agencies through training in project identification, development and investment readiness.

According to him, the platform will promote African Direct Investments by encouraging investors within the continent to finance viable projects in other African countries.

He said the sixth edition of the network would also prepare Nigerian businesses and investment institutions for the next Intra-African Trade Fair, scheduled to be held in Lagos from 5 November to 11 November 2027.

Mr Zanamwe said the broader objective was to stimulate intra-African trade, promote industrialisation and create decent employment opportunities, particularly for young people across the continent.

He expressed optimism that the engagement would strengthen collaboration among governments, entrepreneurs, investment promotion agencies and financial institutions.

The News Agency of Nigeria reports that this year’s AFSNET edition will be held in Calabar between Thursday and Sunday.

World.title: Makinde gives reasons for challenging Tinubu in 2027
World.content:
Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde has explained why he withdrew his support for President Bola Tinubu and decided to challenging in the 2027 presidential election.

The Allied Peoples Movement (APM) presidential candidate cited what he described as the Tinubu administration’s failures in economic development, governance, national unity and the protection of Nigerians from the effects of economic reforms.

Mr Makinde, who will be completing his second and final term as governor in May 2027, said his decision to contest against Mr Tinubu, the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential candidate for the upcoming poll, was not driven by a personal disagreement or an ambition to occupy the presidential seat, but by his loss of confidence in the direction of the federal government.

In a newsletter published on Thursday on his official website, the governor said he supported Mr Tinubu in the 2023 election because he believed the president would build a government of national unity and competence capable of addressing Nigeria’s economic challenges and improving citizens’ living conditions.

“Three years later, I no longer believe his administration is taking us in that direction,” he stated.

Mr Makinde identified four major concerns: economic stabilisation without corresponding development, what he described as the government’s reliance on excuses, the use of political alliances to consolidate power rather than promote national unity, and the implementation of economic reforms without adequate protection for citizens.

On the economy, the governor acknowledged improvements in some macroeconomic indicators under Mr Tinubu but argued that such gains had not translated sufficiently into productive businesses, employment, better incomes and improved living conditions.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Government revenues and external reserves mean little to ordinary Nigerians if those gains do not translate into productive businesses, jobs, better incomes and improved living conditions,” he said.

He also faulted the administration for what he described as its continued reliance on inherited challenges to explain poor outcomes, arguing that Nigerians should be seeing measurable progress in tackling poverty, insecurity and electricity problems.

“Every government inherits problems, but it is elected to solve them,” Mr Makinde said.

The governor further criticised the Tinubu administration for prioritising political objectives over the national interest through its alliances, while expressing concern about what he described as the weakening of opposition parties, which he said were essential to a functioning democracy.

He said he had initially expected Mr Tinubu’s political experience and ability to build alliances across political divides to translate into an inclusive government that would bring capable Nigerians together around a shared national interest.

On economic reforms, Mr Makinde said he supported the need to reform the petrol subsidy and foreign exchange systems but believed the government failed to adequately prepare for the consequences of its decisions.

“I expected those reforms to be implemented with adequate preparation for their consequences. Instead, millions of Nigerians who were already struggling were exposed to further hardship before sufficient measures were in place to protect them,” he stated.

What Makinde says he would have done differently

Using petrol subsidy removal as an example, Mr Makinde said he would have used the presidential transition period to prepare for the policy and its likely effects on Nigerians.

He argued that Mr Tinubu should have anticipated the hardship associated with subsidy removal, recalling that the president opposed the abrupt removal of the subsidy when former President Goodluck Jonathan attempted to end the policy in 2012.

He also pointed to the petrol and naira scarcity crises before the 2023 election, saying Mr Tinubu had witnessed the difficulties Nigerians faced at the time.

He stated that, upon assuming office, he would have convened the National Economic Council to agree on a coordinated response with state governors, identify interventions to protect Nigerians and determine how they would be funded.

He said the federal, state and local governments would also have agreed on how to deliver the interventions, with transparent reporting to show how much was spent, who benefited and what results were achieved.

Mr Makinde maintained that economic decisions should not be judged only by their financial or macroeconomic objectives but also by how they affect the people the government is elected to serve.

“Nigerians deserved better preparation and better protection,” he said.

Makinde pledges one-term presidency

Explaining his decision to seek the presidency, Mr Makinde said his background and experience had shaped his belief that the government should create opportunities for Nigerians to improve their lives.

He recalled growing up in a lower-middle-class family, attending Bishop Phillips Academy in Ibadan and studying Electrical Engineering at the University of Lagos before establishing an engineering business at the age of 29.

He said access to education, useful skills and opportunities enabled him to build a career and expand his business beyond Nigeria, adding that he was concerned that many young Nigerians could no longer reasonably expect similar opportunities.

Mr Makinde said his experience in philanthropy eventually convinced him that helping individuals through personal donations was insufficient to address the scale of the country’s challenges, prompting his entry into politics.

After unsuccessful attempts to win public office between 2007 and 2015, including two attempts to secure a Senate seat and one governorship bid, before he was elected governor of Oyo State in 2019.

He said his experience governing the state had strengthened his belief that public institutions could make a difference when they focused on creating opportunities, building institutions and following through on decisions.

The governor, who declared his intention to contest the presidency on 14 May 2026, said he could not wait until 2031 or 2035 to seek national office because he was concerned that another four years of what he described as the current trajectory could further damage the economy, national institutions and opportunities available to younger Nigerians.

Mr Makinde said his proposed alternative is contained in the Reset Nigeria Agenda, which he described as a plan setting out the changes his administration would pursue, how they would be implemented and the measurable results Nigerians should expect.

He also pledged to serve only one four-year term. “I have committed to serving one four-year term as President, leading a transitional government of national unity focused on measurable progress.”

The 2027 presidential election is scheduled for 16 January, when Mr Makinde will challenge Mr Tinubu and other candidates for the country’s highest political office.

World.title: AFCON Qualifier: We are focused on beating Tanzania, says Chelle
World.content:
Super Eagles coach Eric Chelle says Nigeria are determined to secure maximum points from their two Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) 2027 qualifying matches against Tanzania as they seek to revive their campaign.

The three-time African champions face the Taifa Stars in Uyo on Friday before travelling to Zanzibar for the return fixture on Tuesday, 17 November.

Nigeria head into the double-header under pressure after a mixed start to their Group L campaign, having recorded a 2-1 victory over Madagascar before suffering a 3-0 defeat to Guinea-Bissau.

The results have left the Super Eagles needing a strong response to keep their qualification hopes on track for the tournament, which will be jointly hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

Chelle and captain Wilfred Ndidi have stressed the importance of winning both encounters, with the coach insisting that the players are determined to put the defeat to Guinea-Bissau behind them.

“We must work hard in these two matches and do everything to win. It is important to sustain the hope, and all the players are in that mood to banish the memory of that defeat to Guinea-Bissau and show their true quality.

“The spirit in camp is high, and everyone is focused on achieving victory in both matches,” Chelle said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Franco-Malian tactician will, however, have to manage his attacking options without Victor Osimhen, who was ruled out after sustaining an injury while playing for his Turkish club, Galatasaray.

In the striker’s absence, Nigeria will look to Ademola Lookman, Akor Adams and Tolu Arokodare to provide the goals against Tanzania.

Arokodare, who plays for Ajax in the Netherlands, is among the attacking options expected to shoulder more responsibility, alongside experienced forward Moses Simon.

Chelle also has several options for a possible reshuffle in midfield and defence, with Fisayo Dele-Bashiru, Samson Tijani and Tochukwu Nnadi among them.

Benjamin Fredricks, Chibuike Nwaiwu and Abdullahi Ibrahim Bewene are also expected to provide defensive alternatives.

Tanzania, meanwhile, will be hoping to frustrate the hosts and take advantage of their own attacking options, including experienced forward Mbwana Samatta, Simon Msuva, Selemani Mwalimu and Bernard Kamungo.

The second encounter will take place at the Amman Stadium in Zanzibar on Tuesday, with Nigeria aware that victories in both matches would significantly strengthen their position in the qualification race.

For the Super Eagles, Friday’s meeting offers a chance to respond to their setback against Guinea-Bissau and restore confidence in their bid to reach the 2027 AFCON finals.

World.title: ‘We’ll beat DR Congo all-round’ – Olympic Eagles stars promise ahead of LA 2028 Qualifier
World.content:
Nigeria U23 invitees Zadok Yohanna, Chibuzo Nwoko, and Peter Edokpolor have expressed strong belief in the Olympic Eagles’ ability to overcome DR Congo and take a major step towards qualifying for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.

The Nigerian side faces their Congolese counterparts in Lubumbashi on Friday in the first leg of their qualifying tie, with a place in the Olympic football tournament at stake.

Despite the challenge of playing away from home, the young Nigerians are confident they can return with a favourable result before the decisive second leg.

In a video posted on social media by the Nigeria Football Federation, Brighton and Hove Albion forward Yohanna was particularly emphatic in his message to Nigerians, promising that the Olympic Eagles would not only win in Lubumbashi but also complete the job on home soil.

“Tomorrow, by God’s grace, we will win our game,” Yohanna said.

“We would win both legs. I assure Nigerians that tomorrow, by God’s grace, we will beat DR Congo. We would beat them home and away. Keep us in prayers.”

Benfica forward Peter Edokpolor also backed the team to deliver in the first leg, assuring supporters that the players are determined to return to Nigeria with victory.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I assure Nigerians that we are coming home with the victory,” Edokpolor declared.

Fulham midfielder Chibuzo Nwoko, meanwhile, called on Nigerians to rally behind the team as they prepare for what promises to be a difficult encounter in Lubumbashi.

“We are going to win tomorrow. Please come support us,” Nwoko said.

The Olympic Eagles know that a strong performance away from home could put them in a commanding position ahead of the return fixture, as they pursue Nigeria’s first appearance at the men’s Olympic football tournament in 12 years.

READ ALSO: Zadok Yohanna breaks into 2026 Golden Boy top 100 rankings

Nigeria last featured at the competition during the Rio 2016 Olympic Games in Brazil, where the team, led by Samson Siasia, claimed the bronze medal after defeating Honduras 3-2 in the third-place play-off.

The country subsequently missed the Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 editions, making the current qualification campaign particularly important for a nation with a proud Olympic football history.

A successful two-legged contest against DR Congo would bring the Olympic Eagles closer to ending that absence and securing a ticket to Los Angeles 2028.

World.title: COP31: ‘Africa won’t sacrifice development to decarbonise’
World.content:
African negotiators and civil society groups have said the continent’s shift from fossil fuels must not sacrifice its development, after a Brazil-led roadmap for the transition was presented at COP31 in Antalya, Türkey.

The chair of the African Group of Negotiators (AGN), Nana Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, told journalists in Antalya that Africa needs to make the transition. Still, it has to be a just one, with the finance and technology to implement it.

“African countries have put forward ambitious NDCs and adaptation plans, but most of that ambition depends on finance that has not yet arrived,” he said.

Mr Antwi-Boasiako said ahead of the summit that Africa cannot allow its natural resources to be stranded when it needs them to develop, PREMIUM TIMES reported.

Mithika Mwenda, executive director of the Pan African Climate Justice Alliance (PACJA), a coalition of African civil society organisations, told a high-level dialogue on the roadmap that the transition should be measured by what it adds to energy access, economic transformation and sustainable development, and not solely by how much fossil fuel infrastructure is retired.

Mr Mwenda said developed countries should lead in cutting dependence on fossil fuels, given their historical responsibility for emissions and their greater financial and technological capacity, according to a PACJA statement.

“The roadmap should recognise that Africa’s energy transition must support broader structural economic transformation and must address the structural constraints that prevent African countries from pushing an ambitious and development-compatible energy transition,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

PACJA made the same case in a position paper Mr Mwenda presented at the summit.

“Africa supports mitigation ambition aligned with science and the Paris Agreement—but ambition must be equitable, financed, technology-enabled and compatible with development,” the paper said. “Africa cannot be required to decarbonise without the means to do so.”

The group asked governments at COP31 to recognise energy access as a climate goal. The International Energy Agency said 655 million people worldwide lack electricity, including more than 560 million in sub-Saharan Africa.

The fossil fuels transition roadmap

Brazil’s COP30 presidency published the Roadmap on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels on 3 November as a voluntary guide to help energy systems shift from coal, oil and gas.

The 182-page document was presented in Antalya on Tuesday and is not open to negotiation. It invites countries to prepare national plans for clean energy systems by 2028

Nigeria was among the countries that backed the roadmap, alongside India, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and Australia, according to the report. Nigeria’s representative told the launch that countries’ different starting points were fundamental.

Omotenioye Majekodunmi, director-general of Nigeria’s National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), set out the country’s conditions for the transition in her opening remarks at Nigeria Day at the Nigerian pavilion in Antalya on Wednesday.

“A just transition must be equitable and nationally determined, adequately financed, and responsive to the development realities of emerging economies,” Ms Majekodunmi said.

She noted that Nigeria had come to COP31 to build partnerships that could turn its priorities into action.

“For Nigeria, climate implementation must mean economic opportunity,” she said.

Nigeria’s climate plan puts the cost of meeting its goals at about $337 billion between 2026 and 2035, according to the NCCC.

About $2.5 billion a year went to climate action in Nigeria in 2021 and 2022, counting domestic and international sources, according to data from Climate Policy Initiative.

The UN secretary-general, António Guterres, proposed a climate justice compact on Wednesday to support developing countries’ transition from fossil fuels while protecting people already suffering from climate change.

Mr Guterres called for the roadmap to be fed into the next global stocktake, the review of progress under the Paris Agreement due in 2028. Saudi Arabia and other producers are expected to oppose that.

Call for increased adaptation finance

The AGN is pressing for a target to triple adaptation finance to be given priority in the cover decision, the political text adopted at the close of the summit on Thursday. The group lost its bid on Monday for separate agenda items on the target and on trade.

Mr Antwi-Boasiako told a press conference on Tuesday that the increase needs the right structures and a clear timeline. He addressed the opening plenary on Monday on behalf of the continent, noting that roughly two-thirds of the climate finance reported by rich countries came as loans.

“The transition cannot be called ‘just’ if low- and middle-income countries must mortgage their futures in the process,” he said.

World.title: Obi pledges ₦15 million for Yelewata massacre survivors, nursing college
World.content:
The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has pledged ₦15 million to support survivors and families affected by the June 2025 massacre in Yelewata, Guma Local Government Area of Benue State.

Mr Obi announced the pledges in a statement on Wednesday after visiting the community, where he said he met families affected by the attack.

He pledged ₦10 million to support the education of children orphaned by the massacre and another ₦5 million for the construction of a borehole to improve access to clean water.

“No child should be forced to let the tragedy that has affected their family determine the course of their future,” Mr Obi said.

He acknowledged that the financial support could not compensate for the lives lost or the suffering of survivors.

“Although no financial contribution can restore the lives lost or remove the suffering endured by their loved ones, we have a responsibility to do everything within our power to renew hope, preserve dignity, and create opportunities for those affected,” he said.

The Yelewata community was attacked in June 2025, leaving scores dead and many others displaced.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The incident attracted national and international attention over persistent attacks on rural communities in Benue.

Support for nursing college

During the visit, Mr Obi also pledged an additional ₦10 million to the College of Nursing Sciences in Gboko, established under the leadership of the Catholic Bishop of Gboko, William Avenya.

He said he had supported the institution since its inception and made the latest pledge to strengthen its operations.

“Supporting education and healthcare is an investment in our collective future,” he said.

Mr Obi also visited the Tor Tiv in Gboko, where he said they discussed issues relating to development, peace and the welfare of the people.

Earlier disagreement

Mr Obi’s visit to Yelewata followed previous disagreements with the Benue State Government over his planned visits to communities affected by insecurity.

PREMIUM TIMES reported on 8 September that Mr Obi’s convoy was forced to turn back after suspected thugs and security operatives confronted it along Gboko Road in Makurdi.

His campaign photographer, Esther Umoh, alleged that the men were sponsored to prevent the presidential candidate from entering the state. The NDC governorship candidate, Terhemba Shija, also accused the state government of involvement. The allegations had not been independently verified.

In April 2025, Governor Hyacinth Alia had also cautioned Mr Obi against making what he described as an unscheduled visit to internally displaced persons in the state, citing security and protocol concerns.

Ahead of Wednesday’s visit, Mr Shija again accused the state government of planning to disrupt Mr Obi’s movement to Yelewata. The government denied the allegation, saying it had no plan to interfere with the visit and would ensure visitors’ safety.

In his statement after the visit, Mr Obi thanked Governor Alia, saying he had contacted him before travelling to Benue and the governor had personally returned his call to assure him of a warm reception.

The visit ended with a town hall meeting in Makurdi, attended by Mr Obi, his running mate, Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, and other NDC candidates in the state.

World.title: Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang resigns
World.content:
Nvidia’s Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang has given up his position at the company he co-founded 33 years ago and helped build into a $4 trillion corporation at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom.

He will be replaced at the chipmaker by Colette Kress, the chief financial officer (CFO), as interim CEO.

The company disclosed its board’s decision in a post on its website on Thursday, saying Ms Kress would retain her position as executive vice president and CFO while serving as interim chief executive until a permanent successor is appointed.

The board said it had begun searching for a permanent CEO and will consider both internal and external candidates.

The leadership change followed reports of an affair involving Mr Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, and a company employee named Kimberly Powell.

Mr Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in an email to Nvidia’s employees on 8 November.

Nvidia’s board subsequently announced an independent investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The board said at the time it had no reason to believe Nvidia’s trade secrets or US national security had been compromised, but that its inquiry would examine available information.

The controversy also attracted investor attention, with Nvidia’s shares coming under pressure amid concerns about corporate governance and the potential implications of a leadership change.

“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the company said in the Thursday statement.

Mr Huang co-founded Nvidia alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in April 1993, and has led the company as its chief executive since its establishment.

Ms Kress joined Nvidia in September 2013 and has led its finance organisation, contributing to the company’s growth and development.

Before joining the chipmaker, she spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.

In her first statement as interim CEO, Ms Kress said the company will build on the foundation established by Mr Huang over the past 33 years.

“Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” she said.

She added that the company will continue advancing its work in accelerated computing and artificial intelligence while focusing on customers, partners, developers and shareholders.

The board also appointed Harvey Jones as its first-ever chair. Mr Jones has more than 30 years of experience as an entrepreneur, technology executive and venture investor.

He previously served as chief executive and executive chairman of Synopsys.

Commenting on the appointment, the board chair, Mr Jones, said Ms Kress has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of significant growth and has a deep understanding of its business, customers, operations and financial position.

He stated that the board has confidence in her and the leadership team, adding that it expects the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.
