World.title: Liberia: LDEA Boss, Deputies Test Negative for Drugs Ahead of Senate Confirmation
World.content:
MONROVIA – Newly appointed Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) Director General Daniel Dee Ziankahn, Jr. and his two deputies have tested negative for drugs as they prepare to appear before the Liberian Senate for confirmation.

By Edwin G. Genoway, Jr.

Ziankahn and his deputies, Precious Rue, Deputy Director General for Operations, and Prince Mulbah, Deputy Director General for Administration, underwent drug testing on Wednesday at the Wellness Health Center in Congo Town, outside Monrovia.



A team of journalists witnessed the testing process, and all three officials received negative results. Speaking after the test, Ziankahn said officers responsible for fighting illegal drugs must first demonstrate good character and discipline by setting an example for the public.

He said the decision to undergo testing before their confirmation was intended to show that the new leadership is prepared to follow the laws it is expected to enforce.

“As security officers, especially those fighting drugs, we need to lead the way and set the standards. As you can see here today, we came to do our drug test before going for confirmation,” Ziankahn said.

The LDEA’s fight against illegal drugs is built around four major areas: intelligence-led operations, drug prevention and demand reduction, institutional accountability and professionalism, and coordination with national and international partners under the National Anti-Drug Action Plan.

The agency’s intelligence-led operations are intended to stop the supply of illegal drugs by strengthening border security, monitoring major entry points and targeting trafficking networks that use Liberia as a transit route.

Its prevention and demand-reduction strategy focuses on educating the public, particularly young people, through school anti-drug clubs, community awareness campaigns, treatment and rehabilitation programs.

The agency also seeks to improve discipline and professionalism among its officers through drug testing, proper training and a zero-tolerance approach to corruption and misconduct.

Another key part of the strategy is cooperation among security institutions, health authorities, communities and other partners to ensure a coordinated national response.

Ziankahn has pledged to work with these strategies and strengthen their implementation to make the LDEA more effective, disciplined and professional.

He also urged officers of the agency to remain committed, focused and honest in carrying out their responsibilities, stressing that the fight against drugs must begin with accountability within the institution itself.

His appointment comes at a time when the LDEA has faced public criticism and questions about its leadership and effectiveness in fighting drug trafficking.

The leadership change followed the indefinite suspension of former Officer-in-Charge Fitzgerald Biago amid major cocaine seizures and investigations involving the agency’s previous administration.

The developments raised concerns about accountability, internal discipline and the agency’s ability to effectively fight the illegal drug trade. President Joseph Nyuma Boakai subsequently appointed Ziankahn and his two deputies in an acting capacity to take charge of the agency while the Senate confirmation process moves forward.

Meanwhile, some Liberians are expressing hope that Ziankahn’s appointment will bring meaningful changes to the LDEA and restore public confidence in an institution that plays a major role in protecting the country from illegal drugs.

Some believe his military and security background could help strengthen discipline within the agency, improve its operations and ensure that officers involved in drug enforcement carry out their duties professionally.

Others expect the new leadership to go beyond arresting street-level drug users and focus more attention on major dealers, suppliers and trafficking networks responsible for bringing illegal substances into the country.

There are also expectations that the new administration will investigate allegations of corruption within the agency, ensure that officers found guilty of misconduct are held accountable and prevent powerful individuals from interfering with drug investigations.

Young people and communities affected by drug abuse are also expected to benefit from stronger public education, prevention programs and rehabilitation services of the Zainkahn’s administration.

However, some Liberians believe the real test of the new leadership will not be its promises but its ability to produce visible results, including reducing the availability of illegal drugs, dismantling trafficking networks and rebuilding public trust.

For many observers, Ziankahn’s appointment presents an opportunity to change the public perception of the LDEA and strengthen the country’s fight against drug abuse and trafficking.

Zainkahn’s Senate confirmation still ahead, expectations are high that the new leadership will work with the agency’s anti-drug strategies and turn them into practical results.

World.title: Chipolopolo face Burundi seeking to stay in AFCON race
World.content:
Zambia face Burundi at home on Friday afternoon, seeking to stay in the race for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) on matchday three of the qualifiers.

Kick-off is 15:00 hours at the Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola.

Algeria top Group I with four points, one point ahead of Zambia and Togo, who are both on three points. Burundi are bottom on one point.

Ahead of the match, Chipolopolo coach George Lwandamina said Zambia will need an element of madness to get the edge over Burundi.

“It won’t be an easy game, but what I have asked for from my players is the element of madness that will give us the edge,” Lwandamina said.

On injuries in the squad, Lwandamina said football is a physical game and injuries are expected, but Zambia are not short of replacements.

He said he is confident that those called up to replace the injured players have been working very hard and doing well.

Zambia have suffered injuries to striker Patson Daka, Libya-based Lameck Banda, Gamphani Lungu and Kingstone Mutandwa.

The replacements are Edward Chilufya, Prince Mumba and Derrick Bulaya.

“It is an opportunity for them, but I have to rely on the other players. These players we are bringing in have been feeding from the same pot as those who are injured, so I doubt if we have to bring something else. It is the same pot,” Lwandamina said.

He said the team is ready for the game, and the players are ready for the challenge, as they know what is at stake.

“We have this game; it will give us the perimeter. We are ready for this game, and the players are ready for the challenge. They know what is at stake. We just have to wait for the game,” he said.

World.title: Chipangali brothers cleared of referee murder
World.content:
Four (4) brothers who were accused of murdering a referee in Chipangali district, for allegedly failing to award their football team a foul, have been acquitted by the Chipata High Court.

Judge Ketrina Maimbolwa Walubita, making a ruling on whether the quartet had a case to answer, acquitted them, citing lack of evidence linking them to referee, Donald Tonga’s death.

The Tembo brothers – Aaron, Chimanja, Sole, and Thomas – were accused of murdering the referee after he failed to award Mikango United, a foul during a football match on May 7, 2026.

The Tembos were initially charged alongside four others who were later discharged after the state discontinued the case against them and proceeded to trial with the quartet.

The court heard that, during a football tournament between Leopards United and Mikango United, which was sponsored by Chipangali Member of Parliament, Andrew Lubusha, violence erupted after Tonga failed to award a clear foul to Mikango United.

Tonga fled the pitch toward the tournament executives, but was pursued by irate players, forcing officials to advise him to hide for his safety.

He allegedly ran into the bush, where there was a traditional Gule Wamkulu shrine called, Dambwe.

Three of the accused were allegedly seen running after the referee, but no eyewitness saw them hitting him.

In her ruling, Ms Justice Walubita noted that defence lawyers from the Legal Aid Board, Blessed Mbewe and Newton Tembo, indicated that the referee had run into a Dambwe, noting that there are dire consequences for trespassers into the shrine.

She further stated that the prosecution’s evidence showed that the four brothers had a confrontation with the deceased that started on the pitch and escalated into a nearby bush.

The judge said it was not in dispute that the role played by the four was merely pushing the referee, which did not amount to causing any injury.

Ms Justice Walubita also noted that witnesses called before the court repeatedly said the referee was attacked by Mikango United players and supporters.

She, however, wondered how a mob of players and supporters was narrowed down to just four people.

“Even taking the prosecution’s evidence at its highest, there is no evidence from which malice aforethought may be inferred,” Ms Justice Walubita ruled.

(By Mayengo Nyirenda/Zambia Daily Mail)

World.title: FAZ launches new national cup competition
World.content:
The Football Association of Zambia (FAZ) has launched the KCM-ZFA Cup, a new national cup competition featuring both men’s and women’s tournaments, sponsored by Konkola Copper Mines (KCM).

The inaugural 2026 edition will bring together 32 teams competing across 31 matches in five rounds, culminating in the crowning of the first-ever KCM-ZFA Cup champions.

Speaking at the launch in Chingola, FAZ President Keith Mweemba described the competition as his brainchild and said it will undoubtedly be the biggest cup competition in Zambia.

Mweemba thanked KCM for its continued commitment to football, noting the mining company’s long-standing relationship with FAZ through the provision of vehicles, sponsorship of domestic football and, more recently, support for the senior national teams, the Chipolopolo and Copper Queens.

He said the Cup was conceived as part of his vision for the development of Zambian football, with a determination to introduce new ideas, expand opportunities for clubs and create meaningful platforms for the growth of both men’s and women’s football.

“One of the gaps he identified was the absence of a dedicated national cup competition for women’s football, an imbalance that needed to be addressed given the remarkable progress of women footballers on the continental and international stages,” Mweemba said.

Meanwhile, KCM Deputy Chief Executive Officer Satish Kumar announced that KCM has committed a total investment of US$1.6 million this year towards supporting Zambian football, including the launch of the inaugural KCM-ZFA Cup.

Kumar said the investment includes support for the senior national teams, the Copper Queens and Chipolopolo, alongside broader efforts to strengthen football development at different levels.

Kumar said KCM is steadily ramping up production in support of Government’s ambitious three-million-tonne copper production target, but firmly believes its growth must go hand in hand with the social and economic development of communities.

He said building a strong football nation cannot begin and end with senior national teams, but must start at the grassroots, where young and emerging talent is identified, nurtured and given opportunities to develop.

He urged participating teams, coaches, match officials and administrators to uphold discipline, sportsmanship, professionalism and fair play, and encouraged young footballers to play with passion, work hard, respect the game and believe in their abilities.

World.title: ZDA to invest commitments worth 5 billion US dollars towards IZIC
World.content:
The Zambia Development Agency (ZDA) is targeting investment commitments worth 5 billion United States dollars at this year’s Invest Zambia International Conference (IZIC), as the country seeks to attract more local and international investors into key sectors of the economy.

Speaking during an exclusive interview with the media ZDA Director General, Albert Halwampa, says the conference scheduled for December 9th to 11th, will provide a platform for investors, policymakers and private sector players to explore business opportunities, establish partnerships and conclude investment deals.

Mr Halwampa highlighted that last year’s conference attracted approximately 2,500 delegates, with close to 1,000 participants coming from outside Zambia, demonstrating growing interest in the country’s investment opportunities.

He disclosed that the conference will focus on opportunities in mining, energy, agriculture, manufacturing and infrastructure, which have been identified as key sectors in supporting the country’s economic growth agenda.

The Director General noted that Zambia’s ambition to increase copper production to three million tons annually presents significant opportunities for investors, particularly in mining exploration, mineral processing and value addition.

Mr Halwampa stated that agriculture will also be a major area of discussion, with opportunities arising from the country’s targets to increase maize, soybean, wheat and sugar production, as well as expand beef exports.

He revealed that the conference is not only intended for foreign investors but also provides opportunities for local businesses to establish partnerships, access investment incentives and participate in the country’s economic development.

Mr Halwampa has also disclosed that the minimum investment threshold for wholly Zambian-owned businesses to access investment incentives through ZDA has been reduced from 500,000 United States dollars to 50,000 dollars

He has since encouraged local and international investors, policymakers, private sector players and other relevant stakeholders to participate in the conference, saying the ultimate goal is to translate investment commitments into actual projects, employment opportunities and economic growth.

World.title: Serenje Central MP assures prudent use of CDF
World.content:
Serenje Central Member of Parliament (MP), Friday Katombi has pledged to ensure the prudent use of the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) to drive sustainable local development.

Bishop Katombi emphasized the importance of proper resource allocation and transparency under the current decentralization framework.

Speaking when he featured on Millennium Radio Programme “I Heard Segment,” Bishop Katombi said he will prioritize allocating funds to projects that require urgent attention.

“We have places that need bridge repairs and some other places that need feeder roads fixed,” he stated.

Bishop Katombi said he will work closely with the Ward Development Committees (WDCs) and community members to ensure prudent and accountable use of CDF allocations.

He said there is need to introduce strict measures, work alongside Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) and key stakeholders to ensure all allocated funds are fully utilized and none are returned to the local authority

Bishop Katombi further assured that he will see to it that every member of the community benefits from the CDF, leaving no one behind regardless of their political affiliation.

World.title: Chilanga Council pushes Keep Zambia Clean Campaign
World.content:
Chilanga Town Council Chairperson, Buumba Mulunda, has called on businesses and institutions to take a proactive approach in supporting the Keep Zambia Clean, Green and Healthy Campaign.

Mr Mulunda says maintaining clean frontages is a shared civic responsibility and should not be left to the local authority alone.

He added that all businesses, institutions and residents must take pride in their surroundings and contribute towards a cleaner, greener and healthier district.

Mr Mulunda said this when he engaged various institutions and business establishments, including Chilanga Cement, Indo Zambia Bank and Puma Energy Service Stations, on their responsibility to maintain clean and orderly surroundings.

He explained that the exercise forms part of the Council’s continued stakeholder engagements aimed at enhancing environmental management in the district.

“The exercise is aimed at promoting cleanliness and proper maintenance of business and institutional frontages,” Mr Mulunda stated.

He was accompanied by Council Secretary, Stephen Malenga, and technical officers from the Departments of Public Health, Engineering, Planning and the Public Relations Unit.

Discussions during the engagements centred on clearing litter, maintaining road verges, ensuring proper waste disposal and providing adequate waste bins to discourage indiscriminate littering.

Mr Mulunda further disclosed that the exercise will be extended to more establishments in the coming days to ensure full compliance.

This is contained in a statement made available to the media by the Chilanga Town Council Public Relations Unit.

World.title: Kasama residents welcome relocation of street vendors
World.content:
Kasama residents have welcomed the relocation of street vendors from the Central Business District (CBD) to designated markets.

Some residents who spoke in an interview with the media, observed that the move has restored order and cleanliness in the town centre.

Josephat Mulenga, said the development has also reduced the risk of traffic accidents within the CBD.

Mr Mulenga has since urged all residents to rally behind the local authority in its quest to ensure that all forms of trading and businesses are conducted with sanity.

“What I have observed is that the town is very clean and that congestion which was there before is not there, so even the danger of accidents has reduced,” he said.

Another resident, Jennifer Bwalya commended the Kasama Municipal Council for undertaking the removal of street vendors.

Ms Bwalya said claims by vendors that there is no business in the markets are unjustifiable, urging both traders and residents to comply with the law.

She noted that the development will go a long way in minimising the risk of disease outbreak.

Meanwhile, Joan Chilufya, a trader at Chikumanino market, urged the council to be on the lookout for some vendors carrying their merchandise in bags and baskets.

Ms Chilufya said trading spaces are still available in the markets calling on the local authority not to relent in enforcing the law.

And the Kasama Municipal Council has commended street vendors for responding positively to the relocation order.

Council Public Relations Manager, Charity Chaiwila said the local authority is pleased that there was no resistance from the vendors.

She added that the relocation exercise is being conducted in phases.

“Now that these vendors have moved into the markets, we shall now start dealing with illegal installation of mobile money booths,” she said.

Ms Chaiwila disclosed that both the council and State Police will continue manning the streets to ensure total compliance.

World.title: It’s a full squad as Chipolopolo step up Burundi preps
World.content:
Chipolopolo have stepped up preparations for Friday’s Group I Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Burundi, with Coach George Lwandamina now having a full squad in camp in Ndola.

All the players called in to replace the injured trio of Patson Daka, Lameck Banda and Gamphani Lungu have reported for duty.

Iraq-based Prince Mumba of Al Gharraf SC, Edward Chilufya of Hapoel Jerusalem and Derrick Bulaya of Green Eagles have all joined camp, boosting Lwandamina’s options ahead of the crucial double-header.

Zambia will, however, still be without Kingstone Mutandwa, Ackim Mumba and Jackson Phiri, who were ruled out of the back-to-back assignments due to injury.

Lwandamina has been leading the 30-member team in training, with the final 26 expected to make the cut for the home fixture.

Zambia hosts Burundi on Friday at the Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola at 15h00 CAT.

Algeria tops Group I with four points, one better than Zambia and Togo, while Burundi are rooted to the bottom on one point.

Only the top two teams will qualify to the PAMOJA 2027 AFCON to be hosted by Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.

Meanwhile, forward Kings Kangwa is back in camp after missing the first two qualifiers through suspension.

CAF have confirmed he will be eligible for the return leg against Burundi on 17 November in Bujumbura.

World.title: Africa: Africa Made It: Turning Africa's Cotton Wealth into Jobs, Industry and Economic Power
World.content:
Africa Made It campaign was launched in Lagos, Nigeria, aiming to drive Africa's industrial sovereignty under the theme, "Power, Protect and Purchase."

Africa produces cotton, inspires global fashion and boasts a vibrant creative industry. Yet much of the economic value generated from these resources is captured beyond the continent. Launched during CANEX WKND 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria, the Africa Made It campaign seeks to change that narrative by promoting local manufacturing, strengthening Africa’s textile value chain and encouraging consumers to support African-made products.

Africa’s fashion and textile industries hold considerable potential to drive industrialisation, create employment and strengthen the continent’s economic independence. However, despite its abundant natural resources and creative talent, Africa continues to capture only a limited share of the value generated by its cotton and fashion industries.

The Africa Made It campaign, launched during the Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX) WKND 2026 in Lagos, aims to address this imbalance by encouraging African countries to move beyond exporting raw cotton and invest in a fully integrated fibre-to-fashion value chain.

Built around three pillars “Power, Protect and Purchase” the campaign seeks to mobilise governments, investors, manufacturers, fashion brands and consumers to strengthen local production and retain more economic value within Africa.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The initiative highlights the potential of the sector to contribute an estimated US$34 billion annually to Africa’s GDP through increased domestic textile and garment production.

In an interview with AllAfrica’s Nontobeko Mlambo, Abimbola Ogundairo, Senior Consultant at Africa Practice, discusses the campaign’s ambitions, the challenges facing Africa’s textile industry and the lessons other African countries can draw from Benin’s emerging manufacturing sector.

What inspired the Africa Made It campaign, and why is it important for the continent?

Africa Made It is a movement designed to showcase the investment potential of African-made brands, starting with the fashion industry.

Its significance lies in a challenge we have faced for decades: Africa contributes enormous value to the global economy but captures very little of the wealth generated from its resources.

Take cotton, for example. Thirty-seven of Africa’s 54 countries produce cotton, yet the continent captures less than 2% of the global cotton economy. And cotton is only one example. The same challenge exists in other sectors, including cocoa and gold.

Africa Made It aims to bring these conversations together and address the missing links in our value chains, particularly the lack of local processing and manufacturing capacity. We want to engage policymakers, development institutions, investors, businesses and other stakeholders across the value chain to explore how we can connect these different elements.

The objective is to ensure that more of the value Africa produces remains on the continent rather than being exported for others to benefit from.

How does the campaign align with CANEX’s broader ambition to develop Africa’s cultural and creative industries?

Platforms such as CANEX are incredibly important because the creative industries have long been overlooked as sources of economic value and cultural identity. Across Africa, young people are achieving remarkable things in fashion, music, art and other creative sectors, often despite limited institutional support.

Africa already exports enormous cultural influence and creative talent. Our fashion, music and artistic expressions have a global presence. The question is whether we have the mechanisms in place to capture the economic value associated with that influence.

CANEX provides an opportunity to bring the right stakeholders together. It allows creatives to showcase their achievements while engaging directly with policymakers, investors and institutions capable of providing the infrastructure, financing and policies they need.

What makes these platforms particularly valuable is their ability to move the conversation beyond isolated initiatives towards coordinated, sustainable solutions. We need to institutionalise the support systems that allow creative businesses to grow and ensure that the economic benefits generated by African creativity remain within the continent.

What are the campaign’s main objectives, and what changes does it hope to bring to Africa’s fashion and textile industries?

The campaign aims to unlock the enormous economic potential of Africa’s cotton-to-fashion value chain.

Research estimates that an investment of approximately US$1.8 billion across the continent could help create up to two million permanent jobs and generate US$33 billion in annual household income. For African countries seeking to accelerate industrialisation, increase revenue and create employment, this represents a significant opportunity.

Benin provides an interesting example. Through the development of the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone, the country has begun transforming its cotton industry.

According to the figures we have seen, Benin has moved from exporting approximately 90% of its raw cotton towards processing around 30% locally. The country is also reportedly exporting about 10 million garments annually and aims to create 300,000 permanent jobs by 2030.

These developments demonstrate what can be achieved when investment, infrastructure and industrial policy are aligned. This is why our campaign is built around three pillars: Power, Protect and Purchase.

Power means providing African manufacturers and businesses with the energy, financing and infrastructure they need to operate and expand.

Protect focuses on creating fair trade policies and addressing illicit imports and other practices that undermine the competitiveness of local industries.

Purchase is about encouraging governments, businesses and consumers to buy African-made products.

We must move away from the assumption that foreign products are inherently better. Buying African is not only an expression of cultural identity and pride. It is also an economic decision that supports local businesses, creates employment and strengthens our economies. Ultimately, we want to build a movement that brings all stakeholders together to close the gaps in Africa’s manufacturing value chain.

Why is it important for African consumers to recognise, support and take pride in locally made fashion?

As a Nigerian, I grew up in a society where people take enormous pride in wearing traditional clothing and expressing their cultural identity. For many Nigerians, wearing local styles is already part of everyday life. However, there is an important economic dimension to this conversation.

We may proudly wear African prints and traditional fabrics without realising that some of these materials are manufactured outside the continent. Ankara, for example, is widely associated with African fashion and identity, yet much of the fabric is produced elsewhere.

This raises an important question: when we celebrate our cultural identity through fashion, are we also supporting the local industries and workers who should benefit from it?

Cultural pride should translate into economic empowerment. We need to ensure that the clothes we wear and the products we celebrate contribute to employment, manufacturing and wealth creation within our own countries.

Africa has contributed immense cultural and economic value to the world for generations. We should also be able to capture the financial benefits of that contribution. We do not want to become a continent that proudly wears its cultural identity without benefiting economically from it. We can do both: celebrate who we are and build industries that create prosperity for our people. That is the thinking behind Power, Protect and Purchase.

What specific activities, partnerships or initiatives are needed to turn the campaign’s ambitions into tangible results?

Everyone has a role to play in building a sustainable African fashion and textile industry. The value chain begins with cotton farmers, who need access to agricultural inputs, technical skills and resources to improve the quality and productivity of their crops. It extends to processing facilities, storage, transportation, manufacturing infrastructure and the policies required to attract investment.

Governments have a responsibility to create enabling environments, while investors must recognise the opportunities available across the industry. Fashion businesses also have an important role. They should consider whether they are sourcing materials locally, working with African manufacturers and supporting artisans within their communities. The media and other storytellers can help raise awareness of the industry's potential and highlight successful initiatives. Development institutions and international investors also have opportunities to contribute.

Regional integration is particularly important.

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) provides a framework for strengthening trade and industrial cooperation across African countries. For example, cotton could be grown in Nigeria, processed in Benin and transformed into finished garments elsewhere in the region. Different countries could contribute at various stages of production, allowing more of the economic value to circulate within Africa.

We should also recognise that fashion extends beyond clothing. Technology is creating new opportunities, including the use of artificial intelligence to improve garment design, sizing and the consumer experience.

The industry encompasses accessories, innovation, logistics and many other activities. Our challenge is to connect these different elements and ensure that businesses have access to the resources they need to grow.

You have highlighted Benin as a success story. What lessons can other African countries learn from its experience?

Close 

One of the most important lessons from Benin is the value of creating an environment that encourages private investment. The Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone demonstrates how cooperation between the public and private sectors can support industrial development. The government has played a role in facilitating investment and establishing conditions that encourage manufacturing. Such partnerships are important because building a textile industry requires substantial investment in infrastructure, energy, transport and production facilities.

Benin’s experience also shows the importance of moving beyond the export of raw materials towards local processing and the production of finished goods. The country is now reportedly exporting approximately 10 million garments annually. Other African countries can learn from this approach by developing policies that attract investors, encourage industrial partnerships and support local manufacturers. Ultimately, the lesson is that industrial transformation requires coordination, long-term commitment and a willingness to invest in domestic value creation.

How will you measure the success of the Africa Made It campaign?

The campaign is designed to raise awareness, encourage dialogue and connect stakeholders across Africa’s cotton-to-fashion value chain. In the short term, success will mean generating greater recognition of the opportunities available in the sector.

We want to see more conversations involving policymakers, investors, development institutions, manufacturers and fashion businesses. We also want these discussions to lead to practical collaboration. That means identifying where investment is needed, which policies require reform and how institutions can work together to support local businesses.

African entrepreneurs should not have to succeed despite structural obstacles. They should be able to thrive because the right infrastructure, policies and institutional support are in place. In the longer term, success will be measured by tangible economic outcomes. We want to see investment mobilised, manufacturing capacity expanded and sustainable employment created.

The estimated US$1.8 billion in investment and the potential US$33 billion in annual household income illustrate the scale of the opportunity.

If African countries, investors and businesses work together, we can build stronger industrial value chains and ensure that more of the wealth generated by Africa’s resources and creativity benefits African people. That is the transformation Africa Made It hopes to achieve.

World.title: Niger: UNHRC Calls For Millions in Emergency Aid to Fill Critical Gaps
World.content:
Geneva — The UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, warned on Tuesday of a deepening crisis that has caused tens of thousands of people to flee from Nigeria to neighbouring Niger and Benin, where problems of malnutrition and disease are surfacing.

Dominique Hyde, UNHCR director of external relations, said at a UN press conference in Geneva that nearly 64,000 people have arrived in Niger fleeing violence in northern Nigeria since the beginning of the year.

“They are adding to the growing humanitarian needs in a country already hosting more than half a million refugees and asylum-seekers, including some 327,500 from Nigeria, alongside people displaced within Niger itself,” said Hyde.



In the past decade, attacks by Boko Haram, Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) fighters and criminal gangs have displaced millions of people fleeing the violence.

“The impact of the violence is also being felt further afield, with several hundred Nigerians seeking refuge in neighbouring Benin,” said Hyde.

“Although the numbers remain relatively small compared to arrivals in Niger, these movements highlight the widening geographical impact of insecurity in northern Nigeria and the increasing distances families are travelling in search of safety.”

UNHCR said that most arrivals have sought safety in Diffa, in south-eastern Niger, and Tahoua, in western Niger, both bordering Nigeria, which are already grappling with insecurity, climate shocks and overstretched services.

The refugee agency said in October alone, around 1,200 people crossed into Diffa and another 3,400 into Tahoua, as violence continued to force families from their homes.

THOUSANDS OF NEWLY-ARRIVED REFUGEES

“Thousands of newly arrived refugees, many of them children, are struggling to survive with limited access to food, clean water, shelter and essential services, as humanitarian resources fall critically short,” noted Hyde.

In Diffa, more than 23,000 people, over two-thirds of them children, have arrived since the beginning of the year.

Many are living in makeshift shelters that offer little protection from the elements, while access to clean water remains a major challenge.

“Refugee women describe having to walk several kilometres to collect water for their families. With no nearby health facilities or schools, families are struggling to meet even their most basic needs,” said Hyde.

The UN agency said that protection concerns are growing and only around 5 percent of Nigerian refugees who arrived this year have been registered, due to limited resources.

Close 

Without documentation, refugees face additional barriers to accessing assistance and essential services, leaving them exposed to heightened protection risks.

“Education is another major concern, particularly for children arriving from Nigeria’s English-language-based education system, with no schools or transitional classes at some locations,” explained Hyde.

UNHCR said an urgent increase in humanitarian assistance, stronger coordination and additional operational partners are needed to address critical gaps in water, food, shelter, health care, registration and protection.

Beyond emergency assistance, greater investment is needed in livelihoods and longer-term solutions.

The refugee agency said it urged the international community to urgently fill these critical gaps while investing in more stable, sustainable futures for refugees and host communities, as it calls for $11.4 million for emergency solutions in Niger, Nigeria and Benin.

World.title: Africa: Can Carbon Markets Help Africa Close Its Climate Finance Gap?
World.content:
Aerial view of Monboyo River and peatland forest of Salonga National Park south-east of Mbandaka, Democratic Republic of the Congo. The most carbon-rich tropical region in the world is estimated to store the equivalent of three yearsâ worth of total global fossil fuel.

interview

Africa is in a difficult financial situation regarding climate change. The continent accounts for less than 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions yet is one of the most climate change-exposed regions in the world. Droughts, floods, and increasingly erratic rainfall are all having a major impact on people, their livelihoods, and their economies. At the same time, there are massive climate investment opportunities on the continent, such as renewables, clean cooking, forest conservation, land restoration and sustainable agriculture.

Africa needs hundreds of billions of dollars every year to underpin clean energy, climate adaptation and resilient development, and yet it still receives a very small share of global climate finance. A large proportion of that finance is in the form of loans rather than grants. Local institutions and project developers often find it very difficult to access the finance they need to deliver on the ground.

Private investment and carbon markets are increasingly considered as a way to close the gap. Through mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and voluntary carbon markets, countries can attract private capital to support emissions-reduction projects while advancing their national climate commitments. Several African countries are already moving. Kenya has updated its laws to attract carbon market investment. Ghana is building an Article 6 pipeline covering clean cooking, low-emission rice farming, waste management and electric mobility. Senegal has also authorised initiatives supporting the transition to electric vehicles.

High project development costs, limited access to financing, regulatory uncertainty and concerns over carbon pricing can prevent promising initiatives from reaching implementation. There are also questions about who benefits from the revenues generated by carbon projects, particularly when they involve community land and natural resources.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

At COP31, the real challenge will be in translating those climate commitments into investments that can actually be scaled up.

Jocelyne Landry Tsonang, Co-Founder of Nature Crest, Verified Carbon Market Collaborative (VCM+) Fellow, has over 11 years of experience in structuring carbon and green finance projects across Central and West Africa. She talks about what needs to change in order to unlock climate finance for Africa, how carbon markets can support Africa's development priorities, and why communities need to have a greater share in climate finance, including in relation to the super pollutant projects.

Can you walk us through your journey from environmental and natural resource management and circular economy work into co-founding Nature Crest and becoming a VCM+ Fellow?

I started my career in 2014 at a national consultancy firm in Cameroon, where I was appointed directly as Head of the Natural Resource and Environmental Management Unit. I coordinated proposal development and project delivery with teams of consultants, and led the preparation of major national strategic documents for Cameroon. I then joined an international consultancy firm, where I focused on circular economy roadmaps across Africa. I was part of the team that developed Africa's first national circular economy roadmap for Rwanda, and went on to work on roadmaps for Tunisia, Ghana and Cameroon, among others.

A turning point came when I was selected for the Young African Leaders Programme at the European University Institute's School of Transnational Governance. Those three months of intensive lectures and practical sessions opened my eyes to how far Africa lags in access to sustainable and climate finance. I decided not to return to full-time consultancy and to devote most of my time to closing that gap instead.

I joined Green Bond Corporation part-time as Project Manager for Africa, working on large projects with ticket sizes of at least U.S.$100 million. That work was valuable, but another layer needed attention. So, with a few associates, I co-founded Nature Crest to tackle the problem at the source: building stakeholders' capacity and developing and structuring carbon projects. Carbon finance is a tangible way to fund environmental projects, and their co-benefits attract development finance too. As a market-based tool, it is also far more within reach of national and subnational governments and communities than climate finance mechanisms that are often complex and inaccessible.

Becoming a VCM+ Fellow was a natural continuation, because the platform's core principles align closely with my work at Nature Crest. Through AFRICO2, we are building a one-stop shop that makes Africa's carbon project ecosystem more transparent and accessible. And through Nature Crest, we want to increase the flow of carbon and climate finance into Francophone Africa, which is why Nature Crest and Green Bond Corporation are co-convening the Central Africa Sustainable Investment Forum (CASIF) in June 2027.

You have spent more than 11 years working on carbon and green finance projects across Central and West Africa. What has your experience taught you about the biggest barriers preventing African climate projects from accessing finance?

There are many barriers, but a few stand out.

The first is the low development of regulatory frameworks, which are a prerequisite for attracting investment. Investors want clarity on who owns the carbon rights, how benefits are shared and how authorisations work, for instance under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Where these rules are missing, investors simply wait.

The second is low access to information. You are sometimes surprised that even top government officials don't have access to key information on carbon markets and climate finance opportunities. Without that information, it is hard to put the right policies in place.

Language is also a barrier. Major communications are done in English, and even the media interested in these topics are predominantly English-speaking. Carbon markets don't speak French yet, and Francophone Africa is too often left out of the conversation.

Then there is the lack of technical capacity to structure fundable projects. Many good ideas never reach investors because they are not packaged the way investors need them to be.

Finally, perceived country risk plays a role. Even a solid project can struggle to attract finance, or pay more for it, because of how its country is perceived. That is why capacity building and transparency are at the heart of our work at Nature Crest and AFRICO2.

Africa has huge potential for climate action, from forest conservation and restoration to renewable energy. But many projects are stuck in the transition from idea to implementation due to a lack of financing. What needs to change to unlock more investment into African climate projects?

First, we need to get project structuring right. Most projects don't make it to financing because they are not well structured or not mature enough. A good idea is not yet a bankable project: investors need a clear business model, solid data and a credible implementation plan. Capacity building is the way to bridge this gap, both for project developers and for the public institutions that support them.

Second, project developers need to know exactly which doors to knock on for funding. They have to go out and look for it, and not just sit back waiting for funds to come searching for them.

Third, investors should look beyond the perceived risk of a country and focus on its actual solvency: its track record and how consistently it repays its loans. That gives a much fairer picture than perception alone.

Finally, we need to make climate finance cheaper. Today, the cost of capital for clean energy projects in Africa is two to three times higher than in advanced economies. This has to change, because when it comes to climate, the development of one is the thriving of all. Every project with climate benefits in Africa is a gain for the whole planet.

Carbon markets are increasingly being presented as a way of attracting private financing for climate action. How then can African countries make use of these markets without ending up too dependent on carbon credits or putting their development objectives at risk?

The carbon market is a market-based tool, so it operates on the rules of supply and demand. Prices go up and down, and demand can shift. That is exactly why African countries should treat carbon finance as an additional source of funding, not the only one.

Used well, these markets are an important tool for African countries because they serve not only climate objectives but development objectives too. Imagine a community that develops an agroforestry project. The community benefits from the crops grown on the project land. The project creates jobs for the most vulnerable members of the community, giving them a steady income. It funds local infrastructure such as classrooms and clean water systems, and sometimes even financial literacy training, which can be life-changing. A project like this delivers far more than carbon benefits.

Carbon finance can also be an additional source of funding for clean energy, clean mobility, clean water and clean cooking projects, which all bring real development benefits to local communities.

To avoid dependence and protect their development objectives, countries should make sure that every carbon project developed on their territory is aligned with national development goals and builds lasting wealth. This is where clear national frameworks matter. The money earned from this market should then be reinvested in other development projects, so that carbon revenues drive sustained national development rather than becoming an end in themselves.

Private investment is usually driven by the desire to achieve financial returns, while local communities focus on matters like livelihoods, land rights, and access to resources. How are carbon and green finance projects able to reconcile the interests of investors with the needs of local communities?

It starts with genuine stakeholder consultation, not a box-ticking exercise. Communities must be consulted before a project begins, through a process of free, prior and informed consent, and they must have the right to say no.

Projects should be done with the communities and should work for the communities, not against them, so that their dignity is preserved. In practice, this means clarifying land and carbon rights from the start, agreeing in writing on how the benefits will be shared, and giving communities a real voice in how the project is governed.

Access to information is just as important. Communities need to understand what is happening on their land, what the project earns and what they are entitled to. This requires several layers of information sharing, such as community meetings, local languages, local radio and community representatives, not just technical reports that are not accessible to everyone. Communities must also be able to flag a misalignment at any time, through a grievance mechanism that is easy to use and that actually responds.

On the investor side, profit cannot be the only focus. There has to be a balance between profit and impact. But I would add that the two are not really in opposition. A project that communities support is a project that lasts. When communities feel ownership, they protect the forest, they maintain the infrastructure, and the carbon benefits are more durable. When they feel excluded, conflicts arise, projects stall and investors' reputations suffer. Respecting communities is not only the right thing to do; it is also the best way to protect the investment.

Pollutants such as methane, black carbon, and hydrofluorocarbons have a great effect on global warming, yet they are given less attention than carbon dioxide. What opportunities are there for African countries to draw in climate finance in order to reduce these pollutants?

Poor waste management is one of the biggest sources of these pollutants in Africa, especially in our cities. Open dumpsites release large amounts of methane, and the open burning of waste releases black carbon. Cooking with solid fuels at home is another major source of black carbon, which is why clean cooking is also an important opportunity.

Carbon finance can be used as co-funding to run proper waste management systems across the whole chain: from efficient waste segregation at the source, to collection, to the recycling and processing of organic waste through technologies like composting, black soldier fly farming and others. Methane released at existing dumpsites can also be captured and either flared, which turns it into CO2, a far less potent gas, or used to produce energy.

It all comes down to structuring investable projects that can benefit from blended finance, with carbon finance as an important part of the financing model. Carbon revenues alone will rarely cover the full cost of a waste management system. But combined with public funding, municipal fees and concessional finance, they can make the difference between a project that stays on paper and one that gets built.

All big African cities should seriously consider this, because short-lived climate pollutants are having disastrous effects on the people living in them. Air pollution is estimated to cause around one million premature deaths a year across the continent. A good waste management system will also drastically reduce the open burning of waste, which means cleaner air, healthier neighbourhoods and new green jobs.

How can African countries make sure that the funding from carbon markets intended for reducing super pollutants leads to tangible health benefits for vulnerable communities when achieving reductions in emissions?

Emission reductions should never be the only result we measure. For vulnerable communities, the real test of a super pollutant project is whether people breathe cleaner air and live healthier lives.

Close 

First, it starts with where the money goes. The people most exposed to these pollutants are often the most vulnerable: families living next to dumpsites, waste pickers working on them every day without protection, and women and children breathing smoke from cooking with firewood and charcoal. Projects should reach these groups first. A waste management project, for example, can formalise waste pickers and give them protective equipment, decent working conditions and access to health coverage.

Second, we need to measure health, not only carbon. From my experience leading MRV work, what gets measured gets managed. If we only count tonnes of CO2 equivalent, health benefits remain assumptions. Projects should track simple indicators such as air quality around dumpsites or respiratory illness in households. Some carbon standards already allow clean cooking projects to measure and certify the health benefits they deliver, and African countries should make more use of this.

Third, countries should set clear benefit-sharing rules in their national frameworks, so that part of carbon revenues goes back into community health: local health centres, clean water and awareness campaigns. Carbon revenues should be reinvested in development, and health is one of the best places to start.

Fourth, health authorities should be involved from the design stage, so that environmental data and health data speak to each other. Capacity building has a role to play here too.

Finally, communities must have access to information on the results. They should know what the project has achieved and how the money has been used, and they should be able to raise concerns if the promised benefits don't materialise.

At the end of the day, a tonne of methane avoided is good for the planet. But for a community, what makes the difference is a child who no longer coughs because of smoke from a dumpsite or a kitchen.

What concrete commitments should African governments and international climate finance partners call for to raise super pollutants to a climate negotiation priority at COP31?

Super pollutants offer Africa quick wins for both the climate and people's health. They deserve a much bigger place in the negotiations, in Antalya and beyond.

African governments should commit to clear targets for super pollutants in their NDCs, especially in waste management, clean cooking and cooling. They must also invest seriously in data collection, which is paramount to writing fundable projects, and put in place the regulatory frameworks, including clear Article 6 rules, that make these projects investable. Cities, which are on the front line of waste management, need the means to act.

International climate finance partners should commit to dedicated and predictable funding for super pollutants, with a fair share for Africa. They should also make finance cheaper through guarantees and blended instruments, and support project preparation, capacity building, and MRV systems that track both emission reductions and health benefits.

Both sides must make information accessible to all, including in French, so that no country is left behind.

Super pollutants are not a side topic. They are one of the fastest and most cost-effective ways to deliver on the Paris Agreement while improving lives.

World.title: Africa: Author Simbarashe Kundizeza Cleared of AI Allegations
World.content:
Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of allegations that he had used artificial intelligence to write his award-winning short story, The Blue Fighter. The reports had emerged after an article in The Atlantic cited results from an AI detection tool, which suggested that the story may have been generated by artificial intelligence.

Kundizeza won the 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing, which comes with a $13,000 endowment; however, the allegations prompted the Caine Prize to conduct an internal review, which included interviews with the author, judges, publishers, and independent expert analyses of the story's draft metadata. Following the investigation, the prize's board said it had found no evidence of generative AI use, and confirmed that Kundizeza remains the winner.

The organization explained that the matter is now closed, while announcing the introduction of new measures to help guard against AI misuse in future submissions. The day after winning the prestigious Caine Prize award in October, Kundizeza had told the BBC that he was first inspired to pen the book after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.

He said he had woven that in with fictionalized details from his own life in the early 2000s in Zimbabwe, when the country's economic troubles began. The case meanwhile sparked wider debate about the reliability of AI detection tools and the future of literary awards in the age of artificial intelligence.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Medical Charity Warns Funds for DR Congo Ebola Fight Not Reaching Front
World.content:
Health workers in protective gear inside the Ebola treatment centre at Buniaâs referral hospital in Ituri province, eastern DRC.

Six months into Congo's Ebola outbreak, the virus is still spreading out of control and large sums of international aid are not reaching the front line, French medical charity Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said on Thursday.

The current outbreak of Ebola was first detected in the DRC's conflict-plagued Ituri province in mid-May.

It has since killed more than 5,300 people out of more than 11,000 confirmed cases.

Medical charity MSF warned Thursday that the outbreak, the country's worst, "remains out of control".



It urged more "transparency and accountability" from the Congolese state over the "persistant" gap between resources and action.

"A troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and what is actually reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities continues," MSF said in a statement.

Ambulances without fuel

Despite the hundreds of millions of dollars spent by the international community, "many frontline responders are left trying to contain the outbreak with empty hands and empty pockets," said Javid Abdelmoneim, MSF's international president.

"Our teams are often left speechless by the dysfunctions they witness in many areas. Six months into the response, this situation is simply unacceptable."

MSF cited cases of healthcare workers not being paid or trained, ambulances left to run without fuel, a lack of supplies or support for frontline employees and Ebola monitoring "surveillance teams that exist on paper but are nowhere to be seen on the ground".

The charity also warned that some parts of the vast central African nation were seeing an "excessive concentration of efforts... at the expense of other hotspots where needs are increasingly urgent".

These inadequacies have made some hospitals into "new centres of transmission, rather than places of care", MSF warned.

Inside Bunia's fight to protect families from DRC's deadliest Ebola outbreak

'Problematic' virus surveillance system

In one part of the eastern province of North Kivu, "close to three-quarters of Ebola patients contracted the disease in a health facility".

The charity also criticised a "deeply problematic" virus surveillance system.

While it acknowledged that "community mistrust makes surveillance difficult", given the long absence of the Congolese state from many of the hotspots, "urgent improvements in oversight, staffing, and operational support are essential".

The latest outbreak of Ebola, which is transmitted through contact with infected bodily fluids, has also spread across the DRC's borders to Uganda, Kenya and as far afield as Nigeria.

Close 

The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which no approved vaccine or treatment is currently available.

Development of a virus-specific vaccine is underway but could take months.

MSF has called for people at risk to be given broader access to the ERVEBO® vaccine, saying it's the only one currently available at scale.

"For MSF, the absence of a Bundibugyo-specific vaccine should not prevent the use of the only vaccine currently available," sais Guyguy Manangama, epidemiologist and deputy director of operations at MSF.

"Every month spent waiting for dedicated tools leaves healthcare workers, frontline responders, contacts of confirmed cases, and affected communities exposed to a potentially deadly disease."

(with newswires)

World.title: South Africa: Political Parties Have 14 Days to Form New Municipal Councils
World.content:
About 138 municipalities have no political party with enough seats to govern alone, forcing parties to negotiate agreements to share power.

Minister Velenkosini Hlabisa says political fights must not delay new councils or disrupt water, electricity, rubbish collection and other basic services.

Political parties have just 14 days to form new municipal councils after elections left 138 municipalities without a clear winner.

This means parties that fought against each other during elections may now have to work together to run towns and cities.

The Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs has introduced new rules to help parties reach agreements and prevent political fights from affecting residents.



The 138 municipalities make up about 65% of the country's councils.

In these municipalities, no single party won enough seats to govern on its own.

Parties will have to form coalitions, support minority governments or find other ways to work together.

A coalition happens when two or more political parties agree to work together to run a municipality.

But why does this matter to ordinary South Africans?

Municipalities are responsible for services people use every day, including water, electricity, rubbish collection and fixing roads.

When political parties fight over who should be mayor or who gets important positions, it can make it harder for councils to do their work.

Residents still need their taps to run, rubbish to be collected and broken streetlights to be fixed, no matter which party is in charge.

Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs Minister Velenkosini Hlabisa says political negotiations must not delay the formation of councils or interrupt basic services.

He wants parties to put residents first and reach agreements that will keep municipalities running.

Department spokesperson Pearl Maseko-Binqose said the new guidelines will help parties manage disagreements and protect service delivery.

"The guidelines provide practical guidance to political parties and municipalities on managing coalition arrangements, resolving disputes, and ensuring political stability whilst protecting municipal administration and service delivery," she said.

The guidelines were discussed at a government meeting on 9 November 2026 and presented for approval on Wednesday.

They aim to help parties settle disputes and form councils that can continue working even when political disagreements arise.

Hlabisa said parties must focus on stability and fighting corruption.

"I am very confident that the coalition discussions and political parties who can work together, and who can constitute 50% plus one, will find each other," he said.

Close 

He also called on provincial governments to help municipalities follow the new guidelines and step in when political fights threaten their work.

For ordinary South Africans, the next 14 days will be important.

The parties may be negotiating who gets power, but residents will be watching whether the new councils can deliver the services they need.

World.title: Malawi: Nationwide Protests Planned Over Malawi's Economic Challenges
World.content:
Frustrated Malawians are preparing to take to the streets in nationwide demonstrations on 17 November 2026, piling pressure on the government over worsening economic hardships and failing public services.

The protests, organised by a group calling itself Concerned Citizens, are set to take place in major cities and districts including Lilongwe, Blantyre, Mzuzu, Zomba, Kasungu, Mulanje, Balaka, Mchinji, Salima, Chikwawa and Phalombe.

According to a circular issued by the organisers, demonstrators will demand answers over persistent fuel shortages, foreign currency scarcity, electricity blackouts, shortages of essential medicines in public hospitals, water supply disruptions and alleged passport scandals.

The group says Malawians are no longer satisfied with assurances and want government to provide clear, time-bound solutions to the country's mounting challenges.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In a move likely to increase political pressure, the organisers are also calling for the resignation of three Cabinet ministers whom they blame for failures in key sectors.

The ministers named are Finance Minister Joseph Mwanamvekha, Health Minister Madalitso Baloyi and Energy Minister Jean Mathanga.

"The Concerned Citizens are demanding the resignation of the following Ministers," the circular states.

The planned demonstrations come as households and businesses continue to struggle with rising costs, shortages of essential commodities and unreliable public services.

Organisers say the protests are intended to force authorities to account for the country's challenges and outline when ordinary Malawians can expect improvements.

With anger growing over the state of the economy and public services, the demonstrations are expected to become a major test of public sentiment towards the government's handling of the crisis.

World.title: Kenya: Supreme Court to Hear Fresh Challenge to Affordable Housing Levy
World.content:
President William Ruto handed over 180 new affordable housing units in Milimani, Kakamega on March 17, 2026

Nairobi — The government's affordable housing programme is facing a fresh legal challenge at the Supreme Court, reopening the debate over the constitutionality of the 1.5 per cent housing levy after the Court of Appeal upheld the tax.

Peter Okiro has filed a petition of appeal challenging the appellate court's decision that upheld the Affordable Housing Act, 2024, setting the stage for another round of litigation over the government's flagship housing financing programme.

In directions issued on November 11, the Supreme Court ordered Okiro to serve the petition on the respondents by close of business on the same day, with the respondents required to file their responses within 14 days of service.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Okiro will then have seven days to file a rejoinder, if necessary. The matter is scheduled for a virtual mention on December 4, 2026, for further directions.

The directions do not determine the merits of the appeal or suspend the existing housing levy. They set out the next procedural steps as the court prepares to consider the dispute.

The Supreme Court proceedings follow a September 25, 2026 Court of Appeal judgment in which a five-judge bench dismissed 42 consolidated appeals challenging the Affordable Housing Act, 2024.

The appellate court upheld the legislation, finding that the levy was a lawful exercise of the government's taxation powers and that its collection served a legitimate public purpose.

The judges also rejected arguments that the levy violated property rights because it required employees to contribute towards a housing programme from which they might not directly benefit.

"Taxation enacted through Parliament for a clear public purpose does not violate private property rights," said the court in its determination.

"The Affordable Housing Act seeks to respond directly to the constitutional imperative of providing accessible and adequate housing to citizens."

The court further found that different collection mechanisms for formal and informal sector workers did not amount to unconstitutional discrimination, dismissing concerns that salaried employees were being unfairly targeted.

The government had defended the legislation, arguing that Parliament had fulfilled constitutional requirements on public participation through nationwide consultations, stakeholder hearings and the submission of written and oral memoranda.

The dispute has its origins in November 2023, when the High Court declared the housing levy introduced under the Finance Act, 2023 unconstitutional, partly because it lacked an adequate legal framework and discriminated against salaried workers.

Close 

The ruling prompted the government to introduce the Affordable Housing Bill, which subsequently became the Affordable Housing Act, 2024, after presidential assent on March 19, 2024.

The new legislation established a statutory framework for collecting and administering the levy, leading to a fresh set of constitutional petitions that were dismissed by the High Court in October 2024. The subsequent appeals culminated in the September 2026 appellate ruling.

Under the housing levy framework, employees contribute 1.5 per cent of their gross monthly salary, matched by an equivalent 1.5 per cent contribution from their employers.

Non-salaried earners are also subject to a 1.5 per cent contribution on gross income, subject to the applicable statutory provisions.

The levy is a central financing mechanism for President William Ruto's affordable housing programme, which seeks to expand access to housing while supporting construction activity, employment and investment in the built environment.

However, the fresh appeal introduces another layer of legal uncertainty for a programme whose financing model depends on continued statutory deductions from workers and employers.

The December 4 mention will provide an opportunity for the Supreme Court to issue further directions on the handling of the appeal. No determination on the substantive constitutional questions has yet been made in the proceedings initiated by Okiro.

The SS United States — a vessel that sailed across the Atlantic from 1952 to 1969 — was deliberately scuttled at around 10 p.m. ET on Wednesday, roughly 25 miles southwest of Destin, Florida.

The ship had a storied history, carrying such celebrities as Grace Kelly, Elizabeth Taylor, Jackie Gleason and even a young Bill Clinton on his way to Oxford University as a Rhodes scholar.

WRECK OF DEADLIEST US NAVAL LOSS OF WORLD WAR I FOUND AFTER MORE THAN A CENTURY: 'LOST WITH ALL HANDS'

Video shows the decades-old vessel tilting sharply to one side as it sank into the Gulf of America, with water rushing over the ship.
