World.title: WATCH: Socialist agitators lose it when cameras turn on them
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Far-left activists from the network funded by communist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham can dish it out, but they can't take it.

For years, CodePink activists, easily recognizable in hot pink T-shirts, have heckled lawmakers and officials in public settings with a tactic called "bird dogging," cornering targets, peppering them with hostile questions, like "Why do you support baby killers?" and shaming them on social media with tactics that amount to humiliation rituals.

On Veterans Day, the agitators found themselves on the other side of the lens, and they didn't like it.

For six hours on Wednesday, Fox News Digital followed members of CodePink, BreakThrough News, the People's Forum, the Party for Socialism and Liberation and allied groups in the Singham network through the halls of Congress during a lobbying event organizers called the "Taxpayer Uprising."

But when the cameras turned on them, they angrily refused to answer questions and covered the camera lens, one time with a Palestinian keffiyeh scarf and another time with a backpack designed with the pattern of a watermelon, a symbol adopted by the Palestinian movement. Then, they responded with smears and ad hominem attacks.

Finally, they published their footage of the confrontations, turning their objections to being filmed into content for their followers. One follower congratulated them on their success deploying "psychic militancy."

LAWMAKERS THROW OUT 'TROJAN HORSE' ACTIVISTS THEY SAY ARE ENGAGED IN AMERICAN SUBVERSION

Breakfast with Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y.

The day began just before 10 a.m. inside the Rayburn House Office Building, where activists in pink CodePink T-shirts and keffiyehs walked into a breakfast gathering of the U.S. House Bagel Caucus.

At 9:59 a.m., they surrounded Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., and pointed their cameras at him. Medea Benjamin, co-founder of CodePink, wore a shirt emblazoned with the message "NO WAR ON IRAN" and pressed him on Section 219 of the National Defense Authorization Act, which she called a "merging" of the U.S. and Israeli militaries.

"It is not a merging of the militaries," Goldman said. "It is a collaboration on technology that we depend on Israel for, and they depend on us for, and it is for our own national security."

He asked the activists whether they supported Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Hamas and Hezbollah.

"We're not funding them. We're funding Israel," Benjamin replied.

When the liberal congressman called the situation in Gaza "absolutely horrific" and said he wished Hamas would allow in the aid Israel was trying to send, the group members groaned in unison. CodePink activist Tighe Barry, Benjamin's husband, in a pink shirt and pink hat, yelled at him: "You're a real congressman, and you just made that statement?"

"That was a horrific lie that you just said," Barry shouted at him. "As a sitting congressman, I take deep offense at that."

"Alright, here we are. We're enjoying the Bagel Caucus here," Goldman said before walking away. "Thank you for talking. Take care of yourself."

HOW CODEPINK CO-FOUNDER MEDEA BENJAMIN'S FAMILY FOUNDATION BECAME A MAJOR FUNDER OF LEFT-WING ACTIVIST GROUPS

'I'm sorry, I can't hear you'

CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin moved through the building wearing a backpack designed with the pattern of a keffiyeh, the checkered scarf that has become a symbol of the pro-Palestinian movement.

At 10:06 a.m., the group shuffled to the Rayburn cafeteria, where organizers had set up tables numbered by lobbying group. Pink signs reading "TAXPAYER UPRISING" and "WAR IS NOT GREEN" sat on the tables.

Confrontations began within minutes. "No, no. Hey, out of here," a CodePink volunteer told the reporter at about 10:09 a.m.

Asked for an interview, Barry turned to his fellow activists and balked, saying, "Why would I?"

AS SINGHAM FACES FEDERAL PROBE, WIFE MARCHES IN ANTI-ISRAEL PROTEST LED BY GROUPS HE FUNDED

A woman at the check-in table asked the reporter to "move your camera away." Another activist used a keffiyeh to block the camera's view, and a Muslim woman in a headscarf put her hand over the lens.

At about 10:12 a.m., an activist hoisted a pink backpack printed with watermelons in front of the Fox News Digital camera.

A young man in a keffiyeh, with a name tag that read "Finn," then planted himself in front of the camera and moved with it as it tried to pan around him.

"Is this what you do in your free time, is like, wander around?" he taunted.

Melissa Garriga, CodePink's media contact, refused to answer any questions, priding herself to the team on refusing to answer emailed requests for comment from Fox News Digitai.

Asked a question by the reporter standing right in front of her, she cupped her hand behind her ear and said, "I'm sorry, I can't hear you. Can you speak up?"

Asked again, she responded, "I still can't hear you. You're gonna have to talk a little louder. Sorry."

Then, again: "Can you please speak up?"

Asked about Singham's funding of CodePink, Garriga waved her hand across the lens. "I don't have to respond to you," she said.

At 10:14 a.m., Garriga put her hand fully over the camera: "Just buzz off," she said.

The activist with the "Finn" name tag returned and held a gray jacket over the lens, then a canvas tote bag, then a keffiyeh, one after another.

Minutes later, a red-haired woman in a keffiyeh waved her hands in front of the camera.

'They work for us'

Shortly after 10:20 a.m., CodePink co-founders Jodie Evans and Benjamin took charge of the room. Evans married Singham in 2017 when he sold his company, Thoughtworks, for an estimated $785 million. He used some of those proceeds to pump $285 million into a network of nonprofits that have been pro-China and pro-communist. Several of their leaders hit the halls of Congress on Wednesday.

"Alright, everybody, we want to start our program," Evans said at 10:22 a.m.

Benjamin urged them to confront lawmakers wherever they found them.

"Remember, they work for us. They're not better than us. They are public servants," she said. "And so, if you see them, try to engage them."

She told the activists how to spot members of Congress in the hallways: They wear lapel pins and aren't holding anything, because staff carry documents, binders and other items for them, she said.

"The worst it could be is they say, 'I'm not a congressperson,'" she said.

Singham has denied acting at the direction of the Chinese government. Asked if her husband would do an interview, Evans, the only member of the entourage to respond professionally to questions, smiled and said, "No, he's shy."

Fresh from a propaganda tour to China, the Singham network activists pressed lawmakers to slash the military budget, pull out U.S. troops and end U.S. military ties with Israel — demands that align with China's foreign policy agenda.

Rania Khalek, a co-host of "BT Live" at BreakThrough News, slipped into the cafeteria.

When Fox News Digital asked Khalek about BreakThrough's funding from Singham, she responded, "Oh dear. I'm not speaking to you."

A man in a pink shirt stepped backward to plant himself in front of the camera. Khalek raised her phone, filmed the reporter and asked, "Are you harassing us?" She then answered her own question: "Yes."

Asked whether she was with the Party for Socialism and Liberation, a woman standing with Khalek smiled and replied, "Am I?" She has led Party for Socialism and Liberation protests at the White House and is a member of the Party for Socialism and Liberation.

At 10:26 a.m., two activists stepped in front of the camera at once and another pushed a cafeteria chair into the reporter's path.

At 10:33 a.m., Khalek walked behind Benjamin and Evans with the activist from the Party for Socialism and Liberation to hit offices.

Outside Hakeem Jeffries' office

By 10:35 a.m., the activists had moved to the second floor of the Rayburn building, where U.S. Capitol Police officers stood outside Room 2267, the office of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. A yellow sign taped inside the office door read, "OFFICE CLEARED."

The activists only met with a staffer.

At 11:11 a.m., Benjamin did a stand-up video in front of Jeffries' door, casting the image of a dramatic confrontation between activists who "packed" the small office foyer and Jeffries.

'Nobody cares what you think'

At 11:20 a.m., Khalek exploded.

Near the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. "The fact that you pretend to care about free speech right now while literal journalists in Gaza are being, like, executed, sniped in the head by the IDF with U.S. weapons, is a freaking joke. Okay? Nobody cares what you think."

Holding up her phone, she added, "I'm literally doing journalism right now. See?"

Asked whether it was acceptable for Singham network activists to disrupt Congressional hearings, Khalek answered with a question of her own: "Is it okay to fund genocide?" Then she walked away. At 11:22 a.m., she lashed out, calling the reporter a "genocide apologist."

Another activist stepped in front of the camera and took over. "Shame on you. You're completely shameless," she said. "You are a disgrace to this profession!"

The Party for Socialism and Liberation activist filmed the exchange with Khalek.

BreakThrough News later posted the confrontation on Instagram and X, quoting Khalek, who lives in Lebanon, saying: "Stop justifying bombing my country!"

One follower praised the outburst as "psychic militancy."

Her outburst over, Khalek proceeded to go chase lawmakers.

At 11:25 a.m., a woman in a pink CodePink shirt draped a keffiyeh over the camera lens, then followed the reporter and raised it onto the lens again.

Olivia DiNucci, CodePink's D.C. coordinator, wore an olive jacket that read "STOP ARMING ISRAEL." DiNucci has heckled Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Palantir CEO Alex Karp and scores of others, and has written first-person accounts of her own arrests and disruptions inside Congress. On Wednesday, she threw her hand in front of the camera.

"We just don't wanna talk to you, because you're complicit in genocide," she yelled. "Is that really hard for you to understand?" She continued: "We're not interested in talking to people who support murdering babies."

At 11:34 a.m., Benjamin, Khalek and the Party for Socialism and Liberation activist intercepted a congressman walking past the Rayburn House Office Building sign, pressing him on the activists' demands.

"That's propaganda," he responded.

Scalise: 'Maybe there's another country that they like better'

By lobbying day's end, at 3:28 p.m., on the steps of the U.S. Capitol, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., spoke to Fox News Digital, as the activists stood with their signs, cordoned away behind police barricades. Their signs read "WELCOME TO DC / LET'S END WAR" and "HEALTHCARE NOT WARFARE."

"Some people like yelling and screaming and making a lot of noise," Scalise said. "They sure do want attention focused on them so people can see how radical they are. And some of these people are just against the foundations of what made this nation great."

"We're here at a Veterans Day ceremony of all things and they want to protest," he said. "Anybody who would protest Veterans Day, you know, they need to really check themselves. Maybe there's another country that they like better than America, they're free to go there. We love this country."

Scalise added, "Ask Europe who liberated it. It was the United States with our allies that stopped the Nazis, stopped fascism, and we've always been the ones, America, standing up to the bad guys."

"You just follow the money when you see who funds some of these groups that hate America," he said. "It tells you everything you need to know."

Follow the money

The money behind the groups involved in the lobbying day is substantial.

According to IRS filings, Singham has given $1.098 million to BreakThrough's BT Media Inc., $1.33 million to CodePink and $22.44 million to The People's Forum.

CodePink lists 56 organizations taking part in the Taxpayer Uprising with an estimated $40 million in annual revenues, according to Fox News Digital's investigation. The coalition includes the Council on American-Islamic Relations, American Muslims for Palestine, the Democratic Socialists of America's International Committee and the Communist Party USA, which says on its website that it "is guided by Marxism-Leninism." Other participants describe themselves in socialist terms, including Friends of Socialist China, which calls itself "a platform based on supporting the People's Republic of China and promoting understanding of Chinese socialism," and Qiao Collective, which says it is "committed to the principles of socialist internationalism."

They're not grassroots groups. They have big revenue totals: CAIR Foundation at $9.4, the People's Forum at $7.1 million, the Institute for Policy Studies at $5.7 million, Nonviolence International at $3.7 million, Global Exchange at $3 million, American Muslims for Palestine's AJP Educational Foundation at $2.1 million, CodePink at $1.8 million and BreakThrough at $1.5 million.

Fox News Digital couldn't identify any group registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, according to the Justice Department's FARA database. Last year, Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., wrote a letter raising concerns about CodePink's pro-China lobbying. Rubio has pressed the Justice Department about Chinese Communist Party information warfare through these nonprofits. House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., has sent subpoenas to the People's Forum, BreakThrough News and a related Tricontinental thinktank as allegedly aligned with the Chinese Communist Party propaganda operation.

Overnight, CodePink posted the video where she spoke to her team's camera in front of Jeffries' office, with the caption, telling the world: "We just packed the office of Hakeem Jeffries' office."

World.title: Biden judge rejects DOJ bid to halt probe of prosecutors in botched ICE protest case
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A federal judge investigating whether prosecutors misled her court in the "Broadview Six" case against anti-ICE protesters canceled a hearing requested by the Justice Department to clarify her authority to conduct the inquiry.

U.S. District Judge April Perry, a Biden appointee, has ordered four federal prosecutors, including Chicago's U.S. attorney, to testify under oath as she considers possible sanctions or criminal contempt proceedings.

"Ultimately, the Government’s professed lack of clarity about the Court’s inherent authority to ask lawyers who have made misstatements to or misled the Court to explain their actions is immaterial," Perry wrote Wednesday, canceling the Nov. 17 hearing.

The Justice Department dropped the criminal case against the six protesters in May amid allegations of misconduct involving former federal prosecutor Sheri Mecklenburg, who later resigned. But Perry's investigation into the prosecutors' conduct has continued.

DOJ MOVES TO BOOT FEDERAL JUDGES FROM IMMIGRATION CASES OVER NYT INTERVIEW

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, the Justice Department's third-ranking official, argued in a filing that requiring prosecutors to testify would put them in a "Catch-22."

"They can testify and risk prosecution, or they can assert their rights under the Fifth Amendment and risk antagonizing the court, while it may also be considering non-contempt sanctions," Woodward wrote.

Perry rejected the government's argument, writing that "the Government does not represent at least 3/4 of the individuals who have been asked to testify, two of whom have expressed their willingness to do so."

Perry has ordered U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros and three assistant U.S. attorneys in the Northern District of Illinois — William Hogan, Matthew Skiba and Andres Almendarez — to testify under oath Monday about possible misconduct in grand jury proceedings involving the protesters.

"There is no indication on the docket that the Government represents the fourth individual," Perry wrote, referring to Boutros.

The testimony is expected to address prosecutors' knowledge of possible grand jury misconduct, the accuracy of their statements to the court, why grand jury transcripts were redacted and whether officials outside the U.S. Attorney's Office received information about the investigation. Perry could use the testimony to determine whether sanctions or criminal contempt proceedings are warranted.

DOJ MOVES TO BOOT TWO FEDERAL JUDGES FROM IMMIGRATION CASES OVER REMARKS TO MEDIA: 'EXTRAORDINARILY IMPRUDENT'

The canceled hearing follows a separate dispute over communications the Justice Department has declined to disclose to Perry.

On Monday, Woodward argued in a motion that certain communications involving federal prosecutors were privileged and should not be disclosed. The Justice Department also submitted a privilege log identifying the withheld communications and the grounds for withholding them.

Perry rejected the submission Tuesday, finding it "noncompliant" because the government had redacted information identifying numerous senders and recipients in lengthy email chains. She also questioned the Justice Department's response to her request for an email sent to Boutros containing an expedited transcript of the Oct. 9, 2025, grand jury session, when jurors first declined to return an indictment. The PDF, the judge said, lacked metadata that could help establish whether Boutros had read the email.

Prosecutors were given until Thursday to address her concerns. The inquiry began May 20, when Perry ordered prosecutors involved in redacting grand jury transcripts to appear in court and questioned them during a sealed hearing the following day.

ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS CLASH WITH AGENTS OUTSIDE NEW JERSEY DETENTION CENTER AS GOV SHERRILL DENIED ENTRY

In October, Perry requested communications between federal prosecutors and outside officials concerning investigative and charging decisions in the case, finding that "several aspects of this prosecution were very flawed."

The inquiry stems from a grand jury's refusal to return an indictment on Oct. 9, 2025, and again during a subsequent session convened by Boutros, when two jurors were excused over concerns about their impartiality. Those jurors later returned for a third session on Oct. 23, when the grand jury indicted the protesters on a felony conspiracy charge.

According to court records, grand jury transcripts initially provided to Perry in April contained redactions that concealed evidence of possible misconduct, including allegations of improper "vouching" for the government's case by former Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri Mecklenburg during an Oct. 9, 2025, grand jury presentation.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Six protesters, including former Democratic congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, faced federal charges stemming from a Sept. 26, 2025, confrontation outside an ICE facility in Broadview, Illinois. Prosecutors alleged that the demonstrators surrounded a federal immigration agent's vehicle to prevent him from entering the facility. Members of the crowd allegedly struck the vehicle, damaging a side mirror and windshield wiper, although prosecutors did not identify any of the six defendants as personally responsible.

World.title: AOC taps power player who helped Bernie Sanders defy the odds as major 2028 decision looms
World.content:

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., is tapping a key player behind Bernie Sanders' presidential fundraising operation as speculation swirls over whether the left-wing Democrat could launch her own White House bid in 2028.

Ocasio-Cortez split with her longtime digital fundraising firm, Middle Seat, Axios reported Thursday, citing three sources familiar with the matter. She has now tapped Aisle 518 Strategies, the firm led by Democratic strategist Tim Tagaris, who helped drive Sanders' record-breaking online fundraising operations during his 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns, according to Axios.

The move comes as some progressive groups are calling for Ocasio-Cortez to jump into the White House race in 2028. There has also been mounting speculation that she could seek the Senate seat held by Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., in 2028, potentially setting up a Democratic primary showdown if Schumer seeks re-election.

AOC CAMPAIGN MEMO FRAMES GROWTH FROM PROGRESSIVE FIREBRAND TO NATIONAL DEMOCRATIC PARTY FORCE

Ocasio-Cortez's office declined to comment to Fox News Digital on Thursday.

Middle Seat and Aisle 518 Strategies each did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests seeking comment.

Sanders' 2016 fundraising operation capitalized on major campaign moments and attacks from establishment Democrats to generate surges in small-dollar donations, helping propel the relatively obscure Vermont senator into an unexpectedly competitive primary battle against Hillary Clinton, Politico reported at the time.

"Internet fundraising is about taking potential energy and converting it into kinetic energy, and nobody has done that better than Bernie Sanders," veteran Democratic operative Ari Rabin-Havt told Politico back in 2016. "Tim [Tagaris] and his team are maximizing that. Their emails are superior."

Sanders' office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Sanders' campaign raised $34.5 million in the final three months of 2019, according to the AP. He went on to briefly emerge as the Democratic front-runner in early 2020 before Joe Biden consolidated support and secured the nomination.

AOC OPENS UP ABOUT RACE, GENDER IN WEIGHING POSSIBLE 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID

Ocasio-Cortez previously parted ways with her longtime campaign manager and creative director earlier in 2026, and also recruited a few former aides, according to Axios.

"I know there is a lot of speculation about what I will decide to do in 2028," Ocasio-Cortez said in a recent fundraising email. "I get asked about it nearly every interview and event."

Still, Ocasio-Cortez told The Washington Sun in an interview published Wednesday that she plans to deliberate privately about her political future.

World.title: Nvidia stock falls after Huang resigns, weighing on broader market
World.content:
Major stock indexes declined at the opening bell on news that Jensen Huang, one of the most important executives in the AI boom, was resigning effective immediately as CEO of Nvidia.

Shares of Nvidia sank 12% at the open, before quickly erasing some losses, as the company and its investors grappled with multiple scandals that have engulfed its founder and now-former CEO, Jensen Huang.

Throughout the day, the company was among the biggest decliners on the Nasdaq, Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 indexes.

Major indexes also faced choppy trading. All three were slightly higher after following a similar pattern to Nvidia’s: falling, rising and then declining again.

Without a formal succession plan, the company that designs the chips powering the entire AI sector was thrust into crisis. It’s a pivotal moment for AI, with Anthropic gearing up for its potentially trillion-dollar-plus initial public offering next week.

Anthropic is highly reliant on Nvidia’s chips and has entered into hundreds of billions of dollars worth of contracts with cloud providers to rent them.

Nvidia named its longtime chief financial officer as its interim leader. Huang’s departure from Nvidia came after a New York Times report said the CEO had had a relationship with an executive at Nvidia who reports to him.

That came right on the heels of his admission on Sunday that he was “unfaithful” to his wife, an announcement that was released after the Financial Times reported Saturday that Huang had had a relationship with a woman whom a source told NBC News was a Chinese spy.

There are few companies as important to the artificial intelligence industry as Nvidia.

“We’re probably the only AI company in the world that works with every AI company in the world,” Huang told Bloomberg in an October interview.

As reports swirled around Huang this week, Nvidia’s shares have plunged, erasing about $515 billion in value. Nvidia’s total market value fell below $4 trillion for the first time since 2025 in early trading.

The news surrounding Huang, a confidant of President Donald Trump’s, also raises the prospect of tighter regulations on the chip and AI industry, which could further pressure stock indexes that have been powered for years by the explosion in AI stocks.

“All told, given the national security concerns, we think the risk of more restrictive guidelines on shipments directly or indirectly into China has risen,” JPMorgan analysts said on Thursday before Huang was removed.

Industry experts widely believe that American leadership in AI has been powered by Nvidia. That too could come into question.

“We expect the [Nvidia] team to maintain its leadership in AI,” said JPMorgan’s team, while cautioning that “history has shown that one execution misstep often leads to more.”

“Maintaining flawless execution” will be critical to Nvidia and the sector going forward, they said.

Also pressuring stock indexes was news from AI cloud startup Nebius, which reported that it beat earnings expectations. But the company also gave investors disappointing guidance.

Investors have been on edge about AI-linked firms, especially smaller startups, given that they require tens of billions of dollars to get their data centers up and running. Overall, the sector has poured hundreds of billions of dollars into developing AI systems, data centers and equipment, but investors remain nervous about how soon those investments could pay off.

Nebius shares plummeted almost 20%. Its peer CoreWeave also fell 10% after surging Wednesday.

Together, the Nvidia and Nebius news sent the entire tech sector lower, and it was the worst performing S&P sector on Thursday.

Suppliers to both companies also fell. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell 2%, while an ETF that tracks memory suppliers fell 4%.

World.title: Ukraine faces new Starshield disruptions as Trump envoys meet with Putin
World.content:
Hours after an American delegation touched down in Moscow for peace talks, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country’s military had experienced a renewed wave of “significant disruptions” to the Starshield satellite internet service, hampering its ability to defend itself against Russia.

“These are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions,” he said in a Telegram post. “For us, this primarily means a significant complication in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones.”

His comments came as U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, arrived in the Russian capital for peace talks with President Vladimir Putin, a day after trilateral talks aimed at ending the war were held in the United Arab Emirates.

The two-day Abu Dhabi summit, the first such meeting since February, ended with no major breakthrough, although representatives of Russia and Ukraine agreed on a large exchange of prisoners of war.

In Moscow, Kushner told ‌Putin that Europe wanted ‌a role ‌in future negotiations, according to Russia’s Tass state news agency.

European countries cut communications with the Kremlin and refused to engage with Russia directly after Putin launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but have since expressed concern about the Trump administration’s softening stance toward the Kremlin. Kushner last week said he also wanted to address “long-term European security and stability,” signaling a focus beyond just Ukraine that prompted a firm response from European leaders.

Expanding on that theme on Thursday, Kushner said there was a “very strong momentum and desire” from European leaders to “engage together,” adding that “understanding the long-term security between Russia, Ukraine, and Europe is a conversation that we started having with them.”

While representatives from several European countries were in Abu Dhabi, they did not play a direct role in the talks. Russian negotiators have previously opposed their involvement, citing Europe’s support for Kyiv as an obstacle.

At the meeting in Moscow, the Interfax news agency reported that Putin proposed a joint Russian-Ukrainian humanitarian mission to the city of Kostiantynivka ⁠in eastern ​Ukraine, similar to the Melania Trump-brokered mission in Oleshky which allowed residents to leave the Russian-controlled town.

Meanwhile in Ukraine, Zelenskyy said military units had for several days reported speed restrictions affecting the entire front line and Russian-occupied parts of the country.

A limit of 100 mph is once again being “imposed on Starshield,” he said of the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink communications service. The system normally runs at a stable speed exceeding around 250 mph.

“These are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions,” he said. “For us, this primarily means a significant complication in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones.”

“Unfortunately, there have already been strikes that got through because our interception systems cannot reach sufficient speeds and are unable to intercept in time,” he added.

Zelenskyy, who is set to meet with Kushner and Witkoff in Dublin on Friday, added that Ukraine was trying to ⁠clarify the reasons for the ‌restriction with the ​U.S. side.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NBC News.

Craig Albert, the graduate director of national defense Studies at Augusta University, said decreasing Starshield’s speed would slow down how fast Ukraine’s offensive drones travel, “which makes them pretty much target practice for faster interceptor drones by the Russians.”

It would also slow down Ukrainian interceptor drones and their missile defense systems, meaning “Russian drones can get through their defenses much quicker.”

“The Russians can target more infrastructure, and the Ukrainians just don’t have the speed to counteract,” he said, adding that “for the price, the scale, the scale, the speed, the scalability, and the efficiency,” there were no real options other than Starshield.

Ukraine first raised the alarm last month about speed limits being imposed on Starshield, which is crucial to its battlefield operations and air defenses.

Starlink owner Elon Musk initially put the responsibility for the restrictions on President Donald Trump, who has been trying to pressure Kyiv to make concessions to end the war. The U.S. government said ​that any such decision could only have been ‌taken by Musk.

Trump denied being involved in the decision concerning the slowdown. Musk later said in an X post that SpaceX had acted to close a “loophole” with its civilian Starlink service, accusing Ukraine of violating “Starlink terms of service” by using it for offensive drone strikes, which the country denied.

The aftermath of a Russian air attack on Kyiv, on Thursday. Vladyslav Musiienko / AFP via Getty

Moscow has so far resisted such efforts to bring Europe to the main negotiating table, something Ukraine has long sought.

The talks came against the backdrop of continued fighting on the front lines, where neither side has achieved significant progress for months.

Instead, the focus has shifted to daily attacks with long-range missiles and drones. Russia has targeted Ukrainian cities, aiming to cut off water and power supplies as winter sets in. Kyiv has resumed attacks on energy infrastructure, a campaign that drew Trump’s ire.

Ukrainian officials said Thursday that five civilians had been killed by Russian strikes on the country overnight, and 29 people injured. The Russian Defense Ministry said it had shot down 71 drones.

World.title: She’s delivered 2,000 babies. The measles outbreak changed her mind about vaccines.
World.content:
This is part of The Vaccine Divide, a data investigation into America’s potential loss of its measles-free status as the deadly virus roars back and childhood vaccine defenses continue to crack and crumble.

When Roberta Devers, a midwife in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, did a prenatal check on an expectant mom this week, the woman — a member of the Amish community in her third trimester — had been sick with measles.

Devers said she has cared for dozens of pregnant women infected with the virus since measles began spreading rapidly in the county in April. Lancaster County is largely rural, with sprawling family farms.

“Every single day,” she said, “someone’s calling to ask what they do. They’re pregnant and they’ve gotten it, or their babies have gotten it.”

Devers, 63, estimates she has delivered nearly 2,000 babies in her 38-year career. She has a degree in maternal and fetal health, but she is working as an unlicensed, traditional midwife in Pennsylvania, independent of the hospital systems and without physician oversight. State law bars traditional midwives from practicing medicine.

Devers said pregnant women with measles are having miscarriages. "While our Amish families believe God is always in control, they're emotional people, and like anyone else, they grieve the loss of a baby," Devers said. Hannah Beier for NBC News

Devers said she questioned immunizations as a young mother and never vaccinated her son.

“There was as much information against vaccines as there was about the efficacy of vaccines,” she said. “It was difficult to know who to trust and who to believe.”

Her experiences in Lancaster County’s outbreak have changed her mindset.

“Numbers and books became people,” she said. “It was humanized by watching what was happening to the mothers I was serving.”

World.title: Behind the data: How NBC News tracked the decline in childhood vaccinations
World.content:
Editor’s note: This 2026 NBC News data investigation is an update of The Vaccine Divide, which was originally published in September 2025. The methodology for both projects is similar. The new data was collected from June to October 2026.

For “The Vaccine Divide,” NBC News gathered massive amounts of data from state governments and archives of public records. With the help of infectious disease researchers at Stanford University, NBC News filed scores of requests for documents, including materials obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, and wrestled different types of data into a standardized format to map and compare rates across thousands of counties.

Methodology

How NBC News collected the data

NBC News built a database of childhood vaccination and exemption information using data provided by state governments, primarily health agencies. The data combines public information available for some states and data provided directly to NBC News.

The data covers kindergartner vaccinations for each academic year.

After collection, the data was collated, and exemption rates were calculated in order to be analyzed. The analysis focuses on four facets of the data:

Medical exemptions: Exemptions granted when students have medical conditions that could make vaccination harmful. Nonmedical exemptions: Exemptions for students who opt out of required vaccinations because of personal beliefs or religious convictions. MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccinations: For states where data is subdivided by number of doses, MMR vaccination is counted by the second dose. Some states track measles, mumps and rubella immunization separately; in those states, measles was used to represent MMR rates. Up-to-date vaccinations: Students are considered “up to date” with their vaccinations if they have received the full vaccination series required for enrollment in their schools.

How the data was processed

With a hodgepodge of formats, jurisdictions and collection practices across states, the task required extensive work to ensure that possible inconsistencies in the data were managed.

Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.

Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.

All data was checked for accuracy.

Analyzing the data

This analysis of childhood MMR vaccination rates focused on states that provided MMR figures for the 2025-26 school year. Accompanying the analysis were several variant analyses, which confirmed that the results were robust. The variant analyses all yielded similar results, mostly within 1 percentage point. We also examined the scale of MMR vaccination rate decline across counties, with almost 4 in 10 counties declining by over 5 percentage points since 2019 and about 1 in 8 declining by that amount since 2024. Fewer than 2% of counties declined by 0.1 percentage points or less since 2019.

Variations in the data

Many states collect and report their data differently. Some use health districts instead of counties. Some states provided over a decade of data; others provided only two years’ worth. Some states redacted certain data because of privacy concerns.

World.title: 1 killed, 4 injured in shooting in D.C.; suspect is dead
World.content:
Five people were shot, including one who died, as a gunman opened fire in and outside a gym in Washington, D.C.'s Logan Circle neighborhood on Thursday morning, police said.

The suspect barricaded himself in a unit believed to be his in an apartment building over Logan Circle's Vida Fitness before shooting himself, said Jeffery Carroll, the Interim Chief of Police of the Metropolitan Police Department, at a news conference Thursday morning. Police later confirmed the suspect died on the scene.

Carroll said there were five victims, not counting the shooter. One is deceased, one is in critical condition and three have non-life-threatening injuries. The injured victims have been transported to area hospitals, Carroll said.

Victims found in multiple locations

Carroll said police received a call for the shooting just before 8 a.m. and that authorities responded within 30 seconds.

The person who was killed was shot in the gym. Other victims included members of a construction crew across the street and a person in the lobby or alley outside the gym, Carroll said. The suspect is believed to have used a handgun, Carroll said.

CBS News national security correspondent Nicole Sganga says it appears the suspect opened fire in and outside Vida Fitness, then retreated into a parking garage and ascended into the apartment building before barricading himself in a unit on the seventh floor.

A fire also was set inside the building at some point during the incident, Carroll said. He said sprinklers went off and that the fire has been contained. He said police don't "know for sure" who set the fire, but that authorities "would kind of expect" it was the suspect.

Gunshots continued to be heard for the better part of two hours, while officers with the Metro Police Department negotiated with the suspect. Carroll said the suspect fired through the apartment door at police on two occasions. While on the phone with negotiators, the suspect shot himself, Carroll said.

After hearing the gunshot, officers forced entry into the apartment, where they found the suspect suffering from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Carroll did not say where the suspect shot himself.

Law enforcement respond to the scene of a shooting in Logan Circle on Nov. 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Police say suspect had conflict with homeowner's association

The suspect is a White man, according to Carroll. He said police know the man's identity but did not publicly share it.

The man is believed to be a member of the gym, Carroll said.

Carroll said an investigation into the suspect's motive is ongoing, but said police are aware that he had a conflict with the apartment building's homeowners association.

Jonathan Csapo told CBS News that the suspected shooter was his upstairs neighbor. Csapo said he had not interacted with the suspect "all that much" but knew he was "very disgruntled with the building's management," who he believed "weren't talking sufficient action" about a water issue in his apartment. The suspect aired his complaints on X and had filed a lawsuit against the building, Csapo said. He also complained during board meetings, becoming "a little more upset" at two recent gatherings, Csapo said.

"He invited everybody to his unit to see the damage," Csapo said. "He wanted people to know what was happening. He wanted more attention, and he was getting increasingly frustrated that that people weren't listening to him."

Csapo said he evacuated the building by fire escape after hearing the fire alarm go off. Then he heard shots fired. He and others took shelter around the corner, he said. He said he was shocked that the building, which he described as safe and tight-knit, was at the center of a mass shooting.

"Everybody knows each other. The building is only 99 units. Everbody says hi to each other in the hallway," Csapo said. "We're just a little neighborhood, and we're all, I think, quite shocked."

Multiple agencies respond

The shooting took place about one mile north of the White House. Multiple federal agencies responded because of their proximity to the incident, officials said.

Streets were closed and residents were asked to avoid the area. A shelter-in-place order was issued.

The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms said its Washington Bureau was at the scene and assisting. The Federal Bureau of Investigation said its Washington field office was also aiding the MPD.

The Secret Service, U.S. Marshals and U.S. Park Police were also responding to the scene. There are no Secret Service protectees involved. The agency and FBI responded because of their proximity to the incident, not because of any connection to the White House.

Vida Fitness emailed members on Thursday morning to say that its Logan Circle location would be closed until further notice.

Witnesses describe "horrific" scene

Witness Jennifer Christine said she was on a treadmill in the gym when she heard shots ring out. She said she witnessed one death inside the gym before leaving the building and taking shelter in a local bagel shop.

"There was no way of getting out of the gym other than going past that scene," Christine told reporters. "It was like chaos. It was horrific, honestly."

Another witness told reporters that he was also on a treadmill when he heard a loud bang. He first thought the sound was a ball popping or something falling to the floor. Then he saw blood on the floor. An alarm went off, and the gym was evacuated, he said. The witness said he and other gym attendees ran outside, where police were already gathered. Then, more shots were fired.

"We all just started running and people are scattering everywhere," the witness said.

Witness Max Smith told media that he heard multiple shots around 8:30 a.m. He said he and about 10 other bystanders also took shelter in the bagel shop.

"I'm very shaken up," Smith said. "You know, you don't expect it."

World.title: GOP lawmakers negotiating for Huang to appear before Congress
World.content:
Washington — Republicans on Capitol Hill are negotiating for now-resigned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to appear before Congress about the scandal that has rocked one of the most important companies in the world, lawmakers said Thursday.

"We are in discussions with him right now on a date to come and meet with us," said GOP Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, the chairman of the House Select Committee on China. But he added: "If for some reason that were not to happen, all three committees, all three chairs have said we will use our subpoena power."

Nvidia, whose chips have fueled the AI boom, announced on Thursday that Huang had stepped down following a scandal over his affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at the company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Moolenaar and two other chairs — Reps. Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Rick Crawford of the Intelligence Committee — wrote a letter to Huang on Nov. 4 asking him to appear for a closed-door briefing with all three committees. They said the purpose of the briefing would be to discuss Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset." The lawmakers gave Huang a deadline of Wednesday to respond.

Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Thursday that they received a response. Mast said Huang indicated he's willing to appear. Moolenaar said that Huang's resignation "does change the dynamic" surrounding his potential testimony. Republicans still control Congress until January.

"I think right now our goal is to get him in as soon as possible, so that we have a full understanding of the facts and get to the bottom of the truth of this situation," Moolenaar said.

Huang's resignation from the company he co-founded has not dampened calls from members of Congress for answers about Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to highly prized chips that are banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.

Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said on CNBC on Thursday that he would happily support subpoenaing Huang moments before Nvidia announced his resignation. A Cramer spokesperson said he would still support subpoenaing the tech founder.

President Trump, a friend of Huang's, has downplayed the scandal and said Thursday that Huang had done a "fantastic job."

"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place — TIM COOK of Apple," the president posted to Truth Social.

World.title: Crews begin excavating site of building collapse in Brooklyn
World.content:
The death toll continues to climb after a Brooklyn building collapsed and an adjacent building was significantly damaged.

A three-story, multi-use building on Flatbush Avenue collapsed into a nearby construction site just after 4 p.m. Wednesday, tearing off the side of another building.

At least eight people were killed and 18 others were injured as of Thursday morning, according to the FDNY. Six people were found dead at the scene, and two died at the hospital.

"We know that this morning they pulled out, I believe a couple of construction workers that were on site last night, which added to the death toll this morning," said Councilwoman Farrah Louis.

The structure was fully occupied by residents, and construction workers were in the construction pit performing excavation work at the time of the collapse.

Emergency crews worked through the night under floodlights with the help of drones and K-9 units to get through the massive piles of rubble.

Video showed dozens of firefighters at the scene Thursday morning searching for additional victims.

Members of the New York City Fire Department and first responders search for victims in the rubble a day after a building collapsed in Brooklyn. Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images

After searching through every accessible void by hand, first responders brought in heavy machinery to excavate the remaining debris.

Officials are trying to determine what caused the ground to give way.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the incident devastating, praising first responders for executing a grueling, high-risk technical operation.

"Rescue workers have spent the night searching the site of yesterday's building collapse, working under extremely dangerous conditions to find and save anyone who may still be trapped. I am heartbroken that eight New Yorkers have now lost their lives and at least 17 have been injured, including three firefighters. There are no words for a loss of this magnitude," he said in a post Thursday.

Investigators are conducting comprehensive reviews of the conditions at the collapsed building and neighboring construction site. Investigators said developers have active permits for excavation and foundation work associated with a new building project.

Records revealed the site had been cited for violations months before the disaster. Those were corrected, and work was allowed to resume in May.

Investigators have not determined whether that work contributed to the collapse.

A full stop-work order has been issued as recovery operations continue.

The Brooklyn District Attorney's Office is also investigating whether any criminal conduct contributed to the collapse.

World.title: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who reprimanded group near tomb
World.content:
Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a medal on Thursday to the service member who reprimanded his group for making noise at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day.

Hegseth posted a series of photos on X with the soldier, Specialist Thomas Iglesias, and other members of the unit who guard the tomb at Arlington National Cemetery around the clock. One of the photos showed Hegseth pinning a medal to Iglesias' chest.

"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist," Hegseth wrote. "Carry on Patriots."

We love soldiers.

We love standards.

Well done, Specialist.



Carry on Patriots. pic.twitter.com/Uk6ek6oOso — Secretary of War Pete Hegseth (@SecWar) November 12, 2026

A Pentagon official said Hegseth "welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."

Iglesias was guarding the Tomb following a Veterans Day event that included Hegseth, President Trump and other administration officials. Footage showed Hegseth, his wife, his chief of staff and other aides posing for photos near the tomb. Someone laughed, and Iglesias shouted: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

In the aftermath, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: "The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored-and will always honor-the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

Soldiers reminding visitors to maintain decorum at the tomb is not uncommon. One member of the regiment that guards the tomb said in an Army interview in 2022 that sentinels react to the crowd two or three times per day.

World.title: While many Americans resist, China embraces AI data center boom
World.content:
Ulanqab, China — Off a major highway on the outskirts of Ulanqab, in the Chinese province of Inner Mongolia, Hereford cows roam through corn fields scouring the ground for any dried up remains of the recent harvest.

Hovering over the landscape are shiny new transmission towers linked by power cables that stretch along the plateau for as far as the eye can see. On the ridgeline, covered in snow, wind turbines spin, taking full advantage of the ever-blowing wind.

The energy pulsing from the remote Chinese region — a combination of renewables and fossil fuels — will soon power multi-story data centers being constructed on farmland as part of a sprawling AI data center construction boom.

The construction site is the size of a small American city. It is the biggest, and fastest growing infrastructure project anywhere in China right now.

An image from video broadcast by Chinese state television on Oct. 16, 2026, shows data centers, some still under construction, in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, China. CCTV/Reuters

This corner of Inner Mongolia was famous for generations for growing potatoes. Now, it's fast becoming an AI hub, and Chinese officials hope the expansive, rugged landscape will help power the country's ambition to surpass the U.S. as the global leader in artificial intelligence.

Baletu, a 72-year-old farmer, who has lived here for more than 40 years growing potatoes and corn, said the changes across his local landscape are positive.

"It doesn't affect my farmland, not at all," he told CBS News. "It's good for the area."

A short drive away, CBS News was able to see what all that wind power will soon be feeding. Trucks, cranes and thousands of workers are taking part in the construction project to create one of the biggest data centers anywhere in the world.

We drove miles down new roads with multistory data centers going up on either side. Even from the road it was easy to spot the countless racks that will hold servers, semi-conductor chips and cooling and exhaust fans.

There are dozens of data centers being built in Inner Mongolia, more than any other part of the vast nation. The reason they have chosen Ulanqab is because it offers cheap, abundant energy. Fossil fuels are still the main source of power here, but they also use renewables, including wind and solar.

Ulanqab is one of the most consistently windy locations in the province. The climate is also cold all year, which helps keep cooling costs down, and land and labor are more affordable in the remote region.

An image from video broadcast by Chinese state television on Oct. 16, 2026, shows solar and wind energy infrastructure in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, China. CCTV/Reuters

Experts cited by the Financial Times say data centers in China are built at about one-fifth of the costs incurred in the U.S., not least due to the much higher land and labor costs.

As many as 30,000 workers have been brought in from across China to help build the AI hub, and in a country experiencing an economic downturn and high youth unemployment, these mass infrastructure projects are very much welcome.

"Development is the best thing, especially when it provides job opportunities for many young people," a local businesswoman who sets up a lunchtime food stall outside the construction site told CBS News.

While data centers in the U.S. face major community opposition, which could be emboldened by the "blue wave" of the Democrats' stunning midterm election performance, there are few hurdles for Chinese developers.

While China's government doesn't generally tolerate protests of any kind, and it tightly controls messaging across all media, a United Nations survey last year found that as many as 80% of people in the country support data center construction. At least two-thirds of Chinese people use AI in their day-to-day life, as many embrace the technology and the infrastructure behind it.

Under President Xi Jinping, AI development has become a national strategic priority for China.

"There is no opposition to data centers in China. It's never heard of, whereas in the U.S., it has become a huge movement against data center building in neighborhoods," Henry Wang, founder and president of the Center For China and Globalization, told CBS News.

Huawei, Alibaba, Byte Dance, Deepseek, Baidu, Z.ai, ZData and VNET — China's biggest AI companies — are all active in Inner Mongolia. In areas where construction has finished, fences are up and grounds are landscaped, and avenues through the humming data centers have been named after the AI tech giants.

While Chinese firms' AI models are believed to be about six months behind their U.S. competitors, due largely to restrictions on the sale of high-end microchips, the gap is narrowing.

China has more than double the power generation capacity of the U.S., and some experts believe access to power, not chips, will ultimately be the deciding factor in the global race for AI dominance.

"Chips may not become the latest diving criteria," said Wang. "It may be that power is the bottleneck, and whoever goes through that first gets the advantage. And right now. China has the edge."

World.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns in wake of affair, spy scandal
World.content:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of AI tech giant Nvidia effective immediately following a scandal involving an alleged spy, the company's board of directors announced Thursday.

The decision came amid an investigation into Huang's affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. President Trump said this week the FBI is investigating romantic and business ties between Huang and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The two aren't related.

Nvidia's board had been preparing to oust Huang, two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News on Wednesday night, plans that were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Huang's ouster also follows a New York Times report Wednesday that five employees at Nvidia came forward alleging Huang was romantically involved with a subordinate, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare.

The Times also reported Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were caught on video being affectionate at a conference in March, according to two Nvidia employees. The Times has not seen the video and CBS News has not verified the report.

Jensen Huang speaks at a conference on artificial intelligence on Oct. 21, 2026, in Berlin. John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images

The company's interim CEO will be Colette Kress, who is currently Nvidia's chief financial officer and will continue in that role.

"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Harvey Jones, who was announced as the company's first board chair, said in a statement.

Kress has been Nvidia's CFO since she joined the company in 2013. She previously worked in finance roles at tech companies like Cisco and Microsoft for nearly 25 years.

Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993. It became one of the most valuable companies in the world by designing the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.

Nvidia's stock plunged as news emerged of the company's turmoil, potentially erasing more than $700 billion in value. As of midday Thursday, the company's price was down nearly 5% at around $165.25.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.

Megaspeed grew with the help of access to Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips. According to U.S. investigators, Alice Huang was able to gain access to 240,000 chips that were banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.

In Washington, top Democrats on Capitol Hill have expressed concerns over whether Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang may have compromised U.S. national security.

Following Jensen Huang's resignation, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said his departure doesn't absolve him or the company from the scandal.

"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement.

In a statement accompanying her appointment as interim CEO, Kress said that the company's focus will be on "serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."

"NVIDIA's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said.

The board said it will be conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates.
