World.title: Cuba’s Revolution Is Even Taking Away Our Vices
World.content:
By Fabiana del Valle

HAVANA TIMES – There comes a day when you realize there are things you don’t need, and you decide to give them up as a voluntary, personal choice. But in Cuba, there are things you give up because they have become economically impossible.

My husband, for example, is discovering that the “Revolution” has found a way to force him to quit smoking. Not through anti-smoking campaigns, a terminal illness, the image of a lung reduced to a rag, or a personal decision born of a desire to be healthier.

Here, even vices are subject to inflation, and existential questions begin when, before lighting a cigarette, you look at it as if it were a diamond. Do I really need to smoke? Should I save the money to buy food, or just buy three cigarettes and save a little that way?

Every cigarette becomes an equation, and getting even the most die-hard smoker to develop the skills of an economist when lighting up a Popular brand cigarette is quite a revolutionary achievement.

The famous Popular cigarette, or “ration-store cigarette,” as all Cubans know it, deserves a special chapter in the life of anyone born on this island who has ever smoked.

It’s a domestic product made with so few resources that it seems to have been manufactured from the leftovers of a cigarette someone else already smoked. Sometimes you even find a tobacco stem or a cockroach wing in the filling. Its packaging, white paper with blue lettering, makes you suspect it has been through a war before reaching the consumer’s hands.

It turns up on the informal market at a frightening price, as though every cigarette were wrapped in gold leaf. One thing is for a product to be unavailable; quite another is for it to show up where it shouldn’t be, at a price far above its actual value.

It’s the same old game with every product manufactured in this country. It all begins in the warehouse of some factory, with a worker who knows someone else who knows how to get hold of the merchandise. Then there’s the famous “buddy” who always manages to obtain a few boxes, moves them around, resells them, and at the end of the chain are the same people as always: those trying to survive on wages that are laughable.

I’m not going to blame the person selling them. Unfortunately, that person is also trying to survive. This country’s economy resembles a game of dominoes in which everyone tries to play their tile and move forward however they can before night falls. And while some manage to get their hands on merchandise, others can barely afford to breathe.

I know smoking isn’t a basic necessity. It would never occur to me to convince anyone that a cigarette should take priority over rice, medicine, or electricity. Smoking is bad for your health, and if it’s also expensive, well, you just quit. Simple as that.

Except that the same thing is happening with anything that still gives us a little pleasure. We don’t smoke, we don’t drink coffee, we don’t eat meat because it costs too much, traveling is an impossible dream, and we don’t buy clothes. There are always other priorities. The sad thing is that when someone asks how we’re doing, we answer without hesitation: “We’re fine.” We’ve learned to survive without complaining too much.

In this tropical version of the Holy Trinity, the land of rum, sugar, and tobacco, you’d better have your wallet ready. My husband has the right to decide to quit smoking because he wants to, rather than having his choices dictated by economic misery.

Cigarette packs warn that smoking is harmful to your health, but in Cuba, smoking seriously damages your wallet, leaving it sick, very sick, with no chance of getting an appointment with a specialist.

Read more from the diary of Fabiana del Valle here on Havana Times.

World.title: Paraguay’s banking superintendent arrested in the Ueno Bank investigation
World.content:
Paraguay’s banking superintendent arrested in the Ueno Bank investigation

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 11:20 UTC Full article

Insfrán was named in a criminal complaint expanded by opposition lawmakers last week, alongside the economy minister and other officials

Paraguay’s Superintendent of Banks, Holger Insfrán, was arrested on Thursday as part of the investigation into the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has already led to the pre-trial detention of former President Santiago Peña and former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, according to prosecution sources cited by the EFE news agency. The charges against him have not been disclosed.

The Superintendency of Banks, part of the Central Bank, is responsible for supervising and regulating Paraguay’s financial institutions, including Ueno. Insfrán was named in a criminal complaint expanded by opposition lawmakers last week, alongside the economy minister and other officials.

According to prosecutors, Ueno received large amounts of public funds during Peña’s term, including from five pension funds, while granting allegedly irregular loans to companies owned by its owners, the Vázquez Group. The bank had 2.94 million customers.

Peña, removed by the Senate on November 6, is charged with alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator, and could face a maximum sentence of 15 years, according to prosecutors. He says he is innocent. Carvallo, who headed the finance company from which the bank emerged before Peña appointed him to lead the Central Bank in 2023, is accused of breach of trust, producing false public documents and self-serving administration.

The Central Bank said on Wednesday that 100% of customers covered by the state guarantee have received an advance of up to 40 minimum wages, about 121.8 million guaraníes or roughly US$19,600, under the emergency law passed by Congress. It has until Monday to complete repayments up to the guarantee ceiling of 75 minimum wages, about 228.3 million guaraníes or roughly US$36,600.

World.title: Leo XIV arrives in Peru, his “homeland”, defending international law and reconciliation
World.content:
Leo XIV arrives in Peru, his “homeland”, defending international law and reconciliation

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 10:59 UTC Full article

Leo XIV will remain in Peru until Monday, November 16. On Friday he will celebrate Mass in Pimentel, near Chiclayo, the diocese he led from 2015 to 2023

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Lima on Wednesday, the final stage of his South American tour, and in his first speech in Peru, the country where he lived for some twenty years and whose nationality he holds, called for diplomacy that “respects international law” in the face of wars and for the country’s past events “to be dealt with justice and sensitivity”.

President Keiko Fujimori received him at the foot of the plane, and thousands of people greeted him along the route from the airport. After meeting him at the Government Palace, the Pope addressed the authorities. “Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own history also belongs to you,” he said, referring to a country he regards as his homeland.

In the first international reference of his tour, Leo XIV said, without naming any country, that “the wars and tensions afflicting so many peoples demand patient diplomacy that keeps dialogue open, respects international law and seeks agreements that protect the life and dignity of people”. “Every nation has legitimate aspirations, but none can consider the fate of others alien to it,” he added, encouraging Peru to keep contributing to regional and international cooperation.

The Pope also referred to the country’s recent past. “Peru too has gone through difficult moments that have tested coexistence among its people. The events of the past deserve to be dealt with justice and sensitivity, leaving room for harmony to grow,” he said, adding that “democratic life means recognising that no one can be treated as a problem, but as a person with dignity”. Fujimori, who spoke before him, said “Peru needs to reconcile” and that “no country can live as a prisoner of its wounds”.

The Pope spoke alongside the daughter of Alberto Fujimori, the former president convicted of human rights violations, pardoned in 2017 and who died in 2024. According to El País, in 2017 the then Bishop of Chiclayo Robert Prevost criticised the former leader for apologising only in a “generic” way. On the eve of the visit, victims of state violence during the armed conflict of the 1980s and 1990s and of the crackdown on the 2022 and 2023 protests, in which at least some fifty people died, sent a letter alleging that “some people, from within the Church” are preventing their stories from reaching the pontiff. Former President Dina Boluarte, under whose government those deaths occurred, attended the speech.

Leo XIV will remain in Peru until Monday, November 16. On Friday he will celebrate Mass in Pimentel, near Chiclayo, the diocese he led from 2015 to 2023, where nearly a million faithful are expected; on Saturday he will visit Cajamarca and Zaña, and on Sunday, Cusco and Pucallpa, before returning to Rome.

World.title: Law of the sea tribunal to rule on November 28 on Argentina’s bid to halt Sea Lion
World.content:
Law of the sea tribunal to rule on November 28 on Argentina’s bid to halt Sea Lion

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 10:58 UTC Full article

Because the United Kingdom chose the International Court of Justice and Argentina the Hamburg tribunal, the merits of the case will be decided by an arbitral tribunal

The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea will announce on Saturday, November 28, its decision on Argentina’s request for provisional measures to halt the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, after two days of hearings concluded in Hamburg on Wednesday. Argentina presented final requests that were more specific than its initial ones, and the United Kingdom asked the tribunal to reject them all.

According to the tribunal’s statement, the reading of the order is tentatively set for noon on November 28. The date is later than some experts had anticipated, who had put the decision around November 13.

In its final submissions, signed by Argentina’s agent, Ambassador Mario Oyarzábal, Argentina asks that, pending the constitution of the arbitral tribunal that will rule on the merits, the United Kingdom take all necessary measures to ensure that no new drilling for exploitation and no installation of production infrastructure takes place in the North Falklands Basin, referred to in the Argentine filing as the North Malvinas Basin, in connection with Sea Lion. It also asks that the UK refrain from using information obtained during exploration to the detriment of Argentina’s rights, cease preventing Argentina from complying with its obligation to protect the marine environment of the disputed areas, and refrain from measures that might aggravate the dispute, in particular the granting of new exploitation authorisations. In its October request, Argentina had asked more broadly that the start or continuation of exploitation be prevented.

The United Kingdom, in a filing signed by its agent, Sally Langrish, asked the tribunal to “reject all the requests” by Argentina. Attorney General Ellie Reeves, who led the delegation, argued that the tribunal has no jurisdiction over sovereignty issues and warned that blocking the project would “kill” it, with “devastating” consequences for the islanders, who would lose billions of pounds in revenue. “In reality, what Argentina opposes is the Falkland Islands government licensing hydrocarbon activities for the economic benefit of the Falkland islanders,” she told the judges, according to coverage of the hearing.

For Argentina, jurist Marcelo Kohen said the United Kingdom cannot behave like a 17th-century colonial power treating vast expanses of the ocean as its own, according to The Guardian. Argentina also argued that London cannot invoke the sovereignty dispute to escape the tribunal’s jurisdiction while exploiting the resources “as if the dispute had already been resolved in its favour”.

Because the United Kingdom chose the International Court of Justice and Argentina the Hamburg tribunal, the merits of the case will be decided by an arbitral tribunal. Hamburg can only order provisional measures if it finds that tribunal would have prima facie jurisdiction, that there is urgency and that the right invoked is plausible. Sea Lion, operated by Israel’s Navitas Petroleum and Britain’s Rockhopper Exploration, is expected to begin drilling in January 2027.

The hearing took place while Princess Anne is visiting the islands and ahead of the debate on Argentina’s sovereignty defence bill in the Chamber of Deputies, scheduled for Thursday.

World.title: British Antarctic Survey begins a season featuring the largest-ever penguin census
World.content:
British Antarctic Survey begins a season featuring the largest-ever penguin census

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 10:51 UTC Full article

The season began with the departure from the UK of the polar icebreaker RRS Sir David Attenborough, which is running on hydrotreated vegetable oil, a biofuel

The British Antarctic Survey (BAS), the UK’s national operator in Antarctica, began its 2026/27 research season in late October, including the largest penguin census ever carried out on the continent, with flights from the British Rothera station and from Chile’s Marsh station on King George Island.

The season began with the departure from the UK of the polar icebreaker RRS Sir David Attenborough, which is running on hydrotreated vegetable oil, a biofuel, as part of the organisation’s efforts to reduce emissions, and with the arrival of its aircraft at Rothera. Dozens of scientists and support staff will be spread across the five British stations.

The census will use an aerial camera system aboard a Twin Otter aircraft, successfully trialled last season, to count around 200 colonies of Adélie, chinstrap and gentoo penguins on the Antarctic Peninsula and the South Shetland, Elephant Island and South Orkney groups. The data will help scientists understand population changes and the potential impact of krill fishing, and will feed into the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

New projects also include the first drone-based monitoring system for the body condition and demography of humpback whales, whose populations are recovering after the end of commercial whaling. A multinational study will investigate why the flow of warm water to the Amundsen Sea, a major driver of ice loss in West Antarctica, varies, with the help of the autonomous submarine Autosub Long Range. Other teams will study the compacted snow layer that protects ice shelves from melting and, with NASA and the California Institute of Technology, deploy an instrument beneath the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf.

At King Edward Point station in South Georgia, the groundfish survey will mark 40 years since it began in 1987, one of the longest records in the Southern Ocean and key to studying the effects of ocean warming on fish and the wider ecosystem.

“Collaboration is at the heart of Antarctic science,” said BAS Director Professor Dame Jane Francis, highlighting the participation of researchers from Chile, the Netherlands, the United States and Australia, as well as the value of long-term monitoring programmes.

World.title: Milei in tears as he bids farewell to Leo XIV at Ezeiza, closing the Pope’s Argentina visit
World.content:
Milei in tears as he bids farewell to Leo XIV at Ezeiza, closing the Pope’s Argentina visit

11th Wednesday, November 2026 - 19:49 UTC Full article

The day had begun at the Devoto prison in Buenos Aires, where the Pope listened to some 70 inmates

President Javier Milei was moved to tears during Pope Leo XIV’s farewell at Ezeiza airport, at the end of a four-day visit, the first by a pontiff to Argentina in 39 years. The Pope left for Peru, the second leg of his South American tour, after celebrating his last Mass at the Basilica of Luján.

Milei, accompanied by his sister and presidential chief of staff, Karina Milei, and Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, greeted the Pope and the bishops present and walked him to the steps of the plane, an Aerolíneas Argentinas Airbus A330. While the aircraft was still waiting to depart, the three embraced, as behind a fence a group of children waved small Vatican flags. The plane began taxiing at 2.14 p.m.

Javier Milei in tears, absolutely balling his eyes out, thanking Pope Leo XIV for his visit, as he asks the Pope repeatedly to pray for him. This has been an incredibly well organised trip. Everyone involved should rightly be praised. Argentina you won. https://t.co/1vAO8wZqXp — Catholic Sat (@CatholicSat) November 11, 2026

Earlier, in Luján, the Pope bade farewell to the faithful. “Thank you for receiving me with such affection. Thank you, Argentina, for receiving me with open arms. Farewell, my dear Argentina!” he said. Official figures reported by Argentine media put the crowd at the Mass at more than three million people, which have not been independently verified. At the start, he placed a Golden Rose, the highest honour the Vatican grants to Marian shrines, at the feet of the image of the Virgin. According to Infobae, he said in his farewell message that the country “now has two Popes, one born here and one by adoption”.

The day had begun at the Devoto prison in Buenos Aires, where the Pope listened to some 70 inmates. “I hope to take away the message that a new life is possible,” he said, according to the news site MDZ.

The visit began on Sunday with a speech to the authorities, with Milei present, in which the Pope said that “the economy must be at the service of the person”. On Monday he celebrated Mass in Palermo, with some 2.5 million people according to the authorities, and on Tuesday another in Córdoba, with some 650,000, according to El País. The visit was preceded by tensions between the government and the Catholic hierarchy over austerity policies. Milei, who harshly criticised Pope Francis in the past, described him on Sunday as “the most important Argentine in history”.

The Pope arrives in Lima tonight, where President Keiko Fujimori will receive him at the Government Palace. Between November 13 and 16 he will visit Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa, among other places, and he will return to Rome on the 16th.

World.title: Prosecutors open the vault at Peña’s house and find it empty; two safes found at Ueno Bank
World.content:
Prosecutors open the vault at Peña’s house and find it empty; two safes found at Ueno Bank

11th Wednesday, November 2026 - 11:12 UTC Full article

Prosecutor Silvia González said Peña, through his lawyer, indicated where the key was, which made it possible to open the room. “We found nothing of value inside,” she said

Paraguayan prosecutors on Tuesday opened the armoured vault hidden in former President Santiago Peña’s summer house in San Bernardino, two days after finding it, and found it empty. In a second raid, at Ueno Bank’s headquarters, they found two more hidden safes, one containing about US$14,000 in cash.

Prosecutor Silvia González said Peña, through his lawyer, indicated where the key was, which made it possible to open the room despite its complex security system. “We found nothing of value inside,” she said. According to the defence, the space was built as a “panic room”. Images released show an empty space with ventilation and electrical connections, without furniture. The house, which cost about 7.7 billion guaraníes (US$1.25 million) financed with loans from Ueno Bank, has passed to the administration of Senabico, the state body that manages seized assets.

Neighbours say three SUVs left the residence several times on Friday, November 5, as the Senate began Peña’s impeachment trial, and surveillance cameras reportedly recorded the vehicles’ movements. It has not been reported what they were carrying.

At Ueno Bank’s headquarters, known as La Matrix, investigators found a safe about 1.70 metres tall hidden behind a wall in a rooftop bathroom, linked to the offices of former vice-president and chief executive Miguel Vázquez. It contained documents and drinks, but no money. A second safe was in a false bottom in the bathroom of his office. Prosecutor Jorge Arce opened it and found 87.1 million guaraníes, about US$14,000 in cash, along with documents and empty bags.

An appeals court meanwhile upheld Vázquez’s pre-trial detention and provisionally expanded the legal classification of his case to money laundering and criminal association, so he could face up to 15 years in prison, according to the newspaper La Nación of Paraguay. Peña, charged with breach of trust and self-serving administration, has been in pre-trial detention since Saturday and says he is innocent. Prosecutors estimate the damage at about US$809 million.

Opposition lawmakers criticise prosecutors for not having seized Peña’s mobile phone and for delaying the raids, which they say allowed evidence to be removed, and are calling for the impeachment of Attorney General Emiliano Rolón. The Colorado Party has the votes to block it.

World.title: EU-Mercosur deal, six months on: winners, losers and the question mark over Europe’s top court
World.content:
EU-Mercosur deal, six months on: winners, losers and the question mark over Europe’s top court

11th Wednesday, November 2026 - 11:02 UTC Full article

Supporters highlight tariff savings of about €4 billion and a market of more than 700 million consumers

Six months after it began to apply provisionally, the trade agreement between the European Union and Mercosur, made up of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, combines projected benefits for both blocs, opposition from part of Europe’s farming sector and a legal question mark: the opinion of the EU Court of Justice on its legality, which could take until early 2028.

The interim trade agreement, signed in January, has applied since May 1 and covers trade and investment liberalisation. Mercosur will gradually eliminate tariffs on 91% of imports from the EU and the EU on 92% of those from Mercosur. The European Commission specified that it applies to those South American countries that completed their ratification. The broader, political Association Agreement must be ratified by all 27 member states. On January 21, the European Parliament voted 334 to 324 to ask the court to review the deal. The Commission then said those doubts were unjustified, and provisional application continues in the meantime.

Supporters highlight tariff savings of about €4 billion and a market of more than 700 million consumers. BBVA Research estimates that bilateral trade will grow by 40% by the end of the 16-year implementation period. For Mercosur, the estimates cited by the newspaper point to a boost of up to half a percentage point of GDP in Argentina and one and a half in Brazil.

There are also sectors set to lose. According to BBVA Research economist Juan Ruiz, in Europe these will be extensive beef farming, sugar and bioethanol, and in Mercosur, industry and manufacturing. The agreement provides for closed quotas for beef and poultry, safeguards if prices fall by more than 5% and a €45 billion reserve to compensate European farmers. Ruiz acknowledges that these protections “distort the market”, but give time to adapt. Spanish farming organisation ASAJA argues that one cannot speak of “fair competition” while agreements are signed with countries that do not fully guarantee compliance with EU standards.

That debate was revived on September 3, when the Commission suspended imports of meat, eggs and honey from Brazil over antibiotic use incompatible with EU rules, pending an audit. For the specialists consulted, the measure shows that protection works. “There has been a lot of misinformation in the farming sector, which is the most protected in the world and has nothing to fear,” said Juan Moscoso del Prado of EsadeGeo.

Legal uncertainty worries businesses. “The uncertainty arising from the agreement’s legal status remains, which for now prevents companies from planning,” said Mar Guardiola, head of tax at Andersen. Her colleague Rafael Ripoll recalled that annulment has not been sought, only an opinion on three aspects, and that the formula of splitting the treaty in two was already used with the agreement with Canada.

On the geopolitical front, Moscoso del Prado considers it a deal “clearly alternative to the model imposed by both the US and China”. Experts concede that it arrives late, as China leads in goods trade, but argue it is not obsolete.

World.title: Leo XIV draws some 650,000 to Córdoba with a homily on holiness
World.content:
Leo XIV draws some 650,000 to Córdoba with a homily on holiness

11th Wednesday, November 2026 - 10:55 UTC Full article

On Wednesday, Leo XIV will celebrate his last Mass in Argentina in Luján, in Buenos Aires province, and then fly to Peru

Pope Leo XIV celebrated Mass on Tuesday in Córdoba, in central Argentina, before some 650,000 people, according to the newspaper El País, in a homily devoted to holiness and local saints. “There is no better way to teach than by setting an example with one’s own life,” he told the faithful, urging them to practise their faith concretely in daily life.

The pontiff left Buenos Aires at 7.30 a.m. and landed in Córdoba an hour and a half later. The Mass was held at the grounds of the Argentine Aircraft Factory, covering more than 200 hectares, with 50 giant screens. Many pilgrims came by bus from other provinces, walked the last stretch before dawn and camped in the open. Among them were 28 altar boys from a parish in Jujuy, 900 kilometres away, who raised the travel money by selling food and holding pet shows. “I was left with all my hopes,” said Dora Ponce, 76, who did not manage to see the popemobile pass and followed the ceremony on a screen.

In his homily, Leo XIV recalled figures such as Father Brochero and Mama Antula, venerated above all in the interior of the country, and highlighted Córdoba’s religious history, marked by the arrival of the Jesuits in the 16th century. Its Jesuit Block has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000.

After the Mass the Pope privately received a group of about 20 people from various social struggles, among them Alba Camargo, who as a child was abducted during the last dictatorship (1976-1983) and lost relatives to forced disappearance. Camargo asked him to name the disappeared and for his words to encourage those who know something about those crimes, including members of the clergy, to come forward. The Vatican has not given details of the meeting.

In the afternoon, the Pope greeted crowds from the balcony of the Archbishopric, the same one John Paul II appeared on in 1987, and met members of religious orders at the Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption. “There are stages in priestly and consecrated life in which remaining is already a very concrete form of self-giving,” he told them. The meeting was especially moving for the cloistered nuns who prepared the celebration: they baked 400,000 hosts and polished the chalices and liturgical items.

Attendance at the Córdoba Mass was lower than in Buenos Aires, where authorities estimated some 2.5 million people, and than the million the provincial government had anticipated. On Wednesday, Leo XIV will celebrate his last Mass in Argentina in Luján, in Buenos Aires province, and then fly to Peru, where President Keiko Fujimori will receive him that night.

World.title: Mexico and My Money: Protecting yourself from counterfeit bills
World.content:
After nearly five years in Mexico, I’m now worried about something I never even considered worrying about before: being given counterfeit pesos.

Back in 2008, I received some fake pesos (the Argentine variety) from a taxi driver in Buenos Aires. At the time, I felt like an idiot for being duped. Since then, I hadn’t given it another thought.

Until this year, I’d never even seen this problem mentioned in the press. But it turns out that the threat from counterfeit currency is on the rise in Mexico. So being aware of the risks — and how to spot fake bills — is increasingly important.

How big is the problem of counterfeit money in Mexico?

Banco de México (also known as Banxico) removes hundreds of thousands of counterfeit notes from circulation annually. It remains such a serious problem because Mexico is still a cash-centric economy.

Last year, Banxico seized 291,673 counterfeit notes, up from 286,917 bogus notes in 2024, but below the peak level of more than 350,000 notes in 2022. While those numbers are huge, counterfeit money in Mexico is nothing new.

The problem dates back nearly a century.

Authorities discovered the first massive counterfeiting operation in Mexico City back in October 1934. The operation was masterminded by Alfredo Héctor Donadieu, a Frenchman originally from Marseille known here by the alias “Enrico Sampietro.”

Monsieur Sampietro was a colorful character and supremely gifted artist who forged Mexican banknotes throughout the 1930s and 1940s, living lavishly off the proceeds before he was caught. He served a total of 13 years in Mexico City’s infamous Lecumberri prison before being deported back to his native France.

Fast-forward to the 21st century, Banxico has engaged in a technical arms race against organized crime to protect the currency, introducing ever more sophisticated features to make Mexican banknotes more difficult to forge.

The central bank’s innovations include the addition of security threads, watermarks, color-shifting elements and specialized printing. But these enhancements have been matched by parallel innovations in digital printing, high-resolution scanning and commercial printing equipment, which criminals have embraced in their quest to produce high-fidelity fake currency.

The most commonly counterfeited bills in Mexico

While the data vary a bit from year to year, criminals generally prefer to forge high-denomination bills used in high volumes. The simple reason is that larger bills offer a better return on investment than smaller bills.

In 2025, 51% of all counterfeit notes removed from circulation were 500-peso notes.

The second most frequently forged bill was the 100-peso note, accounting for about 25% of the total. The 200-peso note was the third most common target, accounting for another 19% of bills confiscated last year.

All other denominations accounted for the remaining 3% of fake bills seized in 2025.

Where the risk is highest to encounter forged banknotes

The chance of receiving counterfeit money varies significantly depending on where you are in Mexico.

Mexico City consistently leads the nation, with tens of thousands of fake bills reported annually. The state of Mexico (excluding the capital) and Jalisco, home to both Guadalajara and Puerto Vallarta, are also considered the highest-risk locations.

Outside of big cities, the Yucatán Peninsula is a popular target for counterfeiters due to its heavy tourist traffic and relatively heavy reliance on cash. In this region, Mérida and Valladolid have reported significant counterfeit activity in recent years.

Conversely, states with lower population densities, such as Baja California Sur and Campeche, see the lowest incidence of counterfeit currency.

Penalties are stiff for passing illegal money in Mexico

Under Article 234 of Mexico’s Código Penal Federal, passing counterfeit currency carries a strict penalty of five to 12 years in prison.

If you receive a suspicious note, the recommended action is to hand it over to a bank teller, who will issue a receipt and submit the note or notes to Banxico for forensic analysis. To be clear, when you do this, the bank will not replace your forged note with a legitimate one.

While the federal government doesn’t publish official statistics on cases brought against counterfeiters, independent investigations by InSight Crime and others have found that records from the Fiscalía General de la República (FGR), along with judicial data, reveal a massive disconnect between the huge volume of fake notes seized annually and the number of cases prosecuted.

The large gap exists because the legal bar to convict counterfeiters is quite high. Namely, prosecutors must prove not only that the accused passed fake bills, but that the user had criminal intent. Pleading ignorance is a strategy that works rather well in these cases.

When charges do get brought, they tend to be focused on sophisticated, large-scale counterfeiting operations, not cases against individuals.

Learn to identify genuine Mexican banknotes to protect yourself

Counterfeiters prey on unsuspecting consumers and businesses. So, it helps to be familiar with the signature details of authentic Mexican banknotes to avoid being duped.

Conveniently, your own hands are one of the best tools for detecting fake money.

Real Mexican banknotes have a special texture that you can feel, because they’re made of cotton and polymer. It’s one of the easiest ways to distinguish a genuine banknote from a counterfeit one.

In addition, raised print is used for denominations and signatures, allowing you to easily check their authenticity by running your finger over them.

When viewed against a bright light, you can also see the following features on real Mexican money:

Microprinted security threads that change color when the paper is moved Ink that glows under ultraviolet light Tiny numbers displaying the name and series

Fake notes will have certain flaws and one or more distinguishing features. The most obvious tells are smooth paper and text, uneven colors and blurry faces or monuments.

If you notice any of these things when receiving money at a business, street market or from an individual, decline it and ask for a replacement.

For those who work in Mexico and handle cash regularly, it’s also worth buying a small, portable UV lamp or specialized marker pen like Check It to verify that the notes you receive are authentic.

From tipping and working with local contractors to moving money into Mexico from abroad, check out more from MND’s “Mexico and My Money” archive.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Growing solar panel use drives Mexico’s 9.4% rise this year in distributed energy
World.content:
Distributed generation — electricity produced on a smaller scale near where it will be used — is on the rise in Mexico, having increased 9.4% in the first six months of the year, according to the National Energy Commission (CNE).

Driven by the growing use of rooftop solar panels, Mexico’s distributed generation reached 5,675 megawatts (MW) of cumulative installed capacity, with 485.76 MW and 54,766 new contracts added in the first half of the year

By generating electricity via modular systems located at or near the point of consumption, solar panels and other on-site systems don’t use large, centralized power plants or long-distance transmission lines, thereby helping reduce reliance on the national grid and supporting the nation’s transition to green energy-.

Distributed photovoltaic solar energy accounts for 5,640 MW of the distributed power and over 99.5% of the installed capacity under the CNE scheme. Cumulative investment in distributed generation reached a reported US $14.58 billion at the end of June.

“These investments reflect user confidence in these technologies and drive economic development, the creation of specialized jobs and the strengthening of supply chains linked to clean energy and high-value-added technologies,” the CNE stated.

Jalisco dominates in distributed electricity generation

The states with the largest installed capacity are Jalisco (808.58 MW), Nuevo León (596.22 MW) and Chihuahua (424.85 MW), together contributing 32% of the national total. Distributed generation is also growing in Guanajuato, Coahuila, México state, Sonora and Yucatán, demonstrating progress across various parts of Mexico.

In Jalisco, where distributed generation is expected to surpass 1,000 MW by 2030, the scheme is part of its Sustainable Energy Development Plan. The aim is for the state to generate at least as much energy as it consumes by 2030, with 60% of that energy coming from clean sources, up from 42% today.

“Every photovoltaic system installed in Jalisco frees up grid capacity, strengthens the supply chain, generates savings for families and businesses and reduces emissions,” Manuel Herrera Vega, head of the Jalisco Ministry of Energy and Sustainable Development, told the newspaper El Economista.

Those benefits cannot come too soon. The Mexican Institute for Competitiveness estimates that achieving the Plan México growth targets would increase electricity demand by 10.1% , or an additional 11.9 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity than what is currently considered in the official planning for 2030.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: Indigenous language skills can now open the door to a career in Mexico’s Foreign Service
World.content:
For the first time, Mexico has begun counting Indigenous-language skills toward entry into its Foreign Service — aiming to improve consular assistance for Mexicans in the United States who speak those languages.

Applicants to the service’s technical-administrative branch can now demonstrate proficiency in specified varieties of Maya, Mixtec, Nahuatl or Zapotec to meet a language requirement.

The Ministry of Foreign Relations (SRE) published a recruitment notice Oct. 20 in Mexico’s Official Gazette (DOF), offering up to 80 positions: 44 in administration, 20 in consular affairs, communities and protection, and 16 in information technology and digitization.

Applicants do not have to prove Indigenous ancestry.

Ana Luisa Fajer, president of the Foreign Service Personnel Commission, said approximately 500,000 Mexicans of Indigenous origin live in the United States.

Recruiting speakers of their languages would improve access to documents, legal advice and consular protection, she added.

Rafael Laveaga, Mexico’s consul general in Atlanta, said language barriers complicate assistance for hospitalized patients, immigration detainees trying to understand their rights and crime victims communicating with lawyers.

Consulates provide that assistance, but finding interpreters can delay immediate help, he said. Hundreds of families speaking Mixtec, Zapotec and Nahuatl live in Georgia, Alabama and eastern Tennessee, he added.

The change follows a consular initiative launched last year to provide government information in 15 Indigenous languages at Mexican consulates, embassies and other offices abroad.

Mexico’s consulate in Los Angeles has worked with the local Indigenous advocacy organization CIELO since 2022 to provide interpretation, train staff, and promote Indigenous languages and cultures. CIELO is a women-led nonprofit that stands for Comunidades Indígenas en Liderazgo (Indigenous Communities in Leadership).

Language barriers also affect services inside Mexico. In a June article by Animal Político, specialists identified shortages of bilingual medical personnel and Indigenous-language educational materials among shortcomings limiting access to health care and education.

Though the change was widely reported only this week, the Oct. 26 to Nov. 3 registration period has already closed. Applicants accepted for the next step have until Nov. 17 to submit documents.

The first elimination round includes entrance exams in January; further evaluations and training will be held next spring.

Applicants must also pass a written Spanish exam, but those qualifying with an Indigenous language are not required to demonstrate proficiency in English or another foreign language.

With reports from Infobae, Animal Político and NX Noticias

World.title: Is violence in Mexico really falling, and by how much?
World.content:
The National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) reported over 5,000 more homicides in 2025 than the federal government’s Executive Secretariat of the National Public Security System (SESNSP), the largest gap in more than a decade.

INEGI reported on Tuesday that there were 29,488 homicides (or alleged homicides) in Mexico in 2025. According to INEGI’s “Registered Death Statistics” report, homicide was the eighth leading cause of death in Mexico last year.

INEGI’s homicide count is 5,140 higher than the combined number of homicides and femicides reported by the SESNSP in 2025. In percentage terms, the number of homicides reported by INEGI is 21.2% higher than the 24,348 homicides and femicides reported by the SESNSP.

The gap between the two numbers is the highest in the last 11 years, according to the news outlet Animal Político.

The difference is 95.3% higher than in 2024, when INEGI’s homicide total was 2,632 higher than the SESNSP count. It should be noted that the SESNSP’s homicide data is compiled from statistics it receives from the Attorney General’s Offices in Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

Marcela Figueroa, the head of the National Public Security System, reports the compiled data on a monthly basis at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s morning press conferences.

As Mexico News Daily reported in January, the reliability of the statistics the state-based Attorney General’s Offices provide to the SESNSP is considered by many to be questionable. There have also been claims that the decline in homicides during Sheinbaum’s presidency is related to an increase in disappearances.

“State Attorney General’s Offices don’t work in a vacuum,” Alberto Guerrero Baena, a public security consultant and academic, wrote in a column published by the news outlet Expansión in January.

“They operate under budgetary, political and media pressures. When a homicide is difficult to prove or requires lengthy investigation, there is an incentive to reclassify it as injury, accidental death or a lesser crime. … An unresolved homicide looks bad in the statistics. A [fatal] injury unrelated to homicide looks better,” Guerrero wrote.

The homicides reported by the SESNSP (and referred to above) are homicidios dolosos, or intentional homicides. Homicidios culposos — negligent or culpable homicides — are categorized separately by the federal government agency.

Why the discrepancy?

In a report published on Wednesday, Animal Político noted that the difference between INEGI’s homicide statistics and those of the SESNSP is not new, although it has increased significantly in recent years. The difference, the news outlet added, is explained, “in part,” by their methodologies.

For its homicide count, INEGI looks at death certificates and records as well as information from civil registry offices, forensic services and Attorney General’s Offices. In classifying a death as a homicide, INEGI looks closely at the cause of the death.

The SESNSP simply compiles the statistics it receives from the Attorney General’s Offices in Mexico’s 32 federal entities. It essentially takes the fiscalías, as the offices are called, at their word, despite allegations that they — or at least some of them — are fudging the numbers.

In an Oct. 30 column published by the Saltillo-based newspaper Vanguardia, Víctor Manuel Sánchez Valdés, a professor and researcher at the Autonomous University of Coahuila, wrote that INEGI’s statistics “are usually more reliable” than those of the SESNSP as INEGI “cross-checks various sources.”

Most of Mexico’s fiscalías — but not all— are formally autonomous of the governments in the states in which they operate. Still, there are claims by opposition politicians and others that fiscalías in states governed by Morena, Mexico’s ruling party, are manipulating data to make the country’s homicide toll appear lower than it actually is.

“Morena doesn’t fight violence, it covers it up,” National Action Party Senator Mayuli Martínez said in June.

“… It is concerning that in Quintana Roo there are six times as many homicides classified as negligent [homicidio culposo] as there are those classified as intentional [homicidio doloso],” she said.

“When more cases [involving the death of a person] are classified under categories other than intentional homicide, it creates an artificial impression of improvement in public safety indicators,” Martínez said.

Quintana Roo is one of 23 states governed by Morena. Data showing declining homicide numbers is, of course, politically beneficial to the federal government and Morena.

President Sheinbaum and other federal officials frequently cite the homicide statistics reported by the SESNSP as evidence that the government’s security strategy is working. On Tuesday, Figueroa, the National Public Security System chief, reported that homicides were down 50% in October compared to September 2024, the final month of Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s presidency.

Among the five states that recorded the biggest year-over-year reductions in homicides in the first 10 months of 2026, three are governed by Morena (Nayarit, Quintana Roo and Baja California Sur), one is governed by the Green Party (San Luis Potosí), an ally of Morena, and one is governed by the Citizens Movement Party (Nuevo León).

Sheinbaum has rejected claims that state fiscalías are manipulating statistics.

“Homicide is homicide, there is no manipulation. It’s not that there are crimes that go from [being classified as] one crime to another crime,” she said at her July 14 press conference.

At the same press conference, Figueroa said that the methodology that state Attorney General’s Offices are required to follow when classifying crimes is “very clear” and “public.”

Still, not everyone is buying federal officials’ assurances that state fiscalías’ homicide figures are accurate.

In his Oct. 30 column, Sánchez poses the question on many Mexicans’ lips: Is violence in Mexico really decreasing?

“The quick answer is yes, but we don’t know the exact extent [of the reduction],” he wrote.

“… Despite these [alleged] manipulations that seek to artificially reduce intentional homicides, everything indicates that there has been a reduction [in violence] since Claudia Sheinbaum came to power and the [new] security strategies were implemented by [Security Minister] Omar García Harfuch,” Sánchez wrote.

In other words, he (and many other Mexicans) believes that homicides have gone down, but not as much as the data compiled by the SESNSP indicates.

Security Ministry: SESNSP homicide numbers are ‘complementary’ and ‘show the same trend’

In early August, shortly after INEGI published preliminary homicide data for 2025, the federal Security Ministry (SSPC) released a statement titled “INEGI’s vital statistics confirm the decline in intentional homicides in 2025.”

INEGI’s preliminary statistics showed a 16.6% year-over-year reduction in homicides in 2025, more than four points higher than the 12.1% decline according to the final data published on Tuesday. According to SESNSP data, the year-over-year reduction in homicides in 2025 was 21.2%. At 9.1 percentage points, the difference between the reduction in homicides reported by INEGI and the decline reported by the SESNSP is not insignificant.

In its statement, the SSPC wrote that “the measurement of intentional homicide by INEGI and SESNSP are complementary exercises that use different methodologies and serve different purposes.”

The ministry said that the difference between their homicide numbers is “expected” as “each institution performs different functions, uses different [data] integration procedures, has different collection, validation, and publication periods, and generates information for specific purposes.”

Still, “the trend shown by both sources” is “consistent” with the progress made under the national security strategy, the SSPC said.

“Both sources show the same trend with respect to the evolution of intentional homicide,” the ministry said.

INEGI’s 2025 homicide data in brief

INEGI reported that there were 29,488 homicides in 2025, a reduction of 12.1% compared to the 33,550 homicides in 2024.

Almost nine in ten homicide victims in 2025 (87.5%) were men. Women accounted for 11.3% of victims while the sex of the deceased person wasn’t specified in 1.2% of cases.

Almost three in ten homicide victims (28.2%) were men aged 25 to 34.

Homicide was the leading cause of death in 2025 for men aged 25 to 34 and men aged 35 to 44.

Mexico recorded 22.6 homicides per 100,000 residents in 2025. There were 40.5 homicides per 100,000 men and 5 homicides per 100,000 women.

Among Mexico’s 32 federal entities, Guanajuato recorded the highest number of homicides in 2025 with 3,334. México state ranked second with 2,618 homicides, followed by Chihuahua (2,291), Baja California (2,144) and Sinaloa (1,966).

Mexico City recorded 830 homicides last year, the 16th highest total among the 32 federal entities.

Yucatán was the only entity that recorded fewer than 100 homicides in 2025. There were 59 homicides in the state.

Colima recorded the highest number of homicides per 100,000 residents in 2025, with 92.6. Sinaloa ranked second with 62.3 homicides per 100,000 people, followed by Morelos (58.6), Chihuahua (58) and Baja California (56.8).

The cause of death in 70.6% of homicides was a gunshot wound or wounds. Stabbings were the second most common means of homicide, accounting for 9.5% of cases. About one in 15 homicides (6.6%) involved hanging, strangling or suffocation.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

With reports from Animal Político

World.title: More foreign tourists are visiting Mexico for its culture than for any other reason — including beach resorts
World.content:
Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez Zamora told thousands of tourism industry professionals gathered in Guadalajara this week that Mexico’s total of 67.7 million foreign arrivals over the first eight months of the year was a two-decade high — and that the most common motive for their visit was to experience Mexican culture.

Rodríguez was speaking as the host of the opening ceremony of the first ITB Americas trade show, which will continue through Thursday. It is expected to attract 5,000 representatives from 61 countries, including participation from all 31 Mexican states plus Mexico City, 300 exhibiting companies and organizations and 300 specialized buyers. Its economic impact for Mexico should be around US $13 million.

In a true sign of the times, Rodríguez informed the gathering that approximately 36.3% of this year’s visitors said they came to Mexico for its cultural tourism. That percentage more than doubles the 15%-16% that came for beach tourism.

Meanwhile, sports tourism has been growing in popularity, getting a boost from the 2026 FIFA World Cup, but also traceable to the Mexican Formula 1 Grand Prix, several major international marathons, cycling events, open water swimming competitions and surfing opportunities, as well as tennis and golf tournaments.

Mexico is now the sixth most-visited country worldwide and No. 1 in the Americas, with hopes of moving up to the fifth most popular tourist destination by 2030 under the government’s Plan México national development strategy.

Mexico City has moved ahead of international cities such as London and Singapore in entertainment tourism, largely owing to hosting world-class concerts, said Rodríguez.

The tourism minister announced a planned investment of $42 billion in Mexico’s tourism sector by 2030, primarily directed at hotel and airport infrastructure, training for regional operators and strategies for enhancing tourist experiences across all states.

Rodríguez said that Mexico’s tourism model emphasizes regional service providers who had historically been marginalized.

With reports from LatinUS, Infobae and Informador

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico City man forced to buy event merchandise to obtain tortillas outside his own apartment
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Municipal authorities confirmed Monday that Mexico City is on track to welcome a record-breaking 65.9 million tourists in 2026 — a massive influx driven by a packed calendar of international concerts and sporting events that has effectively transformed central residential neighborhoods into perpetual venue concourses.

The capital’s tourism boom, which has generated over 120 billion pesos in hotel revenue and a 16% jump in lodging tax collections, was fully on display Tuesday morning when local resident Rodrigo Morales was forced to purchase a 1,200-peso commemorative stadium tour hoodie just to reach the tortilleria on his own block.

Morales, 34, reportedly found himself cut off from basic domestic staples after event organizers erected a temporary VIP concourse, three wristband authentication checkpoints, and a corporate sponsor village outside his apartment building to accommodate back-to-back stadium shows and motorsport crowds.

“I simply wanted half a kilo of warm corn tortillas,” said Morales, standing in a two-hour credentialing queue while wearing a neon-laminated media pass. “However, security staff informed me that the sidewalk leading to the corner shop had been designated an exclusive artist-merchandise corridor. My options were either to buy the limited-edition tour fleece or attempt to breach the soundboard barricade.”

City tourism officials praised the interaction as proof of the capital’s booming hospitality economy, noting that as visitor volume reaches double its level from 10 years ago, public infrastructure must seamlessly integrate with event monetization.

“With tens of millions of visitors flooding the capital, our goal is to ensure every square block offers the vibrant commercial flow of an arena,” explained a spokesperson for the local tourism ministry. “When a local resident buys official tour merchandise just to step over an idling broadcast truck and retrieve his groceries, that represents a direct victory for our economic projections.”

At press time, Morales reported that while his tortillas were completely cold by the time he cleared the final security metal detector, he remained optimistic about his evening plans, provided he could secure a general-admission wristband to access his own bathroom.

World.title: Sheinbaum calls NYT report on CIA’s alleged bargain with Chihuahua prosecutor ‘very interesting’: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📰 NYT report spotlights ex-prosecutor who allegedly partnered with CIA: Sheinbaum called the Times article on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, “very interesting.” The report says Zuany’s revoked U.S. visa was reinstated after he helped CIA officers train state forces and join missions. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Tuesday that both the FGR and the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office have outstanding arrest warrants for Zuany.

Sheinbaum called the Times article on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, “very interesting.” The report says Zuany’s revoked U.S. visa was reinstated after he helped CIA officers train state forces and join missions. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Tuesday that both the FGR and the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office have outstanding arrest warrants for Zuany. ⚖️ “ It’s illegal because it violates the National Security Law”: Sheinbaum said her government flagged the CIA’s participation in an April drug lab raid in Chihuahua as illegal as soon as it found out about it. Former Chihuahua attorney general César Jáuregui was detained last month on a treason charge. She said any collaboration with foreign agencies must respect the Constitution and the National Security Law, and that “in this case, [the law] wasn’t obeyed.”

Sheinbaum said her government flagged the CIA’s participation in an April drug lab raid in Chihuahua as illegal as soon as it found out about it. Former Chihuahua attorney general César Jáuregui was detained last month on a treason charge. She said any collaboration with foreign agencies must respect the Constitution and the National Security Law, and that “in this case, [the law] wasn’t obeyed.” 🏥 IMSS Bienestar doctor’s appointments up 55% since 2023: Director Alejandro Svarch said the public healthcare service for people without social security is on track to provide 58.3 million free consultations this year, up from 37.3 million in 2023. Specialist appointments are projected to rise 105%.

Director Alejandro Svarch said the public healthcare service for people without social security is on track to provide 58.3 million free consultations this year, up from 37.3 million in 2023. Specialist appointments are projected to rise 105%. 📈 Opposition-governed states lag: Svarch said “general consultations” rose just 4% between 2023 and 2026 in the eight states that haven’t joined IMSS Bienestar, which operates in 24 of 32 federal entities, while specialist appointments are forecast to rise 27%. “It’s the same country, the same period, but you can see the results are vastly different,” he said.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Wednesday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum responded to a New York Times report headlined “The Man Who Helped the C.I.A. Secretly Operate in Mexico.”

Published on Tuesday, the article focuses on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, the state where U.S. Central Intelligence Agency officers allegedly participated in a drug lab raid in April without the authorization or knowledge of the Mexican government. Two CIA agents and two Chihuahua police officials died in a car accident after the raid, a tragedy that helped bring the CIA’s presence in the state to light.

The New York Times report states that “[w]hen the Central Intelligence Agency was looking to quietly expand its operations in Mexico last year, it found an especially useful partner.”

“… To the C.I.A., Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a prosecutor and former police commander in the border state of Chihuahua, offered a different kind of partnership,” the report says.

“He could pair C.I.A. officers with Mexican police units on counter-cartel operations — and he was in a bind that made him uniquely cooperative, Mexican and U.S. officials said.”

That bind, according to the Times, was that Zuany’s U.S. visa had been revoked “because of his suspected ties to the very cartels the C.I.A. wanted to root out.”

The Times reported that Zuany’s visa was reinstated after he “shepherded C.I.A. officers as they trained Chihuahua State forces, joined those forces on certain missions and provided expertise during ground operations” during a period of more than six months.

Beyond Sheinbaum’s response to the New York Times report, another notable topic at today’s mañanera was the performance of IMSS Bienestar, Mexico’s public healthcare service for people without social security coverage through institutions such as the Mexican Social Security Institute, or IMSS, and the State Workers’ Social Security Institute, or ISSSTE.

The IMSS Bienestar scheme was established by the previous federal government and now operates in 24 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities. Eight states have opted against signing onto the scheme. Those states — Nuevo León, Coahuila, Durango, Jalisco, Querétaro, Aguascalientes, Chihuahua and Guanajuato — are all governed by opposition parties, rather than by Morena, Mexico’s ruling party.

NYT report ‘very interesting,’ says Sheinbaum

A reporter raised the New York Times report about Zuany, noting that it quotes the former prosecutor as saying that Chihuahua Governor Maru Campos was aware of the CIA’s presence in the northern border state, something that Campos denies.

Sheinbaum, who has previously been critical of the Times’ reporting on Mexico, said she read the report and described it as “very interesting.”

🇲🇽#México | Claudia Sheinbaum se refirió al reportaje de The New York Times sobre la presunta facilitación de operaciones de la CIA por parte de Guillermo Zuany, fiscal especializado de Chihuahua. La presidenta calificó la publicación como “muy interesante” y sostuvo que los agentes estadounidenses deben apegarse a la Ley de Seguridad Nacional. “En este caso no se respetó”, afirmó. #ClaudiaSheinbaum #Chihuahua #CIA #SeguridadNacional 🌐 Consulta #ElPortalDeÁngulo7

➡️ https://t.co/14SVC19UGG — Ángulo7 Noticias (@angulosiete) November 11, 2026

She subsequently noted that the former attorney general of Chihuahua, César Jáuregui, was arrested in connection with the CIA’s presence in the state. Jáuregui, who was detained by federal authorities on a treason charge last month, is accused of allowing CIA officers to participate in the drug lab raid in Chihuahua in April without authorization from the Mexican government.

Sheinbaum said that the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) has to continue its investigation of the case. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said on Tuesday that both the FGR and the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office have outstanding warrants for the arrest of Zuany.

Sheinbaum said that Zuany’s alleged conduct is “very relevant” to investigations into the CIA’s presence in Chihuahua.

“It’s worth learning about who this person is and how he collaborated with one of the U.S. agencies,” she said.

Although the New York Times report states that CIA officers joined Chihuahua state forces “on certain missions” and that the CIA “began working” with Zuany “around 2025,” Sheinbaum asserted that “the article doesn’t say that there were operations [with the CIA] since 2025.”

“It says there was [CIA] presence,” she said.

Sheinbaum highlighted that her government pointed out that the CIA’s participation in the drug lab raid in Chihuahua was illegal as soon as it found out about it.

“It’s illegal because it violates the National Security Law,” she said.

“And the Federal Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation,” Sheinbaum added.

“Today, the [former] attorney general of Chihuahua is detained for this reason. The important thing is that … any collaboration [with foreign authorities] has to guarantee respect for the [Mexican] Constitution and the National Security Law,” she said.

“Any agent from a U.S. agency in Mexico has to comply with the National Security Law,” Sheinbaum said.

“In this case, [the law] wasn’t obeyed,” she said.

IMSS Bienestar chief reports sharp increase in doctor’s appointments

At the start of his presentation, IMSS Bienestar director Alejandro Svarch said that “for decades, where a person was born and the job they held determined the range of medical care they were able to receive.”

“Three years ago, IMSS Bienestar began transforming this reality,” he said.

“Today we are the largest network of public health services in our country and above all we’re an institute that is achieving results,” Svarch said.

He went on to report that the number of medical consultations provided by IMSS Bienestar is projected to increase 55% this year compared to 2023. IMSS Bienestar is on track to provide 58.3 million free doctor’s appointments this year, according to the data presented by Svarch, up from 37.3 million in 2023.

“That’s why we say the model works. The results are clear and compelling,” the IMSS Bienestar chief said.

Svarch noted that IMSS Bienestar operates in 24 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities, while eight states have their own public healthcare systems for people without social security coverage.

He reported that “general consultations” increased just 4% this year compared to 2023 in the eight states that haven’t signed on to IMSS Bienestar.

“It’s the same country, the same period, but you can see the results are vastly different,” Svarch said.

He also reported that the number of specialist doctor’s appointments provided by IMSS Bienestar is projected to rise 105% this year compared to 2023, while the increase over the same period in states where IMSS Bienestar doesn’t operate is forecast to be 27%.

“These results are not the product of chance,” Svarch said.

“They are the product of actions and a very specific implementation plan,” he said.

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Eat, dance, swim, run, repeat!
World.content:
One of the things I love most about living in Puerto Vallarta is the variety of entertainment and activities on offer. Case in point, this month you can 1) taste cuisine from some of Mexico’s top chefs at the 31st International Gourmet Festival; 2) listen to live jazz, rock and mariachi at one of Vallarta’s many great music venues; 3) compete in an open-water swimming race; or 4) run a half-marathon. OK, so the last two might not be for everyone, but you can cheer on the racers instead.

Read on to learn more about these exciting events.

31st International Gourmet Festival

Puerto Vallarta’s reputation as a culinary destination is on the rise. Earlier this year, two local restaurants, Icú and Pancho’s Takos, earned spots on the prestigious Michelin Guide’s recommended list, a first for the city. This month, Vallarta will host the 31st International Gourmet Festival from Nov. 12-22. The festival brings some of the most celebrated Mexican chefs together for 11 days of culinary events at more than 25 top-rated restaurants in Puerto Vallarta, Riviera Nayarit and Tepic.

Events include tasting experiences featuring food and wine from more than a dozen restaurants, dining “safaris” where you travel to a few selected restaurants in one night, multicourse fine dining at single restaurants featuring guest chefs and even a drag brunch.

On Nov. 17, the Technological University of Bahía de Banderas (UTBB) will host a panel of chefs who will discuss the latest trends shaping the culinary scene in Mexico. The panel discussion is free and open to the public. Tickets for the dining experiences are available for purchase on the festival website.

Live music up close and personal

I love listening to live music, especially in intimate settings where I can watch the performers up close. In my last events roundup, I promised to share some of my favorite venues. True to my word, here you go:

The Social Club: The Social Club is a modern-day speakeasy located at 447 Basilio Badillo in the Romantic Zone. Just a narrow black door marks its spot. If you’ve never been before, you could easily miss it. I feel transported to another era every time I visit. After entering the front door, you climb up a narrow staircase, pass through red velvet curtains and enter a small parlor-style room with tiny tables lit by tiny lamps. The “stage” is at the back of the room, just a few feet from the tables. Waiters clad in Prohibition-era outfits serve bespoke and classic cocktails. Doors open at 9 p.m., and music starts around 10 p.m., featuring many of the best local jazz musicians and many special events. This is one of our favorite date-night spots in all of Vallarta.

Aquí Nomás: In the mood for a Mexican folk music singalong? Then you want to go to Aquí Nomás in Versalles. On Friday and Saturday nights, the neighborhood cantina hosts a live mariachi band that plays all the classic songs that Mexicans seem to know by heart. On our first visit in early October, we had only planned on staying for dinner and venturing someplace for music. But, being early season, the other venues in Versalles were closed. Our waitress convinced us to stay, and we’re so glad we did. Around 10:30 in the evening, the band showed up — a full 10-person mariachi ensemble — and the tables filled up, too. Pretty soon, the band was passing the mic, and everyone was singing along. It was such a friendly, local vibe; we are looking forward to returning soon with the whole family.

Casita & Garden: Casita & Garden in the Romantic Zone offers a variety of live music from jazz to funk to rock and pop every night of the week except Sundays. Shows are held in its lovely outdoor courtyard during the winter season starting at 7 p.m. In addition to live music, you can sample wine and sake selected by their in-house sake sommelier, and fill up on sushi and wood-fired pizza. The venue also hosts private dinners and wine tastings, but they are popular, so it’s best to reserve well ahead of time.

For the sporting type

View this post on Instagram A post shared by CRUCE VALLARTA (@crucevallarta)

Coming from Boulder, Colorado — arguably the sporting capital of the United States — where every summer weekend is packed with running, biking and triathlon events, I was astounded to find a similar enthusiasm for sports in Puerto Vallarta. It seems there is a race of some sort every weekend. Yet I’ve found the events way more chill and the athletes much friendlier than in Colorado. (Even though they still crush the course.)

Since moving to Mexico, I’ve become an avid open-water swimmer, and recently joined a local swimming group. They convinced me to 

If running is more your speed, the next day, on Nov. 15, Puerto Vallarta is hosting its 22nd Annual Half Marathon. The 21-km run is a grand tour of the hotel zone and the Marina, starting at the Sheraton and heading north along Av. Francisco Medina Ascencio (aka the 200), winding through the Marina and returning to the Sheraton via Av. Francisco Medina Ascencio. There is also a 5 km distance. You can register for either distance online.

I hope to see you out there, enjoying great food, good music and fun sports.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: Spain Poll Puts Sánchez 7.8 Points Ahead
World.content:
File photo, 28 May 2024. Pedro Sánchez speaks at La Moncloa, the prime minister’s seat in Madrid. Photo: Moncloa press office/Borja Puig de la Bellacasa, via Wikimedia Commons.

SPAIN · ELECTION POLLS

Published Thursday, November 12, 11:30 a.m. ET (5:30 p.m. Madrid) · Source: CIS pre-election survey, Polymarket

Spain’s state pollster has handed Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez a head start on the very day the campaign opens, and most private pollsters disagree with it. The Centre for Sociological Research (CIS), the state polling institute led by José Félix Tezanos, gives Sánchez’s Socialist Party (PSOE) 33.3% of the vote against 25.5% for the conservative People’s Party (PP), a 7.8-point lead.

Key Facts Result CIS poll: Socialists 33.3%, conservative PP 25.5%, Vox 18.4% (conservative); lead 7.8 points.

Seats Socialists 134 to 143, PP 98 to 106, Vox 57 to 65; majority needs 176.

Prediction markets Polymarket (a prediction market), 11:30 a.m. ET Nov. 12: PP plus Vox majority 90.5% (US$58,495 traded); PP most seats 83.5%.

Next Campaign opens at midnight Madrid time (6 p.m. ET); Spain votes Sunday, Nov. 29.

This story is part of our coverage of the Spain Election 2026. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Spain Poll Shows Right Bloc Near 200 Seats

In plain English Spain holds a general election on Nov. 29, and parties need 176 of 350 seats to govern without partners. The CIS is a state institute whose polls critics say tend to favour the Socialists, so analysts compare it with private surveys.

The Numbers Behind the Lead

Vox, the conservative party led by Santiago Abascal, is third with 18.4% and 57 to 65 seats. The PP, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, would take 98 to 106 seats.

Even the top of both ranges, 106 and 65 seats, adds up to 171, by our arithmetic. The CIS itself warns that the party ranges should not simply be added together.

Frente Amplio, the left-wing alliance formerly known as Sumar, is fourth with 4.7% and seven to 11 seats. In Catalonia, a joint list of Esquerra Republicana (ERC), the Catalan pro-independence party, and Podemos, a left-wing party, would win 10 to 14 seats.

The Gap Narrowed Since October

In the CIS’s October barometer the Socialists stood at 34% and the PP at 22.2%, an 11.8-point gap. Vox then had 17.1%.

The PP has therefore gained 3.3 points and Vox 1.3, while the Socialists slipped 0.7. The two surveys are not strictly comparable, because the new one is far larger.

File photo, 17 July 2018. Sánchez, left, receives Feijóo, then president of Galicia, at the Moncloa Palace. Photo: Moncloa press office/Fernando Calvo, free use with attribution.

How the Poll Was Run

The CIS conducted about 45,000 telephone interviews between Oct. 7 and Oct. 30. Part of the fieldwork came after the Oct. 28 rail accident at Urda, a town in Toledo province, south of Madrid.

The survey has no question that measures the accident’s effect on voting intention. The election was called early after a housing crisis, which the poll also reflects.

Private Polls Say Something Different

The CIS result departs from nearly all private polls, which have generally put the PP and Vox together above 176 seats. Our Spain election poll tracker follows each survey as it appears, and our earlier poll report covers the right-wing lead.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, traders put a PP and Vox majority at 90.5% at 11:30 a.m. ET, with US$58,495 traded. A separate market gives the PP 83.5% to win the most seats, with US$471,222 traded.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

A split verdict would mean weeks of coalition bargaining in a major euro-zone economy, which matters to holders of Spanish stocks and bonds. The CIS and the markets point in opposite directions, so the first big private polls of the campaign will show which side is right.

What Is Not Known

We do not yet know how the PP, Vox or the government have responded to the poll. We have not reviewed the CIS technical report, and the effect of the Urda accident on voters is unmeasured.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who would win Spain’s election, according to the CIS?

The CIS puts the Socialist Party first with 33.3% and 134 to 143 seats. The PP is second with 25.5% and 98 to 106 seats, and neither bloc is projected to reach 176.

Why does this poll differ from others?

The CIS is a state body and its model differs from private pollsters, which have generally put the PP and Vox above 176 seats. The reasons for the gap are not yet explained, and the CIS says its seat ranges are modelled scenarios, not forecasts.

Sources: Centre for Sociological Research (CIS); Polymarket; Spain’s Congress of Deputies.

World.title: Cuba’s Infant Deaths Jump to 9.9 per 1,000
World.content:
File photo, 2016. Plaza de la Catedral in Old Havana. Photo: Yoeztudioz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Cuba · Health

Published Thursday 12 November 2026 · Source: Cuba’s Ministry of Public Health, January 2026; Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the UN health agency for the Americas, 31 March 2026

Cuba’s health ministry says 9.9 of every 1,000 babies born alive in 2025 died before their first birthday, up from 7.1 a year earlier. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the United Nations health agency for the Americas, says blackouts and shortages of medical supplies are straining newborn care.

Key Facts What. Cuba’s health ministry reports 9.9 infant deaths per 1,000 live births in 2025, up from 7.1.

Births. Births fell to 68,051 in 2025, which is 3,108 fewer than in 2024.

Drivers. PAHO, the UN health body for the Americas, points to power cuts and shortages of medical supplies.

Disputed. The ministry cites the US embargo among other causes; a Washington think tank blames US sanctions.

Not known. No 2026 national rate appears in any ministry bulletin we could find.

Power Index. Cuba ranks 14th of 14 in Cuba ranks 14th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 22.5 points (November 2026 edition).

What the Official Numbers Show

Cuba’s Ministry of Public Health published preliminary data in early January 2026. The infant mortality rate, which counts deaths of babies under one year old per 1,000 live births, reached 9.9 for 2025 against 7.1 for 2024.

That is a rise of about 39%. A ministry series reproduced by PAHO shows 4.9 in 2020, so the rate has roughly doubled in five years.

Births fell to 68,051 in 2025, which is 3,108 fewer than in 2024 (about 4%). PAHO counted 508 infant deaths for 2024, so by our calculation from the rate and the birth count, deaths rose by about a third to roughly 670.
