What Officials Say Is Driving It

The ministry’s own list of causes starts with the difficult economic situation. It adds the tightening of the United States economic, commercial and financial blockade (Havana’s term for the US embargo), which it says limits medicines, supplies and equipment (our translation).

The ministry also names mosquito-borne disease outbreaks, hurricanes and heavy rain, and unfilled staff posts in some services. It gives no breakdown of how much each factor contributed.

PAHO’s report of 31 March 2026 says prolonged power outages, shortages of medical supplies and reagents, and limited transport are constraining obstetric and neonatal care. It says more than 32,000 pregnant women reportedly face higher risks because of reduced access to ultrasounds and delays in diagnosing congenital anomalies.

PAHO adds that incubators, ventilation systems and other life-support equipment depend on a reliable power supply. It dates energy limits from reduced fuel supply to December 2025.

A Cause That Is Disputed

The Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR), a Washington think tank, said in April 2026 that the rate rose 148% from 4.0 in 2018 to 9.9 in 2025. It links the increase to United States sanctions.

Cuba’s health ministry also cites the US embargo but lists other causes, so the two accounts overlap without matching. We found no public data that settles how much each factor explains.

What It Means for You

For readers in the United States, the figures put a human cost into the debate over Washington’s sanctions on Cuba, where the effect on ordinary Cubans is contested. Our reports cover the policy side, including new US sanctions on Cuban oil shippers and the loss of a Turkish power ship amid blackouts.

PAHO also lists lack of income, food insecurity, and insecurity or violence as reasons people leave Cuba. For how the island is changing its migration rules, see our report on the 24-month limit, and for the wider picture our Cuba news page.

What Is Not Known

We found no 2026 national infant mortality rate in a ministry bulletin. One independent report says a meeting of Cuba’s ruling Communist Party acknowledged a rate of about 14 per 1,000 in Havana for 2025, but we found no official bulletin with that figure.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Cuba’s infant mortality rate?

Cuba’s Ministry of Public Health reports a preliminary rate of 9.9 deaths of babies under one year old per 1,000 live births for 2025. The rate was 7.1 in 2024.

Why are more babies dying in Cuba?

The ministry cites the economic situation, limits on medicines and equipment it ties to the US embargo, mosquito-borne diseases, hurricanes and unfilled staff posts. PAHO points to power cuts and shortages of medical supplies.

How does the rate compare with 2020?

A ministry series reproduced by PAHO shows 4.9 per 1,000 in 2020. The 2025 rate of 9.9 is about double.

Has Cuba published a 2026 infant mortality rate?

We found no 2026 national rate in a ministry bulletin. The latest official figure we could confirm is for 2025.

Sources: Cuba’s Ministry of Public Health, preliminary 2025 maternal and infant data, January 2026; Pan American Health Organization, Public Health Situation Analysis No. 2 on Cuba, 31 March 2026; Center for Economic and Policy Research, press release on infant mortality in Cuba, April 2026.

World.title: Trump Threatens to Double Mexico Tariffs
World.content:
Mexican National Guard vehicles at the entrance of Guadalajara International Airport, 4 March 2022; the National Guard is one of the forces named in the operation. Photo: ProtoplasmaKid, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

MEXICO · TRADE AND MIGRATION

On Thursday 12 November 2026, President Donald Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexico if it does not stop migrant caravans marching north. The warning arrives while Washington already charges a 10% duty on Mexican goods outside the US-Mexico-Canada trade pact (USMCA) and while a Honduran caravan crosses southern Mexico.

Threat: Trump says tariffs on Mexico will be doubled immediately if caravans are not stopped.

Caravan: About 1,500 mostly Central American migrants left Tapachula, southern Mexico, on Tuesday 10 November; counts vary.

Tariffs now: A 10% duty applies to Mexican goods outside the USMCA, the US-Mexico-Canada trade pact.

Trade at stake: US goods imports from Mexico reached US$534.3 billion in 2025.

Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 70.8 points (November 2026 edition).

What Trump Said

Trump wrote on Truth Social, his own platform, that large migrant caravans had started a march through Mexico. He said Mexico must stop them now.

He wrote that if Mexico does not, tariffs on Mexico will be doubled immediately. He said the US Border Patrol, the federal border police, and ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) had been notified, and said there would be no leniency.

What Mexico Says

President Claudia Sheinbaum answered at her morning press conference on Thursday 12 November. She said no migrant caravan has reached the northern border since Trump took office.

File photo. The Palacio Nacional, the government palace on the Zócalo square in Mexico City, 2015. Photo: Daniel Case, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

She said two caravans exist now. One formed in Arriaga, in Chiapas state, with about 500 to 600 people and now has fewer than 100, while the second came from Honduras.

She said Mexico’s immigration institute (INM) and the National Guard, Mexico’s federal security force, accompany migrants rather than repress them. Most migrants choose to return home with government help once told entry to the United States is very difficult.

Sheinbaum said US migration policy has not changed since the US elections. No formal reply to the tariff threat from the foreign affairs or economy ministries had been announced at the time of writing.

According to a Chiapas state government source, about 1,500 people, mostly Central Americans, left Tapachula, near the Guatemala border, on Tuesday 10 November. Other reports say about 2,000, and it is not clear whether this is the Honduran caravan Sheinbaum mentioned.

Our earlier report on US removals of migrants of four nationalities to Mexico gives background. It describes how the United States sends non-Mexican migrants to Mexico.

Which Tariffs Apply Today

Since Friday 24 July 2026, Mexican products pay an extra 10% tariff under Section 301, a US trade law against alleged unfair practices. The US Trade Representative’s office (USTR), the White House trade office, set it over a failure to effectively enforce a ban on forced-labour imports.

The duty excludes goods entered duty-free under the USMCA, called T-MEC in Mexico, and articles already under Section 232. That national-security tariff law covers steel, aluminium and autos, which carry separate duties.

Other economies face 10% or 12.5%, depending on their record. Doubling Mexico’s 10% would mean 20%, but that is our arithmetic, because Trump did not say which tariff he means.

The threat comes while the two countries negotiate a trade deal, a track covered in our report on the Mexico tariff talks. No agreement had been announced at the time of writing.

On Wednesday 1 July 2026, USTR said “the USMCA is not renewed”, yet the pact “remains in force pending resolution of these issues”. USTR added that it would meet Mexico the week of 20 July for a third round of bilateral talks.

Why It Matters for US Readers

For US importers the cost lands at the port, because they pay any tariff on entry before goods reach shelves. They should watch the Federal Register, the US government’s daily journal of rules, and note that USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt from the 10% duty, so origin paperwork matters.

US goods imports from Mexico reached US$534.3 billion in 2025, against US$337.3 billion of exports, according to the US Census Bureau. Mexico’s real GDP grew only 0.5% in 2025, says the International Monetary Fund’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook, which leaves less cushion for a tariff rise.

For investors, the peso moved little at first. The dollar traded at about 18.6 pesos on Thursday, close to the previous day.

What to Watch Next

The first checkpoint is any White House or USTR decree, because a post has no legal force until a notice names a tariff and a rate. Until then, current duties stay in force.

The second is the state of the US-Mexico trade talks, where no agreement had been announced. Sheinbaum’s next morning press conference, a daily event, is the first place she may add detail on any formal reply.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether or when a tariff would be imposed, which tariff would be doubled, or under which legal tool. Trump’s post does not say.

Mexico’s formal answer is also unknown, as is the true size of the caravan. Nobody can yet say whether any group will reach the US border, though Sheinbaum says none has since Trump took office.

More: Read more Mexico news in English. The Rio Times covers it every day.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly did Trump threaten?

He posted on Truth Social that tariffs on Mexico will be doubled immediately if Mexico does not stop migrant caravans. The post names no date, rate or legal tool, and no decree has been issued.

What tariffs does the US charge Mexico now?

A 10% Section 301 duty has applied since 24 July 2026 to Mexican goods outside the USMCA. Goods already under Section 232 duties, such as steel and autos, are excluded and pay their own rates.

How big is the caravan?

About 1,500 people left Tapachula on 10 November, according to a Chiapas state government source. Other reports say about 2,000, and no single official count exists.

What does Mexico say?

Sheinbaum said no caravan has reached the northern border since Trump took office, and the Arriaga group has fewer than 100 people. No formal reply from the foreign affairs or economy ministries had been announced at the time of writing.

Sources: Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR), Section 301 forced-labor action, notice dated Thursday 23 July 2026; USTR statement on the USMCA joint review, Wednesday 1 July 2026; US Census Bureau, trade in goods with Mexico, 2025; IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026; President Trump’s post on Truth Social, Thursday 12 November 2026; President Sheinbaum’s morning press conference, Thursday 12 November 2026.

World.title: Ex-Minister Pantami’s Gombe Convoy Attacked
World.content:
Nigeria Politics

A convoy carrying a former Nigerian minister was attacked on arrival in Gombe, and the rights group Amnesty International has urged police to investigate.

A convoy carrying Isa Ali Pantami, a former Nigerian communications minister, was attacked in Gombe, capital of Gombe State in north-eastern Nigeria, on Wednesday 11 November 2026. Amnesty International, the global human rights group, condemned the attack on Thursday 12 November 2026.

Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country, and its 2027 elections will shape politics across the region. Gombe’s governorship vote is about 12 weeks away, so the incident matters to readers abroad.

Key Facts •Who: Isa Ali Pantami, ex-communications minister and Gombe governor candidate for the opposition Peoples Democratic Party (PDP). •What: His convoy was attacked in Gombe city, with burned tyres and smashed glass on Jekadafari Road. •Where: Gombe, capital of Gombe State in north-eastern Nigeria. •When: Wednesday 11 November 2026; Amnesty International condemned it on 12 November. •Next: Nigeria's election body lists the governorship vote for Saturday 6 February 2027.

What Happened in Gombe

Pantami arrived in Gombe on Wednesday 11 November 2026 for a rally and reception with supporters. His convoy was attacked on Jekadafari Road in the city.

Tyres were burned on the road, and windscreens and glass of convoy vehicles were smashed. No one has confirmed how many vehicles were damaged or how many people were hurt.

Pantami is the candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), a main opposition party, for governor of Gombe State. Our explainer on the Gombe candidates gives more background on the race.

The central mosque in Gombe city, capital of Gombe State in north-eastern Nigeria. File photo, 2022. (Photo: Gwanki, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What Amnesty and the Police Said

Amnesty International said the attack appeared aimed at stopping Pantami from entering Gombe town. Its preliminary findings suggest the attackers are suspected to be working for Nigeria’s ruling All Progressives Congress (APC).

Amnesty urged security agencies to investigate and bring those responsible to justice through a fair trial. It said no arrests appeared to have been made.

Buhari Abdullahi, spokesperson for the Gombe State Police Command, confirmed the incident. He said some people took advantage of the movement of the crowd to barricade vehicles and attack them after the main procession had passed.

Abdullahi said no arrests had been made as of Thursday and that an investigation is under way. He said police could not establish how many vehicles were affected because no formal complaint had been lodged.

Usman Murtala, the APC’s publicity secretary in Gombe State, accused supporters of the PDP candidate of attacking residents and damaging property. That is the APC’s own claim, and no suspect has been named.

Who Is Isa Ali Pantami

Pantami served as Nigeria’s minister of communications and digital economy under former president Muhammadu Buhari. He quit the APC governorship race in protest after the party backed Jamilu Gwamna, its consensus candidate, meaning one agreed by party leaders, and joined the PDP.

On 24 September 2026 the Federal High Court in Gombe, a national trial court, nullified the first PDP primary that picked him and ordered a fresh one. He won the rerun on 29 September 2026, and our profile of Isa Ali Pantami explains his career.

The 2027 Election Calendar

The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Nigeria’s election body, lists the presidential and National Assembly elections for Saturday 16 January 2027. It lists the governorship and state assembly elections for Saturday 6 February 2027.

INEC revised its timetable in February 2026 after Nigeria adopted a new election law, the Electoral Act 2026. Its published calendar still shows both votes as upcoming.

So Gombe’s governor race is about twelve weeks away. Campaign incidents like this one therefore land close to polling day.

What It Means for Election Risk

The incident shows how quickly a campaign event can become a security question. Amnesty describes violence against the opposition, while the police describe opportunists acting after the procession had passed.

The strongest counter-view belongs to the APC and the police. The APC’s Usman Murtala says PDP supporters attacked residents, and police say no arrests have been made and no formal complaint has been lodged.

For a US reader, Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country, so the credibility of its vote matters. We follow that test in our Nigeria coverage.

What Is Not Known

It is not established who attacked the convoy. Amnesty’s link to the APC is a preliminary suspicion and remains unproven.

No one has confirmed the number of injuries or damaged vehicles. Police said no arrests had been made as of Thursday and named no suspects.

What to Watch Next

First, watch whether police, who say an investigation is under way, make arrests or name suspects. Police said no formal complaint had been lodged, so any later complaint would be a signal.

Second, watch the INEC dates, with the governorship vote set for Saturday 6 February 2027. Any revision by INEC would reset the campaign clock.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Isa Ali Pantami?

He is a former Nigerian minister of communications and digital economy. He is the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) candidate for governor of Gombe State.

What happened to his convoy?

It was attacked on Jekadafari Road in Gombe on Wednesday 11 November 2026. Tyres were burned and convoy glass was smashed.

Has anyone been arrested?

Police said no arrests had been made as of Thursday. Amnesty International said none appeared to have been made.

When is the Gombe governorship election?

INEC lists it for Saturday 6 February 2027. The presidential vote is listed for Saturday 16 January 2027.

Sources Amnesty International, Nigeria; INEC election calendar. Amnesty International statement of 12 November 2026; statements by the Gombe State Police Command, the PDP and the APC, 12 November 2026.

World.title: Ruto Says Kenya Highway Deal Saves US$446M
World.content:
File photo, 2016. Farmland and homes in the Rift Valley seen from Iten, a highland town in western Kenya. (Photo: Appleslerp, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

On Thursday 12 November 2026, Kenyan President William Ruto said the renegotiated Rironi-Mau Summit highway deal saves the country about Ksh58 billion (US$446 million), where Ksh means Kenyan shillings against a cancelled French-led contract. The road sits on the main freight route from Mombasa port to Uganda, Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo, so its cost and builder matter beyond Kenya.

The Ksh58 billion is our subtraction of two figures Ruto gave, not an audit. Conversions use Ksh129.91 per US$1, the market exchange rate of 12 November 2026.

The cancelled 2020 French-led deal covered 175 km; Ruto says the new road spans 210 km. Exit cost Ruto says Kenya paid Ksh6.4 billion (about US$50 million) to leave the French contract.

What Ruto Said

Ruto spoke at the annual general meeting of the Kenya Comprehensive School Heads Association, a body of school principals, in Nyali, a Mombasa suburb, and the State House press office (Presidential Communication Service) released his remarks. He said the road now being built costs Ksh191 billion (about US$1.47 billion), while the French contract would have cost Ksh249 billion (about US$1.92 billion).

Ruto called the gap “nearly Ksh60 billion”. He dismissed criticism of the deal as propaganda and said he accepts being called a micro-manager “because I have to be accountable”.

President William Ruto of Kenya, official portrait, 2022. Photo: Government of Kenya, public domain.

The French Contract He Cancelled

The previous administration awarded the contract in 2020 to a consortium of Meridian Infrastructure Africa Fund, an investment fund, Vinci Highways SAS and Vinci Concessions SAS, which carry the name of Vinci, a French infrastructure group. The deal covered dualling, or adding a second carriageway to, 175 km of road.

Ruto said the company built not a single kilometre of road in six years, took the government to court and lacked the capacity to build. The consortium’s account is not in his remarks, and we have not reached it.

Ruto said court action held up the works, and Kenya paid Ksh6.4 billion (about US$50 million) to exit the contract. Ruto said staying in court could have cost Ksh25.8 billion (about US$200 million) to Ksh38.7 billion (about US$300 million), “and then no road would be built”.

He said he reached out to French President Emmanuel Macron, adding: “I could clearly see that the matter in court would cost us more money than the negotiation we had.” The saving is before the exit payment, which leaves about US$396 million by our arithmetic.

How the Toll Road Is Built and Paid For

Ruto said the project spans 210 km, against 175 km before. The 70 km Naivasha to Nakuru section has six lanes, not four.

The toll is Ksh8 a kilometre (about US$0.06), against Ksh12 (about US$0.09) in the previous agreement, according to Ruto. He called the financing “innovative” and said it comes “without burdening Kenyans with additional taxes or additional debt”.

China Road and Bridge Corporation, a Chinese state-owned contractor, builds the first stage, as announced at the project launch in late November 2025. The National Social Security Fund (NSSF), Kenya’s national pension scheme, was named at that launch as partner of the contractor on the first phase, which starts at Rironi.

In Plain English A toll concession lets investors build a road and earn the money back through tolls, and a dual carriageway has separate lanes for each direction. The NSSF collects pension contributions from Kenyan workers and invests them, and here it is named as a partner in the road.

What It Means for Drivers and Investors

Drivers on the Mombasa to Uganda freight corridor are promised a wider road at Ksh8 a kilometre (about US$0.06). Completion is expected in 2027.

For investors, the deal shows Nairobi turning to Chinese contractors and a domestic pension fund after a French concession fell through. The savings remain Ruto’s claim, not an audit.

Ruto faces voters worried about prices, so a cheaper road is a political argument too. The feud ahead of the 2027 election adds pressure.

What to Watch Next

The first stage, Rironi to Naivasha, missed its 30 October 2026 deadline, as we reported in our story on the delay. Transport minister Davis Chirchir now wants it open by December 2026 and blamed a bitumen price rise.

Ruto said funds are secured for studies to extend the dual carriageway to Malaba, on the Ugandan border, and towards Kisumu. Details of dualling the Nairobi to Mombasa highway will come shortly, he said.

What Is Not Known

The financing structure, which Ruto’s remarks did not detail.

The scope behind the two prices: at the 2025 launch, 233 km and Ksh184 billion (about US$1.42 billion) were quoted, against Ruto’s 210 km and Ksh191 billion (about US$1.47 billion).

Whether the comparison is like for like: lengths and lanes differ, and no cost breakdown has been published that we could read.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does Ruto say the new deal saves?

Ruto compared Ksh191 billion (about US$1.47 billion) for the new road with Ksh249 billion (about US$1.92 billion) for the French contract. The gap is Ksh58 billion (about US$446 million) by our subtraction, before the exit payment.

Why was the French contract cancelled?

Ruto said the consortium built no road in six years, went to court and lacked the capacity to build. Kenya paid Ksh6.4 billion (about US$50 million) to exit, and the consortium’s account is not in his remarks.

Who is building the road?

The 2025 launch announcement named China Road and Bridge Corporation for the first stage, with the NSSF as partner. Shandong Hi-Speed Road and Bridge International, a Chinese contractor, was assigned the Nakuru to Mau Summit section.

When will the road open?

Ruto said works are 40 per cent complete and completion is expected in 2027. The first stage missed its 30 October 2026 deadline, and the transport minister now wants it open by December 2026.

Sources: Presidential Communication Service text of President Ruto’s remarks, 12 November 2026; project launch announcement, 28 November 2025; market exchange rate of 12 November 2026.

World.title: Dominican Central Bank Backs 4.5% Growth
World.content:
The Dominican flag flying against a clear sky. Photo: Phyrexian, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

The Banco Central de la República Dominicana (BCRD, the country’s central bank) confirmed on Wednesday 11 November 2026 that it still expects the Dominican economy to grow 4.5% this year. Governor Héctor Valdez Albizu gave the forecast to a visiting mission of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the Washington lender whose yearly Article IV review checks each member economy.

For US readers the number matters because the island is a popular Caribbean holiday destination and a large recipient of remittances, the money Dominicans abroad send home. Both flows are among the drivers the central bank names for this year’s expansion.

Forecast The central bank holds its 2026 growth forecast at 4.5%.

The central bank holds its 2026 growth forecast at 4.5%. So far The economy grew 4.6% from January to September; September alone was 5.6% above a year earlier.

The economy grew 4.6% from January to September; September alone was 5.6% above a year earlier. Prices Consumer prices rose 0.58% in October, the central bank reported on 9 November.

Consumer prices rose 0.58% in October, the central bank reported on 9 November. Money in The bank projects about US$12.6 billion in remittances and US$12.2 billion in tourism income.

The bank projects about US$12.6 billion in remittances and US$12.2 billion in tourism income. Peso About 60.5 pesos buy US$1 on 12 November 2026.

What the Central Bank Told the IMF

The BCRD said on 11 November 2026 that growth reached 4.6% in the first nine months of the year. It added that the monthly economic activity index (IMAE) for September came in 5.6% above September 2025, a figure the governor first gave in October.

The BCRD links the outlook to tourism, steady remittances and foreign direct investment (money that foreign firms put into local businesses). It says the 4.5% pace would keep the country among the faster-growing economies of Latin America despite international risks.

On money from abroad, the governor projected about US$12.6 billion in remittances for 2026 and about US$12.2 billion in tourism income. Remittances are money that Dominicans abroad send home.

Prices and the Peso

The central bank reported on 9 November 2026 that consumer prices rose 0.58% in October from September. We cover that release in our October inflation report.

The peso traded near 60.5 to the US dollar on 12 November 2026 in market trading. At that rate US$100 buys roughly 6,050 pesos.

Why It Matters for US Readers

The BCRD names tourism as one of the engines of growth and projects about US$12.2 billion in tourism income this year. A steady economy supports the hotels, flights and services that American travellers use.

Investors should note that Fitch Ratings, a US credit rating firm, lifted the country’s sovereign rating from BB- to BB (still below investment grade), with a stable outlook, in early November. Our report on the September growth figure and our look at who runs the Dominican economy give more background.

What to Watch Next

The next checkpoint is the October reading of the central bank’s monthly activity index (IMAE), which will show whether growth held above 4.5%. The IMF mission’s own statement will show whether its view matches the bank’s.

Each release will show whether the 4.5% forecast still holds. Readers can follow the wider picture on our Dominican Republic news page.

What Is Not Known

The central bank’s public release does not give us a full-year figure for the current account balance or for the size of the economy in US dollars, and we do not state them. We also do not know whether the IMF mission agrees with the 4.5% forecast.

Frequently Asked Questions

What growth does the Dominican central bank expect in 2026?

The central bank expects the economy to grow 4.5% in 2026. It said so on 11 November 2026 to an IMF mission.

How fast has the economy grown so far this year?

Growth was 4.6% from January to September 2026. The September activity index was 5.6% above a year earlier.

How much do remittances and tourism bring in?

The central bank projects about US$12.6 billion in remittances and US$12.2 billion in tourism income for 2026. Remittances are money that Dominicans abroad send home.

Sources: Banco Central de la República Dominicana, news release of 11 November 2026 and consumer price release of 9 November 2026 (bancentral.gov.do); Fitch Ratings sovereign rating action, November 2026; International Monetary Fund Article IV mission, November 2026.

World.title: Brazil Liquidates Two Financial Institutions
World.content:
Brazil’s central bank shut two financial institutions on Thursday, 12 November 2026, and the closures matter mostly to the people who saved or paid into them. It placed the Cooperativa de Crédito Rural do Agreste Alagoano, known as Cooperagre, and the Cooperativa Administradora de Consórcios Roma into extrajudicial liquidation, an administrative wind-down run by the central bank rather than a court.

Neither is a household name, and the central bank described Cooperagre as small. For foreign investors the message is about oversight: the Banco Central do Brasil has now liquidated 21 institutions this year, by Brazilian press tallies.

What the Central Bank Decided

In a statement on 12 November, the Banco Central do Brasil said it had decreed the extrajudicial liquidation of both institutions. Under that regime the central bank takes charge and a liquidator, the official appointed to wind it up, sorts out the assets and debts.

The central bank said the decision does not settle individual blame, which it will examine in separate proceedings. It added that it will keep investigating and that the findings could lead to administrative penalties and referrals to other authorities.

Cooperagre: A Very Small Credit Union

The central bank said Cooperagre was liquidated because of “serious violations of the rules governing its activities”. Cooperagre is a credit union in segment S5 of Brazilian prudential regulation.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 74.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The central bank described that segment as institutions below 0.1% of GDP with simplified risk management. In September 2025 Cooperagre held about 0.0000222% of the financial system’s total assets.

The central bank said Cooperagre’s deposit-type products are covered by the Fundo Garantidor do Cooperativismo de Crédito, or FGCoop, the private guarantee fund for credit unions. By law, the assets of the cooperative’s former administrators are now frozen.

Roma: Problems in How Consortium Shares Were Sold

A consortium, or “consórcio”, is a Brazilian savings club in which members pay monthly into a pool and take turns, by lot or bid, to buy a car, home or other asset. Each member holds a quota, a share in one such group.

The central bank said it found “serious and persistent irregularities” in Roma’s business model, tied to how it sold quotas, to high rates of participant exclusion and to its pay structure. It called the problems structural and said they continued despite earlier supervision and sanctions.

In June 2026 Roma ran 28 consortium groups with about 16,000 active quotas held by 8,300 members. That made it 49th among 129 institutions in the segment by active members.

The central bank said the liquidation aims at an orderly exit from the market. It added that the rights of group participants are protected.

In Plain English

Extrajudicial liquidation: the central bank closes the firm and a liquidator it names handles the winding up, without a court case. FGCoop: a private guarantee fund that repays credit-union savers up to a cap if a member fails.

What It Means for Savers and Investors

Savers at Cooperagre should expect FGCoop to repay covered balances up to its ordinary cap of R$250,000 per depositor at each institution, about US$44,500 at R$5.62 per US$ on 12 November. The fund’s rules set which products count.

Consortium members at Roma should watch for central bank guidance on their groups, because the central bank said participant rights are protected. Roma managed 28 such groups in June 2026.

For US investors in Brazil, the central bank’s figures describe Cooperagre in particular as very small. It has liquidated lenders regularly this year, as with the Credipaiva cooperative in October, the Simpala consortium and finance group in August and the Will Bank lender in January.

The best-known case remains Banco Master, a Brazilian bank liquidated in November 2025. More coverage sits on our Brazil news page.

What Is Not Known

The central bank has not said how many savers or how much money sit in Cooperagre, or how much FGCoop will have to pay. The statement also gives no detail on which of Roma’s consortium groups will continue.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Brazil’s central bank do on 12 November 2026?

It ordered the extrajudicial liquidation of the Cooperagre credit union in Alagoas, a state in north-east Brazil, and the Roma consortium administrator. Brazilian press tallies put the 2026 total at 21 institutions.

Are Cooperagre deposits protected?

The central bank says Cooperagre’s deposit-type products are covered by FGCoop, the credit-union guarantee fund. Ordinary cover is R$250,000 (about US$44,500) per depositor at each institution.

What happens to Roma consortium members?

The central bank says the liquidation protects the rights of group participants and aims at an orderly exit. It has not yet said how the 28 groups will be handled.

Why were the two institutions closed?

Cooperagre was closed for serious violations of the rules governing its activities. Roma was closed for persistent irregularities in how it sold quotas, excluded participants and structured its pay.

Sources Banco Central do Brasil statements on the liquidation of Cooperagre and of Cooperativa Administradora de Consórcios Roma, 12 November 2026; Fundo Garantidor do Cooperativismo de Crédito (FGCoop) rules on ordinary cover; market exchange rate of 12 November 2026 (R$5.62 per US$).

World.title: Mexico Gets 11 Replies on 18 Migrant Deaths
World.content:
Mexico’s foreign ministry said on Thursday 12 November 2026 that US prosecutors have answered 11 of its 22 letters about deaths and injuries of Mexicans in immigration custody or enforcement operations. The ministry counts 18 such deaths, and it says dialogue with the other prosecutors continues.

The statement matters to US readers because a foreign government is writing directly to state and county prosecutors about deaths linked to ICE, the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency that detains migrants awaiting removal. The ministry also says the Harris County prosecutor in Texas has announced an indictment of an ICE agent in one case, which involves an injured person, not a death.

Who: Mexico’s foreign ministry has sent 22 letters to US prosecutors and received 11 replies.

What: It counts 18 Mexicans dead in migration custody or during US enforcement operations.

Houston: The ministry says Harris County prosecutors announced an indictment of an ICE agent in one case.

Courts: Civil lawsuits have been filed in 3 of the 18 cases.

As of 12 November 2026, 15:30 GMT

In plain English: ICE is the US federal agency that arrests and holds people for immigration violations. The foreign ministry, known in Mexico as the Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores (SRE), runs the country’s diplomacy and its consulates. A state attorney general is a state’s chief law officer, while a county prosecutor brings criminal cases within one county. A grand jury is a panel of citizens that decides whether there is enough evidence for a formal charge, called an indictment. Mexico’s consular network is its embassy in Washington plus its consulates in US cities, which help Mexicans in trouble. Harris County is the Houston area of Texas, and Webb County includes Laredo.

What the Ministry Says Came Back

The ministry says it has sent 22 letters, 8 to state attorneys general offices and 14 to county prosecutors. They ask for the status of investigations into deaths of Mexicans in ICE custody or during ICE operations.

So far 11 replies have arrived, and in the ministry’s words “the dialogue continues with the others”. Several prosecutors have shown willingness to hold more meetings with Mexico’s consular network and embassy to follow up.

The embassy is also in contact with prosecutors in Harris County and Webb County in Texas, and Ventura County in California, to monitor investigations. The statement does not say which of the 22 prosecutors have replied.

Where the Cases Stand

The ministry says 4 of the 18 cases are represented through its legal assistance programme for Mexicans, known as PALE (Programa de Asistencia Jurídica a Personas Mexicanas), which uses outside legal advisers. Another 7 have private lawyers.

In 2 cases the families are still looking for a lawyer, and consular staff are accompanying them. In 5 cases the families chose not to take legal action.

Civil suits have been filed in 3 cases, 2 with PALE lawyers and 1 with private counsel. In Harris County, the ministry says, the prosecutor announced a formal indictment, issued by a grand jury, against an ICE agent involved in the case of a Mexican person injured in the Houston area.

The statement gives no date, agent name or charge, but local US reports date the indictment to 30 October and say the agent surrendered on Monday 2 November. The ministry did not say whether this case is counted among the 18.

How We Got to 18

The count stood at 17 in July and is 18 now. The steps below come from the ministry’s own documents.

Thursday 9 July 2026: the ministry announced legal action, counting 17 dead, 14 in detention centres and 3 in operations.

the ministry announced legal action, counting 17 dead, 14 in detention centres and 3 in operations. Monday 13 July: Roberto Lazzeri, Mexico’s ambassador to the United States, filed 20 complaints, 8 with state prosecutors and 12 with county prosecutors, in Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, Missouri and Texas.

Roberto Lazzeri, Mexico’s ambassador to the United States, filed 20 complaints, 8 with state prosecutors and 12 with county prosecutors, in Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, Missouri and Texas. Tuesday 14 July: the embassy passed the complaint of Mexico’s federal prosecutor’s office (the Attorney General’s office) on all 17 cases to the US Department of Justice through the State Department.

the embassy passed the complaint of Mexico’s federal prosecutor’s office (the Attorney General’s office) on all 17 cases to the US Department of Justice through the State Department. Saturday 17 October: a 56-year-old man died at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas.

a 56-year-old man died at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas. Monday 19 October: after the Laredo death, the ministry announced that it would file a complaint with the Webb County prosecutor over the Laredo death.

The official cause of death had not been published when we reported the case in our earlier article on the complaint. The man died at the Rio Grande Processing Center, a detention centre in Laredo.

The National Palace in Mexico City, seat of the Mexican presidency. File photo of 16 October 2013 by Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What It Means for You

Families of Mexicans held by ICE can read the statement as a sign that consulates now press local prosecutors, not only federal agencies. Those who have lost a relative can ask the nearest Mexican consulate about legal help, which the ministry says it offers through PALE.

Other Latin American governments track their people inside the system too. Costa Rica’s count is in our story on its citizens in ICE detention.

US readers who follow ICE oversight can watch whether more prosecutors report progress on their investigations. Our report on ICE’s own death reviews looks at how medical care in custody is judged.

What Is Not Known

The statement gives no content for the 11 replies, and it does not say which prosecutors answered or who the 11 others are. It also gives no dates for the letters.

The date of the Houston indictment, the agent’s name and the charge were not given, and we do not know how the 18 deaths split between detention and operations. We could not open the ministry’s own web page for the 12 November statement, so its figures come from the statement’s text as carried by two Mexican newspapers that agree.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times. Our Mexico coverage includes politics, markets and migration.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Mexico’s foreign ministry announce on 12 November 2026?

It said it has sent 22 letters to US prosecutors and received 11 replies. It counts 18 Mexicans dead in migration custody or during US enforcement operations.

Who did Mexico write to?

It wrote to 8 state attorneys general offices and 14 county prosecutors. It asked about the status of investigations into deaths of Mexicans in ICE custody or during ICE operations.

Has anyone been charged?

A grand jury in Harris County, Texas, issued a formal indictment against an ICE agent in a case of a Mexican person injured in the Houston area. The ministry gave no date, name or charge.

Are the families getting legal help?

Of the 18 families, 4 are represented through the ministry’s legal assistance programme and 7 have private lawyers. Two are still looking for a lawyer, and 5 chose not to take legal action.

Sources: Mexican foreign ministry communiqué, 9 July 2026; Mexican foreign ministry information note, 22 July 2026; Mexican foreign ministry statement of 12 November 2026.

World.title: San Ramón Forests Hold Nearly Half of Costa Rica’s Bat Species
World.content:
The forests around San Ramón shelter at least 56 bat species, nearly half of all those recorded in Costa Rica, according to researchers at the University of Costa Rica (UCR) who are studying how these often-misunderstood mammals cope as their habitat is broken up by farms, pastures and towns.

The work is led by UCR’s Western Campus in San Ramón, where scientists and students are tracking how bats respond to changes in their surroundings and what that means for forests and farming. One study sampled seven sites in and around the Alberto Manuel Brenes Biological Reserve to examine how forest fragmentation and degradation affect bat populations. Researchers captured and studied 407 bats from 39 species, including 10 species that had never before been documented in the area.

Those new records helped raise the known total for the wider San Ramón region to at least 56 species. UCR researcher Daniel Zamora said the findings show the importance of protecting not only large, continuous forests but also the smaller patches of vegetation that link one habitat to another. Landscapes that mix farms, pastures, forest and homes, he said, can still support remarkable biodiversity.

One encouraging result was the abundance of fruit-eating bats. By dispersing seeds, they help plants spread and drive the natural regeneration of tropical forests. Other species eat insects, which could make them valuable to farmers. UCR graduate student Katherine Álvarez is studying whether insect-eating bats help control pests that attack potato crops in Cartago, with the aim of producing evidence that supports conservation and encourages growers to see bats as allies.

The university is also looking at how bats adapt to cities, including the role of protected green spaces in San Ramón and Liberia. Researchers are combining field surveys with acoustic monitoring, which records bats’ echolocation calls, to map where different species live and how they respond to changing environments. A recent urban wildlife survey in Heredia found similar surprises in city green spaces.

Other studies are examining parasites carried by bats, and a project on their anatomy and evolutionary relationships is planned for 2027. Alongside the science, the program runs environmental education activities aimed at dispelling myths about bats. Researchers work with students, community groups, landowners and conservation organizations to share what they find and build support for protecting the animals.

World.title: Luisa Stefani Moves Closer to WTA Finals Semifinals After Dramatic Comeback
World.content:
Brazil’s Luisa Stefani and Canadian partner Gabriela Dabrowski moved closer to the WTA Finals doubles semifinals Wednesday after producing a dramatic comeback to defeat Wimbledon champions Guo Hanyu and Kristina Mladenovic in a match that lasted more than two hours.

The top-seeded Brazilian-Canadian partnership survived a tense encounter at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden, winning 7-6(5), 4-6, 10-5 to remain unbeaten in the round-robin stage of the season-ending championship. Their second consecutive victory put them in control of Group 1 and within reach of a semifinal berth, although their place in the final four was not yet mathematically guaranteed.

The result was particularly satisfying for Stefani and Dabrowski, who lost to the Chinese-French pairing in the Wimbledon doubles final earlier this year. Wednesday’s rematch gave them an opportunity to settle that score, but they needed a remarkable recovery in the deciding match tiebreak to secure the victory.

After splitting the opening two sets, Stefani and Dabrowski fell behind 5-2 in the 10-point match tiebreak. With the momentum favoring their opponents, the Brazilian and Canadian responded by winning eight consecutive points to complete the comeback. The victory took two hours and one minute and demonstrated the resilience that has helped make Stefani and Dabrowski one of the most successful doubles teams of the 2026 season.

The opening set was closely contested, with both teams struggling to hold serve consistently. Stefani and Dabrowski broke their opponents three times but also surrendered three service games of their own. They had an opportunity to serve out the set at 5-4, only for Guo and Mladenovic to respond and force a tiebreak.

The Brazilian-Canadian team eventually claimed the opening set 7-5 in the tiebreak after Mladenovic committed a double fault on set point. The Wimbledon champions responded strongly in the second set. Guo and Mladenovic increased the pressure on their opponents’ service games, breaking twice and establishing a 5-2 advantage. Although Stefani and Dabrowski fought back, the Chinese-French partnership closed out the set 6-4 to force a deciding match tiebreak.

For several minutes, it appeared the Wimbledon champions might repeat their Grand Slam victory. Instead, Stefani and Dabrowski raised their level when it mattered most, improving their serving and returns while putting their opponents under increasing pressure. Stefani acknowledged afterward that the match had been difficult and that the pair had needed to overcome several problems. She said their serving and returning improved during the closing stages, allowing them to regain control.

The victory was their second of the tournament following a 6-3, 7-6(5) win over Belgium’s Elise Mertens and China’s Zhang Shuai in Monday’s opening round. Stefani and Dabrowski now hold a 2-0 record in Group 1, putting them in a strong position to advance from the four-team group.

Their final round-robin match is scheduled for Friday, November 13, against Taiwan’s Hsieh Su-wei and Latvia’s Jelena Ostapenko, who defeated Mertens and Zhang 7-5, 6-3 on Wednesday. The top two teams in each group advance to Saturday’s semifinals, with the championship match scheduled for Sunday, November 15.

For Stefani, the tournament represents another opportunity to reach the season-ending final after finishing runner-up in 2025 alongside Hungary’s Timea Babos. Dabrowski already knows what it takes to win the championship. The Canadian captured the 2024 WTA Finals doubles title with New Zealand’s Erin Routliffe.

Their partnership has enjoyed an outstanding 2026 campaign. Before arriving at Indian Wells, Stefani and Dabrowski had collected six doubles titles together, including three WTA 1000 championships in Dubai, Beijing and Wuhan. They also won tournaments in Strasbourg, Eastbourne and São Paulo, establishing themselves as one of the most consistent teams on the women’s circuit.

Their success has extended beyond those victories. They reached the Wimbledon final and also finished runners-up at the Tokyo tournament earlier this month. The pair entered the WTA Finals as the top seeds, having built one of the strongest records in women’s doubles this season.

For Brazilian tennis, Stefani’s continued success is especially significant. The Olympic bronze medalist has become one of the country’s most accomplished doubles players and is seeking her first WTA Finals championship. Wednesday’s victory did not secure the title or eliminate the challenges ahead, but it moved Stefani and Dabrowski another step closer to their goal.

After surviving a difficult rematch against the Wimbledon champions, the Brazilian-Canadian team will enter Friday’s final group match with two victories, growing confidence and an opportunity to advance to the semifinals of women’s tennis’ season-ending championship.

World.title: Costa Ricans Could Vote on Reopening Crucitas to Gold Mining
World.content:
Costa Ricans could be asked to decide at the ballot box whether gold mining returns to Crucitas, after President Laura Fernández confirmed that her government is weighing a national referendum on the troubled northern mining zone. Speaking at her weekly press conference yesterday, Fernández said she has discussed the idea for months with Minister of the Presidency and Finance Rodrigo Chaves, the former president, and other members of her team.

She stressed that no decision has been made and said she would tell the country in due course whether she will call a referendum on Crucitas or on another issue. Chaves revived the idea earlier this month, saying he would recommend that Fernández put Crucitas to a public vote, while adding that he did not know whether she would. Fernández first said in July that she was studying a referendum as a way around stalled legislation and named Crucitas among the possible topics.

Crucitas, in Cutris de San Carlos near the border with Nicaragua, was the site of an open-pit gold project by Canadian company Infinito Gold that was halted in 2010, the same year Costa Rica banned new open-pit metallic mining. Since then the area has been overrun by illegal miners.

Authorities say the mercury and cyanide used to process illegally extracted gold are contaminating water sources and surrounding ecosystems, and they link much of the activity to organized criminal groups. The government has separately moved to treat illegal mining as organized crime.

Security Minister Mario Zamora has told lawmakers that about 200 police officers are deployed in the zone at a cost of roughly $1 million, and that the area affected by illegal extraction has grown by more than 200%. The government’s answer is Bill 24.717, which would authorize open-pit gold mining at Crucitas and award concessions through public auctions.

The administration argues that regulated mining would cut off illegal extraction and generate revenue it says would go to education, security and health. The bill has been stalled for months in the Legislative Assembly, where opposition lawmakers filed hundreds of motions to amend it.

Fernández blamed the National Liberation Party (PLN) and the Broad Front (Frente Amplio) for the delay. Opposition lawmakers favor alternatives centered on cleaning up and restoring the damaged land, and on issuing digital tokens linked to the gold that would stay in the ground. PLN legislator Diana Murillo has filed a proposal that combines remediation, the sale of gold recovered during cleanup and tokens tied to the remaining deposit.

Fernández argued that none of these approaches would stop illegal miners from entering the area. Costa Rica’s Constitution allows a referendum to be called in three ways: a citizen petition signed by at least 5% of registered voters, approval by two-thirds of the 57-member Legislative Assembly, or a joint call by the executive branch and an absolute majority of lawmakers.

The ruling Pueblo Soberano party holds 31 seats, enough to back a joint call without opposition votes. Opponents say the question cannot legally go to voters at all. Frente Amplio lawmaker Edgardo Araya, an environmental lawyer, has argued that reopening Crucitas to mining would be an environmental rollback, and that such a rollback cannot be decided by referendum.

Any consultation would have to meet constitutional and legal requirements, overseen by the Supreme Elections Tribunal, before voters could be called to the polls. Costa Rica has held only one national referendum, the 2007 vote that approved the Central American Free Trade Agreement with the United States. Earlier this year, the country’s geologists also called for a referendum on Crucitas.

World.title: El Niño Could Leave 306,000 People in Costa Rica Short of Water
World.content:
More than 306,000 people in Costa Rica could face problems getting drinking water as the strongest El Niño on record dries us out, according to estimates from the AyA. Nearly half of them, 48%, live in the Chorotega region, which covers Guanacaste, so if you live in that area, this matters now.

As we all know, the dry season is setting in across Guanacaste and the Central Valley, and the rains that refill wells and springs will not be back for months. AyA has tripled its fleet of water tanker trucks, from 21 to 64, to deliver water where local systems run short. It has also drawn up 149 water security plans for the community-run water associations known as ASADAS and handed out 25 storage tanks to 14 of them.

The utility says it is also bringing new wells online, adding storage, repairing leaks and arranging supply for schools and shelters. The figures were presented Wednesday at the government’s weekly press conference, where Alejandro Picado, president of the National Emergency Commission (CNE), outlined the response.

The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) has classified this El Niño as the most intense since the institute was founded in 1888. The CNE has declared four alerts since May and raised Costa Rica to a red alert on Oct. 22 and the government says more than 20 institutions are coordinating the response.

Every liter you save at home stretches what is left in the system. AyA has already asked households to cut back on water use as the dry season begins. Fire is the other risk and the fire department (Bomberos), bought five tanker trucks that hold about 34,000 liters (9,000 gallons) each and stationed them in Puntarenas and Guanacaste, after what the government describes as a historic rise in forest fires this year.

Farmers, ranchers and fishing families are already feeling the drought. The CNE and the fishing institute Incopesca have delivered food to more than 2,500 fishing families in 43 communities across 11 areas and Incopesca extended the fishing range for 40 boats to 12 nautical miles (22 kilometers, or about 14 miles).

The rural development institute Inder has put more than 645 million colones (about $1.4 million) into livestock feed, equipment, and water and pasture studies in Guanacaste, which it says benefit more than 6,000 families. The irrigation agency Senara says the reservoir serving the Arenal-Tempisque irrigation district can supply its farmers through the end of 2027.

Small businesses and community water systems can also get help. The Development Banking System will offer 5,000 million colones (about $11.2 million) in low-cost financing, with 4,000 million colones for small businesses and producers and 1,000 million colones for ASADAS, the first time those associations can borrow from the system.

With the dry season only beginning here, how far the water stretches will depend on how soon the rains return and how much households, farms and businesses conserve until then.

World.title: Guided Hikes in Costa Rica Would Need ICT Licenses and Insurance Under New Bill
World.content:
Companies that sell or lead guided hikes in Costa Rica would need a license from the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) and insurance covering medical care, evacuation and death under a bill filed in the Legislative Assembly. Trails would also be rated by danger level with a color code.

The Bill was filed Nov. 9 by legislator Eder Hernández of the National Liberation Party (PLN). It applies to people and businesses that regularly organize, guide, sell or lead tourist hikes, and it would not require any permit for people who hike on their own. If you book a guided hike, the operator would have to tell you the trail’s danger category and the ICT’s safety recommendations before you set out. Operators would also have to call off or change an outing when conditions push the risk above what that trail’s category allows.

The ICT would build a national system to rate how dangerous each trail is, weighing terrain, weather, route complexity, how likely and how serious incidents are, access for rescue and medical teams, and past incidents where records exist. The number of categories and the colors themselves would be set later in regulations.

Each outing would need a logbook listing participants’ identification, emergency contacts, the route and its color category, start and expected finish times, relevant health information and how the hike ended. The idea is that operators can account for everyone who starts a route and everyone who comes back.

Operators would have to carry valid insurance before running any tours. Minimum coverage would include medical care for accidents, transport and evacuation, third-party liability, emergency assistance and death benefits where they apply, with amounts varying by the trail’s danger level and the type of activity.

Staff would need minimum training, equipment matched to the danger level and a way to communicate during the route. Clients would have to give informed consent after being told the risks. The ICT would also issue a National Emergency Protocol for Hiking, with separate procedures for injuries, missing hikers and deaths. Operators would have to activate it immediately when needed and coordinate with emergency services.

Running tours without a license, without a valid trail classification, without insurance or without logbooks would count as violations, as would failing to activate the emergency protocol. Penalties would be defined by regulation and could range from warnings and fines to suspension or revocation of a license. The bill sets no fine amounts.

The proposal builds on Costa Rica’s existing regulation for adventure tourism, which already covers hiking and trekking. The ICT would have six months after the law is published to write the detailed rules. Hernández said the goal is to make hiking safer for Costa Rican and foreign tourists alike, and that he will present the bill to the legislature’s Tourism Committee and seek support from other parties. Shirley Calvo, executive director of the National Chamber of Tourism (Canatur), said accidents during peak seasons are a recurring concern but that the proposal needs detailed review with the industry.

The bill has not yet been assigned to a committee. Like any bill, it would need to pass two votes in the full Assembly before becoming law.

World.title: Costa Rica Is One Vote From Co-Hosting the 2031 Women’s World Cup
World.content:
Costa Rica is one step away from co-hosting the 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup, the biggest tournament in women’s soccer. FIFA said Wednesday that the joint bid Costa Rica shares with the United States, Mexico and Jamaica meets its requirements, sending it to a final vote on Nov. 23.

If the bid is approved, it would be the first time Costa Rica hosts games at the main World Cup, for men or women. It has hosted two youth versions of the women’s tournament, for players under 17 in 2014 and players under 20 in 2022. FIFA’s technical evaluation gave the four-country bid an overall score of 4.4 out of 5. FIFA said the bid cleared its minimum hosting requirements and can go straight to its Extraordinary Congress, where its member federations will vote on the hosts.

The bid proposes 20 stadiums in 20 host cities. Costa Rica has put forward the Estadio Nacional in San José, Jamaica its national stadium in Kingston, and the United States 14 host cities. The 2031 tournament would be the first Women’s World Cup with 48 teams, up from 32, and the first hosted jointly by four countries. The bid aims to draw more than 4.5 million spectators and generate more than $4 billion in revenue.

The Costa Rican Football Federation confirmed Wednesday that FIFA had approved the bid’s technical reports. Its president, Osael Maroto, will lead the delegation to the vote. FIFA inspectors visited Costa Rica on Feb. 15 as part of the evaluation. The joint bid is the only one for 2031. FIFA’s review also cleared a joint bid for the 2035 Women’s World Cup, which goes to the same vote.

How many games Costa Rica would host has not been announced.

World.title: US Warns Costa Rica Town Halls Off Chinese Cameras, China Pushes Back
World.content:
The United States and Chinese embassies in Costa Rica have traded public statements over Chinese-made security technology used by the country’s municipalities, the latest in a series of disputes between the two powers playing out in San José. The US Embassy published a message on Facebook warning local governments about the risks of contracting low-cost Chinese technology, including security cameras, license plate readers and digital platforms from Chinese companies.

The embassy cited cybersecurity risks, weak data protection, dependence on a single supplier and a lack of transparency in public procurement. The message did not name any municipality or company. The Chinese Embassy answered with its own Facebook post, rejecting the warnings as unfounded and saying they served US interests. It said Chinese products are widely used in China and abroad, that the cameras and tools help protect people and property, and that commercial activity should not be politicized.

Costa Rica’s government has not publicly responded to the exchange. The camera dispute follows months of friction between the two embassies. In January, US Ambassador Melinda Hildebrand listed Chinese economic influence among the challenges facing Costa Rica. That same month, officials in the government of Rodrigo Chaves linked China to a cyberattack detected against the Costa Rican Electricity Institute (ICE).

In March, Chinese Ambassador Wang Xiaoyao asked Costa Rica for evidence supporting the cyberattack accusation. She said China had sought cybersecurity information from Costa Rican authorities since 2024 without a response. In May, Wang criticized Washington for revoking the visas of several Costa Rican public figures, among them former President Óscar Arias.

In late October, the Chinese Embassy rejected a US Embassy statement on Chinese mining companies, also calling it unfounded. Neither embassy said which Costa Rican municipalities use Chinese equipment or how many such systems are in operation.

World.title: Santa Cruz, Home to Tamarindo, Leads Guanacaste in Murders and Car Break-Ins
World.content:
Santa Cruz has recorded 22 homicides so far this year, more than any other county in Guanacaste and about 29% of the province’s 75 killings, according to figures from the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) covering Jan. 1 to Nov. 9. Costa Rica’s count is up from 20 in the same period of 2025, an increase of 10%. Across Guanacaste, homicides rose from 67 to 75, or 11.9%.

Tamarindo has the most homicides of any area in Santa Cruz, with five. Veintisiete de Abril follows with four, while Cuajiniquil and Cabo Velas, the district that includes Flamingo and Brasilito, have three each. OIJ classifies 15 of the county’s 22 homicides as score-settling or revenge killings. That number is unchanged from last year, so the increase comes from other types of cases.

Santa Cruz also leads the area in break-ins of parked vehicles, with 93 of Guanacaste’s 237 reported cases, or about 39%. Liberia follows with 64 and Nicoya with 34. By district, the most break-ins were reported in central Santa Cruz, with 39, followed by Tamarindo with 25 and Veintisiete de Abril with 23. A further 56 vehicles were reported stolen outright in the county over the same period.

The figures come as OIJ agents and the Public Prosecutor’s Office detained 10 people in Santa Cruz yesterday, among them two officers of the Fuerza Pública and a 16-year-old. Investigators suspect the group of involvement in homicide, attempted homicide, drug sales and violent robberies of cars and motorcycles. Authorities link the suspects to at least 13 motorcycle robberies in which victims were seriously injured.

One case under investigation is a homicide on July 6, 2025, in Belén de Carrillo, where a 56-year-old man was shot and his car was then set on fire with him inside. Investigators also connect the group to an attack on Sept. 10, 2025, in which a 77-year-old rancher was beaten while milking and his pickup truck was stolen. Agents seized three assault rifles and ammunition at the home of a woman who was among those detained. Vladimir Muñoz, the OIJ’s interim deputy director, outlined the violent methods investigators attribute to the group.

None of those detained has been charged, and all are presumed innocent. Prosecutors will determine their legal situation in the coming days. The data follow the death of a French woman who was found shot dead inside her home in Cabo Velas earlier this month. OIJ figures are preliminary and can change as cases are reclassified.

World.title: Basketball excitement as SSBA hosts Elite Annual Celebrity Basketball Game
World.content:
Basketball excitement as SSBA hosts Elite Annual Celebrity Basketball Game

By Zoila Palma: Basketball excitement is building ahead of the SSBA and Elite Annual Celebrity Basketball Game, scheduled for Friday, December 4, at 8:00 p.m. at the Victor Galvez Stadium.

The event will bring together personalities representing Santa Elena and San Ignacio for a night of friendly competition and entertainment.

SSBA has begun introducing players who will represent the two communities, including Whitney Roches and Tyron Peters, known as “Bigs,” for Team Santa Elena.

Representing Team San Ignacio are English teacher Vaneene Juan and Ramon Figueroa, popularly known as “Doc.” More player introductions are expected throughout the week.

The annual game is expected to bring supporters together as San Ignacio and Santa Elena compete for bragging rights on the basketball court.

Residents are being encouraged to come out, support their teams and enjoy the excitement on December 4.

World.title: Belize advances Climate Finance readiness through COP31 side event
World.content:
Belize advances Climate Finance readiness through COP31 side event

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize, in partnership with STUF United Fund and the International Cooperation and Development Fund (TaiwanICDF), hosted a side event at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) on November 11, 2026, focusing on improving access to climate financing for developing countries.

Held under the theme “Advancing Climate Finance Readiness: Expanding Equitable Access through Transparency & Partnerships,” the session brought together international experts and development partners to explore ways to strengthen countries’ capacity to secure climate financing and transform national climate priorities into projects ready for investment.

The Government of Belize presented on its efforts to move from climate priorities to finance-ready action, highlighting the country’s experience in strengthening institutional capacity and addressing challenges that limit access to climate financing. STUF United Fund also emphasized the importance of inclusive partnerships, civil society engagement and collaboration across different sectors.

Other presentations came from TaiwanICDF, the Commonwealth Secretariat and Conservation International. Their contributions focused on technical assistance, development cooperation, institutional strengthening, nature-based solutions, conservation financing and innovative mechanisms to support climate action.

The discussions highlighted the need for transparency, stronger institutions, technical support and meaningful international partnerships to help developing countries access and effectively utilize climate financing. Particular attention was given to the challenges faced by small and climate-vulnerable states.

Through the COP31 side event, Belize and its international partners highlighted the importance of ensuring that countries have the resources, expertise and partnerships needed to turn climate commitments into practical solutions, while advancing a more equitable and resilient future.

World.title: PM: Belize and U.S. collaborating to crack down on illegal activities at Corozal Free Zone
World.content:
PM: Belize and U.S. collaborating to crack down on illegal activities at Corozal Free Zone

By Zoila Palma: Prime Minister John Briceno says that Belize and the U.S. are working together to keep the Corozal Free Zone free from illicit activities.

During an interview with 7news Belize, the PM says that representatives from the U.S. Embassy have visited the Corozal Free Zone.

“I know, as far as I know, we have closed that extra gate that they had through the back. The Americans have visited the Free Zone; we have shown them what we are doing with the operations, and we are doing as best as we can. If we export cigarettes from the Free Zone, it is exported legally. Now, what happens in Mexico, we can’t-we have no control over that, so that is a matter that you need to ask the Mexicans,” the Prime Minister said.

“There have been concerns, obviously, earlier on that we have to ensure that we don’t allow the cartels to come into Belize, which is something I have been saying from the beginning-that we have to do everything possible to keep them out of Belize, and we have been fairly successful for that. And, but we continue to work with Americans, and we always tell them we need help-we need help with the intelligence, with the assets to maybe move from point A to point B very quickly, to stave off these people trying to come into Belize,” the PM added.

The U.S. Department of State reports have routinely cited the Corozal Free Zone as a hub vulnerable to trade-based money laundering and the illegal movement of duty-free or contraband goods across the Mexico-Belize border.

World.title: Fonseca: Belize stands firmly with Taiwan after Smith’s US visa revoked
World.content:
Fonseca: Belize stands firmly with Taiwan after Smith’s US visa revoked

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Foreign Affairs Minister Francis Fonseca is making it clear that Godfrey Smith’s push for closer ties with China is his own view, not the Government of Belize’s.

Smith, a Senior Counsel and former Foreign Minister, believes the United States revoked his visa because of his work to expand China’s presence in Belize. Asked whether that was a valid reason, Fonseca declined to weigh in.

“That’s not for me to say. That’s for the US to determine. They have their own policies. That’s Mr. Smith’s personal position,” Fonseca said.

He then restated where Belize stands.

“Belize, of course, our position is very firmly and very clearly that we are committed to our diplomatic relations with Taiwan. They have been a good friend and partner of Belize for 37 years,” he said.

Fonseca said he only learned of the revocation when it was brought to his attention and that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs was never informed.

“I’m very surprised, very shocked by it,” he said. “The US government obviously has the right to revoke anyone’s visa and they have not provided any reasons for that revocation.”

World.title: PM: Belize will win the Sarstoon fight in court, not in combat
World.content:
PM: Belize will win the Sarstoon fight in court, not in combat

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Prime Minister John Briceño says Belize cannot beat Guatemala in a physical confrontation at the Sarstoon, but it can and will win through diplomacy and the courts.

The PM was responding to last weekend’s incident in which two Guatemalan Navy vessels confronted a Belize Defence Force patrol near Sarstoon Island.

“Certainly, it’s of grave concern to all Belizeans, including us as a government,” Briceño said.

He praised the BDF for its professionalism, saying Belize cannot afford a flare up on the river.

“It’s obvious Guatemala is 18 million, we’re 400,000. It’s a fight we can’t win, a physical fight. But we can win that fight diplomatically and in the courts, and that’s exactly what we’re doing at this moment,” he said.

The PM said Belize continues to gain support by raising the matter at the United Nations, the Organization of American States and with partners including the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom and Canada.

He noted that he raised Belize’s concerns at the recent Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, where leaders included continued support for Belize in their communiqué.

World.title: Prime Minister on tensions in Sarstoon: “We continue to stand our ground”
World.content:
Prime Minister on tensions in Sarstoon: “We continue to stand our ground”

By Zoila Palma: Following recent tensions and Wednesday’s stand off between the Belize Coast Guard and vessels of the Guatemalan Armed Forces in the Sarstoon, Prime Minister John Briceno says that Belize continues to stand our ground.

“I have to commend the BDF on the way they act with such professionalism, because the reality is that we can’t afford a flare-up whereby people are fighting out there, because it’s obvious Guatemala is 18 million, we’re 400,000. It’s a fight we can’t win, a physical fight. But we can win that fight diplomatically and in the courts, and that’s exactly what we’re doing at this moment,” the Prime Minister said.

The PM says that Belize continues to stand our ground in face of continued aggression by the Guatemalan army.

“We have not lost the Sarstoon. We continue to stand our ground. There are instances when these big boats are in front of us with guns. What do you want us to go? We have to face reality. But we are very confident that we continue to win diplomatically when we make it known in the United Nations, or to the OAS, or to the friends of Belize like the Americans and the European Union and the UK, Canada. I was at the Heads of the Commonwealth meeting in Antigua and Barbuda; I brought up the concerns, they took out in their communique their continuous support for Belize, so we continue to win on the diplomatic front,” the PM added.

In addition, PM Briceno expressed confidence in the ICJ.

“And I have every confidence in the court we will also win, and we have been discussing with the Americans, with the UN and the EU and all our partners, that one of the important things is going to be that once that case is over would be the implementation. We have to ensure that Guatemala abides by the ruling,” he said.

World.title: Belizean Pride: Leticia Westby earns Doctorate in Conservation and Restoration of Natural Environment
World.content:
Belizean Pride: Leticia Westby earns Doctorate in Conservation and Restoration of Natural Environment

By Zoila Palma: Belizean Leticia Juanita Westby has successfully earned a Doctor of Conservation and Restoration of the Natural Environment degree after defending her doctoral thesis at the Universidad Centro Panamericano de Estudios Superiores (UNICEPES).

The university awarded her the degree with commendations in recognition of her performance throughout the academic process.

Westby’s doctoral research, titled “Effect of Agroecological Practices on Degraded Soils of Sugarcane Crops in Belize,” examined how agroecological practices can contribute to the recovery and sustainable management of soils affected by agricultural activities.

Her research focuses on the role of sustainable agricultural practices in addressing soil degradation, particularly in sugarcane cultivation, an important sector of Belize’s agricultural industry.

“My doctoral thesis evaluated the effect of agroecological management practices on degraded sugarcane soils in northern Belize. In two farmers’ fields in Corozal, a Vertisol in San Narciso and an Inceptisol in Santa Elena, I compared four management packages based on resources available in the sugar belt (sugarcane bagasse, crop residue retention, and intercropping with a legume) against conventional management with residue burning, using a randomized complete block design. Soil physical and hydrophysical properties were measured,” Westby explained.

The doctoral work was conducted under the supervision of Dr. Susan Smith Pinto.

UNICEPES congratulated Westby on her achievement, recognizing the significance of her academic accomplishment and research contribution to environmental conservation in Belize.

World.title: Magistrate orders 23 names struck from Cayo North voters’ list
World.content:
Magistrate orders 23 names struck from Cayo North voters’ list

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Magistrate has ordered the immediate removal of 23 names from the Cayo North voters’ list, in what the United Democratic Party is calling its first victory for electoral integrity.

In a press release issued on Wednesday, November 11, the UDP welcomed the ruling, saying it shows the value of persistence, hard work and perseverance in safeguarding the democratic process.

The matter is not over. According to the UDP, the Magistrate was scheduled to consider a further 76 names on Wednesday afternoon. That decision is still pending.

“Every lawful vote must be protected. Every voters’ list must uphold the integrity of our democracy,” said UDP Leader and Leader of the Opposition Tracy Taegar Panton.

The party thanked Dr. Omar Figueroa, San Ignacio and Santa Elena Mayor Earl Trapp, former UDP Vice Chairman Alberto August and its legal advisors for pursuing the matter through the lawful process.

The UDP said it remains committed to ensuring that voters’ lists meet the requirements of the law.

“The work continues!” the party said.

World.title: Keep spending tight…
World.content:
The IMF has told Jamaica that revenue mobilisation and restraint in current spending growth are critical to preserve fiscal space for priority investment and return public debt to a sustained downward path.

THE International Monetary Fund (IMF) has applauded the Jamaican Government for its “strong policy frameworks and sustained reforms” which “have underpinned its resilience in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa”.

The category 5 system left severe damage in sections of the island after its rampage on October 28, 2025.

But the IMF has warned that addressing supply-side constraints is essential to raising Jamaica’s potential growth and enhancing the country’s resilience and has urged the Dr Andrew Holness-led Administration to ensure it contains non-priority recurrent spending.

Holness has already announced a pause on several government expenditure items, including non-essential travel, parties, and retreats at resorts, with the IMF agreeing that this should remain a priority.

“Revenue mobilisation and restraint in current spending growth are critical to preserve fiscal space for priority investment and return public debt to a sustained downward path. The authorities’ efforts to broaden the tax revenue base and strengthen administration are welcomed, along with the intention to develop a mechanism to anchor medium-term public wage growth in a manner consistent with the fiscal framework,” the IMF said on Wednesday as it released its ‘Jamaica: Staff Concluding Statement of its 2026 Article IV Mission’.
