According to the IMF, its team, led by W Raphael Lam, held meetings in Kingston with Jamaican authorities, representatives of the private sector, civil society, and development partners during October 27-November 4 to conduct the 2026 Article IV consultation.

In his mission statement, Lam said the Jamaican authorities’ effective disaster risk financing framework, together with the strength of the country’s fiscal, monetary, and financial sector frameworks, have supported an appropriate policy response to cushion the severe impact of Melissa while preserving market access on favourable terms.

“The priority now is to advance reconstruction while preserving macroeconomic stability and deepening reforms, considering the more challenging external environment,” said Lam, who noted that economic activity is recovering gradually in Jamaica.

“Following a contraction of 1.2 per cent in fiscal year (FY)2025/26, growth is projected to recover moderately to 1.3 per cent in FY2026/27, with output returning to its pre-hurricane level by mid-2027, supported by reconstruction efforts and a recovery in tourism.

“Headline inflation, largely driven by higher energy and food prices, has risen above the Bank of Jamaica’s target band of 4-6 per cent, yet is projected to return within the target band by mid-2027 as supply pressures ease,” added Lam.

He pointed out that Jamaica’s risks to the growth outlook are tilted to the downside, while inflation risks remain on the upside.

“Higher energy and food prices from prolonged conflict in the Middle East and drought conditions from El Niño, and a further tightening in global financial conditions, could weigh on growth and intensify inflationary pressures. On the domestic front, delays in both reconstruction and restoration of tourism capacity would also weaken the recovery.”

Lam said the Jamaican Government correctly eased the fiscal stance in response to Hurricane Melissa, although accelerating reconstruction efforts remain essential.

“The multi-layered disaster risk financing provided rapid liquidity, including through IMF’s Rapid Financing Instrument. The Government appropriately activated the fiscal rule’s escape clause to support vulnerable households and hurricane-related reconstruction efforts. Revenue mobilisation efforts to broaden the tax base and strengthen administration are welcome,” said Lam.

“However, efforts are needed to accelerate reconstruction and build back better by closing long-standing infrastructure gaps and strengthening resilience to future natural disasters. The establishment of a new National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) provides an opportunity to do so, although work should continue in enhancing procurement, contract management, public investment management, and interagency coordination to address implementation bottlenecks.

“Meanwhile, containing non-priority recurrent spending remains essential, including by ensuring that the current fuel price smoothing mechanism continues to operate symmetrically to ensure cost recovery over time,” Lam added.

He pointed out that preserving debt sustainability should remain a priority for the Jamaican Government, with fiscal efforts shifted towards rebuilding buffers.

The IMF official applauded the Bank of Jamaica for its September policy rate hike which, it said, was appropriate, given above-target inflation and persistent commodity-price pressures.

“Monetary policy should remain focused on anchoring inflation expectations and limiting second-round effects, particularly as fiscal policy supports reconstruction efforts. Alongside an active monetary policy response to inflation risks, greater exchange rate flexibility would strengthen Jamaica’s capacity to absorb external shocks, including those coming from less favourable terms of trade.

“Over time, scaling back foreign exchange interventions would allow the exchange rate to play a greater buffering role and support foreign exchange market development,” Lam added.

He argued that Jamaica’s financial system remains resilient, but continued vigilance and reforms are needed.

“Continued close monitoring of credit and market risks, insurers’ financial positions, and vulnerabilities stemming from financial groups’ interconnectedness remains essential,” said Lam.

“In addition, cyber security risks require increased attention, building on the sector-wide cyber intelligence sharing hub.”

He called for the strengthening of the country’s energy security and electricity infrastructure, including by accelerating the transition towards renewable energy sources, which would reduce Jamaica’s exposure to imported fuel prices.

“Progress should continue in reducing crime, streamlining the regulatory burden for businesses, improving education outcomes and workforce skills, and addressing broader infrastructure bottlenecks. Continued implementation of reforms to strengthen climate resilience will help Jamaica better withstand future shocks,” declared the IMF official.

World.title: ‘Go make a song of it!’
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness speaking during the National Housing Trust’s (NHT) Construction Scholarship awards ceremony which was held at Jamaica House in St Andrew on Wednesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

WHILE acknowledging that thousands of Jamaicans remain without assistance in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has again firmly rejected claims that his Administration has failed to respond to the devastation, insisting that such assertions are false and must be challenged.

“I will continue to say it over and over again, and I don’t care who vex. Go make a song of it,” Holness declared in what appeared to be a pointed jab at dancehall entertainer Beenie Man amid their public disagreement over the Government’s handling of hurricane relief.

Speaking during the National Housing Trust’s (NHT) Construction Scholarship awards ceremony which was held at Jamaica House in St Andrew on Wednesday, the prime minister acknowledged that questions surrounding the pace of recovery and the adequacy of assistance were legitimate, but insisted that these concerns should not be conflated with allegations of Government inaction.

“That’s a perspective. We can debate that. You may feel $500,000 isn’t enough. Another one may feel, ‘I’m grateful’…We understand that, but don’t say the Government has not done anything,” he said.

“That’s false,” Holness insisted, warning that the repeated circulation of such claims threatened to undermine public confidence in the Government and, by extension, the stability of society.

His remarks come amid a public spat with Beenie Man, whose given name is Moses Davis, after the entertainer questioned — during an interview with British broadcaster ITV News — whether donated hurricane relief funds were reaching those who needed it most.

The dancehall artiste subsequently released a song titled Weh Di Money Deh, drawing attention to Jamaicans still struggling to rebuild their lives after the Category 5 storm which struck Jamaica a year ago.

Holness pointed to the NHT, which he said had spent approximately $13.3 billion on hurricane-related assistance, including $2.9 billion in grants distributed to 7,600 Jamaicans. Individual grants, he reminded, ranged from $75,000 to $500,000.

Holness also disclosed that the Government had spent close to $12 billion on direct assistance, with another $9.6 billion being sought to support outstanding needs.

He said the scale of destruction caused by Hurricane Melissa had presented an unprecedented challenge, with approximately 110,000 households identified as requiring assistance and just over 50,000 having received support so far.

“You would see that just the NHT alone has spent significant resources trying to assist Jamaicans. That is true, but it is also true that there are still many Jamaicans who have got no assistance,” he acknowledged.

Holness said the Government was working to secure the resources necessary to reach the remaining households, stressing that the magnitude of the disaster must be considered when assessing the pace of recovery.

“Did it happen quickly? That’s legitimate. Is $500,000 enough? We can debate that. That’s a legitimate debate. But it is patently untrue, false, to say the Government hasn’t done anything,” he said.

The prime minister further cautioned against the dissemination of misinformation, especially on social media, arguing that it could create widespread public distrust and undermine the country’s progress.

“And what that does is to undermine and destroy the legitimacy of Government. And in undermining the legitimacy of Government, your society ends up in chaos,” he said.

Addressing the 50 NHT scholarship recipients, Holness charged that they too must dismiss illegitimate claims against their country.

“I’m not asking you to defend the Government. But defend your society…Don’t believe that you can step out of the society and succeed in spite of the society. If you tear down your society, you are tearing down yourself. You must be vested in building your society,” he said.

“Ultimately, you will be in charge of the society. And what kind of society will you have if you tear it down?” asked Holness.

He maintained that while he is open to criticism over pace of recovery, he would continue to challenge what he described as inaccuracies presented as facts.

“As I’m talking to a group of young Jamaicans who are native to social media, you will see all kinds of untruths being spread. And the only way to deal with darkness is to shine the light. And at every opportunity, we must elucidate. We must shine light, challenge falsehoods and incorrectly held positions,” the prime minister said.

“Yes, we will always challenge falsehoods. Because in the current landscape of information, it is so easy to put things out which are not true. And it is so easy to have compelling perspectives which may have truth in them but are not contextually correct,” Holness added.

World.title: Macka Diamond pours her heart into new chapter
World.content:
Macka Diamond.

More than three decades in dancehall have given Macka Diamond plenty to celebrate, but behind the flamboyant persona and enduring stage presence is an artiste who says there is still much of her story left untold.

For the veteran entertainer, the next chapter will be a deeply personal one, with her forthcoming EP, The Rebirth, serving as an opportunity to share a more vulnerable side of herself with the world.

Scheduled for release in January 2027, the project is being shaped by experiences that have left a lasting impression on her, including the pain of being separated from her son for more than two years. It is an emotional experience she says has inspired her to pour her heart into the music.

“It was inspired by my son after not seeing him over two years, hurting me so bad, and I had to pour out my heart on this EP. And all the struggles as a female in dancehall I go through, I truly wanna show the world my true talent and another side of my talent they don’t see a lot of,” Macka Diamond shared.

The revelation offers a glimpse into the personal experiences informing The Rebirth, suggesting that the project will reach beyond the familiar sounds and personality that have defined much of her public career.

For an artiste who has spent more than 30 years navigating dancehall, the desire to reveal another dimension of her artistry is significant.

Macka Diamond has built a recognisable identity in a genre where women have often had to contend with their own set of challenges to establish and sustain their place.

Her comments suggest that those experiences, alongside the personal sacrifices and emotional struggles that have accompanied her journey, will form part of the story she hopes to tell through the EP.

While she is keeping much of the project under wraps, the self-styled “Diamond of Dancehall” has promised a musical experience that reflects both her years in the business and a willingness to explore a different creative direction.

“I am not at liberty to divulge much at this time, but all I can say is it’s going to be a very interesting project,” she said.

Details surrounding the track list, featured artistes, and exact release date have yet to be disclosed. However, Macka Diamond intends for the project to resonate with her established supporters while introducing her music to a younger generation of dancehall listeners.

The title The Rebirth is particularly fitting for a project rooted in reflection and personal expression. Rather than simply revisiting the career that has brought her this far, Macka Diamond appears intent on using the next phase of her musical journey to communicate something more intimate about the woman behind the artiste.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: Tighter controls coming for sex offenders
World.content:
Commissioner of Corrections Brigadier (Ret’d) Radgh Mason addressing Parliament’s Internal and External Affairs Committee during Wednesday’s meeting.

The Department of Correctional Services (DCS) is moving towards the use of electronic tags to track registered sex offenders as it seeks to strengthen its monitoring of more than 500 people on its watch list.

Commissioner of Corrections Brigadier (Ret’d) Radgh Mason said the department was working to acquire the equipment and put the necessary legal arrangements in place to introduce the system.

He disclosed that the DCS was monitoring 528 sex offenders, with just over 30 having breached their legal requirement to report to probation officers after leaving prison.

The offenders are required to report to the respective probation offices for up to 10 years after their release. Mason explained that monitoring currently centres largely on ensuring they meet that obligation.

The issue was raised by Member of Parliament for St Thomas Eastern Yvonne Rose-Marie Shaw during Wednesday’s meeting of Parliament’s Internal and External Affairs Committee. Shaw asked about the department’s success in monitoring offenders, particularly given that they may move between parishes and communities.

Mason said the department was looking to strengthen the system through electronic monitoring, which would allow authorities to track offenders’ movements and establish areas they should not enter.

“Our next step will be towards electronic monitoring, and so we are working with the acquisition and all the legislative underpinnings towards monitoring. That is effectively how the modern jurisdictions go about monitoring. They place these monitors on them, GPS trackers, and they geofence the areas that they are meant to remain within,” he told the committee.

Geofencing involves setting electronic boundaries around particular locations. A tracking device can then help authorities monitor whether an individual enters or leaves those areas.

Mason said the department was also developing a course specifically for sex offenders. He noted that preventing further harm, particularly to children, was a key consideration in managing this group.

He maintained that the department was meeting its responsibilities under the law, while acknowledging that offenders who fail to report must be dealt with through the police and courts.

“So the success rate has been good. When persons breach, it is then for the courts, the police, to find those persons, at which point they would be brought back into custody and possibly sentenced,” Mason said.

The commissioner did not provide a percentage success rate for the monitoring programme or explain how many of the 528 offenders had been successfully tracked over a particular period.

The disclosure comes as the DCS oversees approximately 2,678 non-custodial cases, including people serving sentences outside prison, while also monitoring the registered sex offenders.

Mason said probation offices across the country had designated officers responsible for monitoring those required to report. The department also provides confidential professional spaces for counselling sessions in each parish.

World.title: PROVE IT!
World.content:
West Indies’ players share a photo op with the trophy after winning the Test cricket series against Bangladesh at the Sylhet International Cricket Stadium in Sylhet on Monday. (Photo: AFP)

WHILE encouraged that West Indies completed a calendar year without losing a Test series for the first time since 1994, cricket commentator Joseph “Reds” Perreira says the ultimate proof of a turnaround would be success against the game’s top teams.

The Daren Sammy-coached West Indies team surprised some watchers by defeating hosts Bangladesh 1-0 in a two-Test series which ended days ago.

That success away from home followed a 1-1 Test series result against visiting Pakistan between July and August, and a 1-0 triumph over touring Sri Lanka earlier in the summer.

That success away from home pushed former kingpins West Indies up to sixth in the ICC Test rankings, closely followed by Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Pakistan, who hold the seventh, eighth, and ninth positions, respectively.

“Those teams are in the bottom half [of the Test rankings]. And we did well [against] them, but the opposition cannot be described as great,” Perreira told the Jamaica Observer on Wednesday.

“When we start beating the people above us, when we start beating the people in the top five, then you can really assess whether we’re getting back to being a competitive Test team.”

The top five ranked teams include world Test champions South Africa, followed by Australia, New Zealand, India and England.

Looking specifically at the Test tour of Bangladesh, the Guyanese-born Perreira said the signs were positive.

Left-arm finger spinner Jomel Warrican shone for the visitors with 16 wickets in the two matches to claim the player of the series award. Captain and all-rounder Roston Chase, who bowls off-break, was also influential with the ball in typical spin-friendly Asian subcontinent conditions.

The batting unit, spurred by Amir Jangoo, Kavem Hodge and Brandon King, more than held its own, particularly in the drawn second Test during which West Indies twice posted 350-plus scores. Batsman Kevin Wickham, who made his debut in the second encounter, was outstanding, scoring stylish half centuries in both innings. Wickham became only the eighth West Indian to score half-centuries in each innings of his first Test.

West Indies had a two-week camp in India prior to the tour of Bangladesh, which is widely believed to have significantly assisted preparations for the unique challenges of playing on pitches in that part of the world.

“I think you have to look at the series and accept that a one-nil win playing in Bangladesh on their home patch is a successful tour,” Perreira said.

While he noted West Indies could have pushed aggressively for a 2-0 series victory by declaring sooner when they built a big lead in their second innings of the final Test, the veteran commentator acknowledged that they took a safety-first approach.

“It’s easy to say [West Indies should have actively chased the win] when you’re watching from umpteen thousand miles away, [but] a win is a win. And they’re now number six in the Test match table,” Perreira said.

Wayne Lewis, a former Jamaica batsman and the West Indies Players’ Association secretary, credited the coaching staff for their efforts in crafting the positive results given the general struggles of regional Test teams since the mid-1990s.

Lewis pointed to the 3-0 series loss to visiting Australia last year, highlighted by West Indies being humiliatingly bowled out for 27 in the third and final Test.

“There was so much speculation around Daren Sammy taking charge of the red-ball team and all the scepticism around that, but he has delivered now. Yes, it was a rocky beginning when Australia bowled us out for 27 at Sabina Park. That was the lowest moment for West Indies cricket. But kudos to Cricket West Indies and him and his staff. We were not [playing] against Australia or England, but still, playing Test cricket and playing Bangladesh in Bangladesh is always very difficult,” the former player told the Observer.

He reasoned that the camp in India was a boost.

“Playing and getting acclimatised to the conditions will always help. So that’s a plus, and it’s good to see Cricket West Indies invested in the team to really allow the coaching staff to have that type of a camp going into a very important Test series,” Lewis said.

“It’s a happy moment for West Indies cricket, and I hope that come next year they can build on that. This is hopefully the beginning of something good for the future, but I’m quite pleased and happy that West Indies really went to Bangladesh and actually won the series.

“Don’t take Bangladesh lightly… they went to Australia and embarrassed Australia in that first Test match [in a drawn two-Test series in August]. They [Bangladesh] are a formidable team, particularly in their conditions,” Lewis said.

— Sanjay Myers

World.title: Palate Reimagined
World.content:
(Photo: Garfield Robinson)

At ROK Hotel Kingston, Palate is setting the table for its next chapter, with a refreshed menu, a new culinary vision and a renewed appetite for putting downtown Kingston on the dining map.

There is something to be said for a restaurant that knows how to reinvent itself without losing its sense of identity. At Palate, the signature restaurant at ROK Hotel Kingston, that philosophy is finding fresh expression through a reimagined menu, a considered refresh of the dining space and the arrival of new Executive Chef Oji Jaja.

With its fifth anniversary approaching next July, Palate is entering its next chapter with a renewed culinary perspective — one that looks to Jamaica’s rich larder, the restaurant’s waterfront setting and the possibilities of downtown Kingston as a dining destination.

To experience the evolution first-hand, the restaurant invited a particularly discerning table of guests, including Jamaica Observer Managing Director Dominic Beaubrun, Deputy Managing Director Natalie Chin-Samuda, Senior Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Social Content, and Table Talk Food Awards conceptualiser Novia McDonald-Whyte, alongside Food Awards judges. Familiar faces at Palate, the group was well-positioned to appreciate just how far the restaurant has come.

Since opening, Palate has collected some notable Jamaica Observer Food Awards accolades, including the Solomon Gardner Award for Outstanding Service, Best Sunday Spot and Chef of the Year — all within its first year of operation. The latest reinvention signals an ambition to build on that early success while giving diners new reasons to return.

“You’ve all been here before, several times. And I think if there’s anybody that can attest to how much we have reinvented ourselves… you are the guys that can tell those stories for us,” said Marlene Buckridge, director of sales & marketing, ROK Hotel Kingston.

“We really depend on you guys to put the word out there that this is one of the best, and safest places to dine in downtown Kingston… On behalf of our team Sherene Brown, director of Food And Beverage and Amit Mahbubani, our general manager, welcome back to Palate, our reimagined food and beverage outlet. And I hope you have a fantastic time tonight,” Buckridge continued.

Looking ahead to 2027, the team’s wider vision is to position its food and beverage offerings as a compelling reason to venture downtown. That means challenging perceptions, cultivating a stronger dining culture and creating an experience that extends beyond the plate.

The transformation is deliberately nuanced. Think: More inviting cushions, a newly introduced cocktail bar and a collection of rather enticing cocktails. The objective is not simply to refresh the restaurant’s appearance, but to elevate the entire experience.

In the kitchen, Jaja is bringing his own perspective to the table. Having joined the ROK team in July, the executive chef has spent his first months assessing the existing menu and identifying opportunities to give Palate a more distinctive culinary voice.

“Because we’re right here on the waterfront, seafood is really what I want to put forward on the menu — really fresh seafood dishes,” he explained.

That coastal sensibility informed several of the evening’s standout plates, including a crab cake and a turmeric-ginger snapper, the latter offering a fresh interpretation of curried fish, accompanied by bammy and coconut milk. There was also a distinctly Jamaican thread running through the bread service, with a Scotch bonnet and Scallion Milk Roll and roasted garlic pakasa making an appearance.

The seven-course tasting experience began with the warm, pepper-kissed milk roll before moving into a Scotch bonnet Pumpkin Bisque and Quinoa and Lentil Salad. A Scotch bonnet Thyme Crab Cake followed, bringing a familiar Jamaican ingredient into a more contemporary culinary expression.

The Turmeric-Ginger Snapper, served with turmeric-ginger coconut cream, steamed bammy, callaloo, okra and sweet corn, was another highlight. The Smoked Filet Mignon offered a change of pace before the evening concluded with Passion Fruit Pavlova — a bright, tropical finish to the menu.

Beyond the kitchen, the cocktail menu had its own moment in the spotlight. Bartenders Sean Hopkins and Odane Young kept the newly introduced bar in good company, mixing a selection of cocktails as guests took Buckridge up on her invitation to explore the “sexy” offerings.

For Jaja, the refreshed menu marks the beginning rather than the conclusion of the process. Although the new selections had only officially made their debut that day, the early response had been encouraging, with the chef looking forward to hearing what the wider dining public makes of the changes.

At Palate, then, reinvention is less about starting over than refining what is already there. With the waterfront as its backdrop, Jamaican ingredients informing its culinary direction and a renewed focus on hospitality, the restaurant is making a case for downtown Kingston as a destination worth dressing up, showing up and dining out for.

World.title: WATCH: 22 years later, Brick and Lace still ‘Wicked’
World.content:
Twenty-two years after captivating audiences worldwide, Jamaican sister duo Brick and Lace are celebrating a new milestone as their hit single Love Is Wicked recently earned silver certification in the United Kingdom.

Catching up with sisters Nyla and Nyanda Thorbourne, Observer Online reporter Vanassa McKenzie explores the enduring legacy of the song while the duo reflects on their journeys through motherhood, their business ventures and plans for new music.

World.title: Gov’t cautions Jamaicans against employment offers linked to Russia-Ukraine war
World.content:
In this file photo Ukrainian soldiers drive in a military truck along a road in the Kharkiv region on July 30, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Roman PILIPEY / AFP)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Government of Jamaica has become the latest Caribbean nation to warn its citizens to avoid recruitment offers to participate in foreign wars or conflicts.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade issued the warning in a press release on Wednesday amid a wider caution regarding overseas employment opportunities advertised through social media, messaging platforms and other online channels.

The Government mentioned in particular those offering unusually high salaries, travel assistance or expedited immigration arrangements.

“It has come to the Government’s attention that there are international reports of foreign nationals being recruited to participate in Russia’s war against Ukraine including through s on social media,” it said.

Noting that the Government could not verify the legitimacy or authenticity of the reported overseas employment offers, it said it is however aware of international media reports of persons recruited from various countries to participate in that war, including accusations of ill-treatment of Africans and persons of African descent as well as misrepresentation of duties, difficulties in receiving payments and difficulties in returning to their home countries or onward travel.

“Jamaicans are therefore strongly encouraged to avoid such recruitment offers. The ministry further reminds that participation in foreign armed conflicts carries serious risks to personal safety including ultimately to life, and may also expose individuals to legal, immigration and consular complications,” it said.

“ The Government of Jamaica also wishes to advise that neither it, nor international humanitarian organisations can guarantee consular or humanitarian assistance or safe repatriation from active conflict zones,” the Government added.

The warning follows similar bulletins issued by the Dominican Republic.

READ: Lured to war: Caribbean men recruited by Russia with promises of work

The ministry is urging Jamaicans more widely to exercise due diligence in verifying the legitimacy of overseas employment offers, recruitment agencies and prospective employers before making travel arrangements or providing personal documents.

“Particular caution should be exercised where recruiters request passport information, advance payments or the signing of contracts that have not been independently verified or fully understood,” the ministry added.

Jamaicans at home who receive suspicious recruitment offers are encouraged to report the matter to the Ministry of Labour and Social Security. Those already overseas who believe they have been misled or coerced into military service should seek assistance from the nearest Jamaican diplomatic or consular mission, where it is safe to do so.

Persons may consult the Ministry of Labour and Social Security’s list of licensed employment agencies at www.mlss.gov.jm or contact its Employment Agencies Unit to seek verification of overseas employment opportunities.

World.title: De grandes villes européennes demandent à l’UE d’interdire les filtres des cigarettes
World.content:
“Les mégots de cigarette représentent pas moins de 30% de tous les déchets sauvages dans la ville de Bruxelles. Non seulement ces déchets dégradent notre paysage urbain, mais leur ramassage fait peser une charge extraordinaire sur nos équipes de nettoyage”, a pointé Anas Ben Abdelmoumen, conseiller municipal chargé de la propreté publique, auprès de POLITICO.

Plusieurs autres villes de Belgique, d’Allemagne, de Tchéquie, de Hongrie et de Lituanie ont également rejoint cette campagne, qui intervient alors que l’Union européenne procède à la révision de deux textes législatifs majeurs susceptibles d’aboutir à l’interdiction des filtres des cigarettes — ou du moins du plastique qu’ils contiennent.

La révision de la directive sur les produits du tabac par la Commission européenne est l’occasion d’interdire les filtres des cigarettes, estiment les membres de la campagne. S’ils échouent par ce biais, ils pourraient se rabattre sur la révision à venir de la directive sur les plastiques à usage unique pour interdire le plastique dans les filtres.

L’Organisation mondiale de la Santé est elle aussi en faveur de l’interdiction ou de la suppression progressive des filtres, affirmant qu’ils ne présentent aucun avantage pour la santé.

“Le filtre de cigarette est l’objet le plus souvent jeté dans l’espace public, il contient du plastique, il est à l’origine d’une pollution environnementale toxique et engendre des coûts considérables pour les collectivités locales et la société. De plus, le filtre ne rend pas le tabagisme moins nocif”, a argumenté Karl Beerenfenger, responsable de la campagne et membre de l’ONG néerlandaise Fair Resource Foundation.

“C’est un produit trompeur, l’une des plus grandes escroqueries de l’histoire récente. Le filtre de cigarette n’aurait jamais dû être mis sur le marché.”

World.title: ‘Blind spot’ no longer: Austria targets Russian espionage with new law
World.content:
While the new legislation targets espionage in general, it is part of the ministry’s broader shift in policy toward Russia, according to an internal document seen by POLITICO.

Under Austria’s current Criminal Code, operating or supporting a clandestine intelligence service is punishable if it harms Austrian interests. But espionage targeting other countries or international organizations is not covered in the same way, a loophole the government now wants to close.

The proposed legislation would introduce prison sentences of up to five years for espionage targeting EU institutions or international organizations with headquarters or offices in Austria, such as the United Nations, the OSCE and the International Atomic Energy Agency. The maximum sentence for espionage against Austria itself would increase from five to 10 years.

Austria pressured Russia earlier this year to dismantle satellite installations on its diplomatic properties in Vienna over concerns they could be used for espionage. At least three installations have since been removed. The country has expelled eight Russian diplomats since March 2025 for suspected espionage.

“Austria’s lax approach to spies is now firmly a thing of the past. Vienna remains a place for dialogue, but will no longer be a hub for espionage,” Meinl-Reisinger added, acknowledging that Vienna has long been known as a hotbed of spying.

Austria’s neutrality and its status as a non-NATO member have contributed to that reputation. During the Cold War, its proximity to the Iron Curtain made it a meeting point for intelligence services from East and West.

World.title: Trump’s snubbed COP — but he’s on everyone’s lips
World.content:
Whether fretting about the Iran war — or picturing life without him — the U.S. president is looming large in the minds of politicians and campaigners at the global climate summit.

ANTALYA, Turkey — Donald Trump is not at the COP31 climate summit but almost everyone is talking about him — and not in the way he’d like.

The U.S. president’s fateful decision to attack Iran earlier this year, sending global oil and gas prices soaring and compounding an international cost of living crisis, has been invoked — directly or indirectly — by leader after leader in Turkey as a reason to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels.

European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen said disruptions on the Strait of Hormuz are “shaking global energy markets.” The U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham invoked the specter of “wars across two continents” that “have sent fuel prices and gas bills soaring for families and businesses across the world.” U.N. Secretary General António Guterres noted how “recent conflicts made clear” that countries’ dependence on imported fossil fuels “is a recipe for chronic insecurity and a cost-of-living meltdown.”

World.title: Zelenskyy demands Europe become ‘regular part’ of Ukraine talks
World.content:
Speaking on his way into the European Political Community summit in the Irish capital ― a gathering of 50 EU and non-EU leaders ― German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he had received positive signals from the Abu Dhabi talks, but also stressed that Ukraine and Europe must be involved.



“I expect the Russian government and the Russian president to finally agree to these joint talks,” Merz said. “We will also discuss who, if necessary, will represent the European Union. But that is a matter we will discuss behind closed doors and not air publicly.”

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas struck a more skeptical tone, saying she had seen no goodwill from Moscow and insisted that a ceasefire must come before discussions on a peace agreement or Europe’s wider security architecture.

“Americans are representing American interests, Europeans are representing European interests,” she said, adding that EU treaties signal that European Council President António Costa and she should represent the bloc in any talks— a solution backed by Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal in an interview with POLITICO.

French President Emmanuel Macron said that Europe must first agree on its own peace proposals and vision for future European security before deciding who should represent it.

The substance of Europe’s negotiating position should determine the format of any talks, rather than the other way around, he told reporters on the way into the summit.

“Without Europeans there is no support for Ukraine, let’s be honest,” he said, arguing that U.S. involvement has declined. “There is some mediation, fine. But at the end of the day we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans. I have no doubt about it.”

World.title: Ukraine meldet erneut Einschränkungen bei Starlink
World.content:
KYJIW – Die Probleme mit „Starshield“, dem militärischen Tool von Elon Musks Satellitennetzwerk „Starlink“, sind in der Ukraine offenbar zurück, sagte Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj in einer Stellungnahme. „Leider verzeichnen unsere Einheiten seit einigen Tagen erhebliche Störungen des Starshield-Betriebs auf dem Gebiet der Ukraine – entlang der gesamten Frontlinie und in den vorübergehend besetzten Gebieten der Ukraine.“

Bereits vor rund einem Monat hatte die Ukraine gemeldet, dass sich die Starshield-Verbindung bei Objekten ab einer Geschwindigkeit von 161 km/h verschlechterte. Dadurch funktionierten ukrainische Verteidigungssysteme, insbesondere Abfangsysteme, nicht mehr zuverlässig. Die Beschränkung wurde am 24. Oktober aufgehoben. Laut Selenskyj gehen auch die neuen Störungen nicht auf eine technische Fehlfunktion zurück. Vielmehr werde die Verbindung erneut systematisch ab einer bestimmten Geschwindigkeit begrenzt.

„Für uns bedeutet dies in erster Linie eine erhebliche Erschwerung beim Abfangen russischer Düsen-Drohnen“, sagte Selenskyj. Die jüngsten Einschränkungen hätten bereits dazu geführt, dass mehrere russische Drohnen die ukrainische Luftabwehr durchbrechen konnten und weitere Ukrainer getötet wurden, fügte er hinzu.

World.title: Feijóo wants to run Spain like a CEO. Not easy with far-right Vox on the board.
World.content:
But it also presents the party with an identity crisis if — as expected — it needs to team up with far-right populists from Vox to build a majority. If the next government is a business, Vox will be a maverick on the board.

Business leader

The devastating Toledo rail crash that killed 69 people on Oct. 28 offered the PP an opportunity to shift the campaign onto territory where it feels comfortable, as party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo and his close circle doubled down on their strategy to present themselves as steady-handed executives.

Feijóo’s first move after the accident was to chair a closed-door gathering of 15 railway experts to project an image of a jefe interested in technicalities.

A second party official explained to Madrid Playbook that the party’s new mantra was: “Management, management, management.” When Sánchez called the snap election in early October, the PP rolled out posters that read “FINALLY.” In the days following the rail accident, the party added “management” to that original slogan. “Finally, management.”

Feijóo talks during a campaign rally in Madrid on Oct. 10, 2026. | Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images

While that low-drama C-suite approach may appeal to the PP, the obvious political challenge is that Vox — which is eyeing key ministries in the next administration — is running a very different type of campaign. Vox relishes political drama.

It was the only party to push on with campaign rallies immediately after the rail disaster and has accused the government of being “a bunch of crooks” who are planning to “steal the election.” Highly outspoken in its hostility to migration, Vox suggested the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, which sparked nationwide protests, would never have happened if she had been North African.

World.title: EU will examine Israel association agreement after massive public petition
World.content:
Out of 136 registered petitions — known as the EU Citizens' Initiative — in more than a decade, only 14 had reached the 1 million-signature threshold required to be officially brought in front of the EU executive.

The ECI mechanism requires the Commission to examine petitions signed by more than 1 million EU citizens from more than seven countries. Earlier this year, the Commission rejected a petition to expand abortion financing after it was signed by 1.2 million citizens.

The European Left Alliance, an umbrella group for 11 left-wing political parties, started the petition almost two years ago. The group said the EU should suspend its trade and political dialogue with Israel over what it sees as the country's failure to prevent genocide in Gaza.

France accounted for the most signatures with 339,479, followed by Italy with 283,863 and Spain with 151,821. The Commission will reply by May 2027 to say whether it plans to take any action in response to the petition.

Originally signed in 1995 and coming into force in 2000, the association agreement covers political dialogue and trade between the EU and Israel. The bloc is Israel’s biggest trading partner, accounting for about a third of its total trade in goods with the world in 2025, according to EU data.

The wars in Gaza and Lebanon have provoked vehement criticism of Israel and divided European leaders.

World.title: Ukraine Starlink speed restrictions in effect again, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
“For us, this primarily means a significant complication in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones,” Zelenskyy said.

The latest restrictions have already allowed several Russian drones to get through Ukrainian air defense and kill more Ukrainians, he added.

"Connectivity issues have resurfaced," said Serhii Bezkrestnov, an advisor to Zelenskyy on defense technology, "specifically regarding communication with helicopters pursuing 'Shahed' drones, as well as with jet interceptors tasked with shooting down jet-powered 'Shaheds'."

A European official with first-hand knowledge of the situation, who was granted anonymity to discuss the matter freely, said the Starshield limits were first noticed three days ago, when negotiations between the U.S. and Russia began in Abu Dhabi. Ukrainian officials believe this is not a coincidence, but a pressure tactic, they added.

The U.S. Congress bipartisan Ukraine Caucus on Thursday demanded in a statement "a full accounting from the Trump Administration and SpaceX on how and why this occurred and immediate action to restore full access to Starshield."

U.S. President Donald Trump said last Sunday that he couldn't tell who slowed down Starlink for Ukraine for much of October, and wasn't even sure it had been throttled.

World.title: “The rules-based international order is breaking down,” Thailand’s Foreign Minister warns
World.content:
Thailand’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told Euronews that as “we live in a world where we see the rules-based international order breaking down,” “we need to restore multilateralism, because nobody can go it alone.”

 

In a wide-ranging interview for Euronews’ new World Conversation global programme, the veteran top Thai diplomat, with over 40 years of foreign ministry service, outlined how Thailand has managed to secure a balanced approach with the United States and China at a time when the “the main global contestation is between the two superpowers whom both are friends of Thailand.”

“We ask our friends not to force us to take sides,” Sihasak explained, adding that “not taking sides does not mean being neutral as sometimes neutrality does not serve your interest.” He pointed to growing Chinese investment in electric vehicles and the US role in regional security.

A market of 700 million people, Thailand is “a geopolitically safe zone,” the deputy prime minister said in Bangkok, and therefore its strategic objective is to maintain peace and stability. In this context, he emphasized the crucial role played by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) alliance for pan-Asian stability, adding that Thailand was ready to rebuild ties with Cambodia and defended a gradual return to regional talks with Myanmar.

World.title: Commission set to approve Hungary’s €10bn in post-pandemic recovery fund next week
World.content:
The European Commission is set to approve almost all of Hungary’s €10 billion allocation from the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) later this month, Commission officials have confirmed to Euronews.

 

Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who swept to power in a landslide election victory in April, campaigned on a promise to unlock EU funds frozen during Viktor Orbán’s 16 years in office.

In May, Magyar and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen agreed to release €16.4 billion that had been withheld over rule-of-law and corruption concerns under Orbán’s government.

Of that total, €10 billion is due from the EU’s post-pandemic RRF, which expires later this year. All payments have to be authorised by the end of November, to be paid before the end of the year.

Hungary announced in late August that it had met the EU’s conditions for payment, despite the substantial delays accumulated under Orbán. The Commission launched a verification process shortly afterwards.

An official familiar with the file, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the Commission expects to complete its remaining RRF assessments, including Hungary’s, by the end of November.

In Hungary's case, the Commission “has not identified major obstacles”, which could mean Budapest receives 100 per cent, or close to it, of the requested amount.

Euronews understands that the assessment could be published as early as next week.

As Euronews reported in May, one of the main ways the Commission helped Budapest meet the funding requirements was by allowing capital injections through investment institutions.

Under Hungary’s revised recovery plan, adopted in August, €3.6 billion – more than a third of the total – was redirected towards capital injections into the Hungarian Development Bank and a newly created, fully state-owned railway company, the Rolling Stock Company.

However, Hungary still had to fulfil 27 so-called “super milestones” and more than 100 other milestones. Parliament amended more than 100 laws over the summer to meet the requirements, most of them concerning judicial independence and the fight against corruption.

The revised National Recovery Plan also includes measures to modernise the country’s energy grid, railways and rental housing stock.

Once the Commission gives a positive recommendation, EU member states must also approve it before payment can follow.

In September, the Commission approved €4.2 billion in frozen cohesion funds for Hungary after Magyar’s government implemented rule-of-law and anti-corruption reforms.

A further €2.2 billion remains blocked because conditions related to academic freedom and LGBTI+ rights have not been met. Budapest has yet to submit evidence that those reforms have been delivered.

Euronews has asked the Hungarian government for comment but has not yet received a response.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 12th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Antibiotic-resistant infections hit 400 a week in England despite falling drug use
World.content:
More than 400 people a week developed antibiotic-resistant infections in England last year, according to surveillance data published by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) on Thursday, highlighting the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance despite efforts to reduce antibiotic use.

 

A total of 21,129 cases of antibiotic-resistant bacteraemia – a potentially life-threatening infection where bacteria are present in the bloodstream – were recorded in 2025, up 16.8% from 18,086 in 2019.

The continued upward trend comes despite a reduction in antibiotic consumption across the NHS. Total antibiotic use fell by 10.7% between 2019 and 2025, from 17.8 to 15.9 defined daily doses per 1,000 inhabitants per day.

"We can’t rely on reducing antibiotic use alone," Shona Arora, interim chief medical adviser at UKHSA, said in a press release, calling for greater efforts to prevent infections and develop new treatment options. “We need to continue our work with partners globally to prevent infections from occurring in the first place, alongside exploring new treatment options.”

The data also reveal significant inequalities in the burden of resistant infections.

People living in England's most deprived areas had a 44.2% higher rate of antibiotic-resistant bacteraemia than those in the least deprived communities. Older people were also disproportionately affected. Adults over 45 accounted for 89.3% of infections, while almost half of cases were detected in people aged over 74.

The findings point to a wider challenge for policymakers: tackling antimicrobial resistance requires not only responsible prescribing but also stronger infection prevention, vaccination programmes and investment in new treatments.

The UK has set out its ambitions in a National Action Plan for antimicrobial resistance 2024 to 2029. Its objectives include limiting the spread of resistant infections and reducing the need for antibiotics in the first place.

Diana Johnson, the UK's minister for public health and patient safety, urged people to take antibiotics only when advised by a healthcare professional, complete their prescribed course and avoid sharing or saving medication.

“This will help reduce the spread of resistant infections and keep all of us safer,” she said.

World.title: The EU sealed a migration deal with Nigeria. But what did Abuja get in return?
World.content:
Details of the EU's “milestone” migration deal with Nigeria remain unclear, two days after it was signed in Abuja by EU Commissioner Magnus Brunner and Nigeria's Foreign Affairs Minister, Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu.

 

After a decade of negotiations, Nigeria agreed on Tuesday to readmit its nationals residing illegally in European countries, as the EU seeks to speed up the return of irregular migrants.

The agreement establishes “rapid and effective procedures” for returning Nigerians who have no right to stay in an EU country, a pressing issue for the bloc, since only one in three irregular migrants is actually sent back.

Accounts vary over what Nigeria secured in return for the agreement.

According to local press, the EU pledged almost €100 million in additional funding for migration management and security cooperation.

The Nigerian newspaper The Sun, in a report shared on X by the EU delegation in Abuja, attributed the pledge to Johannes Luchner, deputy director general of the Commission’s department for Migration and Home Affairs.

According to these reports, the money would finance legal migration pathways for Nigerians into the EU, as well as anti-trafficking and anti-drug initiatives.

The Commission maintains that the agreement is not “a transactional exchange of concessions.”

“It is part of a broader mutually beneficial partnership between the EU and Nigeria. [...] This is one important step in strengthening our partnership, which is based on mutual trust, shared responsibilities, reciprocity, and common interests,” a Commission spokesperson said on Thursday in response to a question from Euronews.

In a statement, Brunner offered little detail on the agreement, saying only that the EU and Nigeria were “turning the huge potential of [their] partnership into mutual benefit.”

Nigeria's Foreign Affairs Minister and the EU Delegation to Nigeria have yet to respond to Euronews' requests for comment.

The EU has already committed €731 million in grant funding to Nigeria for 2021-2027.

Many Nigerian migrants reach Europe through the dangerous Mediterranean route. Nigerians were the largest national group among irregular arrivals in Italy in 2017 and 2018, but their numbers have dropped significantly since then. Eurostat does not publish figures on the current number of Nigerians residing irregularly in the EU countries.

The agreement is part of a broader effort to raise the share of migrants who are effectively returned after an order to leave. That rate remains around 30%, despite a slight increase in recent months.

Under international law, countries are obliged to readmit their own nationals. However, African governments have often resisted such returns or delayed the process.

To step up cooperation with third countries, the EU is using incentives and leverage across sectors, including visa policy, trade and financial support. Foreign governments, for their part, ask in exchange for substantial visa facilitation or large financial packages.

The EU currently has 18 readmission agreements, most of them with Asian and Western Balkan countries. A 2014 agreement with Cape Verde was the bloc's first with an African nation, but subsequent negotiations with Morocco and Tunisia have stalled.

Some EU member states have negotiated bilateral agreements to return irregular migrants residing on their territory. The EU as a whole has increasingly turned to non-binding arrangements, such as those with Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Ethiopia, or to broader strategic partnerships, such as the memoranda of understanding signed with Tunisia and Egypt.

Under this deal, EU nationals who lack the legal right to remain in Nigeria can also be returned. The agreement still needs approval from EU member states and the European Parliament.

World.title: What is next for Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang resigns?
World.content:
For 33 years, it was almost impossible to separate Nvidia from Jensen Huang. The co-founder, always in his leather jacket, turned a company he started with two friends in a Silicon Valley diner into one of the world’s most valuable firms. He drew stadium crowds to watch him unveil the chips that power tools like ChatGPT.

 

His resignation on Thursday leaves the company facing a question it has never had to answer: what does Nvidia look like without him? He stepped down after admitting an affair with a woman US officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence, and after reports of a second relationship with a subordinate.

Who takes charge?

For now, chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO and keep her finance role. Harvey C. Jones, a former chief executive of chip design software firm Synopsys, becomes the board’s first-ever chair.

Kress joined Nvidia in 2013 after nearly 25 years at companies including Cisco and Microsoft, and is often cited as a leading internal candidate. But the company has no known succession plan, and Huang repeatedly avoided naming an heir.

“There’s not someone who is sort of prepped and ready to go next in line,” said Carmem Domingues, who was a senior AI adviser in the Biden White House.

Martin Peers of tech outlet The Information has said there are “no obvious internal candidates”. He named two possible outside picks: AMD chief executive Lisa Su, who is a relative of Huang, and Rene Haas, CEO of British chip designer Arm. Another analyst has suggested Intel boss Lip-Bu Tan.

Huang’s children, Madison and Spencer, both hold management roles at the company. Domingues said it was unclear how ready they would be to take over.

The ‘Huang premium’

Investors have long paid extra for Nvidia’s leadership.

"Investors have effectively been buying into Nvidia’s technology and Huang’s vision in equal measure," said Stephen Innes of SPI Asset Management. "It may now have to calculate how much of that premium was attached to one individual."

Mandeep Singh, global head of technology research at Bloomberg Intelligence, said Nvidia was unlikely to be “as aggressive” under new leadership. That matters for a company racing to deliver each new generation of AI chips.

Rivals could gain as customers look to spread their orders. Charu Chanana of Saxo Markets said “AI leadership could broaden, rather than the boom ending”, and named AMD, Broadcom, Alphabet and Samsung as possible winners.

The first test comes on 17 November, when Nvidia reports its quarterly results under interim leadership.

Ripples across the AI industry

The bigger fear is contagion. Nvidia sits at the base of an AI economy in which companies fund one another in a loop.

"All the AI companies either owe money to Nvidia and/or depend on them," said Domingues. "One falling can bring down a lot."

Chanana said the "bigger risk is a disruption to AI spending itself". Financing, cloud giants’ spending and the returns on AI investment were already under scrutiny. The turmoil also comes days before AI firm Anthropic’s stock market debut, which is widely seen as a test of investor appetite for the sector.

Not everyone is alarmed. Investor Sheikha Maytha Bint Maktoum said any disruption would be "temporary", given the ecosystem Nvidia has built over decades.

What it means for Europe

Europe has a lot riding on what Nvidia does next. A few weeks ago, at an investment summit in Berlin, Germany, Huang agreed an AI partnership with Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The federal government is reportedly contributing a nine-figure sum in euros.

Around a dozen German companies are expected to take part, including Siemens, Audi and start-up Black Forest Labs, which is based in Freiburg im Breisgau.

Nvidia says it invested almost $1 billion (€900 million) in Germany in 2025. In October, it announced an AI hub for start-ups in Stockholm, Sweden.

Huang championed those projects personally. It remains to be seen whether his successor shares his enthusiasm for each country building a “national intelligence” from its own data.

Losing its voice in Washington

Huang was a close informal adviser on AI to US President Donald Trump, and spent years lobbying against curbs on sales of advanced chips to China. Last year, Trump cleared Nvidia’s H200 chips for export there, overruling China hawks in both parties.

With Huang gone and the spy allegations hanging over the company, that influence may fade. Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have already asked the administration to preserve all documents on Nvidia’s chip exports to China.

Beijing denies the spying claims and has accused Washington of using them as a pretext for a technological “blockade”. Meanwhile, Chinese firms are trying to break their dependence on US suppliers, and Huawei is presenting itself as China’s answer to Nvidia.

World.title: Gunman kills one and barricades himself in building after gym shooting in Washington, DC
World.content:
At least one person has been killed and four others injured in a shooting near Logan Circle, a popular neighbourhood within walking distance of the White House in Washington, DC, according to police in the US capital.

 

The suspected gunman has barricaded himself on the top floor of a nearby residential building. His identity and motive are not yet known.

According to US media reports, an armed man entered the Vida Fitness gym, shot a customer in the back and then ran out of the building. The gym was evacuated, and more shots were fired in the street before people scattered.

Nearby public schools have been placed on alert. For now, pupils are not being allowed to leave, and no one is being allowed in.

Police have sealed off the area and asked people to take cover. A SWAT team and other officers have also been sent to the scene.

One eyewitness, who was in the gym when the shooting started at around 8am local time, said there were about 50 people inside.

“Within seconds, a man fell to the ground and blood started pouring out from under him,” he said. “One of the gym customers rushed over to help him. The man died instantly. He had been shot in the neck.”

He said he and others ran out of the gym. He believed two shots were fired inside the gym and a further five or six outside.

The area has seen violent crime before. In the early hours of a Sunday in August 2025, a group of teenagers attacked a former staff member of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), the cost-cutting body set up under President Donald Trump, and tried to steal the car belonging to him and a woman he was with.

World.title: Gaza: Devastation inside Nasser Hospital after deadly Israeli strike
World.content:
The strike devastated the hospital's surgical department, with damage also reported to operating theatres, recovery facilities and the intensive care unit. Footage shows extensive destruction inside the hospital, with shattered ceilings, twisted metal and rubble scattered across medical equipment and beds. Rescue workers searched through the debris, while grieving relatives gathered outside to pray over the bodies of those killed.

 

Gaza's Health Ministry identified one of the victims as general surgeon Rizk Abu Shaira. The Israeli military acknowledged carrying out the strike, saying it had targeted a senior Hamas commander and other militants allegedly operating from the hospital, but provided no evidence to substantiate its claims.

The attack struck one of the few remaining functioning hospitals in Gaza, where years of war have devastated healthcare services and left medical facilities struggling to meet overwhelming needs. According to the WHO, 1,056 attacks on healthcare facilities and personnel have been documented in Gaza since October 2023, resulting in 1,010 deaths and 1,725 injuries. The organisation warned that approaching winter conditions, including heavy rain, flooding and cold temperatures, could further worsen the humanitarian crisis, particularly as water and sanitation systems remain severely damaged.

Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using hospitals for military purposes, allegations the group denies. Under international humanitarian law, hospitals and medical personnel are protected, although facilities can lose specific protections if used to commit acts harmful to the enemy, subject to strict conditions. The WHO reiterated its call for unhindered humanitarian access and the protection of medical facilities.

World.title: ‘Monstrous injustice’: King Charles condemns slavery as UK agrees to talks
World.content:
In this episode of Spotlight on Africa, we talked to scholars from the continent and the Caribbean about slavery reparations – a key topic discussed at this year’s Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.

Advertising

The Commonwealth is a 56-nation group of mostly former British colonies, 21 of them in Africa. King Charles III remains head of state in 15 of them, including the UK.

Its biennial Heads of Government Meeting took place from 1 to 4 November 2026 in Antigua and Barbuda.

In a final communiqué issued on Wednesday, the group said the time had come for “meaningful, truthful and respectful conversation towards forging a common future based on equity”.

Timetable of talks

While no timetable for talks was announced, the group welcomed the United Kingdom’s willingness to engage “in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms”.

In his opening speech, King Charles III, who is politically neutral, called the slave trade “a monstrous injustice” that filled him with “profound personal sorrow”, but stopped short of a formal apology.

UN backs resolution calling slave trade ‘gravest crime against humanity’

For his part, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was open to saying sorry but ruled out paying the financial reparations demanded by some Caribbean countries.

Britain’s Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also said it was “not feasible” for the country to pay reparations for slavery, but that “there are things we can work on co-operatively”.

According to reports, Britain could issue a formal apology next year, during its G20 presidency.

Britain played a pivotal role in the slave trade, which saw between 10 and 15 million enslaved Africans taken to the Americas over four centuries.

The country abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery throughout the British Empire in 1833. It paid financial compensation, but to plantation owners rather than to the enslaved people themselves.

UN resolution

In March this year, the United Nations adopted a resolution recognising the transatlantic slave trade and the enslavement of Africans as the “gravest crime against humanity”, in a motion spearheaded by Ghana.

Ghana backs Jamaica’s petition to push UK for slavery reparations

For many countries, the time has come for formal apologies and concrete plans for slavery reparations.

To find out how these issues are being tackled on the African continent and in the Caribbean, RFI spoke to a panel of four guests:

Edem Adotey: professor at the Institute of African Studies in Accra, Ghana,

Joel Kibazo: Commonwealth spokesperson,

Matiangai Sirleaf: professor at the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law in the United States,

Verene A. Shepherd: Jamaican historian and one of three vice-chairs of the Caricom Reparations Commission.

This episode was mixed by Nicolas Doreau.

World.title: Can the EU make it harder to trick consumers online?
World.content:
The EU wants to curb subscription traps, misleading sales tactics and features that keep people scrolling. What would the proposed Digital Fairness Act change, and does it go far enough?

You 

Under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA), a company would have to remind you before the free trial ends and get your explicit agreement before it can start charging you. The proposed law would also make it easier to cancel a subscription online and require reminders before certain contracts renew automatically.

The Commission presented the proposal on Wednesday. It wants to give consumers more control over how much time and money they spend online.

"We haven't seen that kind of reform in consumer protection in the last 20 years," Agustin Reyna, director general of the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), told DW.

His organization pushed for stronger EU rules against manipulative online practices. He sees the proposal as a good starting point for tackling problems that frustrate consumers every day.

EU Commissioner for the rule of law and consumer protection Michael McGrath has been pushing for the new regulation Image: Europäische Kommission

Ending doomscrolling and 'dark patterns'

The proposal also includes a ban on manipulative marketing tactics, so-called "dark patterns." A concrete example: You are trying to reserve a hotel room and the website claims that only three are left, a potentially false claim to pressure you into buying.

A concert ticket that gets more expensive while you're waiting in an online queue raises a different problem. The price could still go up in the process, but the seller would have to show the current price while you wait and tell you the maximum you could be asked to pay.

Online games that encourage users to spend their money to advance are also targeted. Children would no longer be able to pay to win or get to the next level of their online game.

Marketing and personalized ads would need to be clearly marked and restricted in the case of children. Consumers should get the option to switch off doomscrolling functions such as the autoplay of videos, showing one clip after the other. With these new rules, the EU wants to make apps and websites less addictive.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised that "Europe has the power to act: It is we who decide our rules, not big tech" (file photo from January 2026) Image: Omar Havana/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Consumer protection versus innovation?

For Christoph Busch, an academic with a focus on consumer law and digital services based at Osnabrück University in Germany, the option to opt out doesn't go far enough. He argues that a version in which consumers actively have to choose to opt into those functions would be more effective.

"But then there is always the question of proportionality," Busch said. "And I think here the European legislators are trying to balance different interests."

These competing interests are particularly visible in the gaming industry, where interest groups have warned that the proposed EU restrictions could hurt developers and leave players with fewer options to choose from.

Video Games Europe and the European Games Developer Federation called the proposal "unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate," arguing that a ban on selling children features that help them win or advance is worded so broadly that it "could cover almost any purchase in a game."

For Busch, this argument doesn't hold. "If your business model is based on addictive design features, then maybe your business model has to be reviewed," he said.

The proposal still has to pass the Council and the European Parliament Image: Alexey Vitvitsky/SNA/imago images

The risk of overregulation

Catalina Goanta, an associate professor of private law and technology at Utrecht University, emphasized in an interview with DW that "regulation can very easily slide into overregulation."

Even though she believes that the DFA is a solid and reasonable compromise, she argues that prohibiting dark patterns and doomscrolling altogether would be too prohibitive. Many of the issues consumers currently face could be resolved by enforcing existing regulation more effectively, she said.

She points to the fact that the EU has made a name for itself in the past by adding new rules and regulations that have made it more difficult to access the European market, especially for small online businesses.

BEUC director Agustin Reyna disagrees.

"Instead of having 27 different regulations to adhere to, companies will now only get one," Reyna said.

For him, this speaks for simplification, especially when the responsibility for compliance is shared between online influencers and the platforms they publish on.

According to the new legislation, the EU would have the possibility to impose fines of up to six percent of a company's global annual revenue should the company violate the law.

What happens next?

The European Parliament and the Council, which represents member state governments, still have to agree on the text and formally adopt it. All experts agree that in that process, changes are still very likely.

"It will be a difficult trialogue, especially in this climate of simplification and deregulation with a focus on strengthening European competitiveness," said Christoph Busch. In that climate, it is not easy to add consumer rights, he adds.

Agustin Reyna is more optimistic. "The parliament is a divided house, much more than in the past," he says. "But consumer protection is a subject that brings parties together because it brings tangible outcomes to people."

World.title: Mercedes-Benz halts all further investment at German facilities
World.content:
The announcement comes as the luxury German automaker faces increasing pressure from the works council and trade unions.

Mercedes-Benz announced on Thursday that it was halting all further investment at its German sites for the time being.

"The executive board has jointly decided to halt all further investments in German sites," Mercedes board member Michael Schiebe said in a memo on the company's intranet that was seen by the AFP news agency.

The company is also weighing plant closures, the memo added.

The announcement comes as the luxury German automaker faces increasing pressure from the works council and the IG Metall trade union.

What else did Mercedes-Benz say?

Mercedes-Benz is "forced to examine, in concrete and detailed terms, which sites in Germany we can still afford to maintain," board of management member Britta Seeger said in an interview published on the company's intranet.

"We all want to avoid plant closures at all costs," she added. "Unfortunately, however, we must now pursue this option in more concrete terms."

Shiebe, the company's chief production officer, said the current cost structures meant it is not possible to invest in Germany.

German labour costs are sometimes five times higher than at plants in Eastern Europe, where administrative costs are also similarly much cheaper.

Schiebe had recently announced that two plants in Germany would have to close unless costs were reduced.

World.title: What have the talks with Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi achieved for Ukraine?
World.content:
The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months have ended with an agreement on exchanging prisoners. Does this mark a genuine breakthrough and a step toward peace?

The two-day talks between delegations from Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a ceasefire agreement.

The main outcome was an agreement on a prisoner exchange.

"We have agreed on the largest humanitarian release of prisoners, and tomorrow we will finalize the numbers," Jared Kushner announced after the talks. US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday, where they are due to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier suggested an exchange of "1,000 for 1,000" prisoners, or "1,500 for 1,500." Russia said a large-scale prisoner exchange with Ukraine could take place within the next two to three weeks.

Following the meetings, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the parties had discussed security guarantees and that "the first step should be ending this war and ensuring Ukraine's security." He also stressed that Europe should be involved "at every stage of genuine diplomacy."

How significant is the prisoner swap?

Experts interviewed by DW agree that the main outcome of the talks is humanitarian.

"The agreement on a prisoner exchange is already a major step forward," says Artjom Bronzhukov of the Ukrainian think tank Polityka.

Pavlo Lakiychuk of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies Strategy XXI also viewed it as a "very tangible result." He told DW that "getting our people back is already a major success. That is why it is worth continuing."

A real breakthrough, he added, would be the release of civilian detainees from territories occupied since 2014, particularly people from Crimea, who have been held in Russian prisons for years.

Russia, Ukraine exchange prisoners as talks end To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Empty diplomacy without a real breakthrough?

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction and Ukraine's representative at the talks in Abu Dhabi, gave a positive assessment of the trilateral talks with the US and Russia, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached by the end of the year.

"I think the Russians came with extremely strict instructions, and it was difficult to ease the tone of the discussion. But the way the US representatives structured the talks with a view to the postwar situation in both countries opened up a dialogue, in my opinion, and allowed us to work together more productively," Arakhamia said at a joint press conference with US and Ukrainian representatives following the talks.

Iuliia Osmolovska of the Kyiv office of the international think tank GLOBSEC cautions against reading too much into the positive assessments of the talks from Washington and Kyiv.

"Diplomats taking part in negotiations will never say that everything went badly and that they have no expectations. Even when no results are achieved, they will still emphasize that the talks were constructive," she said. "For anyone familiar with diplomatic language, these are simply standard phrases."

Experts: chances for Russia-Ukraine ceasefire low as things currently stand

Osmolovska points to a joint assessment by 71 Ukrainian security and defense experts published by GLOBSEC in the summer. According to the assessment, the chances of a peace agreement or at least a ceasefire being reached this year or next stand at just 19%.

She blames this on the fact that neither side is "ready" for genuine negotiations. Russia, in particular, has yet to accept that its objectives cannot be achieved by military means. "What we are seeing now is more of a farce, an attempt by all sides to put a brave face on things and create the impression that something is moving forward," Osmolovska said.

Artjom Bronzhukov sees the talks as a way for Moscow to buy time.

"The visits by the Russian delegation, particularly under the leadership of Vladimir Medinsky, are nothing more than an attempt to stall and sell empty promises to the US administration in the form of grand agreements, in order to continue receiving so-called gestures of goodwill from Washington, such as the lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel," the political scientist says.

Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, briefed journalists during the talks between Russia and Ukraine Image: Altaf Qadri/AP Photo/picture alliance

Redrawing borders to make Putin feel like a winner?

Ahead of the talks, several Western media outlets reported on new US proposals concerning disputed territories. The Economist, for example, reported on a proposal to redraw the administrative boundaries of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. However, a member of the Ukrainian delegation stressed that there had "never been any discussion of concessions on territories occupied by Russia."

Washington made no official comment on the reports.

Kyrylo Budanov, a member of the negotiating delegation and head of the Ukrainian president's office, declined to say whether Russia had used the talks to demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the Donbas. Asked by journalists whether Moscow was still insisting that Ukraine pull out of the region, Budanov said the content of the negotiations would remain confidential until an agreement was reached.

"The issues discussed in the talks are matters for negotiation. The only thing that matters is the outcome. Once we achieve it, it will be made public," Budanov said.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, took a different tone, declaring that "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia one way or another." He was responding to reports in European media that Ukraine was rejecting territorial concessions.

Putin demands large swaths of Ukrainian territory

In addition to the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claims the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson in their entirety as Russian territory, even though Russia does not have full military control over them.

"Putin is not fighting over villages and ruined cowsheds in the Donbas. He is fighting for geopolitical influence and trying to exploit the collapse of the old world order," says Artjom Bronzhukov.

The expert from the Polityka think tank recalls that Ukraine was already asked in early 2026 to withdraw its troops from the part of the Donbas it controls and turn the area into a free economic zone. Such a zone "would very quickly become a Russian-controlled area," he warns.
