World.title: Bulgaria’s Cabinet approves large-scale military joint acquisition deals with Italy, France and Spain
World.content:
Bulgaria’s Cabinet approved on November 11 agreements and memoranda with France, Italy and Spain on the joint acquisition of artillery ammunition, military vehicles and anti-drone systems under the EU’s SAFE programme

The largest of the projects by declared value is for the acquisition of up to 1040 military transport vehicles from Italy. The maximum budget envisaged is 410 million euro, with deliveries to be carried out in two stages.

The first covers the period from 2027 to 2030 and envisages the purchase of up to 700 vehicles worth up to 290 million euro. The financing will be provided through SAFE, and the amount also includes training of military personnel, technical support and spare parts.

The second stage should be completed by the end of 2032 and provides for the delivery of the remaining machines, up to a total of 1040. This will require additional funds of up to 120 million euro.

The project aims to improve the transport provision and operational readiness of the army. Opportunities for industrial cooperation are also envisaged, including the assembly of part of the equipment in Bulgaria with the participation of Bulgarian industry.

Bulgaria will prepare a framework agreement with France for the joint acquisition of 155-mm ammunition for the Caesar self-propelled howitzers.

This is the next step in the implementation of the project for the development of the artillery capabilities of the Bulgarian Army.

In 2025, the two countries signed a framework agreement for the acquisition of the howitzers themselves. The National Assembly is yet to approve the investment expenditure project, after which the individual orders with the specific financial parameters and deadlines will be signed.

Bulgaria will cooperate with Spain in the acquisition of systems to counter unmanned aerial vehicles. The approved memorandum provides for the joint purchase of up to 10 mobile systems and up to 10 container-type systems. Spain is the lead country in the project.

The next steps are for the National Assembly to approve the relevant investment expenditure project and for Bulgaria to join Spain’s contract for the acquisition of the systems.

All three projects are part of the efforts to develop Bulgaria’s defense capabilities through joint European procurement under SAFE. The documents approved by the government mark the beginning of the next stages, but the acquisitions will require additional decisions and the conclusion of specific contracts.

World.title: Sofia signs 282M euro contract on EU grant funding to modernise urban transport, infrastructure
World.content:
Sofia mayor Vasil Terziev signed a contract for 282 million euro in European grant funding for the modernisation of public transport and the construction and renovation of streets and boulevards in Bulgaria’s capital city, the municipality said on November 12.

The contract was signed with Regional Development and Public Works Minister Ivan Shishkov.

The funds are provided under the procedure Support for Integrated Urban Transport and Sustainable Urban Mobility of Sofia Municipality, Priority 1 Integrated Urban Development of the Regional Development programme 2021 – 2027.

“We expect the metro line from the centre to Tsarigradsko Shose, the connection with Obelya and the connection that will provide contact with the railway station, as well as the extension of the Ring Road from the Lyulin metro stations to the Sofia Ring Road, to be built and put into operation soon,” Shishkov said.

The programme envisages large-scale investments in the development of transport.

Among these are the extension of the Third Metro Line through the Slatina district, the construction of a metro station next to the Obelya railway station on the Sofia – Kyustendil railway line, with a tunnel connection to the Obelya metro depot, as well as the acquisition of new metro trains for lines No. 1, 2 and 4.

With the signing of an additional agreement on October 27 for the delivery of eight more metro trains, the total number of new trains planned under the programme for lines No. 1, 2 and 4 will reach 16.

All of them should be delivered by autumn 2028. The new metro trains will provide greater comfort with quieter movement and air-conditioned cabins, as well as higher energy efficiency through an energy recovery system during braking, the municipality said.

The secured financing will contribute to covering part of the investments already made and will support the further development of the metro as the main backbone of public transport in Sofia.

In land transport, the funds will ensure the delivery of 75 low-floor trolleybuses with batteries for autonomous movement – 40 articulated with a length of 18 metres and 35 single ones with a length of 12 metres. 50 low-floor fast-charging electric buses and the necessary charging stations will also be delivered. Of these, 35 will be 12 metres long and 15 will be 18 metres long.

The new trolleybuses will allow for the expansion of the route network. It is planned to extend line No. 3 to Mladost-4 and provide a connection with Vrazhdebna, as well as line No. 8 to Orlandovtsi. New trolleybus connections are also planned between Lyulin and Gotse Delchev and between Nadezhda and Mladost-1.

The electric buses will serve two new ring lines – No. 71 between Levski G and Gotse Delchev and No. 75 between Geo Milev and Pavlovo. The routes will pass through key directions, including G. M. Dimitrov Blvd. and Todor Kableshkov Blvd.

With this European funding, combined with the long-term loan that the Sofia municipality will procure, the aim is for all ground public transport vehicles to be low-floor and air-conditioned by 2030, the municpality said.

This will improve accessibility and travel comfort, as well as connections between neighbourhoods, it said.

Investments for which construction activities have already been completed are also included. They are for the construction of Todor Kableshkov Blvd. between Louis Ayer St. and Cherni Vrah Blvd., which was completed this year, as well as Rozhen Blvd. from the overpass over the railway line to the Northern Expressway. Rozhen Blvd. was completed at the end of last year, and now the municipality is preparing the repair of the section from the railway overpass to the Nadezhda overpass, which will be financed through a long-term loan.

According to data from the Management and Monitoring Information System (MIS), the contract is the largest in terms of value for a project under this programmeme, under which Sofia municipality is a beneficiary, since the first programmeming period 2007-2013.

(Photo: Sofia municipality)

World.title: Bulgaria’s Trakia Motorway tragedy: Recriminations and compensation
World.content:
Recriminations, including opposition calls for the Prime Minister to resign, and a Cabinet decision to award a strikingly large sum to the families and heirs of the deceased, have followed the November 10 chain crashes on Bulgaria’s Trakia Motorway in which 11 people died and 86 vehicles collided.

On November 10, Daniel Mitov, an MP for Boiko Borissov’s opposition coalition GERB-UDF, called for Prime Minister Roumen Radev and the “ministers responsible for the tragedy on the Trakia Motorway” to resign.

“Those in power have become accustomed to lying,” Mitov said.

“Today, (Interior) Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev announced that one of the reasons for the tragedy is that there is no connection between the Road Infrastructure Agency, the Ministry of Interior and the toll administration systems,” he said.

GERB MP Nikolai Nankov said that the section of the motorway where the accidents occured was “a skating rink” and for the first time in the past 30 years, as of November 10, there was still no announced winter maintenance system for the Trakia Motorway.

Kalin Stoyanov, an MP for the opposition Movement for Rights and Freedoms and a former interior minister, called for the immediate resignations of “all those responsible” for the November 10 chain crashes.

However, on November 11, a day after his party called for resignations, Borissov said that a law should be passed to prevent politicians commenting for at least 24 hours after such accidents.

Borissov went on to criticise the government for its lack of moral responsibility after the tragedy. He said that those responsible will not remove anyone, but will put the blame elsewhere.

“I removed three ministers for much smaller disasters, I removed Parliament Speakers for much smaller offences, this is a moral responsibility,” Borissov said.

On November 11, Parliament opened its sitting with a minute of silence for those who died in the chain crashes the day before. The ruling majority voted down opposition proposals for hearings of senior officials in connection with the Trakia Motorway crashes.

Road engineer Iliya Zapryanov told Nova Televizia on November that the Trakia Motorway is designed for a much lower load of heavy lorries.

Zapryanov said that the share of heavy good lorries among the vehicles in chain accidents on the Trakia Motorway is significantly higher than assumed when designing the highway.

He estimated that out of a total of 86 vehicles involved in the accidents, 22 were heavy goods lorries, or about a quarter. The motorway was designed to accommodate five to seven per cent of heavy goods vehicles.

According to Zapryanov, one of the quick solutions to relieve traffic on the motorway is to redirect lorries from Bourgas, Stara Zagora, Sliven and Yambol to Sofia along the Sub-Balkan Road , which is less congested.

“Drivers are worried about the lorries breathing down their necks . When you are moving at 90, 85, 95 km/h, the lorry behind you does not keep distance and bothers you,” Zapryanov. Said.

He also raised the issue of the lack of signs that specify a minimum distance between vehicles.

“Have you seen this road sign installed anywhere in Bulgaria? Who controls it? Where is the traffic police? Where is the Road Infrastructure Agency?” he said.

On November 11, the Cabinet decided to allocate 8000 euro each to the families and heirs of the 11 deceased.

This amount is unprecedented . It is the highest assistance to the relatives of the deceased that the state has ever paid.

Typically, such extraordinary financial support is provided to families of victims of natural disasters.

By comparison, during the floods in Tsarevo municipality in September 2023, the cabinet allocated 15 000 leva (about 7669 euro) each to the legal heirs of the four deceased.

The same amount of aid was also determined for the heirs of the four people who died in the floods in the Bourgas region on October 3 and 4 2025.

There is no other case where the government has provided financial assistance of this type to the relatives of people who died in road accidents.

In the bus accident near Svoge in August 2018, when 20 people died, the Social Assistance Agency announced that the families of the deceased and injured were legally entitled to receive a one-time benefit of up to 375 leva.

Meanwhile, the Romanian lorry driver whose vehicle reportedly was the first vehicle involved in the crash has been detained and questioned, but according to Bulgarian National Television, the Prosecutor’s Office will not press charges.

World.title: Remembrance Day 2026 observed in Bulgaria’s capital Sofia
World.content:
November 11, Remembrance Day, was observed in Bulgaria’s capital city Sofia with commemorations at the British and Commonwealth, German, Italian and French war graves.

This year, in addition to the traditional observances, speeches and prayers also honoured Bulgaria’s national day of mourning for the victims of the November 10 chain crashes on Trakia Motorway.

Remembrance Day commemorates and honours the dead in the wars of the 20th century. The November 11 date arises from the anniversary of the Armistice at the close of the First World War.

As is traditional, proceedings began at the Commonwealth War Graves section, with an address by British ambassador Nathaniel Copsey, a service led by Father Patrick Irwin, and with poetry reading by Irish ambassador Catherine Bannon and by William Gladstone school pupils Anna Filipova, Evelin Vassileva and Yana Borissova.

Floral tributes were laid by ambassadors and diplomatic representatives of several countries, Bulgaria’s defence and foreign ministries, Nato and military veterans from Britain and South Africa.

World.title: Vis Archipelago Retains Status as UNESCO Global Geopark
World.content:
November the 12th, 2026 – The Vis archipelago has successfully retained its status as a UNESCO Global Geopark for another four years as all 10 recommendations from the previous evaluation have been fulfilled.

The above was confirmed on the 4th of November at the 11th session of the UNESCO Global Geoparks Council, held at UNESCO headquarters in Paris. The Geopark Vis Archipelago has been part of the UNESCO Global Geoparks Network since 2019.

Morski reports that the re-validation, which is carried out every four years, included a review of documentation and a field mission by international evaluators from the 22nd to the 27th of June 2026.

During their stay on the Vis archipelago, the evaluators visited numerous geological sites, geotrails and visitor centres, and held talks with representatives of the local community, institutions, scientific organisations and partner organisations.

The international evaluators praised the way the sites are presented to visitors, the cooperation with schools and scientists, and the support given to local producers. They also highlighted how the geopark has connected Vis and Komiža in caring for the heritage of the entire archipelago.

World.title: New Dawn for Luxury Tourism in Kaštela With High-End Hotel Brand
World.content:
November the 12th, 2026 – A new dawn for luxury tourism in Kaštela is beginning with the arrival of one of the world’s most recognisable brands in the high-end hotel segment.

It’s genuinely no exaggeration to say that a new tourism dawn of sorts in Kaštela is now beginning. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the international Odien Group, headquartered in Prague, is bringing Sofitel, one of the world’s most recognisable brands in the luxury hotel segment, to Kaštela and Croatia. The contract with Accor, one of the world’s leading hotel groups that includes the Sofitel brand in its portfolio, was formally signed at the Renaissance Vitturi Castle in Kaštel Lukšić.

high-end tourism

Sofitel Kaštela, which will be constructed on the site of the former Zeničko resort in Kaštel Stari, is expected to open its doors in 2029 and will be managed by Odien Hotels, the hotel division of the Odien Group. The hotel will have 137 rooms and apartments, including spacious junior suites and higher-category accommodation units with private balconies or terraces overlooking the sea. Guests will have access to several restaurants and bars, a spa centre, indoor and outdoor pools, a beach club, and spaces for business meetings and various events. It goes without saying that this is an important milestone for Croatian tourism, and especially for Kaštela, which with this project is positioning itself on the international map of luxury hospitality. For the Odien Group, Sofitel represents much more than a new hotel project. It is an important part of the group’s long-term investment strategy aimed at developing Kaštela into an internationally recognisable tourist destination.

a luxury hotel brand blends with heritage

Kaštela will get an internationally recognisable luxury hotel brand, as well as an intimate heritage hotel located in a Renaissance building.

“Our ambitions go beyond the mere construction of luxury hotel facilities. We want to contribute to creating a destination with a strong international identity, recognised for quality, authenticity and the experiences it offers. Kaštela has exceptional potential: a rich history, valuable architectural heritage, an authentic Mediterranean character and an ideal location between Split and Trogir. Combining all these qualities with the international recognition and reputation of the Sofitel brand, which is synonymous with quality, will undoubtedly open a new chapter in the city’s tourism development,” said Mike Saran, owner of the Odien Group.

“Croatia has become one of the most attractive European tourist destinations, recognised for its unique combination of natural beauty, rich culture and authenticity. We are proud that, through this exceptional project with the Odien Group, we are bringing Sofitel to the Croatian market as the first international luxury hotel brand in the country. Sofitel Kaštela will embody the elegance of French luxury while embracing the spirit, heritage and lifestyle of the Adriatic coast, creating a unique destination for travellers from around the world,” said Maud Bailly, CEO of the Sofitel, Sofitel Legend, MGallery and Emblems brands. The arrival of this prestigious hotel brand is part of the Odien Group’s long-term development strategy and commitment to Kaštela. As part of that strategy, the group will, through its companies Odien Hotels and Odien Real Estate, invest more than 100 million euros over the next five years. In addition to the new Sofitel Kaštela hotel project, the company this year also purchased the historic Štafileo Castle in Kaštel Štafilić, which it plans to renovate and convert into a luxury heritage hotel.

These two projects bring two different but harmoniously connected hotel concepts: an internationally recognisable luxury hotel brand and an intimate heritage hotel located in a historic Renaissance building, which will offer guests an authentic experience of local heritage. Together with the group’s existing hotel operations in Croatia, these projects are part of its long-term vision of creating new tourism content and value in Kaštela and throughout Dalmatia.

international luxury tourism for Kaštela

“These projects give the Kaštela the opportunity for a significant step forward in the segment of international luxury tourism. The city’s growing recognition as a tourist destination, its rich cultural and historical heritage and its geographical location form solid foundations for the development of a tourism offer that goes beyond the framework of traditional seasonal tourism,” said Denis Ivanović, Mayor of Kaštela.

“This is an extremely important moment for Kaštela. The arrival of an international luxury hotel brand and the Odien Group’s investments in our city confirm that Kaštela has the potential to become a recognisable high-end tourism destination. It is particularly important to emphasise that this is not just about one hotel project, but about a series of investments that can contribute to the development of the city, open new jobs, strengthen the local economy and extend the tourist season. For us, it is of key importance that this development takes place in parallel with the preservation of Kaštela’s identity and in close cooperation with the local community,” the mayor added. The Odien Group has otherwise been present in Croatia since 2015, when it took over the Le Méridien Lav Split resort in Podstrana.

World.title: Zagreb-Podgorica Direct Flights Coming on November the 26th
World.content:
November the 12th, 2026 – New Zagreb-Podgorica direct flights are coming on November the 26th, with the two capitals being linked in this way after several years.

Travel between Croatia and Montenegro will soon become significantly faster and simpler. Index reports that Montenegro’s national airline Air Montenegro has announced the introduction of a new direct route between Zagreb and Podgorica, with the first flight scheduled for the 26th of November this year.

The flight between the two capital cities will last only 50 minutes, allowing passengers faster and simpler travel without transfers. The new route will operate three times a week, and the flights will be operated by Embraer E195 aircraft, which can accommodate 118 passengers. The introduction of this route is part of Montenegro’s Public Service Obligation (PSO) programme, whose aim is to improve Montenegro’s international transport connectivity and enable more regular air links with important European destinations.

the upcoming flight schedule

According to the announced timetable, aircraft will operate between Zagreb and Podgorica on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays. From Zagreb, these flights will depart at 08:50 and are expected to arrive in Podgorica at 09:40. In the opposite direction, departure from Podgorica is planned at 07:20, with arrival in Zagreb scheduled for 08:10. All departure and arrival times are given in local time, and the schedule is of course subject to change.

the price

One-way ticket prices start at around 50 euros, depending on the direction of travel and the chosen date. On the official Air Montenegro website, the currently listed price for the first flight from Zagreb on the 26th of November is 58.30 euros. The ticket price includes all mandatory fees, as well as one piece of hand luggage weighing up to eight kilograms and one piece of checked luggage weighing up to 23 kilograms. The final price will depend on the travel date, seat availability and the time of booking.

The new air route could also be interesting for travellers who want to get better acquainted with Podgorica, the capital and largest city of Montenegro. Located in the area where the Morača and Ribnica rivers meet, Podgorica combines modern city life, historical sights and natural beauty. One of the places worth visiting is Stara Varoš, the historic city quarter that preserves traces of the Ottoman past. There you will also find the Clock Tower (Sahat-kula), one of Podgorica’s recognisable landmarks. A walk through this part of the city is an opportunity to get to know traditional architecture and local culture.

Among the best-known modern symbols of the city is the Millennium Bridge, which stretches across the Morača River. Visitors can also walk to the place where the Ribnica flows into the Morača and view the old stone bridge on the Ribnica. Nature lovers can head to Gorica hill, after which the city is named, which is a popular place for walking and recreation. Near Podgorica there are also waterfalls on the Cijevna River, known as the Montenegrin Niagara, which are especially impressive when the water level is high. For those who want to explore the surroundings of the city as well, an interesting choice can be Lake Skadar, known for its rich plant and animal life, picturesque landscapes and opportunities for boat trips.

World.title: Invasive Asian Giant Mantis Sighted in Mljet National Park
World.content:
November the 12th, 2026 – An invasive Asian giant mantis has been seen within Mljet National Park, with more favourable weather conditions for this particular species causing them to spread.

This insect is a species of praying mantis belonging to the family Mantidae, one of the largest families within the order of praying mantises. As we all know, the weird and wonderful family of praying mantises earned their name from the characteristic position of their front legs, which they hold raised and folded, resembling hands clasped in prayer.

Index reports that the authorities at Mljet National Park have noted that changes in weather conditions are creating increasingly favourable conditions for the survival of this species across Europe. They add that, as a result, the Asian giant mantis has spread across the eastern Mediterranean in recent years, including Croatia.

we’re unsure what the consequences of their arrival will be yet

They also explained how this invasive species can be distinguished from the native common praying mantis (Mantis religiosa). The Asian giant mantis has a significantly larger body and is recognisable by a white or yellowish spot on its front wings. Unlike the native species, it tends to stay high up in the tree canopies. Its body is mostly green, but it can also have brown or yellow shades, according to the park. They emphasise that this species feeds on other insects, but warn that its long-term impact on local populations of other species is not yet known.

As they point out, only in the coming period will it be possible to determine what consequences the presence of the Asian giant mantis may have on the local ecosystem, if any.

World.title: Bilić and Kovačić Promise a Different Croatia Against England at Wembley
World.content:
Croatia take on England at Wembley on Thursday at 20:45 CET (19:45 local time) in the fifth round of the Nations League, and Slaven Bilić heads to London with a depleted squad. Injuries, illness and suspensions have ruled out several key players, and Croatia arrive on the back of three straight defeats, including the 7-0 loss to England in Rijeka last month.

Bilić named his final 25-man squad on Saturday, but new problems

emerged over the weekend. Josip Šutalo injured his hamstring playing for Napoli against Lazio and will miss both November matches. Dinamo center-back Niko Galešić has been called up in his place, his first senior international call-up.

Kristijan Jakić is also a concern after injuring a knee ligament in PAOK’s match against Olympiacos. The midfielder has joined up with the squad but needs further medical tests. Bilić admitted the situation does not look good, though he hopes the injury is not serious.

Luka Sučić is also a major doubt. The Real Sociedad midfielder has come down with a fever, and Bilić said he is 99 percent certain to miss the England match. Lovro Majer, who was on the preliminary list but missed the cut for the original 25, has been called up as cover.

Ivan Perišić will also miss the England match. The veteran winger is suspended after his red card against Spain last month, but unlike the injured Šutalo, he will be available again for Sunday’s game against Czechia.



Kovačić opened the press conference.

“It’s a big and special game, as it always is against England. We need to be 100 percent focused. We need to be aggressive and give everything, especially after that tough defeat to England last month,” he said.

“I’m healthy and training, and that’s the most important thing. We have a big motive. We want to show who we really are and that we are still Croatia. That game against England in Rijeka was like a blackout.”

Kovačić, who played under Thomas Tuchel at Chelsea, was asked about the England head coach.

“I had a really great relationship with Tuchel. He helped me a lot and has a special place in my career and in my heart. It’s hard to tell the difference between Southgate’s England and Tuchel’s England. Both are aggressive and both are tough. We know England are always one of the top national teams.”

“We always give everything. What happened against England is something we still can’t explain. We had a really tough night in Rijeka, and that defeat still doesn’t sit well with us. We are motivated, and we want to prove it was only a blackout and that we are who we are.”

Bilić then addressed the media.

“We didn’t have time to train in this window. We only got together on Monday,” he said. “Last month’s game against England is still in my head. We showed against Spain that we are who we are, and we want to show that last time was just a bad day.”

“It’s very important for us to stay in League A of the Nations League. If we finish third in the group, it’s great for the Euro 2028 qualifiers.”

“I told the players that the way we played against Spain last month is our standard. That is how we want to play, with togetherness, aggression and everything else. We will see tomorrow whether we show that.”

“The young players were called up for a reason. They’re all in competition for tomorrow. They all bring something to this team. We have enough players to cover for the ones we’re missing. Tomorrow we have a chance to show that what happened in Rijeka was just a collective bad day.

I told the players after the game and again when we went to Split that the game against England was so bad that we need to remember it, to use it as motivation. The game against Spain is our absolute standard.”

World.title: Croatian Unemployment Rate Continued to Fall in October 2026
World.content:
November the 11th, 2026 – The Croatian unemployment rate is continuing to drop, with the figure having fallen by 15% in October this year compared to October 2025.

In October this year, 20,075 persons or 30.2 percent of the total number of unemployed used state monetary benefits. Poslovni reports that back at the end of October this year 66,425 unemployed individuals were recorded at the Croatian Employment Service (HZZ), which is 11,400 persons or 14.6 percent less than in October 2025, HZZ data published this week revealed.

a mixed bag

Compared to September the number of unemployed increased by 6.1 percent or 3,830 persons. According to HZZ daily data, currently 67,308 unemployed are registered at the service, and 13,099 free job positions have been advertised. During the month of October, a total of 16,792 new persons were registered in the unemployment register, which is 7.1 percent less than back in October last year. In this sum, the majority came from an employment relationship, that is 12,476 of them or 74.3 percent.

1,746 people from regular education (10.4 percent of the total number) and 2,570 persons from inactivity (15.3 percent) also entered into the unemployment register in the past month. The latest HZZ data shows that 12,962 persons left the unemployment register, which is 12.5 percent less than in October 2025. Of that 7,554 persons were employed, namely 7,029 persons or 93.1 percent on the basis of establishing an employment relationship and 525 persons or 6.9 percent on the basis of other business activities.

manufacturing reigns strong

The most frequent employment was established in the manufacturing industry. This October, 1,128 persons or 16 percent were employed in this sector. Wholesale and retail trade followed relatively closely with 983 individuals or 14 percent. This was followed by people coming directly from education, with the number totalling 903, or 12.8 percent. In October, 5,408 persons were removed from the unemployment register due to other reasons, e.g. leaving the force corps (retirement, inclusion in regular education), non-compliance with legal provisions (not actively seeking a job, unavailable for work), personal de-registration from the register and others.

Looking at the situation on a county by county basis, employment was led by Split-Dalmatia County (986 persons or 14 percent of the total number of those employed by establishing an employment relationship), the City of Zagreb (984 persons or 14 percent) and Osijek-Baranja County (736 persons or 10.5 percent). Split-Dalmatia County is also currently the home of the largest number of registered unemployed persons – 10,657 or 16 percent of the total number in all of Croatia. Looking at the situation based on the number of registered unemployed persons, the City of Zagreb (9,013 or 13.6 percent) and Osijek-Baranja County (7,757 or 11.7 percent) follow next.

In October this year, 20,075 persons or 30.2 percent of the total number of unemployed used the monetary benefit. The number of monetary benefit users decreased compared to the same month last year by 1.8 percent or by 374 persons. In October, 13,886 job positions were advertised through HZZ, through which the requirement for 21,519 employees was expressed. The number of sought workers decreased by 6.1 percent compared to the same month last year, the latest HZZ data shows.

World.title: Pantheon Data Centre Boss Refuses to Say How Much Water it Will Consume
World.content:
November the 11th, 2026 – The Pantheon data centre boss has refused to reveal just how much water the giant, guzzling centre will actually consume in Topusko. Criticism of the planned centre in Topusko is growing louder and louder.

The project manager of the data centre in Topusko has openly rejected claims that the enormous consumption of electricity and water would endanger the public or raise their bills. Poslovni reports that Pantheon project manager Mario Gudelj appeared on HRT’s Dnevnik, stating that the data centre’s investors plan to invest more than 500 million euros in new electricity infrastructure, including around 300 kilometres of brand new transmission lines and a new substation.

“If we were to connect to the existing system, then that would be an overload. We’re building new infrastructure, 300 kilometres of new transmission lines and a new substation, and we’re handing all of that over into the ownership of HOPS,” Gudelj said. HOPS had earlier confirmed that the project requires the construction of four new 400-kilovolt transmission lines with a total length of around 300 kilometres and that the investor would bear the connection costs.

one gigawatt – a massive consumer

Pantheon has been conceived as a data and AI campus of one gigawatt power, or 1,000 megawatts. This is an exceptionally large new consumer. HOPS representative Igor Šumonja at the end of October said that the current load of the Croatian electricity system ranges between 2,000 and 3,000 megawatts and that connecting Pantheon by itself would increase the load by approximately a third. Back in July, HOPS initially accepted the study of the optimal technical connection solution, and the investor and the network operator expect the conclusion of the connection contract. The start of construction is planned for 2027, and the investors want to put the first computing capacities into operation in 2029.

“electricity won’t be more expensive” gudelj claims, but topusko locals aren’t having it

One of the main criticisms of the project relates to the question of whether such a large new consumer can increase electricity prices. Gudelj just keeps on claiming that this will not happen. According to his words, the construction of the new network infrastructure will enable the connection of approximately five gigawatts of new renewable energy sources, whose production should be greater than the needs of the data centre itself.

“I don’t know on the basis of what someone made calculations that the price of electricity will rise because of us. I think that those calculations were impossibly made in the way they are presented to the public,” he said. In doing so he also reacted to an earlier statement by a HOPS representative that the operator cannot predict how the project will affect electricity prices. Gudelj emphasised that HOPS manages the transmission network and does not determine market electricity prices.

“we won’t take water from the public water supply” – but refuses to reveal what the water consumption will actually be

The second major question relates to the amount of water needed for cooling the data centre. Gudelj said that Pantheon will not connect to the public water supply system of Topusko or Sisak-Moslavina County. The investors, according to his words, are researching their own wells from which they would draw water, and the final quantity will depend on the results of the research. He did not, however, specify what the total water consumption of the data centre will be. That is quite telling.

criticism and protest against harmful data centres are growing louder and louder…

In more recent weeks, the contested Pantheon project has been encountering increasingly strong opposition from part of the political parties, local initiatives and environmental organisations. Green Action (Zelena akcija) has warned of the possible consumption of large quantities of energy and water, noise, electronic waste and the impact on the local environment. From that organisation they consider that Croatia before approving a project of such proportions needs to determine a national strategy for the development of large data centres. Criticisms have also been expressed by individual SDP deputies and local initiatives from Topusko, who are seeking additional information on the impact of the project on water, the energy network and the local population.

Gudelj, of course, rejects such claims. None are in his interest.

“Those are well-placed untruths that have no basis in anything. Our project will in no way affect things the way it is being pushed through public opinion,” he claimed for HRT. It will be interesting to see how those claims hold up when we take the likes of what happened in Ireland and Finland into account.

Despite Gudelj’s assurances, the project has not yet passed all the procedures necessary for construction. Sisak-Moslavina County has launched amendments to the spatial plan and the procedure of strategic environmental impact assessment. A main assessment of the acceptability of the intervention for the ecological network is also planned. Gudelj himself earlier said that the project cannot start construction before the completion of the spatial planning procedures and the acceptance of the necessary environmental studies. Therefore the final impact of Pantheon on water, the environment and energy infrastructure cannot for now be considered established.

Gudelj also commented on the accusations due to his earlier function in HOPS. He said that he left the executive function of president of the HOPS Management Board in 2019, after which until 2023 he remained an adviser, when he left the company at his own request. He rejected claims that due to his previous work in the transmission system operator he finds himself in a conflict of interest. Gudelj also considers that the current resistance to large data centres in Europe and the USA will not in the long term stop their development, but he expects that future projects will have to invest significantly more in their own energy infrastructure.

World.title: Zagreb Airport Attraction Wins Yet Another Prestigious Award
World.content:
November the 11th, 2026 – Zagreb Airport has an attraction that has won yet another prestigious award. The Museum Zone took home silver and has done very well in attracting passengers.

The Museum Zone at Franjo Tuđman Airport, a commendable project realised in cooperation between the Croatian History Museum and Zagreb International Airport, has won the silver the! Award in the multi-stakeholder and multi-sectoral cooperation category at the KoMference of the Croatian Public Relations Association. Poslovni reports that this is otherwise the second professional recognition for that particular project, which in the spring of this year took home the Grand PRix.

The Croatian History Museum, located in Zagreb’s Upper Town (Gornji grad) palaces, was severely damaged in the March 2020 earthquake, because of which it could no longer use its space for exhibiting its museum holdings. On the initiative of the Val Group, cooperation between the Croatian History Museum and Zagreb International Airport began. It was then that the Museum Zone was formally established, within which the exhibition “Stars of Croatian History – The Sky Is Their Limit. Get to Know Them!” was officially opened.

The exhibition presents 24 important figures from throughout Croatian history who, with their work spanning four areas – science, culture, politics and society, and sport – contributed to the development of Croatia and left a mark on the European and global level. “We’re pleased that a project that connected a heritage institution with Zagreb International Airport has been awarded and that this has been recognised as a very good model of communication,” said Minister of Culture and Media Nina Obuljen Koržinek at the KoMference.

Director of the Croatian History Museum Matea Brstilo Rešetar emphasised that when they entered that project they wanted to prove that heritage can meet the public even outside museum walls. According to her words, the Museum Zone has become the second most visited exhibition space in all of Croatia. President of the Management Board of Zagreb International Airport Huseyin Bahadir Bedir said that passengers have been given the opportunity to get to know Croatian history and cultural heritage in an interesting and accessible way, turning the time spent at the airport into an educational experience.

World.title: Potential CSC Telecom leak exposes 125 million text messages across Baltics
World.content:
More than 125 million text messages may have leaked from the Latvian branch of telecom provider CSC Telecom , potentially affecting people and businesses across the Baltics.

While initial information indicated that the Latvian leak also affected businesses and individuals in Lithuania and Estonia, CSC Telecom Estonia sales director Rain Aasmäe later said the SMS service provided to Estonian customers runs on separate server infrastructure and a separate database from the Latvian service.

As a result, Aasmäe said, the vulnerability in the telecom's Latvian platform did not provide access to the Estonian platform or customer data.

He added that the company nonetheless plans to review the security requirements for its Estonian platform and strengthen them based on lessons learned from the incident in Latvia.

SEB communications manager Maarja Lumiste also said that no customer data from the bank's Estonian branch had been leaked.

From big banks to airBaltic and CityBee

The unsecured database, discovered by Latvian outlet Cybernews on Clickhouse on September 28, contained messages dating from October 2022 through September 2026, including more than 3 million messages sent this September alone.

The database contained full message contents, customer names, phone numbers and metadata such as timestamps, with exposed information including temporary passwords, medical test results, booking details, delivery addresses, travel reservations and bank notifications.

Because it was updated in real time, attackers may have been able to access messages before they reached recipients.

Cybernews identified text messages from Latvia's Swedbank and SEB, insurers ERGO, Compensa and Artea, the emergency number 112 and businesses in Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, including Porsche dealerships, shared mobility platform CityBee, online grocery service Barbora, home improvement chain DEPO and the Latvian airline airBaltic, among others.

Swedbank suspends telecom's services

Swedbank Latvia spokesperson Kristīne Čekstere told news agency LETA that their bank immediately launched an investigation and took all legally required measures after learning of the incident.

The bank has suspended its use of CSC Telecom's services and requested information to assess the scale and potential impact of the breach. It urged customers to be wary of suspicious messages, calls and emails requesting personal information or authentication codes.

"Our priority at present is to fully assess the incident and ensure the protection of our customers' interests and data," said Čekstere.

Businesses and officials are warning against suspicious calls and texts. Source: Kaupo Meiel/ERR

SEB: Our sensitive customer data not at risk

SEB Latvia spokesperson Anete Igaune told LETA that their bank used CSC Telecom only to send limited marketing messages related to pension funds, stressing that sensitive customer information is transmitted through other channels and that SEB's systems, sensitive customer data and clients' funds are not at risk.

She said CSC Telecom has not notified SEB of a security incident.

"We are currently assessing the situation based on the information at our disposal," Igaune noted.

AirBaltic said it was aware of reports of a possible data security incident involving an external service provider and was working with providers and regulators to assess its potential impact.

The airline said it was too early to determine how much data may have been exposed or how many customers could be affected. It urged passengers to be cautious of messages or calls requesting urgent action, payment details or login credentials.

Latvian CERT wants answers

Latvia's cybersecurity incident response agency CERT.lv told LETA it had asked CSC Telecom to investigate and establish whether there was evidence of a data breach from the company's infrastructure. The agency offered the company its assistance and forwarded its information on to law enforcement.

Founded in Toronto in 1995, telecommunications provider CSC Telecom expanded into the Baltics in 1998 and is now a leading landline provider in the region.

According to Latvian business database Firmas.lv, CSC Telecom SIA reported revenue of €4.48 million and a profit of €110,554 in 2025.

Registered in 2022, the company is 89.99 percent owned by Estonian-based Global Telecom Invest and 10.1 percent by Sergejs Buzaks (Sergei Buzak).

World.title: Southeastern Estonia inks pledge for more Võro and Seto in schools
World.content:
As the nationwide shift to Estonian-language education picks up, southeastern leaders and organizations have pledged to give Võro and Seto a bigger role, including in schools.

Late last month, 15 municipalities and organizations signed the joint Uma lepe agreement at a seminar at Võru Kreutzwald School. Among the signatories are nine municipalities in Võru, Põlva and Valga counties.

Võru County Development Center (VAK) board member Tiit Toots hailed it as a historic moment for the Vana-Võromaa and Setomaa regions, noting that the municipalities and organizations involved are committing to preserve the local Võro and Seto languages and cultures.

"To my knowledge, no such broad cooperation agreement has ever been signed by these parties before either," Toots continued. "Together we are making it clear that the Võro and Seto languages and cultures matter to us, and that we want to preserve them and pass them on to future generations."

Schools and kindergartens will be central to that effort, bringing Võro and Seto into everyday classrooms.

Craft instructions in Võro in a special edition of Estonia's Täheke children's magazine. 2021. Source: Täheke

Põlva Mayor Maris Neeno said she was pleased to see so much of the region willing to stand and work together like this.

"The Võro and Seto languages are our home and our memory, so I'm glad every local government in Põlva County is joining the agreement too," Neeno said on their behalf.

15 full immersion kindergartens

The Uma lepe agreement sets a 2030 target for at least 20 percent of instruction in Võru County schools and 25 percent in kindergartens to be in Võro or Seto.

It also aims to increase the number of full immersion Seto- or Võro-language kindergarten classes to at least 15, expanding on the handful that already exist in Setomaa Municipality and Võru.

Municipalities in Põlva and Valga counties will expand local-language and cultural education as well.

Schools, kindergartens and teachers will receive training, mentoring and teaching materials in support of these efforts, while local governments, cultural institutions and language experts likewise strengthen their cooperation.

Signatories of the Uma lepe agreement for the promotion of the Võro and Seto languages and cultures. October 2026. Source: Setomaa Municipality

Local efforts backed by bigger institutes

The Uma lepe agreement was signed by the municipalities of Võru, Rõuge, Setomaa and Antsla and the city of Võru in Võru County; Kanepi, Räpina and Põlva in Põlva County; and Valga Municipality. Other signatories include the Võro Institute, Seto Institute, Võrumaa Development Center and Setomaa Union.

The Institute of the Estonian Language (EKI) and the University of Tartu's Institute of Estonian and General Linguistics joined as partners.

University institute director Ann Veismann said the university would continue researching both languages and supporting their use in their traditional regions, contributing to Estonia's linguistic diversity as a whole.

"Both Võro and Seto are taught at the university, and interest in them is high," Veismann said.

It's not just linguistics students taking these courses either. "Students in other majors are taking them as electives too," she added.

World.title: Estonian state ordered to pay €300,000 over unlawful collection of communications data
World.content:
Tallinn Administrative Court upheld a claim for damages filed against the Estonian state by businessman Parvel Pruunsild and politician Priit Humal, ordering the state to pay each of them €150,000 in compensation.

In a ruling issued Thursday, Tallinn Administrative Court upheld a claim filed by Pruunsild and Humal against the Republic of Estonia, seeking compensation for nonpecuniary damages over the state's failure to protect their right to privacy and the confidentiality of their communications.

The court ordered the state to pay each claimant €150,000 in compensation for nonpecuniary damages. It also ordered the state to reimburse the claimants' legal costs of €25,000 and €8,302.40, respectively.

According to the claimants, the Estonian state has for years unlawfully required telecommunications service providers to collect and retain their customers' personal data. They argued that, in doing so, the state violated individuals' rights to privacy. On this basis, they sought compensation for the nonpecuniary damages they had suffered.

The court noted that Estonian law had been in conflict with European Union law since a December 21, 2016, ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union. At the latest, following the entry into force of a June 18, 2021, ruling by Estonia's Supreme Court, the relevant state authorities should have been fully aware that the Electronic Communications Act's provisions requiring the general and indiscriminate collection and retention of significant amounts of communications data were incompatible with EU law and could not lawfully be applied in Estonia.

The court found that, following those rulings, the relevant state authorities should have immediately stopped requiring compliance with the legislation, while government agencies should have ceased requesting data collected and retained under its provisions. The authorities should also have initiated the necessary measures and procedures to repeal the provisions found to be incompatible with EU law or bring them into compliance with both EU and Estonian law.

In this case, however, neither the executive nor the legislative branch had taken steps to resolve the conflict for more than three years after the Supreme Court confirmed that the legislation was incompatible with EU law.

Moreover, the court found that, even after the Supreme Court's 2021 ruling and despite the clear legal situation, executive authorities continued submitting new requests for data collected by telecommunications companies under an invalid legal provision and using the data obtained in criminal proceedings.

The court acknowledged that collecting certain communications data may be necessary and justified to protect national security and maintain public order, as the state had argued. However, these interests do not justify the general and indiscriminate collection of the personal data in question from all telecommunications service users.

According to the court, it is clear that such a system of data collection is unacceptable in democratic countries, is seriously disproportionate and is inherently incompatible with the general principle of liberty, including, in a broader sense, the presumption of innocence.

Under the State Liability Act, compensation can be awarded only if all of the following conditions are met: the damage was directly caused by legislation or a failure to enact legislation, the individual suffered damage, the damage resulted from a serious breach of duty by a public authority, there is a causal link between that serious breach and the damage suffered, the legal provision establishing the breached obligation is directly applicable and the individual belongs to a group of people who have suffered particular harm as a result of the legislation or the failure to enact it.

The court found that all these conditions for awarding compensation for nonpecuniary damages had been met in this case. It emphasized that Section 14 of the Constitution obliges the state, through its competent authorities, to protect individuals' rights.

The court stressed that protection against violations of these rights must be effective and prompt and that the complexity of the relevant legal framework cannot justify a prolonged failure to fulfill the obligation to protect individuals' rights. It also noted that, based on past experience, the state has sufficient resources to swiftly regulate even complex matters through legislation when necessary.

The court further noted that, at a minimum, lawmakers and the relevant executive authorities, including the Ministry of Justice or the Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority, should have initiated the repeal of the statutory provisions directly conflicting with EU law.

To safeguard citizens' fundamental rights, the state should also have informed telecommunications companies through its relevant authorities that compliance with the provisions conflicting with EU law was no longer required. The companies should have been informed that, pending the possible adoption of new legislation, they could limit their collection and retention of data to what was necessary for their business operations, retain it only for as long as necessary and disclose it to state authorities only in circumstances prescribed by law.

The state took none of these steps. Instead, it knowingly continued requesting unlawfully collected data from telecommunications companies to carry out its functions.

The court also found that the claimants belonged to a group of individuals who had suffered particular harm. In both cases, unlawfully collected data had subsequently been used unlawfully in criminal proceedings brought against them.

Although the claimants had not yet been acquitted when they filed their claim, their acquittals in the criminal case in which the data had been collected had become final by the time the administrative court issued its ruling. This placed them in an entirely different category from ordinary citizens and individuals who had been convicted of crimes.

In determining the amount of compensation, the court was required to consider the general principles governing compensation for nonpecuniary damages, under which compensation must be proportionate to the severity of the violation, taking into account the nature and degree of culpability.

The court found there was no doubt that the case involved an extremely serious violation of individual rights. The volume of unlawfully disclosed data was substantial, allowing extensive intrusion into the claimants' private lives and significantly violating their right to the confidentiality of communications. The court therefore considered it justified to award compensation substantially higher than amounts typically awarded in Estonian court practice.

An appeal may be filed with Tallinn Circuit Court by December 14.

Background

The corruption case against Parvel Pruunsild and former Tartu Deputy Mayor Priit Humal (Isamaa) centered on allegations that Humal violated Estonia's Anti-Corruption Act in 2022 by participating in city decisions to forego acquiring the former Estonian National Museum exhibition building in Tartu — a move aided and abetted by Isamaa sponsor Pruunsild that allowed the property to be auctioned and bought in January 2023 for €1.22 million by the student fraternity Korp! Sakala, of which Pruunsild is a prominent member. The men were acquitted by the first two court instances, with the Prosecutor's Office deciding against bringing the case to the Supreme Court after that.

Following their acquittal and the reimbursement of their legal defense costs by the state, Pruunsild and Humal filed administrative lawsuits against the Estonian state (as well as a separate civil suit by Pruunsild against telecom provider Telia) seeking damages over what they contend was the unlawful collection and use of their personal telecommunications data during the investigation.

World.title: Estonian films could reach Russia without local producers' knowledge
World.content:
The Ministry of Culture recently received a letter alleging, among other things, that some Estonian businesses are selling their films to Russia. Edith Sepp, a member of the management board of the Estonian Film Institute, said that while this does indeed happen in Europe, it does not happen in Estonia. The Ministry of Culture confirmed this. However, it emerged that there are other ways in which both Estonian films and money reach Russia.

Sepp said Estonian companies have purchased films for distribution in Estonia through Russian intermediaries. The intermediary companies are registered in countries such as Malta or the United Kingdom, outside the European Union. However, their parent companies are based in Russia. As a result, payments from Estonia for the distribution of certain films reach Russia through intermediary companies. "The situation has certainly improved considerably over the past couple of years and we no longer have to purchase very many films through intermediary companies," Sepp said.

Edith Sepp. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

An international agent can also sell on Estonian film in Russia

Another way money can reach Russia from Estonia is through international sales agents that acquire the rights to Estonian films and hold licenses to represent them. Karlo Funk, an adviser on audiovisual and digital culture at the Ministry of Culture, said an international sales agent can then sell a film anywhere in the world without the direct involvement of the Estonian film company. The Estonian producer only learns about the sale afterward, within three to six months.

Most European sales agents are companies registered in France. Funk gave the example of a French sales agent acquiring the rights to films from Latvia, Poland or Belgium and selling them internationally. The same applies to Estonian films that have received public funding. "The solution here would be for Estonian film producers that have received public funding to clearly stipulate in their contracts that the film cannot be sold for distribution in Russia," Funk said.

He acknowledged that an international sales agent could also acquire the rights to a film currently showing in Estonian movie theaters and sell it to Russia. "Films are not subject to sanctions," he said. After the outbreak of the war, French film exports to Russia increased rather than decreased. "French films took advantage of the opportunity created by Hollywood's withdrawal from the Russian market," Funk explained.

He said this was also because, in the film industry, advance purchases for major projects are sometimes made two to three years ahead of time, meaning existing contracts were not terminated. "As far as we know, the share of French films in the Russian market has declined by now, but they are still being shown there," Funk said.

Sepp said France has no intention of completely stopping the sale of its films to Russia. According to her, France argues that if European films were not shown in Russia, the country's residents would become increasingly disconnected from European values.

Karlo Funk. Source: Estonian History Museum

Another way Estonian films can reach Russia is through international co-productions, for example, when Estonia is a co-producer of a French film. If the French producer, as the lead producer, decides to sell the film to Russia, Estonia has no say in the matter. Funk said that if Estonia were to introduce a rule prohibiting films made with Estonian public funding from reaching Russia in any form, the French co-producer would likely withdraw from the project.

The European Commission's Creative Europe program aims to support Europe's cultural and creative sectors, including the film and audiovisual industries. Funk explained that the Creative Europe programs in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have been addressing the issue of film sales to Russia for the past two years.

Member States decide whether companies can work with Russia

This year, Creative Europe introduced a rule under which film projects cannot receive European Union funding if their distribution rights in the Baltic states are sold to Russia. This means that European film sales agents receiving EU funding for their operations will lose that funding if they enter into such a deal. However, Funk emphasized that ultimately, it is up to individual member states to decide whether to allow their companies to do business with Russia.

Pirated copies of Estonian films also circulate in Russia. Sepp acknowledged that this has always been a problem. She explained that these films are stolen and screened, but no one sells them or receives any money for them. "At least not to my knowledge," Sepp said. Such piracy cannot be stopped.

World.title: Argo Ideon: Politics has become a profession devoid of passion
World.content:
It would be unrealistic to expect a spark of enthusiasm to glow in a lawmaker's eyes every moment of the day. Yet voters are still drawn to those who keep moving 24 hours a day like the Energizer Bunny, writes Argo Ideon.

When members of Mart Laar's second government took office, they were given a copy of "Yes, Minister" by Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay. For the ministers, it was both a comedy and, in some ways, a practical guide that helped explain how public-sector bureaucracy works.

In the book, Jim Hacker heads the Department of Administrative Affairs. He wants the best but constantly finds himself trapped in absurd situations. One thing, however, cannot be held against the characters: a lack of passion. Their enthusiasm overflows whether they are waiting by the phone for an important call or trying to figure out why a newly opened hospital has no patients. Even an invitation to pop in for a drink with the PM's adviser is accepted with enthusiasm, despite the inevitable dressing-down.

Watching today's political maneuvering and party switching in Estonia, however, one quickly gets the sense that the spark and enthusiasm are long gone. Passion is not renewable energy but a rapidly depleted fossil fuel. Modern politics, to borrow a line from the Estonian punk band Propeller, is guided by "cold calculation and strict discipline."

To some extent, this loss of momentum is inevitable. Gone are the days when the country had to be built from scratch and inner conviction kept office lights burning late into the night. Over 35 years, many things have settled into place and it is no surprise that people have settled as well.

There are exceptions, but on the whole politics has increasingly become a matter of earning a living in a particular field. There is nothing shameful about that. Everyone wants something to put on their bread and seeks a place in life where they can earn it more easily. Someone who gets up before dawn and works hard deserves respect, even if their eyes no longer sparkle. The same applies when that person's profession is politics.

Still, to accept politicians' lack of enthusiasm in the midst of yet another election campaign would be close to heresy. Voters prefer candidates who seem to operate around the clock like the Energizer Bunny and can still string together coherent sentences after a sleepless night.

"Over 35 years, many things have settled into place, and it is no surprise that people have settled as well."

On a weekend morning, a prospective candidate rises early to brave the cold and hand out tea, pancakes and pens from a party-branded tent outside a shopping center. Then comes a party council meeting, where they enthusiastically listen to the leader's speech and propose a brand-new plan to revive the Estonian economy, a fresh recipe so simple that no one else could possibly have thought of it because everyone else is obviously wrong.

And once that Smaug's hoard of hidden treasure has been discovered, the one that will supposedly bring prosperity to schools, clinics and rescue stations, the politician's work for the day is done.

It sounds noble to say that a politician's employer is the people, but in practice, for most functions, the real boss is the political party. In that sense, switching parties is a pragmatic move not very different from a baker crossing the street to work in a competing bakery. Condemning party swappers and pointing fingers at them is a relic of an earlier era when some politicians really were driven by pure enthusiasm.

From time to time, the argument resurfaces that politics does not pay well enough, that the private sector offers higher salaries and that lawmakers and other politicians should therefore receive pay raises to attract talented people. In the previous parliamentary term, when salaries were somewhat lower, there was even a member of parliament who occasionally drove a taxi during parliamentary sessions to earn extra money.

Yet when Estonia's average gross monthly salary this year, according to second-quarter figures, stands at €2,243 and the salary of an ordinary member of the Riigikogu is €6,655.81, it is easy to see that the overwhelming majority of working people in Estonia will never come close to that level of income during their careers. Against that backdrop, the notion that financial motives play no role in a political career sounds rather thin.

Finally, one must also admire the optimism of parliamentary candidates. In the most recent election, in 2023, a total of 968 candidates competed for seats in the Riigikogu, more than nine candidates per seat. As a rough guess, perhaps only one in four of them had anything resembling a realistic expectation of being elected.

But why did the remaining three quarters, hundreds of people, take part? They invested their time, attended campaign events and paid candidate deposits. Quite a mystery, isn't it?

Or perhaps somewhere inside those hardened political hearts there is still a small remnant of that lost passion and burning conviction.

World.title: Opposition against 2027 state budget, says state will be fine until April
World.content:
Opposition parties do not support next year's draft state budget in its current form and will vote against it in the final vote if necessary.

The opposition had also planned to suspend the second reading of the draft state budget on Wednesday, but the attempt failed because four members of the Riigikogu were absent from the sitting.

Those absent were unaffiliated MPs Kersti Sarapuu and Tõnis Mölder, as well as Henn Põlluaas, who is also unaffiliated but belongs to Isamaa, and Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) Chairman Martin Helme.

According to Social Democratic Party Chairman Lauri Läänemets, the key issue now is what happens at the third reading, when the final vote takes place.

"If the coalition fails to take the opposition's proposed amendments into account in the meantime, it is entirely possible that the entire opposition will vote against this budget," Läänemets said.

"Ultimately, the governing coalition needs to produce a budget that has the support of a parliamentary majority. If it fails to do so, it is simply taking the risk of leaving Estonia without a budget. It is now up to Prime Minister Kristen Michal and the Reform Party to decide whether Estonia will have a state budget for next year," Läänemets added.

According to Läänemets, €20 million should be allocated to special care services. Under an amendment proposed by the Finance Committee, the Ministry of Social Affairs would receive an additional €7.47 million to improve access to these services. Läänemets said a Supreme Court ruling also requires an increase in funding for special care services.

Läänemets called on the governing coalition to seek common ground, adding that it could lose even more MPs from its ranks before the final vote on the state budget.

"Another decisive factor could be whether the coalition still has 50 MPs in its ranks by then, or whether that number has fallen to 49 or 48. I would not rule out the possibility of the coalition having significantly fewer MPs. I assume the leaders of the coalition parties understand this as well and will seek solutions in the meantime," Läänemets said.

According to Läänemets, this also means the coalition is becoming less likely to be able to count on the support of unaffiliated MPs.

Finance Committee Chair Annely Akkermann of the Reform Party has said that obstructing the draft state budget would also hamper efforts to strengthen Estonia's national defense.

"If defense spending is planned at €2.3 billion for next year, an annual plan is drawn up based on that amount and procurement procedures and contracts covering the entire year's budget begin in January. If that cannot happen, it will not be possible to spend that money over the course of the year, which would weaken Estonia's defense capabilities. I do not believe the opposition actually wants to do that simply for the sake of political gamesmanship," Akkermann said.

Läänemets dismissed the argument as a rhetorical tactic.

"These decisions can actually be made within the limits of the previous year's budget. But this is a rhetorical tactic: You create a problem yourself and then blame others for it. If a state budget drawn up under the Reform Party's leadership does not have the support of a parliamentary majority, there is no point in pointing fingers at anyone else. Instead, they should consider why they lack that majority support," Läänemets said.

Center MP: Estonia will continue to function without a state budget law

Center Party whip Lauri Laats said Kersti Sarapuu and Tõnis Mölder would likely vote with the coalition and that the opposition could not count on their support.

According to Laats, nothing tragic would happen to Estonia if next year's budget were not adopted.

"Estonia will continue to function perfectly well without this budget. Nothing will break down. This year's figures will simply be used as the basis and operations will continue under those figures. It won't be the end of the world, and we all understand that, including members of the coalition," Laats said.

"The state budget certainly should not be adopted in its current form. It lacks ambition and the drive to move the country forward. It includes a large budget deficit, with spending partially financed through borrowing," Laats said.

According to Laats, the country could easily operate without a new budget until April. The Riigikogu elections are scheduled for early March.

"By then, the elections will have taken place and a new government will be in office, one that will certainly be able to present a better budget to the Riigikogu," he said.

Failure to adopt next year's state budget would also leave planned pay raises for rescue workers and police officers, totaling €7.3 million, unapproved. Laats said these increases could be approved retroactively and promised even larger raises.

"If the decisions made after April result in employees in these essential sectors receiving larger pay raises, I am confident they will understand the situation and support this approach," he added.

Finance Committee chair: Leaving Estonia without a budget would affect most adults

Annely Akkermann said that if the state budget cannot be adopted, the government will be able to spend one-twelfth of this year's budget each month next year.

"Several expenditures related to tax revenue transfers will also increase next year, as tax revenues are expected to grow, particularly those linked to gross wages. We expect gross income to rise by 4.6 percent by the middle of next year, which means that allocations from income tax revenue to local governments, as well as allocations to pension insurance, the Health Insurance Fund and the Unemployment Insurance Fund, will increase. And if we cannot transfer these increased revenues, we do not even know what the consequences might be," Akkermann said.

According to Akkermann, another issue concerns pensions.

"Will we be able to pay pension increases if we are constrained by a limit of one-twelfth of the previous year's budget? Pay raises for teachers, police officers and rescue workers will certainly be canceled," she said.

"Leaving the country without a state budget will affect most adults, and not in a good way. Is it a catastrophe? I don't know, but it will certainly cause difficulties," Akkermann said.

Independent MP: State must not be left without a budget over political maneuvering

Unaffiliated Riigikogu member Tõnis Mölder criticized the opposition's actions, saying it lacked a plan.

"Simply opposing the budget is not a substantive plan. The opposition has not presented a single, comprehensive alternative to the budget that would simultaneously ensure Estonia's security, economic competitiveness and people's livelihoods," Mölder said.

"I have not decided whether to support the 2027 budget, but I consider it irresponsible to leave the country without a budget for the sake of political tactics," Mölder said.

"The budget can still be improved before the third reading and, after the elections, further changes can be made through a supplementary budget based on a new mandate. The fact is that, given our current budgetary constraints, we simply do not have money lying around," he stressed.

"For me, the state budget is not something to be used for political horse-trading. The Social Democrats' desire for us to automatically oppose the budget appears to stem from their wish to increase their leverage in budget negotiations. There is nothing statesmanlike about their approach," Mölder said.

The government-initiated draft 2027 State Budget Act passed its second reading in the Riigikogu on Wednesday.

The Riigikogu began debating the draft state budget at around 4 p.m. Following the Finance Committee's report, debate and consideration of proposed amendments, the second reading concluded at 12:56 a.m.

Parliamentary groups have until November 25 to submit amendments ahead of the third reading. The state budget's third reading and final vote are scheduled for December 9.

The article was updated to add comments by Tõnis Mölder.

World.title: Baltic communal singing may no longer bring everyone together, study finds
World.content:
Communal singing across the Baltics may not be as inclusive today as its reputation suggests, with a new study finding some groups are increasingly left out of the experience.

The Integration Foundation presented the findings Wednesday from "Crises Established Singing: investigating the inherent potential of collective singing in times of social crises in the Scandinavian and Baltic regions" (CRIES), a research project involving cultural scholars from the Baltic states and Denmark.

The study examined how communal singing, long seen as a force for bringing people together, can also exclude certain groups.

Researchers found that growing numbers of people in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania do not identify with the idea of being a "singing people."

Those who do not speak the local language also take part in communal singing less often, as do unemployed and older people, who may lack the means or money to attend public gatherings and large events.

Generations of men's choir singers performing at the XXVIII Song Festival in Tallinn. July 6, 2025. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

In Estonia, choral singing is even losing ground in larger cities, where residents have more leisure activities to choose from.

Chances for 'not good' singers

"We're used to thinking that singing together includes everyone and that everyone in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania sings," said Rūta Muktupāvela, a lead researcher and professor at the Latvian Academy of Culture who led the study.

Each country, however, is also home to people who don't belong to its primary ethnic group and are less likely to take part in communal singing or song and dance festivals, she added.

Muktupāvela likewise noted that some people would like to take part but feel like they aren't good enough singers.

She said opportunities should be created for those who may not consider themselves talented enough but would still like to join in communal singing.

Choir singers of all ages and backgrounds at the XXVIII Song Festival in Tallinn. July 6, 2025. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

World.title: Estonian pilot: We keep our jets at least a kilometer from Russia's border
World.content:
Estonian pilots stay at least a kilometer from the Russian border, never flying east of Lake Peipus, one Air Force flyer told Maaleht.

In an interview with the weekly, Second Lieutenant Jasper Vimm, a 28-year-old captain, said no aircraft takes off without a planned route; pilots keep away from the border once airborne, and as GPS signals are liable to evaporate once you near Russia, flights are planned around ground landmarks.

Estonia's Air Force (Õhuvägi) is small compared with some other countries', but has four main aircraft: two Czech-made L-39 Albatros trainers leased from an Estonian firm, one of which is currently undergoing maintenance, and two Polish PZL M28 Skytruck transport aircraft used for maritime patrol and exercises.

The L-39s date from the 1980s and 1990s, fly at subsonic speeds of about 700 km/h, carry no weapons, cannot climb vertically, and have airframes with a service life of 5,000 flight hours, of which this one has a little over half left.

The Air Force currently has between 10 and active 20 pilots, Vimm said, though changes are afoot - the Estonian National Defence College will graduate its first class of pilots next year, after which new Air Force pilots will come through every year.

With its relatively compact size, flying from one end of Estonia to the other takes 30–40 minutes in a trainer; about half that in a larger fighter at cruising speed.

There have been proposals recently for Estonia to take on light fighters, what type is not yet known, but Vimm said once in country these would perform the same roles as the full-blown fast jets, differing mainly in size and speed.

He said new aircraft would be "a source of joy" for pilots, who would be able to do more in the air and practice using aircraft weapons using their own aircraft.

As for drones, Vimm said 'these are suited to destruction and reconnaissance and are replacing some missile roles, but pilots are not going anywhere for the time being: human-piloted planes perform a wider range of tasks and someone must still sit in the cockpit to achieve this.

While the disparity of state of the art fighters costing millions going out to intercept cheap drones, Vimm said the cost of human lives lost, infrastructure destroyed, far outweighs aircraft maintenance and the cost of air time; Ukraine has even mounted machine guns on slower, old piston-driven aircraft to hunt quadcopter-type drones, he noted.

The original Maaleht interview is here.

Since the Air Force, organizationally a part of the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) currently has no fast jets, NATO allies provide that capability flying out of Ämari and from Šiauliai in Lithuania. Turkey's Air Force currently holds that role at Ämari with its F-16s.
