For foreigners living in Poland, this means, above all, keeping an eye on government and parliamentary decisions that directly determine the rules governing residence, employment and state assistance.

For now, there are no grounds to claim that the conflict surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal threatens migrants’ right to remain in the country.

But Poland’s crisis illustrates a broader problem: even in a democratic state, political confrontation can weaken institutions for a prolonged period, undermining the mechanisms that protect human rights. For migrants, particularly refugees whose status often depends heavily on decisions made by the authorities, this has very practical implications.

World.title: ‘The ball is in Armenia’s court’: Yerevan voices on Armenia losing its voting rights in Russia-led CSTO
World.content:
CSTO strips Armenia of its voting rights

The Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO) has stripped Armenia of its voting rights. The country has also officially lost the right to appoint representatives to key positions, a right it had effectively stopped exercising long ago. The CSTO member states’ leaders made these decisions on 11 November at a meeting of the Collective Security Council. Armenia’s prime minister did not attend.

The CSTO officially has six member states: Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Armenia. Armenia froze its participation in the CSTO in February 2024. The country no longer takes part in the organisation’s activities or pays membership fees. Yerevan made the decision because the CSTO failed to fulfil its obligations under its charter. The organisation did not respond when Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s sovereign territory in 2021–2022, despite the Armenian authorities’ appeals for help. The CSTO allies explained their inaction by saying it was “impossible” to confirm the incursions because Armenia and Azerbaijan had not delimited their border. Armenia’s prime minister responded: “If we say there is no border between Armenia and Azerbaijan, then there is no CSTO. The CSTO has an area of responsibility defined by borders. If there is no border, there is no area of responsibility. And if there is no area of responsibility, there is no organisation.”

Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the leaders had taken into account Armenia’s failure to meet its obligations for several years. He was referring in particular to the country’s unpaid membership fees.

Under the organisation’s charter, Armenia can regain its rights in the CSTO once it clears its outstanding debt.

Yerevan has not yet officially responded to the CSTO’s decision. Perhaps the Armenian authorities saw no need to repeat their position, which they have stated many times before. A week ago, during a press briefing, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said, among other things: “I want us to make this clear once and for all: our interest in the CSTO has been exhausted.”

But Security Secretary Alen Simonyan had commented on the decision by the time this article went to publication. On his personal Facebook page, he wrote: “They stripped us of our voice in a place where everyone remained very loudly silent while they were collectively killing us.”

The CSTO member states’ leaders did not surprise experts or the public with their decision. Moreover, they believe Yerevan should not have waited for the organisation to strip it of its voting rights. Many argue that Armenia should have left the CSTO long ago.

Babken Harutyunyan, a politician and former member of the Hayrenik (Homeland) party, described the CSTO as a “pro-Azerbaijani organisation”. He explained his view by saying that Armenia’s allies treat their own member state and Azerbaijan, which they call a “friendly country”, as equals.

“The organisation is leaving the final step [leaving the CSTO] and the last word to Armenia itself. Or perhaps it hopes that forces it finds acceptable [pro-Russian forces] will come to power and once again bring Armenia back under the CSTO’s feet. After Azerbaijan’s years-long occupation of Jermuk and other Armenian territories, Armenia should leave the CSTO,” he said.

Пустующее кресло предназначалось для премьер-министра Армении

CSTO secretary-general: ‘Armenia’s expulsion from the organisation was not on the agenda at the Moscow summit’

CSTO Secretary-General Taalatbek Masadykov stressed that the organisation had not discussed expelling Armenia.

“For the past three years, Armenia has not paid its membership fees or sent staff to the CSTO Secretariat or the CSTO Joint Staff. In other words, although Armenia has formally remained a member, […] it has not taken part in discussions. If Armenia pays its membership fees, it will be able to regain its voting rights in the organisation. The decision is up to the Armenian leadership.”

Masadykov had previously said that Armenia had effectively already left the organisation:

“They listen to weekly reports, but do not take part in our main events, exercises and so on. So I think Article 25 [of the CSTO Charter] applies here. Essentially, they have already left of their own accord.”

Under Article 25 of the CSTO Charter, a member state loses its voting rights if it fails to pay its contributions or fill positions allocated to it under the organisation’s quotas.

‘A sign of deepening political and diplomatic tensions’

Vahan Babayan, chairman of the Reformist Party, said the CSTO’s decision to strip Yerevan of its voting rights was not merely a “technical or financial matter”.

“This is another sign of deepening political and diplomatic tensions between Armenia and the CSTO.”

He believes such decisions have the following implications:

“Armenia is losing its ability to influence the organisation’s decision-making process;

distrust between Armenia and Russia is growing in security and political matters.”

Babayan also warned that Armenia’s institutional standing within the organisation was weakening, even though the country formally remains a member of the military bloc. The politician said he expected the authorities to go beyond statements and provide serious, considered assessments in the interests of national security:

“We need real security guarantees, clear alliance relations and a foreign policy guided by national interests.”

Social media reactions

“Since the CSTO was founded, Armenia has been the only country that dared to speak up — and that is why it was stripped of its voting rights. Just like in an ancient Greek tragedy: you don’t know whether to laugh or cry.”

“They are still hoping that ‘Samvel from Kaluga’ [Russian businessman Samvel Karapetyan, who is under arrest and heads the opposition Strong Armenia party] or someone like him will come to power. Then they will restore Armenia’s voting rights. Otherwise, they would have kicked it out long ago.”

“Armenia should have left these stupid organisations, the CSTO and the Eurasian Economic Union [a Russia-led economic bloc], a long time ago. The only guarantee of Armenia’s security in the future is membership of the European Union and NATO.”

“Armenia decided to leave on its own. Nobody stripped it of any rights. Don’t delude yourselves.”

“And we didn’t need the right to vote anyway. They helped us in our time of need, and now they are taking away our rights? How hard this will be to bear. They don’t even recognise our state border.”

“And what even is the CSTO? A useless, unnecessary Putin-run organisation [a play on the Armenian abbreviation for the CSTO, ՀԱՊԿ, using different Armenian words]? The pointless ‘Putin office’ demands membership fees from Armenia but turned a blind eye to Azerbaijan’s invasion.”

“We have been stripped of our voting rights in a dead organisation.”

“Is it even worth worrying? What has this treacherous organisation ever done apart from betray us?”

“Thank God! I can’t wait for the day when Armenia has nothing in common with this rotten remnant of the Soviet Union.”

World.title: What has changed in Georgia–Russia relations and what comes next? Views from Abkhazia – video discussion
World.content:
Russian-Georgian relations

This discussion focuses on the appointment of Giorgi Zurabishvili as Georgia’s Prime Minister’s Special Representative for Relations with Russia and First Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs. This personnel change has sparked a strong reaction in Georgian media and among experts, raising questions about a potential shift in Georgia’s foreign policy.

Key points and arguments:

Zurabishvili’s appointment and the Geneva International Discussions – Astamur Tania considers it premature to draw conclusions about Zurabishvili’s appointment. What matters most is not the position a person holds, but whether there is the political will and fresh ideas needed to overcome a deadlock that has persisted for many years. Combining the positions of Deputy Foreign Minister and Special Representative could indicate a reconfiguration of approaches, although this is not necessarily the case. According to host Inal Khashig, the appointment may be aimed at restoring diplomatic relations with Russia. Despite criticism, the Geneva International Discussions are not considered useless, as they remain the only functioning platform that can be used to address existing problems.

– Astamur Tania considers it premature to draw conclusions about Zurabishvili’s appointment. What matters most is not the position a person holds, but whether there is the political will and fresh ideas needed to overcome a deadlock that has persisted for many years. Combining the positions of Deputy Foreign Minister and Special Representative could indicate a reconfiguration of approaches, although this is not necessarily the case. According to host Inal Khashig, the appointment may be aimed at restoring diplomatic relations with Russia. Despite criticism, the Geneva International Discussions are not considered useless, as they remain the only functioning platform that can be used to address existing problems. The main obstacle: Georgia’s Law on Occupied Territories – Astamur Tania emphasizes that Georgia’s Law on Occupied Territories is the main obstacle to establishing dialogue and resolving even basic issues. The law ties the Georgian side’s hands, preventing it from signing any documents with Abkhazia. He considers this absurd, given that documents were signed even during the war. Repealing or substantially amending the law would not mean recognizing Abkhazia, but would make it possible to pursue a more constructive policy.

– Astamur Tania emphasizes that Georgia’s Law on Occupied Territories is the main obstacle to establishing dialogue and resolving even basic issues. The law ties the Georgian side’s hands, preventing it from signing any documents with Abkhazia. He considers this absurd, given that documents were signed even during the war. Repealing or substantially amending the law would not mean recognizing Abkhazia, but would make it possible to pursue a more constructive policy. The need for new ideas and formats – A format involving the parties to the conflict (Georgia and Abkhazia) is needed. This would not necessarily imply mutual recognition, but rather a willingness to share responsibility for addressing security and humanitarian issues. Abkhazia has agency, even if it does not possess the same level of influence as major powers, and can participate in resolving issues affecting the interests of the local population.

– A format involving the parties to the conflict (Georgia and Abkhazia) is needed. This would not necessarily imply mutual recognition, but rather a willingness to share responsibility for addressing security and humanitarian issues. Abkhazia has agency, even if it does not possess the same level of influence as major powers, and can participate in resolving issues affecting the interests of the local population. The global and regional context – Global politics remains highly dynamic, and major geopolitical shifts make developments difficult to predict. Neither Georgia nor Abkhazia can influence global politics, but both can contribute to shaping the situation in their own region. If Zurabishvili’s appointment helps ease tensions and facilitates the development of de facto relations between Georgia and Russia, even without the restoration of diplomatic relations, this would also benefit Abkhazia, as improved relations between neighboring countries could have positive implications for the entire region.The idea that Russia could simply revoke its recognition of Abkhazia is naive. Abkhazia is a factor that cannot be ignored.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=ukUtFdwibA8%3Ffeature%3Doembed

Inal Khashig: Hello, this is Chegemskaya Pravda on the air. Today we’ll be talking about Georgia, or more precisely, about the Geneva negotiation process, about Georgian-Abkhaz-Russian relations in the context of a new appointment. A new special representative of the prime minister for relations with Russia has been appointed in Georgia; he is also the first deputy minister of foreign affairs, Giorgi Zurabashvili. In this context, in the context of the personnel question, when personnel decide everything, we’ll talk with our regular expert, Astamur Tania. Astamur, good afternoon.

Astamur Tania: Good afternoon.

Inal Khashig: On the face of it, an ordinary personnel matter. He was appointed, so he was appointed, but I’ve been reading the Georgian media, and there’s literally a kind of storm there, a kind of suspicion that some big moves will follow this appointment. But so far he hasn’t been officially confirmed, Zurabashvili hasn’t been confirmed as head of the delegation at the Geneva talks, but, as the Georgian social networks and media write, experts are saying that it’s a done deal. What do you think about this appointment in general? It seemed the process was just going along and going along, and nothing was changing. And suddenly such an appointment, where a new person, an official, is deliberately brought in.

Astamur Tania: For now, I think, it’s too early to say. I’ve read the comments. I consider them completely premature, because what difference does it make what position a person holds, whether he’s a deputy minister, a first deputy, or has no post in the Foreign Ministry at all? What matters is whether there is political will to solve the problem and whether some kind of model exists. For overcoming at least part of the contradictions that exist.

Of course, one can suppose that combining the posts of deputy minister and special representative for dialogue with Russia may point to some kind of reformatting. Or it may not mean that. After all, we live in such a volatile state, the region is such that it may well mean nothing at all.

I just want to express some wishes. We probably need some ideas for overcoming a deadlock that has lasted many years. I have to read about the uselessness of the Geneva discussions. I don’t think they are useless, because there is a functioning format that can be turned into something useful, or used to highlight some problems. There is no other. This is better than nothing.

Criticizing the Geneva format is the same as criticizing the UN. The UN doesn’t take proper measures to restore order in the world. What instruments does the UN have? Does it have an army or something? Or do the leading states obey the UN Secretary-General as if he were an emperor?

Everything depends on how the context changes, what political will there is. The only thing, I’m coming back to it once again, is that we need ideas for a way out of the deadlock. In my view, the deadlock is created by the existence of this legislation on the occupied territories. It gets in the way of the Georgian side itself. Repealing this very law would not mean recognition of Abkhazia, and neither would transforming this law. But this law prevents the Georgian side itself from establishing a dialogue on the most elementary issues. Even if some dialogue is established, it’s unclear how to implement it, because there are no parties to the conflict.

We keep saying, regularly, from broadcast to broadcast, that we need a format in which there are parties to the conflict. That does not mean any mutual recognition. It means that we are ready to be jointly responsible for resolving certain issues. Security issues, humanitarian issues, what agenda could be built around that. Otherwise, we can demand forever, on our side, a legally binding document on the non-use of force. By the way, several such documents were signed with us in the course of the negotiations. And then, in our day, to believe that a piece of paper will give you something is, in my opinion, completely naive. How long will it last, this legal obligation? It depends on the context, after all. From the Georgian side [the line is]: we will not talk to anyone under any circumstances. This is not a Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, it is a Georgian-Russian conflict. One can keep spinning one’s wheels like this endlessly and get nowhere. In general, maybe this situation actually suits someone just fine.



Inal Khashig: What I see in this appointment. Look. Since he, Zurabashvili, will also be overseeing the Geneva negotiation process. You have to know that, in fact, ever since Saakashvili’s time the Geneva negotiation process…



Astamur Tania: It’s not a negotiation process. It’s a discussion. If it were a negotiation process, that would be a different matter. They didn’t know what to call it, they thought, let’s call them discussions of experts who are not responsible for anything and don’t represent anyone.



Inal Khashig: Fine, discussions. So, the Georgian side at these discussions, this Georgian delegation, which, just like the Abkhaz one and all the others, takes part in a personal capacity, as it’s recorded in the document.



Astamur Tania: Whoever wanted to came, that’s what it’s called.



Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, there is a delegation. And ever since Saakashvili’s time it has been headed by Lasha Darsalia. Who regularly speaks of the occupation of Georgian territory, of occupied territories. Even though after Saakashvili the government changed radically, and Georgian Dream is also doctrinally completely different. It differs from what Saakashvili and his party, the United National Movement, said. Nevertheless, Lasha Darsalia was, as it were, the only connecting link with his thesis about the occupation.



Astamur Tania: He didn’t just walk in off the street either, right?



Inal Khashig: He didn’t , but I read Paata Zakareishvili. Paata Zakareishvili says there were two different centers. That is, when he headed, say, the Ministry for Conflicts and there was a special representative, Abashidze, that is, they didn’t get in each other’s way; more precisely, Abashidze dealt with purely situational things.



Astamur Tania: When was that, anyway? Ten years have passed already?



Inal Khashig: Yes, they have.



Astamur Tania: So what? Can nothing change? People can grow older, their, I don’t know, functions, some vision may change. In our case, they’ve already changed a thousand times. .



Inal Khashig: But it seems to me that the main thing in this, still, is the goal, which isn’t stated separately now; it is, probably, after all, the restoration of diplomatic relations with Russia.



Astamur Tania: And how is that possible without repealing the legislation on the occupied territories?



Inal Khashig: That’s already a detail, which, one way or another, must lead to this. What we’re talking about here, it seems to me, is either a serious revision of the law on the occupied territories, or its repeal. Because it hinders the deeper development of economic and other relations with Russia, since Tbilisi has seriously distanced itself from Brussels. On the other hand, other factors also have to be taken into account. Right now the Constitutional Court of Georgia is considering the question of banning five opposition political parties. It seems to me that Georgian Dream has gone all in, building its system of governance on the Azerbaijani model. But Azerbaijan has oil. Georgian Dream doesn’t.



Astamur Tania: We shouldn’t fall into the trap of these extrapolations at all. Because what’s good, as the saying goes, one man’s meat is another man’s poison. Of course, international experience matters, but you always have your own specifics. I don’t think people sit around drawing inspiration from Azerbaijan’s experience. We should look. Azerbaijan has its own history, Georgia has its own, Armenia a third, and we a fourth. Everywhere there are differences in the state of society, in the configuration of society. The authorities choose the toolkit that suits them best.

Frankly, I don’t see near-term prospects for repealing this law or restoring diplomatic relations. This is a question not so much from the rational sphere. Rationally, it would be beneficial to repeal this law, both for Georgia and for everyone. Because, I say again, it deprives Georgia itself of the ability to pursue any constructive policy in this direction, it ties its hands. Declaring what has been as never having been won’t work anyway. The law proceeds from the premise that what has been never was.

There is also the domestic political situation. The Georgian authorities are under serious domestic political pressure. And if they don’t talk about this law, people there will shout at them through the window from the street. We can see, after all, how the topic of conflict settlement is used for speculative purposes.

There are some completely exotic ideas there. I recently read Bokeria, Giga Bokeria. A man who seems not to live in Georgia at all. He says that civic nationalism and a single civic nation must be created. Georgia is multiethnic. Fine, let’s leave the Abkhaz and the Ossetians aside. Georgia itself is a multiethnic country. There, formulas of consensus have to be found, including against the background of these differences, national, religious, economic, regional. Georgia is practically meant to take the path of federalization.

Putting it mildly, we called them right-wing populists. Maybe someone has the idea that if Georgian Dream goes, wonderful, wonderfully stuffy liberals will come to replace it. That’s not the case at all. Because the state of society predisposes toward right-wing populists coming. Which is dangerous for Georgia, for its prospects, and for its neighbors, such as us. That’s why they are forced to… Georgian Dream will maneuver. Certain steps in the propaganda sphere that would be perceived negatively, they are unlikely to take.

In general, I think we need to think about how to get out of this deadlock. What could the model be? We had a good model, in which there were parties to the conflict.



Inal Khashig: Before 2008.



Astamur Tania: Before 2008 there was a functioning negotiation format. Of course, one can convince oneself that Abkhazia lacks agency, that it can’t conduct negotiations. But it’s obvious to everyone that Abkhazia has agency. Naturally, we can’t have the same kind of agency as Russia or the United States of America. And yes, Georgia too is far from that kind of agency. But there is a range of issues. Let them be small at this stage, but they can contribute to a transformation, a change in the climate, which we could agree on and resolve.

We recently had the fuel situation. It’s clear that the Georgian authorities showed goodwill. We may have issues that are more prolonged in time and need to be resolved, issues that concern the interests of the local population, security, and so on. But if some model could be worked out, agreed, and fixed in some way, that, the fixing, we can’t do now. Because this legislation obstructs such an approach. Certain bold steps are needed here.

Relatively recently I listened to Paata Davitaia. He was commenting on the situation in Abkhazia, and, on the other hand, he said that we ourselves propose nothing. Indeed, if you look at it that way, there are the positions of certain expert groups, there are some comments, Saakashvili said something, Bokeria said something, Gvaramia said something. But from any more or less significant group, whether in power or not, no models are being proposed. Because the Abkhaz theme is used exclusively for domestic political purposes. For stirring up certain sentiments. And in fact both we and Georgia have gigantic problems. Apart from whipping up these sentiments, such harsh ones.

If you look, there are gigantic demographic problems. Gigantic economic problems. We can see, after all, what protests are happening there over the sale of land. We had that too, by the way. Our protests were connected with real-estate issues. But with us that is banned. And in Georgia it’s allowed, it’s legalized. In effect, the most liquid land is being bought up.

Gigantic demographic problems. For example, I looked at both ours and Georgia’s. For example, in 2016, 59 thousand children were born in Georgia. And in 2025, 37 thousand. That is, over 20 thousand fewer children were born. In Abkhazia too, I looked. In Abkhazia it’s unclear where children are born, because many of us are born in Sochi, but there are other indicators. You look, and our situation isn’t very wonderful either. Roughly the same.

These issues need to be dealt with. In my opinion, they determine the future of a people altogether. And here, perhaps, to discuss some ancient myths, fairy tales and so on, that’s entirely a matter for specialists. One can sit for hours pulling the wool over people’s eyes, distracting them from real, pressing problems.



Inal Khashig: The first pithecanthropes were…



Astamur Tania: Yes. Who, when, and whose blood is better, purer, and the like.



Inal Khashig: Still, it seems to me that this appointment is a kind of unease on the part of some of the Georgian expert community.



Astamur Tania: Something has to be commented on, after all. And you and I also have to comment on something. But fortunately, there are very few issues to comment on. Everything is so calm, for now.



Inal Khashig: But still, it seems to me there’s some more thought-out action here than just a personnel appointment, where you simply took one, replaced him, and don’t know what you replaced him for. It seems to me there’s a deeper strategy here, probably, after all.

Astamur Tania: We don’t know about that, you and I.



Inal Khashig: We don’t, but, again, we should probably proceed from the circumstances.



Astamur Tania: But taking the opportunity, we can appeal to them to tell us why they did it.



Inal Khashig: Yes.



Astamur Tania: So that there would be more opportunities.



Inal Khashig: I think the next round of the Geneva discussions will take place literally in the first days. Yes. In November, it seems, in the first days.



Astamur Tania: Let’s wish the next round success. You know, the main success of the next round is that after it there be another one, at the very least, a following round, that it take place. But I’m not joking. If this round takes place, and then the next round takes place, that’s already not bad.



Inal Khashig: It seems to me that nothing at all threatens the Geneva discussions right now. Maybe something did some time ago, but now, it seems to me, the whole thing is probably, after all, heading toward an end, toward some agreements on the Ukrainian-Russian [issue].



Astamur Tania: That’s unclear.



Inal Khashig: Unclear, but still there is a desire to arrive at some common denominator.



Astamur Tania: You know, when such tectonic plates in international politics have shifted, it’s very hard to change this inertia. A great deal has changed in the world over this period. I think the world will remain in motion for a long time yet. It’s not calm around us either.



Inal Khashig: The dynamics, with the end of the conflict, say, in Ukraine…



Astamur Tania: It’s not a chessboard at all, unfortunately. The world is not a chessboard. There are a great many unpredictable factors. There are climatic and economic factors, a mass of others. In Iran, for example. The situation in Iran. Which way will it go, does anyone know? It seems to me that Trump himself doesn’t know.

Inal Khashig: Trump announces every time that he has won.

Astamur Tania: Possibly, yes. But where this situation will go, we don’t know. Elections are being held in Israel right now. Our task, I think, neither we nor the Georgians can influence global politics, [is] to take our minds off all of this a little, the mythology, the fairy-tale creativity. It is developing, by the way. The fairy-tale creativity, I see, especially in the comments, where people are working very productively. I don’t want to retell these new interesting ideas. Ingorokva is ready to jump out and applaud these people, I think.

We need to work on keeping our region calm. On that front we can do something. If Zurabashvili’s appointment helps ease the situation, even if, say, diplomatic relations with Russia are not established, but some de facto relations develop, I think that’s beneficial both for us and for the Georgians.

Inal Khashig: What do you mean by de facto?



Astamur Tania: Some economic issues will be resolved. Some transport issues will be resolved. Some coordinated positions. There are issues, say, issues of the Black Sea. Russia’s and Georgia’s positions may coincide, can’t they?



Inal Khashig: On a par with the Strait of Hormuz, that’s the most dangerous.



Astamur Tania: They may coincide. You can find a mass of problems. If their approaches to solving these problems dovetail, I see a positive factor in that. If this appointment of Zurabashvili is aimed at solving such tasks, then that’s good. That’s what I think. I don’t see a direct threat here.

Some of ours say: the Russians and the Georgians will strike a deal over our heads, and then we’ll be done for. Well, first of all, that’s a very primitive picture of the world, because, I say again, what has been can’t be made not to have been. Abkhazia, of course, is not a gigantic factor, but it is a factor.



Inal Khashig: Well, in general, it’s hard for me to imagine this picture, when, say…



Astamur Tania: What, from tomorrow we close the doors, is that it?



Inal Khashig: Like Dmitry Medvedev, as in 2008, [who] spoke from the rostrum, that’s when he talked about recognition, Abkhazia will now speak out there and say, “Sorry, we made a mistake, we’re stopping.”



Astamur Tania: Well, that’s a completely naive idea of the world.

There are factors, you may like them or not. Neighbors can be difficult, with a difficult character, but they exist, they’re not going anywhere. Iran, for example, isn’t going anywhere. Many people don’t like Russia, Russia isn’t going anywhere. We can see how the Trump administration’s policy toward Russia is being carried out now. Because there is a factor in play. Everyone reckons with it.

So the fact that it’s quieter here is good. If our neighbors are searching for some mutually acceptable approaches, if things go well for our neighbors, Georgia and Russia, I don’t think things will go badly for us. So perhaps some configurations will start working here, including in the area of transport, transit. There are other issues too. There are also other issues that may arise. Issues of security for the local population, of cross-border contacts. It seems like a minor issue, but for us these are big issues. For Georgia and for Russia too.

I say again, if we could influence a change in the climate of our relations, every such opportunity should be used. The decision, say, to supply fuel at a difficult moment for us, didn’t it contribute to improving the climate?



It seems that such steps… But they are one-off. That’s why I say, if there were no obstacles in Georgian legislation, it would be possible to find some kind of systematic model for interaction on various issues. We had that; now it’s perceived as some sort of know-how, but all of it happened in our own, actually, not in some Martian history, it happened in our history.

I don’t believe in big decisions yet. But big decisions rarely come about by shooting straight up to the peak in one go. Usually in politics it goes step by step, little by little. And then, what big decisions there will be will depend on what set of small decisions has been adopted. That also affects the situation, the mood. And what’s happening in the world around us also has an effect. That has to be taken into account.



Inal Khashig: What do you consider a big decision? Say, repealing the occupation law, is that a big decision?



Astamur Tania: It seems to me that repealing the occupation law is not a condition. The occupation law forbids the Georgian authorities from signing with us the slightest piece of paper, even on the most pressing problems. Isn’t that an absurd situation? During the war we signed documents with each other. But that didn’t lead to Georgia recognizing us and us recognizing [Georgia’s] integrity. After the war, too, that didn’t mean that our positions on these issues were radically different. But, by the way, we discussed these problems too.





Many issues, by the way, were cut off precisely because the Georgian authorities of various formations and periods were concerned, first of all, about the domestic political context, and not about regulating the conflict.



Inal Khashig: But, say, not repeal but adjustment, a revision of certain specific articles.



Astamur Tania: I’m saying that we need to think, step back, there has to be some kind of brainstorming. What issues, not of astronomical scale but down-to-earth ones, small, mutually beneficial, could we resolve right now. Create a menu of these issues. Then think about how we could set about resolving them.

Now, if somewhere this runs up against legislation, it seems to me that legislation can become outdated, right? Which means legislation at the very least needs transformation. If we’re talking about a shared desire to resolve the conflict. If there’s, say, a desire to build a Great Wall of China, that’s a different matter. That’s also a possible solution. So, after all, we were given heads to model things and to think with.



Inal Khashig: I think there’s a heap of things here, because nothing has changed all these years. Nevertheless, there should be some cases in the interests [of both sides]. I’m not talking about unrealizable interests, I’m talking about some real things that interest someone. Both the Georgian and the Abkhaz side. Each has things it is interested in. The Georgians also have enough of these issues, connected with the residents of the Gali district.



Astamur Tania: The Gali residents… I believe that we ourselves need to work on changing policy, on correcting our own mistakes regarding the Gali district.

You’re talking about cases. A lot of our positions today have been raised to the rank of some kind of religion. Even though they arose relatively recently. Everyone is afraid to touch them. Sooner or later they will have to be touched. .



Inal Khashig: And what do you mean by that?



Astamur Tania: I mean that constantly engaging in propaganda that doesn’t lead to solving practical issues, sooner or later that will become obvious. You can’t keep being hostages to your own propaganda. It’s clear that it’s also propaganda that materializes. That too has to be taken into account. That’s why I think it’s too early for us to say what this appointment attests to. Maybe it attests to nothing at all, but I’ve voiced some wishes of mine on the subject.



Inal Khashig: Well, I’ll wrap up here. At the very least, the new appointment to the post of special representative for relations with Russia has given us a reason to talk about today’s Georgian-Abkhaz conflict.

I’ll be saying goodbye to you. With you were our regular experts Astamur Tania and I, Inal Khashig. See you. Keep watching us on our YouTube channel, comment, like. Stay well!

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website

World.title: Georgian PM Kobakhidze on ‘Global War Party’: ‘It is neither EU nor US, but can influence them’
World.content:
Georgian PM on the “Global War Party”

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has once again spoken about the so-called “Global War Party”, claiming that real individuals stand behind the term, but that naming them publicly would be “dangerous”.

Kobakhidze is in Dublin attending the ninth European Political Community (EPC) summit. On 12 November, he will attend the plenary session opening the summit and take part in a roundtable discussion on security and defence in democratic Europe. The European Political Community was established on the initiative of French President Emmanuel Macron as a forum for political dialogue and cooperation among European countries. Georgia has traditionally taken part in these summits, despite political contacts between the European Union and the Georgian government having dwindled in recent months.

According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” is neither the European Union nor the United States, although the forces behind it can influence official institutions within both.

“We have never specified exactly who we mean by the ‘Global War Party’, but there are real individuals behind this term. We make it clear that the ‘Global War Party’ is not the same as the European Union or the United States, although these people do use official channels to exert influence on Georgia,” Kobakhidze said.

The prime minister also spoke about a meeting attended by himself and his predecessor, Irakli Garibashvili. According to Kobakhidze, someone at the meeting urged Georgia to open a “second front”. He did not identify the individual or the official organisation they allegedly represented.

Kobakhidze said the Georgian government was firmly convinced that the individual belonged to the “Global War Party”. However, he stressed that neither the European Union nor the previous US administration was behind the incident.

He also referred to the term “deep state”, used by the current US administration, explaining that the Georgian government had a similar set of forces in mind, although it did not necessarily attach exactly the same meaning to the term.

The prime minister said the government was withholding the names of those involved in the interests of the country, as publicly discussing the matter would be “dangerous”. He also claimed that these forces used official channels to influence the policies of other countries, including Georgia.

During the interview, Kobakhidze also addressed the 2008 Russian-Georgian war, saying it could have been avoided. Drawing parallels with Ukraine, he argued that both the first and second wars in Ukraine could also have been prevented.

“Of course, Russia started these wars, just as it started the war in Georgia, which was provoked by foreign agents holding official positions in the Georgian government. At the same time, I am convinced that all three wars – the 2008 Russian-Georgian war and both wars in Ukraine – could have been avoided. Unfortunately, certain influential figures did not want these wars to be prevented,” he said.

Kobakhidze was asked why Georgia was seeking EU membership if, as the government claims, some representatives of European institutions had tried to drag the country into a war or interfered in its democratic elections.

In response, the prime minister said that the value of the European Union for Georgia lay in the EU itself, rather than in the particular politicians or bureaucrats who happened to represent its institutions at any given time.

The prime minister also discussed the geopolitical and economic importance of Georgia and the South Caucasus. He noted that the war in Ukraine and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East had made transport and economic routes connecting Europe with the East particularly important.

According to Kobakhidze, the outbreak of the war in Ukraine had cut the European Union off from the Russian market, which had previously played a significant role in the European economy. The EU had also lost access to relatively cheaper natural resources.

He added that the ongoing conflict in the Middle East was creating further obstacles to maintaining links with the East. “Under the current circumstances, Georgia and the South Caucasus remain the only route connecting Europe with the East. Maintaining close cooperation and strong ties is therefore crucial, not only for Georgia but also for Europe itself,” Kobakhidze said.

How the term “Global War Party” emerged and why Georgian Dream turned it into a political message

The concept of the so-called “Global War Party” entered Georgian Dream’s political rhetoric in 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Initially, representatives of the ruling party used the term “War Party” to refer to the opposition United National Movement. However, they later broadened its meaning, claiming that influential informal political groups in the West stood behind it.

According to Georgian Dream, these forces aim to drag Georgia into a war with Russia, effectively opening a “second front” alongside the conflict in Ukraine. Government representatives have linked this claim to statements by Ukrainian politicians, calls for Georgia to join sanctions against Russia, and political pressure on Tbilisi from Western countries.

The term “Global War Party” gained particular prominence in April 2024, when Bidzina Ivanishvili, honorary chairman of Georgian Dream, told a rally in Tbilisi that an international force was seeking to change Georgia’s government and drag the country into a war. Ivanishvili later explained that he had coined the term himself to distinguish between the “War Party” operating inside Georgia, which he used to describe the opposition, and the international forces allegedly backing it.

Although the authorities do not equate the “Global War Party” with the European Union or the United States, they have at various times referred to representatives of Western political institutions, MEPs, US politicians and international organisations in this context. Nevertheless, Georgian Dream has yet to name a single individual or organisation or present evidence to substantiate the existence of such a coordinated group.

The “Global War Party” narrative has become one of the central elements of Georgian Dream’s political rhetoric. Ahead of the 2024 parliamentary elections, the ruling party built its campaign around a choice between war and peace. It frequently portrayed the opposition and government critics as agents working in the interests of international forces seeking war.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s proposed hourly wage system: Who stands to benefit – workers, employers or state?
World.content:
Introduction of hourly wages in Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan plans to introduce a minimum hourly wage from 2027. The announcement was made on 11 November by Deputy Minister of Labour and Social Protection Zaur Aliyev during a meeting of the Milli Majlis Committee on Labour and Social Policy. According to Aliyev, the new system will initially apply to agricultural production and the catering sector.

Back in 2024, we reported that the introduction of hourly wages was under discussion in Azerbaijan. The main provisions of the proposed amendments to the Labour Code have now emerged.

The government and MPs have presented the initiative as a way to make employment more flexible and bring informal employment into the formal economy. However, critics have raised a different question:

Who will benefit from hourly wages, and could the system be used to split full-time positions into part-time roles in the public sector?

What does the draft law propose?

According to media reports, the draft law provides for hourly wages in two cases: when an employment contract is concluded for less than one month or when the working week does not exceed 20 hours. The Cabinet of Ministers will determine which sectors the new system will apply to.

The draft law also includes several safeguards for employees:

If an employee works less than one hour in a day, they must be paid at least the minimum hourly rate. Any part of an hour must be paid as a full hour.

For part-time employees paid a monthly salary, wages cannot fall below the minimum wage calculated in proportion to their working hours.

In organisations funded by the state budget, hourly wages can only be introduced if the organisation’s existing pay system allows for them, according to APA.

The minimum hourly rate has not yet been announced. According to Musa Guliyev, chairman of the Milli Majlis Committee on Labour and Social Policy, the draft law stipulates that:

The minimum hourly rate cannot be lower than the hourly equivalent of the minimum monthly wage.

However, the deputy minister of labour and social protection said that the proposed minimum hourly rate would be set above this level.

Since January 2025, Azerbaijan’s minimum monthly wage has stood at 400 manats (approximately $235). According to calculations by economist Natig Jafarli, this translates into around 2 manats and 50 gapiks per hour (approximately $1.47) for a five-day working week, or around 2 manats (approximately $1.18) for a six-day working week.

What do authorities say?

Musa Guliyev believes that hourly wages could make it easier for women with young children, students and pensioners to enter the labour market. According to him, the current minimum monthly wage system creates “inequality and social injustice” for part-time, seasonal and short-term workers.

However, the minimum wage cannot serve as a universal benchmark for all working arrangements.

Guliyev described hourly wages as a “social instrument that helps formalise informal employment”. Deputy Minister Zaur Aliyev, meanwhile, said the changes would allow for greater flexibility in applying the minimum wage system and make wage calculations more transparent.

The introduction of hourly wages has not come as a surprise. In May 2026, the government, the Confederation of Trade Unions and the Confederation of Entrepreneurs of Azerbaijan signed a General Collective Agreement for 2026–2028, committing to securing legislative amendments introducing a minimum hourly wage.

What concerns have critics raised?

Natig Jafarli, an economist and chairman of the Republican Alternative Party, raised three questions in a social media post.

The first concerns the benefits for workers. What would they gain from the introduction of a minimum hourly wage? Jafarli gave an example: if someone were hired for two hours a day and paid 5 manats (approximately $3), “who would benefit from this?”

The second question concerns the public sector. According to Jafarli, nearly half of all salaried employees work in the public sector, and it would be difficult to introduce hourly working arrangements for teachers, doctors, police officers and judicial employees. According to figures from the State Statistical Committee, as of 1 September, 834,200 of Azerbaijan’s 1,776,800 salaried employees, or around 47%, worked in the public sector.

The third question concerns the private sector. Jafarli argues that hourly wages should not be “imposed on the private sector, but rather encouraged through incentives”. In his view, employers spend time and money recruiting and training staff and may therefore have little incentive to hire two or three hourly paid employees instead of one full-time worker.

Economist Akif Nasirli argued last year that Azerbaijan was not ready to introduce such a system. He identified the lack of effective mechanisms to monitor compliance with labour legislation as the main obstacle.

Human resources manager Royal Ahmadov told Bakupost on 6 November that introducing hourly wages would not automatically lead to higher salaries. According to him, much would depend on the minimum hourly rate and how working hours are recorded.

“The main goal is not to provide employers with cheaper labour,” he stressed.

Could full-time positions be split into part-time roles?

Jafarli’s most serious concerns relate to the public sector. He believes the new system will primarily be used in state-funded organisations.

The economist gives the following example: a ministry employing 100 people on an average salary of 1,500 manats (approximately $882) could hire another 100 employees without dismissing anyone. If each of the two employees sharing a position worked four hours a day and earned 600 manats (approximately $353), the cost of one full-time equivalent position would fall from 1,500 to 1,200 manats (approximately $706).

According to Jafarli, this would allow the authorities to report the creation of “new jobs”, while saving the state budget 300 manats (approximately $176) per full-time equivalent position.

The economist describes this as “an attempt to create the appearance of sweeping changes without changing anything in substance”.

Government representatives have not yet responded to the criticism. However, the draft law does not exclude state-funded organisations from the new system: hourly wages would be permitted where the organisation’s existing pay structure allows for them.

Jafarli’s example of a four-hour working day also falls within the conditions set out in the draft law, as it would amount to a 20-hour working week over five days.

These concerns come against a backdrop of declining public-sector employment. In 2025, the number of public-sector employees fell by 2%, equivalent to around 17,000 jobs. Employment also declined in education and public administration, while private-sector employment grew by 5.2%.

Who could benefit?

Supporters of the new system argue that workers currently employed without formal contracts stand to benefit the most. MP Razi Nurullayev explained the reasoning last year:

“Workers will be paid for the hours they actually work.”

Economist Khalid Kerimli said in May that the current monthly wage system is primarily designed for full-time employees. In his view, introducing a minimum hourly rate would help protect the rights of part-time workers and give the Labour Inspectorate greater scope to monitor compliance with labour legislation.

However, Kerimli stressed that “introducing a minimum hourly wage does not mean an increase in the minimum wage”.

The impact of the reform will therefore depend on two decisions that have yet to be made: setting the minimum hourly rate and approving the list of sectors in which it will apply.

The new system will first be introduced in agricultural production and the catering sector. If hourly wages help bring informal employment in these industries into the formal economy, supporters’ expectations will be met. However, if the system leads to full-time positions being split into part-time roles and lower labour costs, critics’ concerns may prove justified.

World.title: Court removes leaders of Coalition for Change from hearing on banning political parties in Georgia – day 10 recap
World.content:
Georgia opposition ban trial

On 11 November, Georgia’s Constitutional Court held the tenth day of hearings on a lawsuit brought by ruling party Georgian Dream seeking to ban five opposition parties.

The hearing was at the question-and-answer stage, with judges questioning representatives of Georgian Dream, which brought the case.

Context. The case sets a precedent. The lawsuit was signed by 88 MPs from the ruling party. It seeks to ban five opposition groups: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. Georgian Dream argues that these parties have violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties that seek to overthrow or forcibly change the country’s constitutional order. The ruling party cites their refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the current government as one of its arguments. The application also accuses them of attempting to overthrow the government. The application also accuses Unity – National Movement of undermining the country’s independence and territorial integrity. The stated reason is the party’s alleged responsibility for the August 2008 war with Russia over South Ossetia, when the United National Movement was in power. All five parties deny the allegations. The court must deliver its final ruling by 24 June 2027. A simple majority is required to uphold the lawsuit, meaning at least four of the seven judges must vote in favour.

The main development on 11 November was the removal of Coalition for Change leaders Nika Gvaramia and Maia Kopaleishvili from the courtroom by Constitutional Court Chairman Revaz Nadaraia for arguing with the court and the plaintiffs.

Unless their request to be allowed back into the proceedings is granted, Gvaramia and Kopaleishvili will be barred from attending further hearings until the case is concluded.

Both have been among the most active representatives of the defendants. Kopaleishvili is a former Constitutional Court judge.

What led to Gvaramia and Kopaleishvili being removed

Judge Eva Gotsiridze asked the plaintiffs whether they had evidence that the opposition parties had taken part in or incited violence. In response, Georgian Dream MP Archil Gorduladze named Murtaz Zodelava and Paata Burchuladze. Both have been charged in connection with the events of 4 October 2025, when a group of activists attempted to storm the presidential palace.

Gorduladze said both men were linked to the United National Movement.

Nika Gvaramia objected: “Neither of them was a member of that party. If people were prosecuted simply because someone happened to be their former classmate, half of Georgia would be in prison – because all of you who have ruined this country were classmates!”

“As for those who have ruined it – well, here you all are!” Gorduladze retorted.

Gvaramia then asked whether being friends with someone meant belonging to the same political party: “If I acknowledge that someone is my friend, does that mean we are all conspirators plotting a coup?”

Constitutional Court Chairman Revaz Nadaraia deemed the exchange disruptive and ordered Gvaramia, followed by Kopaleishvili, to leave the courtroom.

Maia Kopaleishvili: “This is a show of force”

Kopaleishvili described her removal from the courtroom as a restriction on access to justice. “This was a deliberate act. It was an instruction from Georgian Dream,” she said. She then asked Nadaraia: “Why are you laughing? Have you already made your decision?”

Nadaraia replied that a formal request could be filed, adding that it was regrettable that Kopaleishvili did not know the law despite having worked at the Constitutional Court for 10 years.

“This is an insult,” Tengiz Tevzadze, another representative of Coalition for Change, told the presiding judge.

“Keep your colleague in check,” Nadaraia retorted.

Before those ordered to leave the courtroom departed, Nadaraia asked them: “For the past two days, have you deliberately been trying to get yourselves removed? Are you perhaps just trying to avoid answering questions?”

As she left, Kopaleishvili told the judges that they should be guardians of the Constitution, not people who restrict the rights of participants in legal proceedings. “This is a show of force,” she said.

She added that Georgian Dream would probably be pleased that the defendants would no longer be able to ask questions.

A day earlier, on 10 November, Nadaraia had repeatedly threatened to remove Kopaleishvili from the courtroom and accused her of trying to discredit the court.

Gvaramia, meanwhile, threatened to file a motion to have the presiding judge recused.

170 injured police officers and photographs on a laptop

The first point of contention during the day’s hearing concerned the evidence.

Judge Vasil Roinishvili asked the plaintiffs whether they had calculated the material damage caused to the state by the defendants, both domestically and internationally.

He cited problems related to visa regimes, critical international resolutions and cases of law enforcement officers being injured during mass unrest.

Gorduladze replied that around 170 law enforcement officers had been injured in November and December 2024 alone.

Opposition representatives demanded to know where this figure appeared as evidence in the lawsuit.

“Did we not agree to skip the examination of evidence, Mr Chairman?” Gvaramia asked sarcastically, referring to a decision taken the previous day.

“The court did not skip anything. Please do not exaggerate,” Nadaraia retorted.

Gorduladze then opened photographs of injured police officers on his work laptop and showed them to the court.

This triggered another verbal clash with Gvaramia. The presiding judge issued him a warning and threatened to remove him from the courtroom.

Giga Lemondzhava, another representative of Coalition for Change, also tried to speak. Nadaraia refused to give him the floor, saying: “Take your seat, or I will order you to be removed. I am not giving you the floor.”

The presiding judge explained that at the questioning stage, the parties were required to accept their opponents’ answers, even if they found them unsatisfactory.

Ana Buchukuri, a representative of the Gakharia for Georgia party, demanded that the court reprimand Gorduladze for making “offensive remarks” about the defendants.

Judge Gotsiridze: “Seeking to ban five parties at once is unprecedented”

Judge Eva Gotsiridze questioned the plaintiffs about the criteria for banning political parties.

She noted that seeking to ban five parties at once was truly unprecedented.

Gotsiridze also pointed out that the lawsuit describes several other parties as “anti-constitutional”, yet the plaintiffs are not seeking to ban them.

In her view, the term “anti-constitutional” was being applied to political parties too loosely. Following this logic, she said, more than 10 parties in Georgia – effectively a majority – could be classified as anti-constitutional.

The judge questioned whether the criteria proposed by the plaintiffs were sufficiently clear, suggesting they might be too vague, and asked how such an approach could be reconciled with democratic principles.

What happens next

The hearing will resume on 12 November at 12:00, with the question-and-answer stage continuing. This time, judges will question representatives of the opposition parties.

The presiding judge said the questioning is expected to continue until next Tuesday.

Hearings in the case have been held at the Constitutional Court in Batumi since 21 October. Since then, the defendants have filed around 14 motions, of which only one has been granted, and that only in part.

News in Georgia

World.title: ‘Who could be closer friend to us than Armenia?’ – Key takeaways from Iran’s vice-president’s visit to Yerevan
World.content:
Вице-президент Ирана – об объемах поставок газа в Армению

Iranian Vice-President Seyed Hamid Pourmohammadi arrived in Yerevan to attend the 19th session of the Armenian-Iranian Intergovernmental Commission. Armenian journalists asked him about economic ties and Iran’s position on the Armenian-American TRIPP project project, known as the “Trump Route”, which would run through Armenian territory. Armenian media also wanted to understand why Iran’s religious and secular authorities hold different positions on the issue.

Seyed Hamid Pourmohammadi stressed that Tehran’s official position was reflected in statements by Iran’s Foreign Ministry.

“Armenia and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan are our reliable partners, and we remain in constant contact. Tehran considers it important that the countries of the region themselves ensure and maintain security and peace. Iran welcomes any steps aimed at preserving and strengthening peace and security among the countries of the region,” the Iranian vice-president said.

Just days earlier, Ali Akbar Velayati, a senior adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, had sharply criticised Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan over the TRIPP project. Velayati accused Pashinyan of making Armenia increasingly dependent on the West, saying this “opens a new chapter of hostility and tension in the South Caucasus”. Velayati’s remarks prompted a response from Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei. He stressed that the Armenian authorities had assured Tehran that the implementation of the TRIPP project, near Iran’s borders, would involve neither the deployment of US military forces in the region nor any changes to existing borders. Baghaei added that, although Iran enjoys excellent relations with Armenia, it would continue to monitor developments and make its position public if necessary.

On increasing Iranian gas supplies to Armenia

Against the backdrop of discussions about a possible increase in the price of Russian gas supplied to Armenia, journalists asked whether Iran could increase its gas exports to the country.

“Iran is one of the countries with the largest gas reserves in the world. And if we have the capacity to export gas, who could be a closer friend to us than Armenia, to whom we would export it?” the Iranian vice-president replied.

Pourmohammadi said that one of the commissions established under Armenian-Iranian cooperation deals specifically with energy issues. According to him, the two sides discussed all possible areas of cooperation in this sector, including supplies of gas and diesel fuel, as well as issues related to Armenia’s long-term energy security.

However, the specific details of the agreements reached with Iran have not been disclosed.

Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan, who co-chairs the intergovernmental commission on the Armenian side, offered only the following details:

“There is not a single area in which we have not reached agreements. These include trade, energy (particularly gas and electricity), opportunities to expand existing project agreements, as well as infrastructure development and its mutual integration.”

The Iran–Armenia gas pipeline has a designed capacity of more than 2 billion cubic metres of gas a year. However, only a small fraction of this capacity is currently being used. Since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline has been under the control of Russian company Gazprom. Some experts believe that Iran cannot increase its gas exports without Russia’s consent. However, in July this year, Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan said there were no restrictions on receiving gas under the Armenian-Iranian “gas-for-electricity” programme. The programme began in 2009 and has already been extended until 2030. The minister assured that Armenia could at least double its gas imports from Iran.

Outcomes of the intergovernmental meeting

The Armenian government said that the intergovernmental meeting covered the implementation of joint projects in the following areas:

energy;

transport;

trade;

infrastructure;

business ties.

Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan particularly emphasised Armenia’s readiness to develop regional connectivity. He expressed confidence that unblocking regional transport links “would create new opportunities for the countries of the region”. In this context, he stressed the importance of Iran’s support for the Crossroads of Peace initiative. The Armenian government’s project aims to fully unblock transport links to and from Armenia in all directions.

The two sides also signed a memorandum of understanding following the intergovernmental commission meeting.

Connectivity also on the agenda of bilateral meetings

According to the Armenian prime minister’s office, Nikol Pashinyan discussed joint Armenian-Iranian programmes during his meeting with the Iranian vice-president. He said their successful implementation would “help develop and expand bilateral relations”.

“The interlocutors discussed issues related to the development of Armenia-Iran border infrastructure, joint road construction projects, as well as cooperation in energy, agriculture and other sectors,” the statement said.

Pashinyan and Pourmohammadi also discussed the unblocking of regional transport links and the opportunities this process could create for both countries.

Armenian Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan also discussed regional connectivity and the unblocking of transport links with the Iranian vice-president. Following their meeting, officials said that both countries saw “great potential” for further developing trade and economic ties and elevating bilateral relations to a strategic level.

World.title: Georgian authorities respond to Metropolitan Iov’s scathing sermon
World.content:
Georgian metropolitan criticises government



Metropolitan Iov (Akiashvili) of Ruisi and Urbnisi has sharply criticised the Georgian government, saying the ruling team has run out of steam and that the country needs better governance. In his sermon, the clergyman also addressed relations between the Church and the state, accusing the authorities of seeking to bring the Church under their control, turning a blind eye to corruption and neglecting national interests.

A sermon delivered on 10 November at Urbnisi Cathedral was published on the diocese’s social media page. Particular attention was drawn to Metropolitan Iov’s remarks, in which he criticised not only the government but also the Church’s senior leadership.

The metropolitan said the Georgian authorities lacked faith and were distant from the Church, warning that growing ties between the Church and the state threatened the independence of the clergy. He noted that, as the state provides funding to the Church, it is becoming increasingly difficult for clergy to speak openly about the government’s failings.

He also addressed the situation within the Church, saying that a significant proportion of the clergy had come to resemble government officials. He pointed out that while priests urge their congregations to endure poverty, help those in need and practise humility, their own behaviour is quite different.

The metropolitan also raised the issue of transparency in state funding for the Church. In his view, parishioners should know how every tetri (the smallest unit of Georgian currency) allocated to the Church is spent.

“Each of you, as parishioners, should know what the money is spent on and where every tetri goes,” he said.

Metropolitan Iov also recalled the reigns of David the Builder and Queen Tamar, noting that during periods of Georgia’s historical greatness, secular rulers worked in harmony with the Church. In his assessment, however, the current government has departed from this historical example.

A significant part of the sermon was also devoted to the so-called State Security Service “dossiers”. According to the metropolitan, the circulation of materials documenting private conversations and the personal lives of members of the clergy was intended to discredit the Church. He also recalled a statement by Bidzina Ivanishvili, in which he suggested that it was legitimate to criticise the Patriarch because he, too, was human and could make mistakes.

The so-called “dossier scandal”, involving the State Security Service (SSS), concerns alleged secret recordings and documents that emerged in the media in September 2021. The materials reportedly contained recordings of private conversations and phone calls, as well as information about the personal lives of senior representatives of the Georgian Orthodox Church, including metropolitans, bishops, priests and monks.

The documents pointed to widespread surveillance and wiretapping of the clergy. They covered internal Church disputes, relationships between members of the clergy, their private lives and political views. The authenticity of the recordings and the precise circumstances in which they were obtained have never been fully established.

The scandal became particularly serious because the State Security Service was named as the alleged source of the leak. The authorities were forced to respond to the allegations and seek to identify those who had made the documents public. However, it remains unclear to much of the public who was behind the collection and dissemination of the material.

Iov questioned why the identities of those who circulated the recordings had still not been established, despite promises from the authorities.

The metropolitan criticised the government over the spread of drug addiction and gambling addiction, the promotion of casinos, corruption and demographic problems. He noted that young people were leaving the country and villages were becoming deserted, while the scale of new construction, against the backdrop of a declining population, raised questions.

Iov also addressed the issue of David Gareji (the subject of a long-standing territorial dispute between Georgia and Azerbaijan over an undemarcated section of their border running through the sixth-century monastery complex – JAMnews), saying that the authorities’ response to the territorial challenges facing Georgia was inadequate.

“We must sound the alarm, because things cannot continue like this. It has become clear that the current government has completely exhausted its potential. Just as changes of government are commonplace around the world, we too should choose a better government in the future,” the metropolitan said.

He added that discussing the need for a change of government did not mean being hostile towards it, and that pointing out the government’s mistakes was a duty of the clergy.

Government and opposition reactions

The metropolitan’s sermon prompted mixed reactions from representatives of the government and the opposition.

Levan Machavariani, a Georgian Dream MP, said Metropolitan Iov’s political assessments were detached from reality and incorrect. He said he regretted that a senior clergyman was using the Church and the pulpit to make political statements.

Machavariani said the authorities were ready to provide comprehensive answers to any questions raised by the clergy. However, he stressed that such issues should be discussed through consultations before being made public.

“The people of Georgia know perfectly well how our government treats the Mother Church. If any problems or questions arise, we are accustomed to discussing them in a constructive manner,” the MP said.

Metropolitan Iov’s remarks were also criticised by Giorgi Gabunia, chairman of the parliamentary Committee on Culture. He described the metropolitan’s accusations as unfounded and said any confrontation between the Church and the state ran counter to the country’s interests. According to Gabunia, attempts are being made both inside and outside the country to provoke a conflict between the Church and the state.

The opposition took a different position from the ruling party. Pikria Chikhradze, a member of the Lelo – Strong Georgia party, described Metropolitan Iov’s sermon as significant and forceful. In her view, the Church’s criticism of the authorities may even have come too late.

Chikhradze drew attention to the so-called State Security Service “dossiers”, noting that the materials contained information about the private lives and correspondence of members of the clergy. In her view, it was virtually impossible to imagine that information on such a scale could have been collected without state involvement.

She also recalled the so-called “cyanide case” (a high-profile criminal scandal in 2017 involving allegations of a plot to murder a senior figure within the Georgian Orthodox Church – JAMnews), which, she said, still left many questions unanswered. Chikhradze argued that both cases were linked to attempts to undermine the Church’s authority.

The opposition politician said that Bidzina Ivanishvili could not tolerate the existence of independent institutions or influential figures capable of shaping public opinion. As an example, Chikhradze cited a plan to establish cannabis plantations, noting that the Church’s firm opposition had played an important role in halting the project. She also pointed out that, despite the Church’s objections to tax breaks for casinos, the authorities had gone ahead and adopted the relevant legislative amendments.

Pikria Chikhradze

Levan Bezhashvili, one of the leaders of the Unity – National Movement party, welcomed the metropolitan’s remarks. He said that Iov himself often criticises the party and is not a supporter of the National Movement, but that this did not diminish the significance of his latest statement.

“He made a very good statement – well done,” Bezhashvili said.

He added that Metropolitan Iov’s assessment reflected a reality recognised by both society and the Church.

Representatives of People’s Power, a pro-Russian movement that supports the ruling party, also responded to Metropolitan Iov’s criticism.

Tamta Megrelishvili said the metropolitan had used the church pulpit to deliver a political appeal, presenting his partisan position as a religious duty. She argued that accusing the authorities of “lacking faith” and calling for a change of government undermined the Church’s authority.

“In essence, this is an open political call from the church pulpit for a change of government,” Megrelishvili wrote.

Another People’s Power representative, Davit Kartvelishvili, took a much harsher view of Metropolitan Iov’s remarks. He accused the cleric of aligning himself with Saakashvili’s political camp and suggested that his calls for a change of government were driven by personal interests. Kartvelishvili also recalled previous allegations against Iov concerning the situation within his own diocese.

Pro-government commentator Davit Chikhelidze said Metropolitan Iov was accusing the authorities of “turning away from faith”, even though, in Chikhelidze’s view, the metropolitan’s own actions did not reflect the values he claimed to defend. He argued that the sermon harmed the country’s interests and was “playing into the enemy’s hands”.

The Church and Georgian Dream: Why Metropolitan Iov’s Statement Matters

The Georgian Orthodox Church occupies a unique position in the country’s political life. Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has established itself not merely as a religious organisation but as one of the most influential institutions in Georgian society. For decades, its authority has far outweighed that of individual political parties or government officials. As a result, maintaining good relations with the Church has been a major source of political legitimacy for virtually every Georgian government.

Georgian Dream, which came to power in 2012, forged particularly close ties with the Church. Bidzina Ivanishvili and members of the ruling team publicly emphasised the unique role of the Orthodox Church, while some influential members of the clergy openly expressed support for the new government. Over time, these ties became a key element of the ruling party’s political and ideological identity.

However, relations between the Church and the authorities have not always been smooth. Clergy members have previously criticised decisions made by the ruling team on a number of issues, including an initiative to legalise cannabis cultivation, as well as gambling and other matters of public concern. Nevertheless, such direct criticism of the government’s overall political course by senior Church figures remains rare.

What makes Metropolitan Iov’s statement particularly noteworthy is that he goes beyond criticising individual government decisions. He questions the established relationship between the state and the Church, raises concerns about the clergy’s financial dependence on the government and internal problems within the Church, and directly tells the authorities that they have exhausted their capacity to govern the country.

The statement carries additional weight given that, following the political changes of 2012, a significant part of the Church was favourably disposed towards Georgian Dream. Metropolitan Iov himself acknowledges that Church representatives supported the government, although he no longer regards that support as unconditional loyalty.

Trust between the Church and the government became a particularly contentious issue in 2021, when media outlets published materials suggesting possible covert surveillance by the State Security Service (SSS). Thousands of documents pointed to possible surveillance of clergy members, politicians, journalists and diplomats. The scandal raised serious questions both within the Church and in Georgian society more broadly, but those responsible have yet to be identified.

It is also worth noting that, according to the Centre for Social Justice, the Orthodox Church received more than 283 million lari (approximately $109,158,525) from central and municipal budgets between 2020 and 2024.
