World.title: New Plymouth-built storage tanks headed for Australian fertiliser plant
World.content:
The export of three massive ammonia storage tanks from New Plymouth is being heralded as evidence the Taranaki engineering sector still has a future.

Built by Dialog Fitzroy for Hiringa Energy, the 35-metre long, 3.5-metre diameter, 100-tonne pressure vessels have been transported across town at night this week to Port Taranaki, before shipping to Australia.

As a huge ammonia bullet approaches on State High 3 amid a blaze of flashing lights and pouring rain, its scale becomes immediately apparent.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408289076112

Standing more than 5m high, it's carried on a 12 axle trailer - six axles each end with an 8m spacer - and it seems to go on forever.

Jarvis Miller of PTS Logistics is behind the wheel.

PTS Logistics driver Jarvis Miller said navigating such a long load was challenging. RNZ / Robin Martin

"The length of it is one of the key issues. It's 36m long, so that's just over a standard truck-and-a-half's length, without being able to turn in the centre.

"The total length of the unit is about 56m, because the average truck is about 21m."

Supplied

He is about to take the load over a bypass ramp built especially for similar transports headed out to the 'Think Big' project at Motunui in the mid-1980s.

"It's a bit of a greasy night, and it's all wet and slippery, so we're hooking up another truck just to give us a little more power over the climb here.

"All up, we're about 215 tonne, with just the main truck. One truck won't quite do it, so we've got another one on standby."

The pressure vessels are on their way to Hiringa Energy's $120 million Good Earth Green Hydrogen and Ammonia project in Moree, New South Wales.

Chief executive Andrew Clennet says they will be used in Australasia's first green fertiliser production plant.

Hiringa CE Andrew Clennett says the partnership with Dialog Fitzroy is an example of what Taranaki firms can achieve when they work together. RNZ / Robin Martin

"We have a large solar farm, we have some batteries, and obviously, the sun goes up and down, and it stores that energy and we feed it into an electrolyzer that makes hydrogen.

"Then we take that hydrogen and turn that, combined with nitrogen from the air, into ammonia, which is what goes into these bullets."

He says the partnership with Dialog Fitzroy is a perfect example of what Taranaki companies can do on an international stage.

"They are out there helping us lay out all the equipment coming in, helping us tie it in... all the pipework to bring it together.

"Utilising all the expertise that we've developed over years of activity here in Taranaki, bringing in modules from international, and getting really good at placing and them hooking them up, and making sure that's done safely and efficiently, and it works." .

Dialog Fitzroy general manager Doug Timanus says such projects are vital for retaining skilled workers in the province.

Dialog Fitzroy project manager Shareece Kahukaka-Taylor and general manager Doug Timanus. RNZ / Robin Martin

"It's important for Taranaki and New Zealand, as well as Dialog Fitzroy, because it's very competitive trying to do something like this in New Zealand, rather in Asia, and like Andrew said, the skillset is going out of tradespeople and apprentices, so it is really important and we've been really lucky to be involved."

Meanwhile, Miller reflects on a cool cruise across town.

"There were a couple of corners where we turned at a 90-degree angle, but it's not only the angle, it's the change in elevation of the road, and because it is such a long load, we have to lift and lower the suspension, so it doesn't bottom out.

"It's a bit of fun, especially on a night like tonight, but I enjoy it. This is what I live for."

World.title: Once thought safe, South Island's giant wētā are disappearing
World.content:
Conservationists fear the clock is ticking for New Zealand's "large and charismatic" Southern Alps giant wētā.

A new study shows numbers of the native insect have plummeted by more than 90 percent at historical strongholds high in the mountains - long thought to be beyond the reach of introduced predators.

Recently published in the New Zealand Journal of Zoology, the research was instigated by Wētā Conservation Trust chair Danilo Hegg, an avid outdoorsman, who was bewildered by his own lack of encounters with Deinacrida pluvialis.

"I have been tramping in the Southern Alps for decades... and I started asking myself questions. I said, if this species is not threatened, how come I never come across it?

"The problem was basically that we had one single survey in time done in '92... and because the species was assumed to be doing fine, nobody ever checked again for nearly 30 years."

Hegg and other researchers scoured a site in Westland, finding just three living Southern Alps giant wētā, where 36 of the insects were recorded in 1992.

They then searched a site in Fiordland, where two adult male were recorded in 2023.

Over the course of 36 hours, the researchers did not spot a single wētā - instead recording evidence of rats.

An adult female Southern Alps giant weta in Westland. Supplied/Danilo Hegg

"What was written in the 90s was that this species was safe, because it was above the level of rat invasion," Hegg said. "Basically, they thought rats don't go that high."

Deinacrida pluvialis were unable to fly, too heavy to jump, too big to hide and did not have a strong bite, making them highly vulnerable to predation, he said.

The species was reclassified as 'Threatened - Nationally Endangered' in 2022.

Although there was at least one other known population in Mt Aspiring National Park, it was almost impossible to determine how many of the insects remained across the South Island, he said.

Hegg and other conservationists were keen to figure out where predator control work should be scaled up.

"The population number... eventually it will go to zero, so we do need to do something about it," he said.

Department of Conservation technical advisor Warren Chinn said the "large and charismatic" critters had long fascinated him and other entomologists.

Southern Alps giant wētā were remarkably resilient, slowing right down in winter and surviving under cold alpine rocks for extended periods, he said.

The nocturnal insects could measure up to 5.5cm long, not including their legs or antennae.

Chinn said the new study highlighted a collision between "two profoundly different evolutionary trajectories of animals".

One of the sites surveyed for Southern Alps giant weta in Westland. Supplied/Emma Gregg

"You've got the rodents and the stoats coming from the northern hemisphere... into Aotearoa, where we have a strongly avian and invertebrate fauna isolated since its break-up 65 million years ago from Gondwana," he said.

"Rare species in isolated lands like our country are extraordinarily valuable, as books of genetic and biological information that represent the diversity of all life on Earth."

Predator Free New Zealand chief executive Jessi Morgan said New Zealand too often lost species faster than expected.

"It's been such a long time between studies and we've seen such a massive decline - and if that study hadn't been done, we'd have no idea," she said.

Morgan said improved tracking technology showed rats, hedgehogs and feral cats all penetrating high-alpine areas above 2000 metres.

World.title: Three-week vote count no barrier to negotiations - expert
World.content:
The 20-day wait for the final vote count is about accuracy, not just special votes - and if politicians are anxious there's nothing stopping negotiations starting now.

That's the view of constitutional law expert Graeme Edgeler, who along with the Electoral Commission is pointing to technological changes to speed up the process next time.

'The real count'

A week after the election, and with a fortnight left before the final result, chief electoral officer Karl le Quesne told RNZ most of the time taken was to ensure accuracy.

"We take a great deal of care to make sure it's complete and accurate, so people can trust the result," he said.

Audio player for " The Aftermath 2026: How each party is feeling post-election... and that phone call " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2567882%2Fthree-week-vote-count-no-barrier-to-negotiations-expert

The Aftermath 2026: How each party is feeling post-election... and that phone call Caucus Download MP3 59m

Improvements had already been made since 2023, when a rushed process meant multiple errors were missed.

"We've strengthened not only that those checks get done, but we've reviewed those checks and improved them to make it easier to actually apply them, and that's one of the real reasons we still need the 20 days to get a complete set of results produced," le Quesne said.

The process includes recounts of ordinary votes, checking votes against enrolments, tallying the number of electorate and party votes to ensure they match, removing any ineligible votes, waiting a legally mandated 10 days for the special votes to be sent to their electorate (many from overseas), counting the special votes, and doing a final series of quality assurance checks.

Le Quesne said a key thing slowing down the count was the need to combine the rolls from the 2700 voting places into one for each electorate, to ensure names had not been crossed out twice.

Edgeler said such cases then needed to be investigated.

"Maybe it was a mistake - you know, Dan Smith voted at one, and they accidentally crossed off Dean Smith's name ... [but otherwise] if you vote twice, all of your votes get cancelled."

Constitutional law expert Graeme Edgeler. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The actual special vote count would happen at the end, which he said aimed to avoid votes being disallowed due to bias from those doing the counting.

"Sort of, someone objecting because 'oh, this is a vote for the other person, my scrutineer is going to try and object and say that shouldn't be counted', so just a protective measure."

Edgeler said New Zealanders should be assured any mismatch between the election night result and "the real count, the careful count" was not only because of special votes but thorough checks and tallies.

Le Quesne said the commission was making good progress.

"It's going really well. We've just about completed the production of one roll for every electorate; we're well into doing the second count of the ordinary votes that were cast before election day and on election day; we're getting the special votes repatriated, they're starting to land in their home electorates.

"We've already started the process on validating and qualifying those - so, we don't do the steps one after each other, we do them at the same time."

A chart showing the post-election process. Supplied / Electoral Commission

'Nothing stopping politicians from starting their negotiations'

Some political parties have been meeting since the election but with the result "too close to call" have largely delayed negotiations for forming a government until the final vote count.

But Edgeler said there was no need, pointing to John Key's first government formed in 2008.

"With the Māori Party as it then was, with United Future, and with ACT, they form a four-party [government], John Key is sworn in as prime minister and announces government ministers before the final count is released. There is nothing stopping politicians from starting their negotiations now if they want."

He said with the result so close, they probably should wait until the final count before announcing a government, but National could be talking to both ACT and New Zealand First at least - and with Opportunity having promised to talk first to the party with the most seats, to Qiulae Wong's negotiating team as well.

"National, plus ACT, plus New Zealand First, plus Opportunity - even if the special votes go badly for the government ... it seems it's almost inconceivable based on historic patterns of special votes that group of four parties would not be a majority.

"It's just a question of whether the three opposition parties and Opportunity could also form - but given that Opportunity said they want to speak to the largest party first, based on the votes we have, that is almost certainly the National Party."

Chief electoral officer Karl le Quesne. RNZ / Russell Palmer

Future voting: Barcodes and auto-updates

For the impatient, changes are coming for future elections that would help speed the process up.

Le Quesne said the commission would soon be trialling a new digital roll mark-off system.

"Instead of having a paper-based roll in every voting place, you could have a electronic roll and you mark people off by scanning a barcode on their Easy Vote card.

"That would make it much quicker to produce that one roll for each electorate, but it would also help you to avoid people voting more than once because you'd be able to identify straight away that they'd voted in another voting place."

Edgeler also pointed to changes that had passed the legislative hurdles but were not installed in time for the 2026 election, which would automatically change someone's enrolment when they changed details like their address with other agencies like Work and Income, or the Transport Agency.

"That information will be passed along to the Electoral Commission who will just say 'okay, this person was enrolled here, they've moved, we're going to change their enrolment'.

"The system we currently have is that information will be passed to the Electoral Commission and they'll write to you saying 'oh, it looks like you've moved, could you please enrol?'".

World.title: Explainer: What is a hung Parliament and could it actually lead to a new election?
World.content:
Explainer: What happens if nobody can agree who should be in charge of the country?

The extremely close preliminary election results - both Labour and National are locked only a few thousand votes apart - have raised fears of a 'hung parliament', which could prolong the wait for a next government or even theoretically lead to a new election.

We're all waiting around for the special votes to be counted by 27 November, but in the meantime, many wonder what happens if the election basically ends in a tie.

What exactly is a hung parliament?

Quite simply, it's a Parliament that's evenly divided between factions, meaning no one group can form a majority.

Often, that just means a coalition must be formed to create a majority, as happened in the 2017 and 2023 elections, but what if the Parliament stays hung? That's where it gets tricky.

Our Parliament has a base number of 120 MPs (before any possible overhangs), which means a 60-60 tie between blocs is quite possible.

With the very likely overhang after election results, it gets a little trickier. RNZ's current tally of the preliminary vote shows a Parliament with a whopping 131 seats - 11 as the result of an overhang.

Until we get the final count on 27 November, there's no way of knowing if we have an even or odd number of Parliament members. Even numbers make the possibility of a hung Parliament, with the current tight vote margins, considerably higher.

Hung parliaments are not unique to our MMP system, which is marking its 30th anniversary.

Under the old first-past-the-post system, the 1922 and 1928 elections both left no single party with a parliamentary majority. Governments were subsequently formed with support from other MPs or parties.

We're technically under a caretaker government until National leader Christopher Luxon finds out if he has the numbers. MICHAEL BRADLEY / AFP

What would happen next?

Right now, as you may have heard, the government is under a 'caretaker convention'. In the event of a hung Parliament, that would continue to be the case.

That means the current government is still in charge, until the results are resolved, but "significant decisions will be deferred or attended to with a light touch", as political scientist Grant Duncan wrote recently.

Coalition talks are intended to create the next government and they've been known to last anything from just over a week to nearly two months.

The waka-jumping or party-hopping law also prevents MPs from going rogue and crossing sides to break up a stalemate.

Audio player for " What power does the caretaker government have? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics/2567881%2Fexplainer-what-is-a-hung-parliament-and-could-it-actually-lead-to-a-new-election

What power does the caretaker government have? Checkpoint Download MP3 9m

"Our beautiful caretaker convention gives the negotiations the time and space needed to deliver an outcome, however long that takes," said Dean Knight, an expert in constitutional law at Te Herenga Waka Victoria University of Wellington.

Labour's Chris Hipkins, Opportunity's Qiulae Wong and Nationals's Christopher Luxon RNZ

Is there any way to break up a stalemate?

The governor-general could "gently remind the parties and their leaders of their obligation to the country to try and reach some negotiated solution", Otago University law professor Andrew Geddis has written.

"But the governor-general can't force anyone to do anything and she shouldn't try to engineer any particular outcome (because she needs to remain politically neutral)," Geddis wrote.

If a prime minister was holding up the next government's formation, they could also be rolled by their own party.

"PMs serve as long as they maintain the confidence of their cabinet colleagues, their party caucuses and, ultimately, the House on behalf of the electorate," Knight said.

"The lifeblood of confidence applies equally within the parliamentary interregnum and process of government formation.

"If a PM's stubbornness is not supported by their colleagues, they could roll the PM, and replace them with someone more prepared to deal or to return to the polls."

A request for a new election would have to go to Governor-General Dame Cindy Kiro. Mark Papalii

Wait, could there actually be a new election here?

In a speech in March this year, Governor-General Dame Cindy Kiro said that "if it... became clear that no government could be formed, another election may be required".

If a hung Parliament persists, there are mechanisms to have a new election, but don't place any bets on that happening.

Such an act would be subject to the caretaker convention and require effective majority support in the House, Knight said. A request from the prime minister for a new election would then go to the governor-general.

"The caretaker prime minister would be expected to consult other parties and seek majority support for calling a new election," Dame Cindy said in her own remarks.

"In that situation, it would be up to members of Parliament to ensure that the governor-general is never required to consider calling an election without ministerial advice."

"The governor-general won't accept a request for a fresh election during the caretaker period unless the PM demonstrates a majority of MPs in the incoming Parliament support such a course," Knight said.

That would be an absolute last resort, pretty much everyone would agree.

"There should be no need for a fresh election," Duncan wrote.

"It's up to the parties now to find a majority. There are strong incentives for them to do so and no party wants to be blamed for forcing the country to return to the polls."

The governor-general does also have the reserve powers to dismiss a prime minister, to force a dissolution of Parliament and call new elections, to refuse a prime minister's request for an election and to refuse assent to legislation - but really, nobody wants that to happen.

"It is the responsibility of the members of Parliament to resolve matters, so that the governor-general is not required to consider dissolving Parliament and calling an election without ministerial advice," the Cabinet Manual notes.

"These powers to act without or even against ministerial advice are reserved for the most extreme situations, and with the exception of the appointment of a prime minister following an election, no New Zealand Governor-General has ever needed to use them," the governor-general's own office notes.

What's happened in other countries?

Many countries have had elections where no one party has a majority.

For instance, Israel is currently wrestling with its most recent election, where opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been tasked with forming a new government.

Israel had to hold two new elections, after an April 2019 vote repeatedly failed to result in a coalition.

Bulgaria, Spain and Green have also held more elections, after governments failed to form.

"Precedents abroad like Belgium and Northern Ireland show us [we] could be in a twilight for an extended period without the sky falling," Knight said.

"Importantly, while we haven't needed the caretaker convention for a long period or even after Parliament's first sitting, it is capable of managing a long period of throttled-back government and does so in a way faithful to democratic principle."

The grand champion for going without a formed government is Belgium, which went more than 500 days without settling their next government in 2010/11.

World.title: Thousands of operations delayed during winter flu season
World.content:
New figures show thousands of patients had their operations put off at the height of this winter's flu season.

They show the impact winter had on the health system, specifically on patients waiting for surgery in the public system.

In August, several hospitals said they were deferring planned procedures during one of the worst flu seasons for years.

Health NZ figures show about 5000 fewer planned operations were done in July and August, compared with May and June - a drop from 38,824 to 33,778.

Planned or elective surgeries were considered non urgent, but included procedures such as hip replacements or gallbladder removal for conditions that could have big impacts on patients' lives.

A Health NZ spokesperson said the "unprecedented surge" in influenza and other respiratory illnesses meant hospital care was in a lot of demand this winter.

Planned care could be deferred during busy illness seasons for several reasons. One was staff sickness, as doctors, nurses and other staff were hit by the same illnesses impacting the rest of the community.

Another was that hospital beds were more likely needed by acutely unwell people, meaning fewer beds were available for post operative care.

Health NZ said surgery was only deferred when it was clinically safe to do so.

"The decision to postpone surgery is not taken lightly," the spokesperson said.

"Decisions are made on a case-by-case basis by clinical teams, with patient safety and wellbeing the highest priority."

Released to RNZ under the Official Information Act, the figures showed the system managed a small increase in operations carried out this winter, compared with last winter.

About 370 more surgeries were done this July and August than the same months in 2025, despite many health professionals saying this winter was the worst for illness in a decade.

Health NZ said its $25 million winter plan to increase care in the community, as well as beds and staffing in hospital, was behind the improvement.

World.title: Defence Force personnel primed to cover for striking fire crews
World.content:
Fire and Emergency has asked the Defence Force for help to man trucks if 10-hour strikes by firefighters go ahead.

Contingency plans laid out this week and seen by RNZ are for trained NZDF firefighters to man FENZ firetrucks at up to 20 "priority" fire stations.

The first of a series of 10-hour strikes by Professional Firefighters' Union members has been notified for 27 November.

FENZ's plan requires the Defence Minister's approval. RNZ has gone to the minister for comment.

"NZDF is asked to advise how many crews could be made available," said one plan.

The agency has been doing a "proximity" analysis to pick the priority stations.

Both FENZ and the union say the industrial action is unprecedented, and FENZ says it could have "fatal consequence". The union says the agency's long-running failure to do a deal is putting the public at risk.

The plans show each four-crew firetruck with defence personnel on board could fight building and vegetation fires, and rescue anyone trapped.

FENZ ladder trucks used on the likes of multistoreys and industrial fires would not be available, nor would medical co-responses, or responses to cliff rescues, hazardous substances callouts, or urban search and rescue.

"Our ability to deliver our functions under our legislation are reduced considerably and, in some functions, withdrawn completely," said another plan around the use of volunteers.

The defence plan shows the troops would stay under the command of their own officer, but under FENZ control, with a FENZ commander at each station.

Volunteer firefighters have also been primed to provide cover, but their union said they will not be asked to do anything they were not trained for.

"They're not going to do anything that they don't do now," said United Fire Brigades Association head Bill Butzbach.

"Here's an example. If there's a major chemical spill on the Ferguson container terminal in Auckland, they're not going to it."

Volunteers had been advised to expect any 10-hour strike period to be busier than normal, especially in the big cities, Butzbach told RNZ.

The strike action follows a years-long fight over pay and conditions that culminated in mass rejection of a pay offer last week.

The minister in charge of FENZ is now Nicole McKee, as Brooke van Velden, who was internal affairs minister, did not stand for re-election.

World.title: Most questions about RNZ's budget blunder could be answered by Christmas - expert
World.content:
The former head of Audit New Zealand says there's no reason why most of the questions surrounding RNZ's shock financial loss cannot be answered by Christmas.

The public broadcaster is commissioning an independent review of its nearly $12 million budget blowout after a litany of financial blunders.

It also plans to cut dozens of jobs.

The broadcaster's chief financial officer Hilary Parker resigned unexpectedly in October.

A spokesperson for RNZ said at this stage, the full terms of reference for the inquiry had not been established and there was no timeframe for completing the review.

The former executive director at Audit New Zealand (now the Audit Office), Stephen Walker, who is familiar with such reviews, said the terms of reference would dictate what could be achieved, but expected most of the review could be completed before Christmas.

Stephen Walker. Supplied / OAG

"The work on the review could take several weeks or so. It will be tight to get it done before everybody shuts up for the end of the year.

"But that makes it even more important to get it underway, right?" he said, pointing to the proposed job cuts.

Walker said such an inquiry would involve interviewing a "good dozen or more" people from the board, leadership team, and finance team, and a range of information to consider.

"I think it could be done, or it may be done in a couple of phases. You may have some sort of interim views this side of Christmas and then maybe a final report [early next year]," he said.

Walker said it meant a reviewer would have to be up and running in the next couple of weeks.

RNZ chairman Brent Impey - who assumed the role in July - earlier said the review would look into RNZ's culture, why its own reports failed to pick up the errors, whether it had the right disciplines and accountabilities in place, and whether senior leaders had been intentionally misled.

World.title: Trio killed in Diwali horror crash named
World.content:
The three people killed in a horror Diwali crash in Auckland on Sunday night have now been named.

The newlywed couple and their brother-in-law died after the car they were in lost control at a roundabout on Great South Road, came off the road and tore through a Takanini BurgerFuel restaurant.

RNZ understands the vehicle is believed to have been travelling at more than 150 kilometres per hour.

Daljit Singh. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Daljit Singh, spokesperson for the Supreme Sikh Society, said the bodies of the victims had been identified as Sukhdeep Singh, 33, his 29-year-old wife, Sukhvir Kaur, and brother-in-law Gurpreet Singh, 38.

Of the couple, husband Sukhdeep had lived in New Zealand for seven years, Daljit said, while wife Sukhvir had arrived six months ago.

Gurpreet had a young son and wife in India and had called Aotearoa home for three years. He worked as a courier driver for New Zealand Post.

Daljit said it was a "huge tragedy".

"They were actually celebrating Diwali at the Manurewa Gurudwara, where they were coming from when this incident was happened," he said, adding that the circumstances of the crash were unclear.

"I'm actually in regular touch with the police and we're talking to them almost every two or three hours, but so far, about the investigations, they haven't actually released any information because they still interviewing some other people as well ... we know that they've been to their employer ... but just waiting for their outcome."

Three people died after the car they were in crashed through the front of a BurgerFuel restaurant in South Auckland. RNZ / Nick Monro

It was hoped their bodies would be released by the coroner on Friday morning, Daljit said. Once that happened, they would be washed and a Sikh preacher would say prayers before they were sent back to India for cremation, as per the families' wishes.

He had also been in contact with the victims' families back in India. Gurpreet's brother was yet to break the news to his parents when Daljit last spoke to him on Thursday morning, but had agreed to do so before it broke via the media.

A Givealittle page in support of the victims' families had raised more than $13,000 within 11 hours of being set up, and Daljit said others were calling him to ask how they could contribute.

"There is so much generosity in the community," he said.

"It's not [just] Sikh communities, it's the wider communities, everbody is helping. There's a lot of calls we're receiving from politicians and local councillors, local boards and wider whanau, even our Māori iwi organising a prayer, to do the karakia on Monday."

Glass is strewn across the ground outside. RNZ / Nick Monro

Creator of the Givealittle page, Mandeep Singh Brar, said the victims' "sudden loss has left their families, friends and loved ones devastated".

"Your kindness, support and prayers mean more than words can express".

Emergency services were called to the crash just after 10:15pm on Sunday night.

World.title: FA scrambles for Jordan alternative with Socceroos reluctant to travel
World.content:
Socceroos players remain unwilling to travel to Jordan as Football Australia (FA) scrambles for alternatives to playing an upcoming friendly in Amman.

But US Soccer's decision to withdraw its team from the under-17 World Cup in ‌Qatar over safety concerns is not expected to affect either the Socceroos or their Joeys counterparts.

The Socceroos and Joeys are both in camp in Doha ahead of their respective friendlies and World Cup campaigns.

Popovic refuses to blacklist Socceroos who pull out of Jordan friendly Australia coach Tony Popovic insists Socceroos players who are reluctant to play Jordan due to security concerns will not be blacklisted from the national team set-up if they elect to withdraw from his squad.

The senior team is due to face Qatar on Saturday (AEDT) before travelling to Amman to face Jordan on November 18.

The latter is the issue, with PFA boss Beau Busch saying last week that Socceroos players had "overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated".

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel to Jordan "due to the unpredictable security situation" and the "threat of terrorism".

FA had been keen for the game in Jordan to proceed, but has said it was monitoring the security situation in the area.

The friendlies against Qatar and Jordan were arranged as preparations for January's Asian Cup, but the postponement of the tournament to December 2027 due to conflict in Saudi Arabia has decreased their significance.

Martin Kugeler has flown to Doha to find a solution. (Getty Images: Ayush Kumar)

FA heavy hitters including chief executive Martin Kugeler and football director Heather Garriock flew to Doha this week, as did Busch and men's head of player relations Jon McKain.

Players are not expected to back down and agree to play in Jordan, likely leaving cancellation or relocation as the options.

One option is Australia remaining in Qatar and playing Jordan in Doha.

But that proposal is understood to have been met with some reluctance from both the Qatari and Jordanian football associations.

Jordan has already had to deal with Indonesia pulling out of a friendly this window.

Playing the Jordan game somewhere in southern Europe is another option, along with cancelling or postponing the game altogether.

Coach Tony Popovic, due to speak to media in his pre-match press conference on Thursday night, has indicated no players would be blacklisted from future selection if they withdrew from his squad for security reasons.

Elsewhere, in ‌a letter sent to players, US Soccer said it was cancelling its team's pre-tournament camp and its participation in the under-17 World Cup "in light of current circumstances".

US Soccer cited US State Department's Level 3 travel advisory for Qatar and related ‌directives for ‌embassy ⁠staff and families.

But the Joeys are not expected to follow the US in withdrawing from the under-17 tournament in Qatar, while the Socceroos are understood not to have issues with being in Qatar.

AAP

World.title: Kiwi duo Ponga and Waaka claim Golden Boot awards after stunning seasons
World.content:
New Zealand duo Kalyn Ponga and Stacey Waaka have been named the men's and women's Golden Boot winners after outstanding individual seasons at their respective clubs.

Ponga scored six tries as he led Newcastle to the NRL grand final before scoring two further tries for the Kiwis at the Rugby League World Cup despite suffering a broken arm.

Waaka, a cross-code star, scored nine tries for the Warriors in just 10 NRLW appearances and added nine tries in four World Cup appearances.

Both players will be in action for New Zealand's men's and women's sides in their respective World Cup finals this weekend as they take on Australia.

Ponga is New Zealand's eighth men's Golden Boot winner, joining Hugh McGahan, Stacey Jones, Benji Marshall, Shaun Johnson, Roger Tuivasa-Sheck, Joseph Manu and James Fisher-Harris.

Waaka is the third New Zealand player to win the women's award, joining Raecene McGregor and Georgia Hale.

Ponga edged out his Cup final counterpart Reece Walsh, Samoa powerhouse Francis Manulelua, Tonga centre Robert Toia and Kiwi centre Casey McLean who were all shortlisted for the men's award.

The Wheelchair golden boot was taken out by England's Rob Hawkins ahead of Friday night's final in Wollongong between England and France.

World.title: Addo-Carr free to leave Eels as club rejects extension opportunity
World.content:
Josh Addo-Carr is free to leave Parramatta immediately after the Eels advised the former Test winger the club would not offer him a contract extension beyond 2027.

After a series of bizarre twists and turns, the Eels have decided Addo-Carr is not wanted after next season and he can start hunting for a new NRL club.

The development comes despite the NRL integrity unit clearing the 31-year-old to return to Parramatta after failing a roadside random drugs test in October.

The ex-NSW State of Origin and Kangaroos star received an unexpected lifeline when his B sample came back negative earlier this month.

"The Parramatta Eels would like to provide an update regarding Josh Addo-Carr following a driving incident in September," an Eels statement read on Thursday.

"After reviewing all relevant information, including the negative result of the B sample, the club has cleared Josh in relation to the issues raised following the incident.

"The NRL has also confirmed it will not be taking any further action, and the club now considers the matter closed.

"Separately, the club has informed Josh and his management that it will not be seeking to extend his current contract beyond the end of the 2027 season."

The Eels will keep the door ajar for Addo-Carr to see out his 2027 contract, but will not stand in his way if he secures a new contract with a rival club.

The 31-year-old is due back at pre-season training with the Eels next week, as his management looks to secure the flyer a future elsewhere.

AAP

World.title: Cummins to 'respond properly' to Khawaja claims tomorrow
World.content:
Australia Test captain Pat Cummins is set to break his public silence on the sandpaper scandal after taking time to "better understand" the allegations of ex-teammate Usman Khawaja.

Test captain Cummins announced on social media that he would speak to reporters tomorrow morning at Cricket NSW's headquarters in Sydney.

"Happy to speak with any and all media about the events of this week," Cummins posted today.

"I've taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly."

Cricket Australia is yet to confirm an official time but Cummins said he would speak at 9:30am AEDT between a training session and the start of day three of NSW's Sheffield Shield clash with South Australia.

Many in Australian cricket circles have been demanding Cummins publicly respond to Khawaja's explosive claims in his book about ball tampering in Australia's Test team.

Khawaja told Nine Newspapers of the plot to use sandpaper on the ball in the infamous 2018 Test against South Africa in Cape Town: "It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us."

The retired batter also wrote of Australia's ball tampering in the preceding Ashes Test series against England.

Cummins and fellow fast bowlers Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood, and spinner Nathan Lyon, have previously denied knowledge of Australia taking sandpaper onto the Cape Town ground. Starc reiterated that stance on Tuesday.

AAP

World.title: Vescio won't quit this habit even if 'it's uncomfortable to watch'
World.content:
There was a moment in Darcy Vescio's press conference for their 100th game where they hesitated on a word.

The inaugural Carlton player has long been a voice and face for the competition, including for the LGBTQ+ community, and particularly so after coming out as non-binary in 2021.

They have always championed that AFLW is for everyone — and everyone is welcome.

Want to win an AFLW flag? Club culture matters, data shows AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher says the gap between AFLW clubs getting workplace culture right is widening and the results can be seen on the field.

But while that is true, they do not exactly want everyone to feel comfortable at their home semifinal on Saturday.

As Princes Park, Carlton's HQ, is used as a home venue for many teams, a lot of the Blues' opposition have become very familiar with the ground.

North Melbourne star Ash Riddell spoke very publicly about loving the ground ahead of the Kangaroos' qualifying final with Carlton last week.

"You want [opposition] people to not feel… welcome," Vescio said, to laughter.

"When they come here. Even heading into last week's game … Riddell was very public in saying she loves playing at Ikon Park because they've built great memories here and they're really home here.

"So that's something we do want to wrestle back."

Darcy Vescio is the first Carlton player to reach 100 AFLW games. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Vescio has said it has been tough to watch other teams play at their home during finals series. Carlton did not make the final eight from 2022 to 2024.

The Blues will have that opportunity when they come up against Hawthorn this weekend in a semifinal.

When Vescio runs out for that game, they will become the first Carlton player to reach 100 games in the AFLW.

Over the course of their career, Vescio has also played a pivotal role in the AFLW collective bargaining agreement negotiations over the years, helping drive the league's pay, conditions and professionalism forward.

"That adds, not weight, but it makes the footy experience a lot more rich," Vescio said.

"I love the game and every challenge that that brings, physically and mentally."

Darcy Vescio sees their role as more than just a football player despite 100 AFLW games. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

"But when you can extrapolate further and see the way you can shape things and push the game into a better space and I guess impact different communities who might not have always seen themselves in footy, for me, that adds to my experience of being a human playing footy.

"From the outside, it can be tempting to just want footy players to just focus on footy. But the reality is when you step out onto the field, you're a fully formed human with a brain and with things going on in your life.

"So if you're able to, I guess, service all areas of yourself whilst playing footy, it just makes it feel like a lot more worthwhile experience."

A lot has changed over the 11 seasons Vescio has played, including the number of teams in the competition (from eight to 18), season length and start date, and the skills and evolution of the game on-field.

Darcy Vesio has been a stalwart of the competition since its conception. (Getty: Morgan Hancock)

One thing for Vescio themself, is the length of their socks.

"They're a bit of a fidget toy for me at this point. They kind of come up, they come down. But I am enjoying the long socks," they said.

"I feel like for a long time the socks we were given were very small, like I've got size 11 feet, so they were really squeezing in and some games they would be around my heel.

"So I feel like after 10 seasons of that, I'm trying to just hit back with maximum length. But yeah, I know it is uncomfortable for some people to look at."

World.title: What is in Usman Khawaja's book Sabr and what did he actually say about Sandpapergate?
World.content:
Usman Khawaja's revelations about the sandpaper scandal have reopened a massive rift in Australian cricket: who knew what? Who's lying? Who's telling the truth.

Much of the problem lies in the ambiguity of language that Khawaja has used in his interviews and moreover in his newly release autobiography, Sabr, which he is now publicising.

When Khawaja told the Nine newspapers that "It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," what exactly did he mean?

Was he inferring that the entire team knew about the plot to sandpaper a cricket ball during the third Test in Cape Town in 2018?

Cameron Bancroft was banned for nine months and Steve Smith for a year for their roles in the sandpaper scandal. (Photo by Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images/Getty Images) (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman)

That clearly is how most of Australia understood that statement.

Or was he saying that everyone in the Australian set-up needed to take responsibility?

We don't know and that is because of Khawaja's deliberate attempts to not name names as he told Sarah Ferguson on 730 this week, "it's never been for me about pointing fingers."

"This is my story," he wrote in his book.

Loading...

But what is clearly inferred from the book is that even if he wasn't pointing fingers at individuals, the knowledge of the ball tampering was widespread and discussed within the team and on the field.

So, what exactly is in Khawaja's book?

The sandpaper chapter is dedicated to three players who were banned for their involvement in the incident, then captain, Steve Smith, Cameron Bancroft and "my childhood friend David Warner".

"The truth will set you free," he wrote.

The set-up happened before the first test in Durban when he alleges a member of the coaching staff told the team: "I don't care what you have to do, or how, but we need to get it moving in the air."

The Australians celebrate the final wicket of the first Test in Durban in 2018. (Getty Images: Lee Warren/Gallo Images)

"It was so much harder to bat when the ball was moving in the air, particularly when it was reverse swinging. "We had to keep doing what all of us had been doing for years in domestic and international cricket: finding a way to make it go reverse. "We were all complicit. "Reverse swing on those older, flatter Test wickets was how you won matches, come day four and five."

The first reference to sandpaper in the chapter comes in reference to the size of the change rooms during the South Africa series.

"Of course I bloody knew what was happening with the sandpaper. "There wasn't much in those small change-rooms that got past me. It was a room full of banter and it was very hard to hide anything. Let alone when you used sandpaper on the ball and it would leave these huge swirl marks on it."

Sandpaper, he explains, is readily available in cricket change rooms, because batters use it to clean up their bats.

On day two of the second test at Port Elizabeth (now Gqeberha), he described an experiment to use sandpaper on a cricket ball.

Steve Smith and David Warner appeal for a wicket during the second Test of the series. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

"What we saw was unbelievable. The ball was completely dry and extremely scuffed on the side we'd sandpapered. There was no way it wouldn't reverse if we bowled with it. Everyone had a look at the ball and was laughing their heads off."

He wrote that a plan was hatched to sandpaper the ball in the Test immediately after breaks in play when the umpire would drop the ball on the boundary before the players went onto the field.

Cameron Bancroft offered to do the deed, because David Warner was conscious that the TV cameras were focused on him.

Khawaja recounted Bancroft saying: "No worries — it'll be easy."

"At this stage, Steve Smith put his hands up and said, 'I don't want to know about anything about this,' and walked out of the room."

Smith used almost the exact same words to describe his actions in a press conference during his subsequent one-year ban.

Nevertheless, the plan went ahead as Khawaja described in his book.

Australia cut through the South African batters after Cameron Bancroft had taken to the ball with sandpaper. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

"The next session, we absolutely went through the South Africans. Bangers (Bancroft) had walked on the field after the break, picked up the ball that the umpires had left on the field, and given it a few twists and turns. The ball came up a treat. The shiny side was shiny and the buffed and, thanks to the sandpaper, the reverse side was really rough and dry. "Every time during that session the ball was passed to me at gully, I'd take a look and think, wow, even I could reverse swing this ball. It was ridiculous. The bowlers went to work and bowled beautifully. Reversing it around corners. We got four wickets for 28 runs. "It was moving so much that, at one point, one of the bowlers said in the huddle after a wicket, 'Guys, it's going heaps now. Just don't do anything else to it, because it's silly how much it's going'.

Khawaja doesn't name the bowlers who took the four wicket in the book, but the scoreboard shows Mitchell Marsh took two, while Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc took one each.

Even so, Australia lost the test. Khawaja claimed that the South African bowlers were reverse swinging the ball "everywhere", starting after about 21 overs.

"We didn't know what they were doing with the ball — all we knew was that they were better than us at getting it go reverse. And we were using sandpaper!"

Come the third test at Cape Town, drizzle was making the ball wet and hard to swing.

Khawaja described a member of the coaching staff approaching Bancroft who he was sitting next to.

"Bangers, whatever you're doing, we need more of it. It's wet out there — we just need more of it," Khawaja says the coach said.

Khawaja wrote the sandpaper helped take the wet surface layer off the ball, making it dry and more conducive to reverse swing.

It was the next session when the infamous shots of Bancroft trousering a small yellow sliver of sandpaper were broadcast on the big screen at Newlands.

Bancroft, he wrote, was "catatonic".

Cameron Bancroft was called over by the umpires after being caught with the sandpaper. (Gallo Images via Getty: Ashley Vlotman)

"Every one of the boys on the field was shitting themselves."

Khawaja wrote it was after the game he had a conversation with the team manager, Gavin Dovey.

"We need to cop this as a team. We did it as a team, so we cop it as a team. "[Dovey] said I was right but that two guys in the team disagreed."

During a subsequent team meeting, Khawaja wrote he expressed the same view that the entire team should accept responsibility.

"There was silence when I said that. Most of the guys agreed, but Painey (Steve Smith's replacement as captain, Tim Paine) knew not everyone felt that way. And so, my idea fell flat."

Khawaja concludes the chapter saying: "I can only speak for myself, and it's very clear I knew what was going on."

Khawaja wants the rest of us to draw our own conclusions.

World.title: Warner hits out as batting coach calls Khawaja claims 'absolutely false'
World.content:
The fallout from Usman Khawaja's 2018 South African tour ball-tampering allegations shows no sign of abating after Australia's former batting coach Graeme Hick weighed in to insist they were "absolutely false".

Hick's strong denial of Khawaja's assertion that the whole team knew of the plan to use sandpaper to alter the state of the ball in the series eight years ago also dragged David Warner back to social media as he launched further barbs at Cricket Australia.

In his new book, former Test batting luminary Khawaja's revelations about the infamous "sandpapergate" tour have received both strong support and vehement denials.

The latest rebuttal of his claims has come from former Zimbabwe-born England batting star Graeme Hick, who joined paceman Mitchell Starc and former head coach Darren Lehmann.

Sandpapergate continues to wound Australia Usman Khawaja and David Warner's Sandpapergate revelations may have set the scene for civil war in Australian cricket as the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to captivate and damage.

Hick, who worked with the Australian team from 2016 to 2020, told the Sydney Morning Herald: "I have seen the various statements around the coaches and I'm very disappointed with the broad nature of them.

"Khawaja puts it simply: 'It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.' To me, what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false.

"In regard to any discussions around the ball-tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything.

"My first knowledge of all this was, like many, when it appeared on the big screen in Cape Town as I was sat on the outside balcony at the time."

Khawaja's fellow opener Warner, who was one of three players who took the blame for the 2018 sandpaper scandal at Cape Town along with captain Steve Smith and batter Cameron Bancroft, has backed Khawaja's stance and thanked him, saying: "It's 100 per cent accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."

After reading Hick's comments, Warner returned to social media with another post that seemed to imply the English Test player was hardly at the heart of the team as Cricket Australia's appointment after the popular Michael Di Venuto resigned.

"Let's get the facts straight," Warner wrote. "Graeme Hick was only appointed because Cricket Australia was unwilling to pay Michael Di Venuto what he deserved.

"As players, we valued Michael so highly that we even offered to contribute from our own salaries to retain him.

"These discussions were taking place during the New Zealand tour. That alone speaks volumes about how highly we regarded him and how determined we were to keep him involved. Adds to why Graeme has spoken!!"

AAP

World.title: The Wallabies-Scotland rivalry born in a Melbourne backyard
World.content:
Sione Tuipulotu used to smash Isaac Kailea in their Melbourne backyard battles, but Wallabies prop Kailea hopes to get revenge when his "lippy" cousin leads out Scotland at Murrayfield.

Tuipulotu is another who got away from Australian rugby, a centre who forged his own path before using his ancestry to become Scotland's Aussie braveheart, an inspirational captain who led them to victory over the Wallabies two years ago.

None of which surprises his old mate Kailea, who as a kid always looked up to the guy he saw as a role model in their close-knit Tongan community in Melbourne.

It is also why Sunday's (Monday AEDT) international also means so much to 26-year-old Kailea, who came off the bench in that 2024 clash when Tuipulotu scored a try in the Scots' 27-13 victory.

"If I get the chance again, I'd love to get a win over him," Waratahs loosehead Kailea said, reflecting on the close bond between his family and the Tuipulotu brothers, Sione and younger rugby-playing siblings Sese and Tavi.

Tuipulotu toured Australia with the British and Irish Lions last year. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"Sione's probably one of the most competitive people I know, so when he puts on that Scottish jersey, he's going to give it 100 per cent.

"Whether he goes extra hard because we're Australia, I couldn't say. I just know he's always putting in that effort, especially now he's their captain.

"I know him quite well. I grew up with him and his younger brothers, we pretty much just call each other cousins. Our dads, both of Tongan heritage, met in Melbourne, and there's a couple of other Tongan families there we all grew up with.

"So a lot of boys, a lot of pretty rough games in the backyard, but Sione was always the leader among the kids, as the oldest. We played a couple of times in the backyard. He used to run amok — he'd smash us to bits.

"The younger kids just followed his lead, and the leadership he showed there is something I can see him doing now with Scotland. Even the way he talks, it's still the same. It's pretty cool to see."

Kailea said the rest of the younger boys saw saw Tuipulotu as a role model, especially once he played for the Melbourne Rebels.

Kailea has joined his "cousin" on the international stage. (AAP Image: Joel Carrett)

"It was a bit tough for him in Australia, he went on his own little journey, through Japan, and now he's ended up in Scotland, and his brothers are over here as well, chasing the dream," Kailea said.

Hooker Tavi plays alongside Tuipulotu at Glasgow Warriors and centre Sese is at Edinburgh Rugby.

"It's pretty crazy to be honest," Kailea said.

In that 2024 clash, Tuipulotu played like a man with something to prove.

"He can be pretty lippy on the field, just like he is off it, so he was throwing a bit of chat, but nothing too crazy. I don't think he'd get too disrespectful," smiled Kailea, recalling how Tuipulotu collected the match trophy off his Scottish gran, Jaqueline Thomson.

He also got flattened by a thunderous tackle from Joseph Aukuso-Suaalii in that match which actually caused an arm injury to the Australian and left Tuipulotu reflecting: "I've never been hit like that in my career."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

Tech.title: ‘The end of Tesla!’: Cybertruck diehards turn on Elon Musk after he pulls the plug
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Cybertruck is heading to that shiny cyber-dumpster in the sky, leaving the folks who built online identities around Elon Musk’s polarizing pickup feeling bereft. Usually, Musk’s fanbase treads lightly around their idol’s mercurial decisions. This time, however, the truck’s demise has sparked rare backlash within the Tesla community — aimed squarely at the guy who signed its death warrant.

Troy Meekhof, who posts on numerous social platforms under the moniker “The Cybertruck Guy,” has been vocal about his disappointment in Musk’s decision to wind down Cybertruck production by the end of summer 2027. (The original plan was to start winding down production in the spring, but then Musk decided to extend it a few months.)

In a 33-minute video on YouTube, Meekhof argues that Tesla never fully committed to making the Cybertruck a success, citing a lack of advertising, confusing pricing changes, and the decision to shift focus before the truck could fully establish itself in the market.

“It feels like they didn’t try to make Cybertruck a success,” he said.

He also had choice words for Musk’s reasons for ending the Cybertruck’s short run to make room at Giga Texas for the fully autonomous Cybercab: “Cancelling all of your best products... in favor of an autonomous platform that remains both software and regulatory constrained... seems like an absolutely terrible idea,” Meekhof vented.

The Cybertruck wasn’t the only Tesla product to meet an untimely end — at least according to those with stakes (and often stock options) in the company’s success. Earlier this year, Tesla discontinued the Model S and Model X, two of its flagship vehicles. With the end of the Cybertruck, Tesla is now left with just the Model 3 and Model Y as vehicles you can actually buy. (The Semi is strictly a commercial vehicle, while the Cybercab’s availability as a consumer product remains dubious, at best.)

“Cancelling Cybertruck after all the years of getting it to production to ‘make room for CyberCab’ is a lame excuse,” @TeslaXplored wrote on X. “There are like 500 CyberCabs in one city that only Tesla influencers are riding in. Taking away consumer cars instead of building what the people want will be the end of Tesla!”

He added, “Very sad what happened to Tesla over the last 5 years.”

Meanwhile, at least one prominent aftermarket company is offering to step in and pick up the mantle. Unplugged Performance, which makes aftermarket accessories, said it would produce the Cybertruck and other vehicles on the truck platform under license, with investors funding the effort: “Worth a conversation?”

Musk, for his part, seems less interested in litigating the particulars of Cybertruck production and more intent on selling a vision of Tesla’s future centered around the Cybercab and humanoid robots. “Cybercab will do a majority of all passenger miles in any jurisdiction where it is not prohibited by law,” Musk wrote on X earlier this week. “Obvious to anyone with eyes and a brain.”

He also pushed back on claims that the Cybertruck was killed because it was unprofitable. “The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate,” Musk said. “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”

To be sure, Cybertruck sales have been disappointing over its entire production run. Musk initially theorized that Tesla could sell 250,000-500,000 Cybertrucks annually, but the actual numbers have been far below those projections. Last year, Tesla is estimated to have sold around 20,000 trucks; the company is on track to sell fewer than that this year.

Whether Musk’s autonomous utopia pans out or ends up joining the Cybertruck in the vaporware graveyard remains to be seen. For now, the stainless-steel wedge that was supposed to be the ultimate symbol of an indestructible future has become a monument to Musk’s shifting attention span — and a stark reminder to Tesla’s most loyal boosters that in Elon’s world, nothing should be taken for granted.

Tech.title: 25 years later, Xbox is trying to reinvent itself again
Tech.content:
Microsoft has spent the past 25 years trying to shake up the game console market. The original Xbox, which launched on November 15th in 2001, took on an industry dominated by Sony and Nintendo. Twenty-five years later, Xbox finds itself in a similar position. It’s not starting from scratch this time around, but to reach another 25-year milestone, it needs to do something radically different.

The original Xbox was radically different. Born out of a fear of Sony putting a PC in the living room, Microsoft built its first game console around familiar PC technology. A custom Intel Pentium III processor powered the original Xbox, alongside an Nvidia GPU and 64MB of unified RAM. It was different from the fully custom architectures that Sony and Nintendo used at the time, allowing Microsoft to entice developers to its platform with tools that were more familiar to PC game makers.

Microsoft also included two hardware features that were unusual for a console at the time: a built-in hard drive and Ethernet port. The hard drive let game developers cache content without having to rely fully on optical discs, and Xbox players could also use it for game saves without having to purchase a separate memory card. You could even rip CDs to an Xbox and listen to custom soundtracks while playing games.

Xbox wasn’t the first to bring online gaming to consoles, but Microsoft took a different approach. Instead of relying on a built-in modem like Sega’s Dreamcast, Microsoft included an Ethernet port, anticipating a shift toward broadband internet connections. Xbox Live, which launched in November 2002, really nailed the entire online experience. There were friends lists, unique gamertags, voice chat through a bundled headset, and integrated multiplayer services. Microsoft created an entire platform for online gaming, making it easier for developers to support and fundamentally changing how people played games together.

The Xbox 360 took these ideas a step further, with swappable hard drives, digital game downloads, wireless controllers, and backward compatibility. It also turned Microsoft’s game console into an entertainment hub for the living room, complete with streaming video apps. Kinect was perhaps its most radical addition. Launched in 2010, the motion-sensing device used cameras and microphones to let players control games with their bodies and voices. It quickly became the fastest-selling consumer electronics device in early 2011.

But the success of Kinect and Microsoft’s ambition to turn Xbox into a home entertainment device helped lead to its first major strategic misstep with the Xbox One. Microsoft positioned the successor to the Xbox 360 around TV, entertainment, and an always-online future, instead of focusing on the games that had made Xbox successful. Its plans for online DRM and restrictions on used games sparked a huge backlash, while bundling Kinect pushed the console’s price $100 above Sony’s PlayStation 4. Six months after launch, Microsoft was forced to drop Kinect from the Xbox One console bundle to close that price gap.

The Xbox One showed what happens when Microsoft loses sight of what gamers want. The company spent most of that generation playing catch-up to Sony’s impressive PlayStation 4 sales. But its weakened position also forced Microsoft to once again try something radically different with Xbox Game Pass.

Introduced in 2017, Game Pass shook up the very economics of how people play games. The subscription service lets you access hundreds of games instead of buying them individually. Microsoft went on an acquisition spree to power its Game Pass ambitions, buying up smaller studios, Bethesda, and eventually Activision Blizzard.

Game Pass has become one of Xbox’s most compelling features, but it has also raised difficult questions about the economics of putting all of Microsoft’s first-party games into a subscription service on day one. It has pleased Xbox fans, but Microsoft hasn’t demonstrated that it can turn the service into the mass-market success it once envisioned. Microsoft has also stopped regularly disclosing subscriber numbers, making it harder to judge if the service is growing or not.

These days, Microsoft is spinning many Xbox plates. The Xbox Series X and S consoles that launched in 2020 are way behind Sony’s PS5 sales numbers, and Xbox Cloud Gaming hasn’t yet been able to reach the millions more players that Microsoft has always wanted for its ecosystem.

Xbox Cloud Gaming promised to make games accessible on phones and tablets without needing a dedicated console, and combined with Microsoft’s messy project to bring Xbox games to PS5 and Nintendo consoles, the efforts have raised questions about what the Xbox brand actually represents these days. Microsoft hasn’t quite decided whether it wants to be a full third-party publisher, an ecosystem owner, or an unusual combination of both.

Some of Microsoft’s recent radically different Xbox bets haven’t paid off, so it’s now turning its attention to a much smaller Xbox division, with a restructuring that will see overall Xbox headcount reduced by 20 percent by the end of Microsoft’s fiscal year in June 2027. “I believe the future of gaming will look more like its beginning, when a small team with a big idea could change how the world plays,” Xbox CEO Asha Sharma wrote in a message to Xbox employees today.

Microsoft is celebrating 25 years of Xbox today with an event in Seattle for fans, where it’s launching Xbox Playback, a personalized look back at players’ 25-year Xbox history. There will be more fan-focused announcements throughout the day, but I’m not expecting any news on the next Xbox console. The celebration is awkwardly timed, because rumors have suggested that Microsoft is also preparing for more Xbox layoffs in November, during the same month it’s celebrating a milestone.

The reset also comes as Microsoft is preparing for a next-generation Xbox console, codenamed Project Helix, which will play both Xbox games and PC titles. It sounds like an effort to combine Windows and Xbox like never before. The next Xbox could also play every Xbox game ever made, thanks to Microsoft’s impressive bets on backward compatibility over the years.

It’s an interesting full-circle moment. The original Xbox was essentially a PC built for the living room. Project Helix appears to be taking a similar approach, but this time around bringing the flexibility of PC gaming into a console experience. If Microsoft gets it right, it could open Xbox up to a much bigger library of games, and entice people trying to decide between a console or a gaming PC.

The problem for Xbox is getting consumers to care about this next console, especially when its games are available on PC and sometimes on Sony’s and Nintendo’s platforms. “Xbox has the best console ecosystem around, packed with consumer-friendly features like free cloud saves, Game Pass, and my preferred controller,” says Jon Clarke, cofounder and editor-in-chief of DayOne. “None of these things are particularly sexy or flashy. They’re simply features that work, and that can make them difficult to get customers excited about.”

Rebuilding the Xbox brand and launching a new console gives Microsoft an unusual opportunity to make another bold bet on the future, just like it did 25 years ago. But the risks this time around are greater, after more than a decade of trying and failing to catch up to the competition.

“Up against competitors that have firmly established their place in the market, Xbox finds itself in a difficult position,” says Clarke. “Rebuilding the brand will be an expensive endeavor, and the bold ambition of combining the best of console gaming with the openness and flexibility of PC is easier said than done.”

Xbox also needs good games, and after years of studio acquisitions it now has plenty of IP to play with. “Many of those franchises have lost their luster owing to years of mismanagement and potentially a generalized lack of vision,” says Jez Corden, executive editor at Windows Central. “Microsoft from the top will need to be willing to invest here to ensure Xbox’s franchises can not only find new audiences, but simply maintain what they already have.”

Xbox also faces the challenge of RAMageddon’s impact on the hardware industry right now, pushing the prices of components beyond levels that consumers can comfortably afford. “If Xbox is to reclaim any of its former glory, innovating on the costs of the traditional video game ‘console’ will be absolutely paramount, otherwise it’s hard to imagine that it will continue to exist in its current form,” says Corden.

A console projected to cost between $1,200 and $1,800 won’t grow the Xbox ecosystem. It could make more sense to let PC makers build their own Xbox hardware, opening up the platform to a wider range of prices and devices rather than relying on expensive flagship consoles.

Twenty-five years ago, Microsoft built a PC and called it an Xbox. Now it’s preparing to build something that looks increasingly like a PC again, only this time it needs to convince people that it should still be called an Xbox. Microsoft has another opportunity to shake up the console industry, but its biggest challenge might be convincing players that Xbox needs to exist as a console at all.

The pad

I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there.
